en: Now begins the first chapter: the Cow, the Earth.
jmā kṣmā kṣā
Kṣamā, kṣoṇī, and kṣiti are earth.
The earth is vast and wide.
The Earth is Aditi, the remover of hostility.
May Nirṛti become favorable to us.
The earth is Pūṣan, the path.
"Gotrā" refers to the earth; "gotrā" consists of twenty-one names for the earth. 1.
Hema-candra.
Gold, iron, and precious metal.
Flesh,
gold, and iron.
Gold, the yellow metal, bharma.
O Maruts, you have granted the gift of immortality.
"Jātarūpa" refers to gold; [these are the fifteen names for gold]. "Ambaram" refers to the sky.
The sky is the sacrificial grass, the bow is the firmament.
The intermediate space, the ether, and the waters.
The earth is the ground, the self-existent.
The path,
the lotus,
and the ocean.
"Samudraḥ adhvaram" refers to the intermediate space;
"adhvaram" is one of the sixteen names for the intermediate space. 3.
The speckled vault of heaven.
"Earth," "the summit," and "the sky" are common [to all]; ["the sky" is one of the six that are common]. 4.
The rays of the sun are called *khedayaḥ*, *kiraṇāḥ*, and *gāvaḥ*.
The rays are the reins;
the prayers are the reins.
The rays of light are like forests at dawn.
The Vasus are the rays that drink the light.
"The seven seers, the Sādhyas, and the Suparṇas" refers to the rays; [the Suparṇas are fifteen names of the rays]. 5.
The near and distant quarters are stretched out.
The quarters,
the intermediate directions,
and the sky.
"Kakubhaḥ haritaḥ" refers to the directions; "haritaḥ" refers to the eight names of the directions. 6. Śyāvī.
Kṣapā,
śarvarī, and aktuḥ are words for night.
Flowing with waves,
delightful,
and harmonious.
The night has passed; the faults have departed.
Tamas and rajas are black.
Abounding in milk,
abounding in darkness, dripping with ghee.
Through glory,
one is freed from sorrow.
Milk from the udder, snow.
"Vasvāḷ" is a name for night; [the twenty-three names of night include] "vasvī. Vibhāvarī, Sūnarī.
Radiant, bright, variegated, and wealthy.
The daughter of Arjuna,
rich in steeds,
possessed of abundant vigor.
Bestowing bliss, radiant, and shining.
The white, the ruddy, the bountiful one.
"Sūnṛtāvatī, sūnṛtāvarī"—these are the sixteen names of Uṣas (the Dawn). 8. At the break of day.
The light of heaven is the day.
The heat is scorching the dwelling places.
The day is bright by day.
"Day by day, dyavidyavi"—this refers to the day;
"dyavidyavi" is one of the twelve names for the day. 9.
The mountain is the pressing-stone, the cow-pen.
The breaker of strongholds,
the eater of food,
the one who nourishes many.
The stone, the mountain, is firm.
The mountain, the cow-pen, and the sacrificial vessel.
Varāha, Śambara, and Rauhiṇa.
Raivata,
Phaliga,
and Upara.
The stone, the cup, the serpent.
Abhra, valāhaka, and megha all mean cloud.
A skin-bag, boiled rice, and a water-vessel.
Vṛtra, Asura, and Kośa—these are names for clouds; "Kośa" is one of the thirty names for clouds. 10.
The verse: the stream,
the refreshing draught.
Gauḥ, Gaurī, Gāndharvī.
Deep, profound, and resonant.
The low-pitched voice, the sharp-edged tool, and the lute.
Speech is the arrow, speech is the blade.
The Sarasvatī is the vessel,
the channel.
Menā with her smiles, like Sūryā.
Sarasvatī is the Nivid; Svāhā!
Speech, the sound of the press-stone,
and the lowing of the cow.
The palate is the tongue;
the resonance is sound.
Svara is sound; it is noise.
The Ṛk is the Hotṛ’s song.
The Gāthā,
the Gaṇa,
the Dhenā.
O Gnas, you who cause things to ripen!
The whip is our vessel of inspiration.
The imperishable, the great, the infinite.
Śacī Vāk is the Anuṣṭubh.
The cow is beautiful and flowing with milk.
*Saraḥ*, *suparṇī*, and *bekurā*—these are names for speech; [according to the tradition that *bekurā* is one of them, there are fifty-seven names for speech]. 11.
The flood, the surge, the destruction.
The sky is a waterless cloud.
Water is a forest.
Clarified butter, honey, and excrement.
Pippala, milk, and poison.
Semen, the penis, and birth.
The chaff and husk of Tugrya.
The bubbling,
well-secured, supporting foundation.
The Surā destroys the obstructing, dust-covered [powers].
The nights have their weapons as kinsmen.
The serpent is the imperishable stream.
Satisfaction is the essence;
it is water.
Milk is the lake of medicine.
Overpowering, victorious, and enduring.
Vitality is the happiness of the ruling power.
The Yadu has brought us auspiciousness.
The past, the present, and the future.
The waters are the great space.
Great glory,
the gatherer of wealth.
The well-ordered, well-strung, and dense thicket.
Deep, indeed, is he.
Food, the oblation, the dwelling place.
The dwelling is the Law, the womb.
The womb of cosmic order, truth, and water.
Wealth is truly full.
The sacrificial grass is entirely imperishable.
Clarified butter is indeed water.
The purifier,
the immortal, the moon.
The golden creations of heaven.
The illusory, monstrous form of Śambara.
Ambu, toya,
and tūya mean water.
The fire-wood is the seed, the brilliance.
Svadhā is the water of libation.
"Jalāṣam idam" refers to water; [these are one hundred and one names for water]. 12. Rivers.
The furrows are prepared for the barley.
The rivers are indeed roaring.
The pains, the flanks, the cavities, and the floods.
The green rivers have wheels of obstructions.
The young maidens,
like surging streams,
are brides.
Golden-colored, ruddy, and flowing forth.
The waves, the rivers, and the streams.
The wide,
refreshing waters are to be chosen.
The mountain-born rivers are full of vigor.
Abounding in milk,
abounding in vigor,
abounding in wisdom.
The roaring ones,
the bank-bound ones, the radiant ones.
"Swift mothers,
the rivers"— this is [the section concerning] rivers; [namely, "the rivers," which consists of thirty-seven names of rivers].13
The steed, the courser, the racer.
The vigorous steed, the carrier, the bearer.
Dadhikrā,
Dadhikrāvan,
the one with swift-moving horses.
Etaśa,
Paidva,
Daurgaha.
Tārkṣya, the son of Ucchaiḥśravas, is swift.
The ruddy sun,
the one who bestows nourishment.
The falcons, the well-winged ones, who do not falter.
The men are like moths among those who waver.
"Hamsāsas" and "aśvās" are names for horses [the list beginning with "aśvās" consists of twenty-six names of horses]. 14. "Harī" refers to Indra's [horses].
The red horse belongs to Agni, the bay horses to Āditya, and the donkeys to the Aśvins.
The goats belong to Pūṣan;
the spotted deer belong to the Maruts;
the ruddy cows belong to the Dawns.
"Dark, multiformed are the teams of Savitṛ; those of Bṛhaspati and Vāyu..."—these are the ten prescribed applications. 15.
It shines, it blazes, it gleams.
It shines, it glows, it is dimmed.
It resounds, it shines, it blazes.
"dyotate" and "dyumat"—these eleven [terms] denote the action of flaming. 16.
"jamat" [is also among them].
Flashing with intense brilliance,
flickering and shimmering with light.
Radiance, glow, and heat.
Tejahara is Hṛṇi.
"Śṛṅgāṇi, śṛṅgāṇi"—these eleven blazing [objects] are the names of the blazing ones. 17. Thus ends the first chapter in the Nighaṇṭu;
now begins the second chapter.
The waters,
the wealth,
the wondrous deed.
The garment,
the trembling, the trembling, having pervaded.
The conduct is cruel and merciless.
The will is capable of performing its functions.
Performing deeds, making them happen, she who cuts away.
The agent has done what was to be done;
the agent has done it for the agent.
Having performed the act,
having fashioned the thought.
Śacī, Śacī; Śamī, Śamī; Śimī, Śimī.
Power, power, craft—this refers to action [“craft” being one of the twenty-six names for action]. 1. tuk.
offspring, son, seedling;
offspring, son,
seedling.
The remnant of Takman is gone.
The offspring born from Gayā.
He is the son, the grandson.
"Progeny is the seed"—this refers to offspring; [the term "seed" includes fifteen names for offspring]. 2. Human being.
Men, horses, and living beings.
The clans, the settlements, the people.
The human tribes,
O Nahuṣa,
are like tawny steeds.
O mortals, you are mortal beings.
The tribes of Turvaśa and Druhyu.
The Āyus, the Yadus, and the Anavas.
The ancestors of all that moves and stands still.
"Pañcajanāḥ," "vivasvantaḥ," and "pṛtanāḥ" refer to human beings; "pṛtanāḥ" is one of the twenty-five names for humans. (3)
The reins have been lengthened for the departing one.
The two hands, reaching out, grasp the two [soma] stalks.
The two hands are the arms; they are the *bhurij*.
"O swift Śakvarī, [place me] on the two carriers"—this refers to the two arms; "on the two carriers" refers to the twelve names for the arms. 4.
The young maidens,
the subtle ones,
the swift fingers.
The arrows are the reins.
The daughters, the unwearied ones, the inspired songs.
The golden-green waters flow like girth-straps.
Sisters, kinswomen, and those of common descent.
The yokes, the harnesses, and the poles.
"Branches," "reins," and "rays" are names for the fingers; "hands" is another name for the twenty-two fingers. 5.
I desire; we desire; he desires.
He seeks, he goes toward, he desires.
He desires, he attains, he enjoys.
The desiring one longs for and celebrates him.
He thinks, he sings, and he desires.
"Desiring, he shines; he has shone"—these eighteen [roots] denote the act of shining. 6. *andhas*, *vāja*.
Milk, fame, and nourishment.
The son [takes] the debt of the father.
You are the bestower of food.
O Earth,
O Lord, grant us nourishment.
Sustenance is the essence; it is the svadhā offering.
The sun is the limit of the earth.
Sasama, homage!
Long life!
Truthfulness and the splendor of sacred knowledge.
“Kīlālam” means food; “kīlālam yaśaḥ” (glory is *kīlāla*)—these are twenty-eight names for food. 7. Ā vayata.
He becomes,
he consumes, or he pervades.
Desiring to eat,
you devour; you consume.
*babdhām* means "he calls"; these are ten roots meaning "to eat. [The root *hvarati* is also among the ten roots meaning "to eat. 8.
Vitality, power, and strength.
Thou art swift; thou art powerful.
The host, the oppressor, the manly strength.
O you of mighty strength,
[slay] Śuṣṇa.
Dakṣa, the powerful one, the source of creative energy.
Strength, conquering power, and vigor.
Slaughter, the host, the enclosure.
O Vṛka, by your might and manly deeds.
O Indras, you hold wealth in your hands.
Śambara—this is a name of Bala [Śambara is one of the twenty-eight names of Bala]. 9. Magha, Rekṇas.
The inheritance is the Veda;
it is wide space.
Refreshing wealth, a treasure.
May Bhaga bestow the warrior power upon us.
The buffalo [is] splendor and power.
Wealth, the granting of riches.
This food is manly strength.
A kinsman, wisdom, and glory.
Brahman is the treasure, the glory.
"Vṛtram ṛtam" refers to wealth; "vṛtam" consists of twenty-eight names for wealth. 10. Aghnyā.
The dawn has shone forth.
Great Aditi, the goddess of devotion.
The *śakvarī* of the world; the *śakvarī* of cows—[these are the nine names of cows]. 11. Relata.
It is seen,
it is perceived,
and it is heard.
He stirs;
he moves, shaking.
"Vanuṣyati," "kampate," and "bhojate"— these ten are the verbal roots for the action of being angry. 12.
The whole;
the remover;
the wrathful one.
Abandonment,
wrath,
and desire.
The crookedness,
the heat, and the flame.
"Manyu-vyathis" refers to anger; "vyathis" is one of the eleven names for anger. 13. It occurs.
It rolls, it tumbles, it rolls about.
Flow, scratch, and crawl.
Flow down, flow forth, fall away.
Flow down, drip, and fall away!
The crooked he straightens;
he stirs.
Shake it,
move it, and cause it to sway!
Churn it, grind it, crush it!
It will sink and it will float.
Falling away, moving about, wandering.
Do not fall,
do not perish.
They have approached, they have entered, they have united.
Come quickly;
hasten!
Do not delay!
He goes toward the Atata;
he desires to sacrifice.
Follow, creep,
and hasten!
It strives, it wanders, it glides.
Silver and gold are exhausted.
By his nature he measures;
he brings them forth.
He hears;
he flows forth from his own source.
The most excellent one bestows [it] upon the most excellent woman.
He moved,
he trembled, he was stirred (the reading is *dadhyata*).
He overcomes;
he fights; he wields the bow.
He has roared;
he has gone forth from the noble one;
he has flown away.
It was given easily and with little effort.
Strike! Slay!
Afflict!
Crush them, pursue them, and destroy them!
The beloved one speeds forth;
he moves.
They move, they rush, they are invigorating.
Go,
O you who go about and wander!
Quicken, exert yourselves, go forth!
Support! Support! Support!
The chariot speeds along, rushing forward.
Tomorrow he will eat the mushrooms.
He blows; he goes; he moves.
It flows,
it glides, it stirs.
Moving swiftly, rushing, and deceiving.
The wind blows and destroys.
Drive away the non-Aryan, drive away the stranger.
Come hither, fly down, and urge them on!
Run! Run!
Go!
O father,
come; let us go.
"ayūyuḥ"—these twenty-two hundred [verses] concern the action of going; 14. "nu," "makṣu."
Flowing swiftly,
they are quick.
The blazing ones,
the pierced ones, the swift-moving ones.
Swiftly,
three times, quickly.
Swift, agile, and restless.
Swiftly, very swiftly, quickly.
Impelling, impelling, being impelled.
The fields are the companions of the sky-dweller.
"Swiftly he crosses, with the speed of the wind"— thus [the phrase "with the speed of the wind" contains] twenty-six names for the swift. 15.
From that seat, he reached the sky.
In Turvaśa,
in the nearby dwelling.
Nearby, close at hand,
among those who are nearest.
*Avame* and *upame* are [two of] the eleven names for "nearness" (*antika*). 16. *Raṇaḥ*.
The one who calls out,
the devourer, the roaring one.
Fill [us] with cries in the battle!
In battle,
you are the leader of the army in the encounter.
In the encounter, my truth is at the rim of the wheel.
The assembly, the gathering, the meeting.
O Mīḷhuṣa, crush the hostile armies.
Vanquishers in battles and in conflicts.
In the battle,
in the confusion, O powerful one.
In battle, in calculation, in assembly.
In the encounter, the joining, and the battle.
In the overcoming of Vṛtra, for nourishment, at the impulse.
In the battle for heroes, in the battle for booty, in the encounter.
O Khala,
display your manly prowess.
In the great contest for wealth and booty.
"Sadma saṃyata saṃvataḥ"—these are names for battle; "saṃvataḥ" is one of the forty-six names for battle. 17.
He speeds along, he approaches,
having reached his goal.
He has attained,
he has reached,
he has obtained.
He has not attained, he is attaining, he has attained.
"He attains" (aśnute)—these ten [roots] have the sense of pervading (vyāpti). 18.
"He deceives" (dabhnoti), "he pierces" (śnathati).
He strikes down, he injures, he excludes.
He cuts, he fashions, he carves.
It breathes, it bellows, it afflicts.
He spreads, he moistens,
he causes to go.
It throbs, it sparkles;
let them offer oblations.
Descend, fly forth, and cross over.
There Indra strikes down the tree.
He delights,
he destroys, he pacifies.
He brings rest to the grass and the palm trees.
He eradicates, he destroys, he diminishes.
"He blows" refers to acts of killing; [the phrase "he blows" refers to thirty-three acts of killing]. 19.
The lightning's rim.
The thunderbolt is named the rim of the wheel.
The sharp-edged weapon, the slaying blow, the thunderbolt.
Arka, Kutsa, and Kuliśa.
The impelling, sharp, and piercing one.
The axe, the arrow, and the hatchet—these are names of the thunderbolt; [the hatchet is one of the eighteen names of the thunderbolt]. 20.
He rules,
he governs,
he dwells.
"He reigns" (*rājati*): these four [terms] have the function of sovereignty (*aiśvaryakarma*). 21.
*Rāṣṭrī*, *aryaḥ*.
"Ni-yut-vān," "Inaḥ," "Inaḥ"—these are names of Īśvara. [Inaḥ, inaḥ—four names of Īśvara.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Nighaṇṭu.
Now begins the third chapter: "Wide and many."
Very much, always.
Pervading the entire expanse of the world.
A hundred thousand [drops] of water.
*kuvit* is one of many; [the twelve names for "many" are as follows]. 1. *ṛchan* becomes short.
The grinding,
illusory foundation.
The ant is small and insignificant.
*Arbhakaḥ*, *kṣullakaḥ*, and *alpakam*—these are synonyms for "small" (*hrasva*). [The term *alpaḥ* is also included; thus, there are eleven names for "small. 2.
The lofty, radiant one of the great [host].
The great, grown, and powerful one.
Powerful,
mighty,
and immense.
R̥bhukṣan, the bull,
the far-extending one.
O Yahweh,
you have grown great; you grow great.
Resounding, majestic, and profound.
Exalted,
impetuous, and mighty.
Exulting, most wondrous,
and most expansive.
"Barhiṣi"—thus there are twenty-five names for "the Great" (mahat), beginning with "Barhiṣat. 3.
Gaya, Kṛdara.
The pit became a palace;
the setting [sun] became a mansion.
He has settled in his own dwelling as a guest.
The difficult paths lead away from the dwellings.
The skin is my womb.
The dwelling, the refuge, the protection.
Vomiting,
a roof,
and a nourisher.
"Śarma ajma" refers to houses; "ajma" is one of the twenty-two names for houses. 4.
He rules.
We shall worship, serve, and pay homage.
He honors; he prospers; he pierces.
"ṛcchati," "sapati," and "vivāsati"— these ten are verbs denoting the act of attending upon. 5.
Śimbātā, Śatarā, and Śatapantā.
Śilgu is the seam,
the growth of the woven cloth.
Maya [has brought] a pleasant day with auspicious fortune.
Strength,
prosperity,
and power.
Medicine, cooling, and auspicious.
A pleasant, auspicious, and propitious sleep.
*Śam* and *kat* are [the first two of] the twenty names for happiness (*sukha*). 6. *Nirṇik*.
An enclosure,
a form, a wondrous shape.
Amati is the one whose essence is water.
One's own form, ground into a paste.
The golden,
bright ornament, O Maruts.
Copper, ruddy, and edible—these are the names for form; "craft" is the sixteenth name for form. 7.
Without blood, without breath, and without decay.
Blameless, beyond reproach, worthy of praise.
Sunītha,
Pāka,
and Vāma.
*vayuna* means "praiseworthy" [the ten names for the praiseworthy are: *vayuna*, etc.]. 8. *ketuḥ*, *ketaḥ*.
Cetas, citta, and kratu.
The breath is the thought,
the power.
"Māyā, vayuna, and abhikhyā" refers to wisdom; "abhikhyā" is one of the eleven names for wisdom. 9.
Truly,
we have heard it all together.
"Truly, thus is *ṛta*," so it is said; these are the six names for truth (*satya*). 10.
He has observed and desired;
we have seen.
He looks on and looks around,
he who observes all people.
"Viśvacarṣaṇiḥ avacākaśat" (The one who observes all people gazes down)—these eight [words] have the sense of "seeing. 11. Hikam.
Pleasure, happiness, and the daily routine.
From of old,
none at all;
not even one.
"Neither the *ākṛta* nor the *amiśrāṇi*": these nine subsequent words, beginning with *ākṛta*, are for the purpose of enumerating all the words.
12. "Like this."
This is just as when one who bestows even four [cows] is like fire.
O much-invoked one, these Brahmins observing their vows are indeed the branches of your tree; you are their lover and bringer of fortune.
Having become a ram, he went toward the iron; he was of that form and that color.
In that way, "so" (*tathā*) constitutes a comparison (*upamā*). 13.
He honors.
He sings, he chants, he utters cries of joy.
He shall celebrate, he praises, he sings aloud.
He calls out, he roars, he questions.
He licks, he blows, he shows compassion.
He acts miserably;
he praises; he extols.
He speaks pleasantly,
he speaks slowly,
he speaks with derision.
He desires and he conceals himself while performing penance.
He pleases, he colors, he praises.
He praises, he unites, he cries out.
he praises, speaks, or bargains.
He bargains, he wins over,
he desires to satisfy.
He magnifies, he strengthens, he honors.
He thinks, he is intoxicated, he sounds.
He sounds forth, he yearns, he utters a low, sweet tone.
"Jalpati"—these forty-four are verbs meaning "to praise. 14.
Bhandate, bhaṇati.
He speaks and sleeps, desiring to satisfy.
He magnifies, he extols, he honors.
It tastes sweet,
it intoxicates, it delights.
She is crooked,
she fancies herself clever,
she prattles on.
"Mantrayate" (he advises) and "vandate" (he salutes) are verbs meaning "to worship";
[the word] "vipraḥ" (the sage).
The one who is free from conflict,
the skillful, the wise.
Vena,
Vedhas,
Kaṇva.
R̥bhu is the wise one who knows all things.
The wise Mandhātṛ, the ordainer.
The inspired one,
whose mind is wise, is the seer.
The praisers, the seekers, the yearning ones.
The Kīstasas,
the true seekers,
are our thoughts.
*Matuthāḥ* means "the wise ones"; thus, these are the names of the wise (*medhāvin*). [*Vāghataḥ*—these twenty-four are the names of the wise. 15. *Rebhaḥ*.
The singer, the poet, the roaring one.
The lowing cow stood still.
The sage is Nāda; the metre is Chandas.
"stup," "rudraḥ," and "kṛpaṇyuḥ"— these are the thirteen names of the singers. 16.
The sacrifice is Vena, the ritual.
Wisdom, the assembly, and the noble ones.
The pressing,
the invocation, and the sacrifice.
In the state of divinity, Viṣṇu is the sacrifice.
Indu, Prajāpati, and Gharma—these are names of the sacrifice; [Gharma is one of the fifteen names of the sacrifice]. 17.
The Bharatas, the Kurus,
and the Vāghatas.
O Maruts, for whom the sacrificial grass has been strewn and the ladles are extended.
"Beset by affliction, seeking the gods"—this refers to the officiating priests; "seeking the gods" is one of the eight names for officiating priests.
We implore them.
I go; we consider; give!
Be able; fill us full; refresh us.
Measure it;
bestow it; grant it.
May the guides lead us across.
We seek you; may we rejoice; we meditate upon you.
"Māyate" and so forth—[seventeen] are the verbal roots of the sense of begging (yācñā). 19.
"Dāti," "dāśati."
He gives,
he bestows, he grants.
You satisfy; he satisfies; he bestows.
"Press for the great one"—these are the ten acts of giving.
20. Flow around.
"Flow on; flow toward our blessings"—these four [verses] have the function of a request. 21.
The two terms *svapiti* (he sleeps) and *sasti* (he lies down) denote the actions of sleeping. 22.
*Kūpaḥ* (a well) is that which is dug.
The cutter is the wood-cutter.
The pit, the well, the worm.
The cook, the spring, the giver of the Rishya.
From the *kārotara* [vessel], the *kuśaya* and the *kevaṭa*.
Thus [the fourteen names of a well are: *kūpa*, *kevaṭa*, etc. 23.
*tṛpuḥ*, *takvā*.
The Ribhvan, the Ripu, the Rikvan.
The thief who steals from the river.
The forest-dweller, the deceiver, the thief.
The thief, the one who utters evil, the wolf.
Thus, "thief" (*stena*)—[including "wolf" (*vṛka*), making fourteen names for a thief]—is the secret name. 24. It is hidden within.
Far away, apart, toward the west.
"Apīcyam" and so forth are six names for that which is determined or hidden. 25. "Āke" and "parāke."
"Far away, from afar, from the distance"— these are five names for the distant. 26.
Ancient,
from of old,
possessing vital power.
"May we know the ancient one for the sake of the day"—thus [the word] "ahnāya" occurs in the Purāṇa; [ahnāya constitutes six names of the Purāṇa]. 27.
New, fresh, recent.

Herein begins the Nirukta composed by the sage Śrī Yāska.

Now begins the first chapter. The traditional collection has been handed down; it is now to be explained. This traditional collection is called the *Nighaṇṭavas*. Why are they called *Nighaṇṭavas*? Because these are *nigamas* (Vedic citations). Having been gathered together from the various *chandas* (Vedic meters), they have been handed down. Aupamanyava says that although they are indeed *nigantas* (those that have gone forth), they are called *Nighaṇṭavas* because of their "gathering" (*nigamana*). Or rather, they may be so called because of "striking" (*hanana*); for they are struck together, or rather, they are gathered together.

Now, those four classes of words are nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*). Regarding these, they provide the definition of nouns and verbs: "A verb has action as its primary meaning; nouns have substance as their primary meaning. Where both [the verb and the noun] have action as their primary meaning, one expresses the action as a process consisting of prior and posterior stages by means of the verb—as in *vrajati* ("he goes") or *pacati* ("he cooks"). From the beginning of the undertaking until its completion, that which is manifested as a concrete entity is expressed by means of nouns denoting substance.

"Going," "cooking"—these are the designations for substances (*sattva*), such as "cow," "horse," "man," or "elephant. "Exists"—this is the designation for a state of being (*bhāva*), such as "he sits," "he lies down," "he goes," or "he stands. Audumbarāyaṇa maintains that speech is constant with respect to the sense organs;
in that case, a fourfold classification is not tenable, or [it applies] to things produced non-simultaneously.

There is the mutual instruction of words and the application [of them] as established by the treatises. However, because sound possesses pervasiveness and yet is extremely subtle, the assignment of names by means of sound is for the sake of worldly transaction. Among these, there is the designation of deities as if they were humans. Because the knowledge of the person is eternal, there is the accomplishment of ritual action through the mantra in the Veda.

Vārṣyāyaṇi maintains that there are six modifications of being (*bhāvavikāra*): "it is born," "it exists," "it transforms," "it grows," "it declines," and "it perishes. The term "is born" denotes the beginning of a prior state; it does not denote a subsequent state, nor does it negate it. "It exists" is the affirmation of the existence of that which has arisen. "It transforms" refers to a modification of that which does not deviate from its essential nature (*tattva*). "It grows" refers to the increase of its own constituent parts, or the increase of associated qualities; or it means it grows by way of victory.
Or, "it grows by means of the body. By this very [term], "it diminishes," the reverse process is explained.

"It perishes" expresses the beginning of a subsequent state; it does not express the prior state, nor does it negate it. Therefore, he said: "The other modifications of being are merely variations of these [three]. These are to be inferred according to their respective descriptions.
Śākaṭāyana maintains that prepositions (*upasarga*) are not bound [to the verb] and do not express meanings;

rather, they serve to indicate the connection with the object (*karman*) of both nouns (*nāman*) and verbs (*ākhyāta*). Gārgya holds that words have various and diverse meanings. Therefore, whatever meaning these [prepositions] convey is a modification of the meaning of the noun and the verb.

*Ā* signifies "hither" (*arvāk*). *Pra* is the opposite of *parā*. *Abhi* signifies "facing toward" (*ābhimukhya*). *Prati* is the opposite of this [i.e., *abhi*]. *Ati* and *su* signify that which is highly praised (*abhipūjita*). *Nir* and *dur* are the opposites of these two. *Ni* and *ava* signify restriction (*vinigraha*). *Ud* is the opposite of these two. *Sam* signifies unification (*ekībhāva*). *Vi* and *apa* are the opposites of this [i.e., *sam*]. *Anu* signifies similarity and posteriority (*aparabhāva*). *Api* signifies conjunction (*saṃsarga*). *Upa* signifies proximity (*upajana*).

*Pari* signifies "on all sides" (*sarvatobhāva*). *Adhi* signifies "above" (*uparibhāva*) or "lordship" (*aiśvarya*). Thus they speak of various meanings, high and low; these should be disregarded [in this context]. 1.3 Now, the particles (*nipāta*) fall upon various meanings. *Api* is used in the sense of comparison (*upamā*), in the sense of including an action (*karmopasaṃgraha*), and as a mere filler (*padapūraṇa*). Among them, these four occur in the sense of comparison:
*iva*, and in common speech (*bhāṣā*), and throughout each chapter (*anvadhyāyam*).
"Like Agni," "like Indra"—in common speech, "na" is used for the purpose of negation; both [forms] are to be studied according to the traditional text. "They did not honor Indra as a god."

Thus, [the particle] has the sense of negation; its occurrence before [the word] is that which it negates, as in "durmadāso na surāyām" (like those intoxicated by wine). It has the sense of comparison; its occurrence after [the word] is that with which one compares, as in "na mṛtyurāmṛtam" (not death, but immortality).

The particle *cit* has many functions. In the sense of reverence: "The teacher (*ācārya*) might say this. Regarding the word *ācārya*: why is he called an *ācārya*? Because he causes one to grasp right conduct (*ācāra*). Or, because he gathers (*ācinoti*) meanings, or because he gathers wisdom (*buddhi*). In the sense of comparison: "Dadhicita" (like Dadhica). In the sense of contempt: "Bring some *kulmāṣa* beans, even if only a little (*cit*). For *kulmāṣa* beans sink down in the houses. The particle *nu* also has many functions. In the sense of stating a reason: "Will he do this, now? In the sense of an inquiry: "How will he do this, now? And also: "Has he not indeed done this? (in the sense of a challenge or emphasis).
Moreover, it is used in the sense of comparison:

"O you who are invoked by many, your branches are like those of a tree"; "O you who are invoked by many, your branches are like those of a tree. *Vayāḥ* and *śākhāḥ* are derived from the root *vi* (to spread). They are windows; they are branches because they extend (*khaśayāḥ*). Or else, they are derived from the root *śak* (to be able).

Now, that for which the distinctness of meaning is understood from the traditional source (*āgama*), but not through a separate analytical statement (*vigraha*) as in the case of *auddeśika*, is a "compound of actions" (*karmopasaṃgraha*).
And the particle *ca* is employed with both [words] in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), as in:
"I and you, O slayer of Vṛtra."
In this very sense: the vowel *ā* [is used] in the phrases "to the gods" (*devebhyaḥ*) and "and to the ancestors" (*pitṛbhyaḥ*);
*vā* is used in the sense of deliberation (*vicāraṇa*).
"Alas! I shall not support this earth here or there.
Furthermore, it also has the sense of conjunction, as in: "Either Vāyu [supports] you, or Manu [supports] you."
The particles *aha* and *ha* are used for the purpose of restriction (*vinigrahārthīya*). They are joined with what precedes them, as in:
"Let this one do this," or "This one will do this, and that one will not do this.
Furthermore, the particle *u* is used in this same sense with what follows, as in: "They speak falsely; they speak the truth to you. Moreover, it serves to fill out the meter (*padapūraṇa*).
*Idam*, *tad*, and *hi*—this [group] has many functions. *Idam hi kariṣyati* (for he will do this) is used in the indication of a reason (*hetvapadeśa*).

*Katham hi kariṣyati* (how indeed will he do it? is used when something is asked in return (*anupṛṣṭe*). *Katham hi vyākariṣyati* (how indeed will he explain it? is used in the sense of censure (*asūyā*).

*Kila* signifies excellence of knowledge (*vidyā-prakarṣe*). Thus: *evaṃ kila*. Furthermore, when not followed by a question, it is used in conjunction with *na* and *nanu*: *na kilaivam* (it is certainly not so), *nanu kilaivam* (is it indeed not so?). *Mā* is used for prohibition: *mā kārṣīḥ* (do not do), *mā hārṣīḥ* (do not take). It is also used with *khalu*: *khalu kṛtvā* (having done), *khalu kṛtam* (it has been done). Moreover, it serves as a verse-filler (*padapūraṇa*): *evaṃ khalu tad babhūva* (thus indeed it came to pass).
Surely there is nothing for us tomorrow; who knows that which is mysterious? For the mind of another is difficult to fathom, and even what has been learned may perish.
Surely may that wealthy sacrificial gift of yours, O Indra, yield a boon for the singer; bestow it upon those who praise you.
Let not fortune fail us; may we, blessed with brave sons, speak aloud at the assembly.
She has milked for you a boon for the singer; a boon is to be chosen. The singer is the one who praises.
The sacrificial gift (dakṣiṇā) is wealthy, possessing riches. "Magha" is a name for wealth.

[The word] *dakṣiṇā* [is derived] from the root *maṃh*, which has the sense of giving. Or [it is derived] from the root *dakṣ*, which has the sense of making successful (*samardhayati*). It makes successful that which was unsuccessful. Alternatively, it is so called because of moving to the right (*pradakṣiṇāgamana*), with reference to the [southern] direction. The right hand is the prototype for the "hand of the direction" (*dig-hasta*). [It is derived] from the root *dakṣ*, which has the sense of exertion (*utsāha*). Or it may be from the root *dāś*, which has the sense of giving. The "hand" (*hasta*) is from the root *han*; [the suffix -as-] is used in the sense of striking (*prāśu-hanane*). [Thus, the meaning is: "Grant desires to the singers; do not strike us excessively; do not give to us by passing us over. May fortune (*bhaga*) be ours."

"May we speak aloud in our own knowledge. *Bhaga* is derived from the root *bhaj*. *Bṛhat* is a name for the great; it means "extensive. Or, [the phrase] "possessing heroes" (*vīravantaḥ*) means having auspicious heroes. A hero (*vīra*) exerts himself against enemies. It may be derived either from the root *vi*, meaning "to go," or from *vīrayati*.
*Sīm* is either a particle used for the purpose of inclusion or a filler for the meter. "The Āditya has sent forth *sīm*."

Or [it means] "he cast forth"; or "he cast forth on all sides. And [as in the verse]: "Vena revealed from the horizon the bright ones. The Sun revealed them on all sides. "The bright ones" refers to the rays of the Sun, because of their beautiful shining. Or rather, one may take the word *sīma* as a meaningless prefix (*anarthaka-upabandha*) functioning as an ablative.

From the boundary, from the limit, from the border; "sīmā" means a boundary or a limit. He sews together two regions. The particle *tvaḥ* is used for the purpose of specification (*vinigrahārthīya*). It is unaccented as a pronoun (*sarvanāman*); some say it is a name for "half" (*ardha*). One, having thrived, sits nourishing the growth of the *ṛc* verses; another sings the *gāyatra* chant upon the *śakvarī* meters; another speaks the sacred knowledge (*brahman*) born of wisdom; and yet another measures out the proportions of the sacrifice.

Thus he explains the distribution of the duties of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*): One, having nourished them, sits [watching] the nourishment of the *ṛc*s; this is the *hotṛ*. The *ṛc* is that which is to be recited. One sings the *gāyatra* among the *śakvarī* verses; this is the *udgātṛ*. The *gāyatra* is so called from the root *gai*, meaning "to praise. The *śakvarī* verses are so called from the root *śak*, "to be able. It is known from scripture: "Because they were able (*aśakat*) to slay Vṛtra with these [verses], therefore the *śakvarī*s have their name 'śakvarī'. One, at every birth [of a son], declares the sacred knowledge; this is the *brahmán*. He is the possessor of all knowledge; he is worthy to know everything.

*Brahmā* is derived from *parivṛh*, meaning "to increase"; *brahman* is increased on all sides. One [person] measures out the measure of the sacrifice: the *adhvaryu*. He is called *adhvaryu* because he is one who "joins" (*yunakti*) the sacrifice (*adhvara*), or because he is the leader (*netṛ*) of the sacrifice, or because he desires (*kāmayate*) the sacrifice. Alternatively, the suffix *-yu* is added to the root *dhī* (to think/meditate) with the prefix *upa*. *Adhvara* is a name for the sacrifice; the root *dhvarati* means "to injure," and this word is its negation. Some say it is a particle (*nipāta*). But how could that be a noun whose original form is unaccented? However, its declension is observed.
"Moreover, they say that in friendship there is firm drinking"—thus in the second [verse].
"And moreover, to him he has revealed his body"—thus in the fourth.
Friends with eyes and ears have become unequal in the swiftness of their thoughts;
some appear reaching only to the mouth or the armpits, while others look like deep lakes after one has bathed.
"Friends possessed of eyes and ears. [The word] *akṣi* is derived from the root *cakṣ* ("to see");
[it is derived] from the root *añj*, according to Āgrāyaṇa.
Therefore, these two appear as it were more distinct.
Thus it is known: *karṇa* is derived from the root *kṛt*, for its opening is cut away; [it is derived] from the root *ṛcch*, says Āgrāyaṇa, for they seem to reach upward through the openings.

Thus it is known: they were unequal in the swiftness of their thoughts. Some reached only to the mouth; others reached only to the armpits. *Āsya* comes from the root *as*, "to eat," or perhaps from *āsya*, "it flowed," for food flows into the mouth. *Daghnam* comes from the root *dagh*, which means "to flow," or it may come from *das*, "to perish," for it becomes more easily digested. Some have seen them as being like lakes (*hrada*) that are to be bathed in (*prasneyā*). *Prasneyā* means "fit for bathing. *Hrada* comes from the root *hrad*, which denotes the act of making sound, or it may come from *hlād*, which denotes the act of becoming cool.
Furthermore, it is used in the sense of a collection: "The *āśvina* [cup] is like a series of turns (*paryāyāḥ*)."

And [there are] the *āśvina* and the *paryāyas*. Now, those which occur as sentence-fillers (*vākya-pūraṇa*) in prose works (*pravṛtta-artha*) or in metrical texts (*amitākṣara-grantha*) are called word-fillers (*pada-pūraṇa*); they are meaningless (*anarthaka*) in metrical texts. For example: *kam īm id vṛṣaṇvasū* (1.9), *niṣṭvaktrāsaścid indraḥ*, and *bhūritokā vṛkādiva*.
Trembling with fear, they bellowed for the sake of coolness and for life.
The cool [season] is for the sake of life; "śiśiram" is derived from the root *śṛ* (to destroy) or from *śam* (to pacify).
"Emenaṃ sṛjatā sute"—"pour him forth at the pressing"; "āsṛjatainaṃ sute"—"let him be poured out at the pressing.
"May our songs of praise increase him."
May our songs of praise increase him; "giraḥ" [is derived] from the root "gṛṇāti" (to praise). This one belongs to you; this one belongs to you. This one belongs to you; this one belongs to you.
It is also seen as if [something] were visible, as if well-known, or as if well-understood. Nevertheless, this particle *iti* is joined with *id* in cases of apprehension:
"Some attend to the oblations with the Svarita accent; others, pressing the Soma, [attend] to the Somas at the libations. (RV 1.10)

"Rejoicing with our wives and with sacrificial gifts (dakṣiṇā), let us not go crookedly, lest we fall into *naraka*. Here, *naraka* means "going down" (*nīcair-gamana*). Or, it may mean that there is not even the slightest place of pleasure (*ramaṇa*) in it.
Furthermore, the particle *na* is joined with *cet* and *id*, as in the phrase "if they do not drink *surā*.
*Surā* is derived from the root *sū*. Thus, these particles fall upon various high and low meanings; they are to be disregarded [as mere particles]. 1.11

Thus, these four classes of words have been enumerated: nouns (*nāman*), verbs (*ākhyāta*), prefixes (*upasarga*), and particles (*nipāta*). Regarding this, Śākaṭāyana and the tradition of the etymologists (*nairukta*) maintain that all nouns are derived from verbs; Gārgya and some grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*) maintain that not all are so derived. This is the case where both accent and grammatical formation are capable [of indicating the meaning] and are endowed with a localized modification. Those are recognized as such, for example: "cow," "horse," "man," and "elephant."

Now, if all nouns were derived from verbs, then whatever being might perform that action, they would have to call it by that name. Whatever horse might traverse a path, it would have to be called "path-traverser. And whatever grass one might eat, it would have to be called "grass-eater. Furthermore, if all nouns were derived from verbs, then a thing would receive as many names as there are things with which it comes into contact; in that case, a single pillar would be called both "support" (*daraśayā*) and "connector" (*sañjanī*). 1.12
Moreover, they would have explained these [words] according to their etymological derivation (*kārmanāmika*) and their conventional meaning (*pratīta-artha*), as is logical.
For instance, they would have called the person "one who lies in the city" (*puri-śaya*);

they would have called a horse "that which goes to the eight" (*aṣṭā-gāmin*); and they would have called grass "that which pierces" (*tardana*). Furthermore, when a word has already been established in common usage, they reflect upon it: "They say 'earth' (*pṛthivī*) because of its expansion (*prathana*); but who expanded it? And what was its support? Now, Śākaṭāyana, regarding words whose meanings were not yet connected and whose modifications were not yet established, composed secondary meanings for them from the constituent parts of the words.
That which is caused by these [roots] begins with *yakāra*, and that which ends the action of *asteḥ* (the root *as*) is pure and begins with *sakāra*.

Furthermore, they say that "being" (*bhāva*) is preceded by "existence" (*sattva*). [The objection: "It is not possible for a modification (*pradeśa*) of the former to occur from a subsequent state of being. This is untenable.

For indeed, when both accent (*svara*) and grammatical formation (*saṃskāra*) are capable and joined with a localized modification (*prādeśika-vikāra*), then everything is indeed localized; such being the case, this objection does not hold.

As for the argument that "whatever action anyone performs, one should call all such beings by that [action]," we observe that those who perform the same action receive the same name, while others do not—just as, for example, a carpenter (*takṣan*), a wandering mendicant (*parivrājaka*), a professional beggar (*jīvana*), or a digger of roots (*bhūmija*).

By this very point, the previous objection is answered. As for the further claim that "they should call them by names whose meanings are well-known," there are indeed words of single syllable origin (*aikapadika*) that have only limited usage, such as *vratati*, *damūnā*, *jāṭya*, *āṭṇāra*, *jāgarūka*, and *darvihomī*.

As for the statement that "they deliberate upon what has been expressed," for indeed, the investigation of the application (*yoga-parīṣṭi*) occurs once the expression has been completed. They say, "The earth (*pṛthivī*) because it was spread out (*prathanāt*). But who would have spread it out, and what would have been its support? Or rather, it is "broad" (*pṛthu*) by virtue of being seen; even if it were not spread out by others. Furthermore, all such theories based on what is observed are subject to criticism. As for the claim that "one has compiled the second halves of the words from the [first] words," whoever has compiled them when the meaning is not connected is blameworthy for that reason. This is a censure of the person, not a censure of the scripture.

Regarding this point that it is not possible for the designation of a prior entity to arise from a subsequent entity, we observe that for some beings who have already arisen, the acquisition of a name occurs due to a subsequent state, while for others it does not—just as, for example, one might be called "Long-Haired" (*lambacūḍaka*) because of a *bilva* fruit. [The word] *bilva* is derived either from supporting (*bharaṇa*) or from splitting (*bhedana*). 1.14

Moreover, without this [science], there is no comprehension of the meaning within the mantras. For one who does not comprehend the meaning, the instruction regarding accent and grammatical refinement cannot be carried out to its full extent. Thus, this field of knowledge is the completeness of grammar; it accomplishes its own purpose. As for Kautsa’s claim that it is useless because it serves to comprehend the meaning of the mantras—[we reply: the mantras are indeed meaningless. This [objection] should be disregarded. The formulations of speech are fixed, as are their specific sequences.
Furthermore, they are prescribed by the Brāhmaṇa as being endowed with specific formal characteristics.
"Spread yourself wide," with these words he spreads it; "May I push forward," with these words he pushes it forward.
Furthermore, there are also [formulas] whose meaning is not applicable.
"O herb, protect him! O axe, do not harm him!"—thus he says while inflicting injury. Furthermore, there are also statements of contradictory meaning:
"Rudra remained alone; there was no second."
"The thousands of Rudras who are upon the earth—O Indra, you were born without a rival. Indra conquered a hundred armies all at once. Thus it is said.
Moreover, he may dispatch one who already knows [the ritual], saying:
"Recite for the fire as it is being kindled.
Furthermore, he says: "Aditi is everything."
"Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the intermediate space"—
this we shall explain later.
Furthermore, there are also [passages] whose meaning is not clearly expressed.
"amyak," "yādṛśmin," "jārayāyi," "kāṇukā"—these [words] possess meaning because they share commonality with the words [in the mantra].
And the Brāhmaṇa states: "This indeed is the success of the sacrifice, that it is successful in form—when the Ṛg or Yajus verse speaks in accordance with the rite being performed."
"Playing with their sons and grandsons"—thus [it is said].

As for the claim that "formulations of fixed speech possess a fixed sequence," this is also observed among worldly matters, such as "Indra and Agni" or "father and son. As for the claim that "they are prescribed as endowed with specific forms by the Brāhmaṇa," that is merely a restatement of what has already been said.
And as for the claim that "they contain meanings that are untenable," from the very words of the sacred tradition (Āmnāya), non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is understood.

As for the claim that these [Vedic statements] have contradictory meanings, this is also the case among worldly people; for example: "This Brāhmaṇa is without rivals," or "The king has no enemies. As for the claim that one gives instructions to someone who already knows, it is like saying "one greets someone who already knows," or "one offers the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*) to one who already knows. As for the claim that Aditi is everything, this is also the case among worldly people; for example: "Water contains all flavors. And as for the claim that these [Vedic statements] have unclear meanings, it is said: "It is not the fault of the tree stump that the blind man does not see it."

That is a human error. Just as among the people of the countryside a distinction between persons is known by their learning, so indeed among those who know the sequence of what precedes and follows, he who possesses greater knowledge is to be praised.
Furthermore, without this [knowledge], the division of words is not possible, as in:
*avasāya padvate rudra mṛḷa*. 1.16.
The cows go along the path; the path is their food. The root *ava* has the sense of "going," and this [prefix] is used for naming. Therefore, they do not pause (*avagṛhṇanti*).
[As in the example: "having unyoked the horses. The root *syati*, when preceded by a prefix, means "unloosing"; therefore, they do pause.
"The messenger of Nirṛti has come here"—this is either to be understood as having the sense of the ablative case, or as having the sense of the genitive case. [The word] ends in the vowel *ā*:
"Proclaim [the one] who is beyond Nirṛti. Thus.
An examination of the meaning of the fourth [case]. [The word] ending in *ai* is [the subject].

"Close proximity" (*paraḥ sannikarṣaḥ*) is *saṃhitā*. *Saṃhitā* is the original state of the words (*padaprakṛti*). The *pārṣada* texts of all the *caraṇas* have the words as their original state. Nevertheless, there are many instances in the sacrificial ritual where [the deity] is indicated by the name of the divinity (*daivata*). Therefore, this [rule] should be disregarded. If they should say, "We are here as those who know the *liṅga*," [one might cite]: "Indra, indeed, [is invoked] with strength; the gods satisfy Vāyu. Thus it is said.

The characteristic of Vāyu and the characteristic of Indra appear in the mantra addressed to Agni: "O Manyu, blazing like fire, prevail! Likewise, in the mantra addressed to Manyu, [Agni] is described as "tviṣitaḥ," meaning "flaming. *Tviṣi* is also a name for radiance. Furthermore, there is praise of knowledge and a censure of ignorance. 1.17
"This man is a mere wooden post, a mere bearer of burdens, who, having studied the Veda, does not understand its meaning.
He who knows the meaning attains all auspiciousness; with his sins shaken off by knowledge, he goes to the heavenly realm."
That which is grasped without being understood and is merely recited as a sound,
like dry fuel in a place without fire, never blazes at all.
*Sthāṇu* comes from the root *sthā*; *artha* comes from the root *ṛ*. Or rather, it is one who stands in the forest (*araṇastha*).
But some, though seeing, have not seen Speech; and some, though hearing, do not hear her.
Yet to another she has revealed her body, as a longing wife, well-adorned, reveals herself to her husband.

"Even one who sees does not see Speech; even one who hears does not hear her"—thus [the seer] spoke of the ignorant person. "She has revealed her body to one"—he thus discloses his own self. Knowledge is the illumination of meaning; he says this by means of this Speech, that is, by means of the highest Speech. "Like a wife desiring her husband, well-dressed at the proper seasons"—well-dressed means wearing beautiful garments, desiring him at the proper seasons. Just as he sees her and hears her when she is thus [adorned], so it is for the knower of the meaning; this is a praise of the one who knows the meaning. The following verse is for a further explanation. 1.19
Moreover, they say that in friendship he drinks deeply; they do not urge him on even in contests for prizes.
He moves by means of a barren illusion, having heard speech that is without fruit and without flower.

Even a single [word] regarding the friendship of Speech—firmly drunk, calling out, sporting, yet having its meaning drained away—[is used] regarding the friendship of the Gods, or as "in a delightful place. Its meaning is thus understood: that which they do not attain among the objects of speech, even when those objects are powerful; for he moves by means of a deceptive power that is like a barren cow.

By means of speech that is merely a semblance, one who has heard speech that is fruitless and flowerless among the realms of gods and men does not milk for himself the desires that are to be milked from speech. Or rather, speech becomes fruitless and flowerless for him; or it may produce some slight flowers and fruits. [The text] states that the flowers and fruits of speech are its meaning (*artha*). The flowers and fruits are the sacrificial and divine, or the divine and the spiritual (*adhyātma*). There were seers (*ṛṣi*) who had directly realized the Dharma; they transmitted the mantras by instruction to later generations who had not directly realized the Dharma.

Failing in their instruction, the later ones handed down this book for the purpose of memorizing the *bilma*—the Veda and the Vedāṅgas. *Bilma* means "learning" (*bhilma*) or "illumination" (*bhāsana*). So many are the verbal roots that have the same function; *dhātu* [is derived] from the root *dhā* (to hold). So many are the names of this being; so many are the meanings for which this is the designation. This is the *naighaṇṭuka* section concerning the names of deities. It is called "principal" because it refers to that which, when occurring in a mantra addressed to another deity, belongs to the *naighaṇṭuka* category—as in:
"Like a horse, you who are desirable... (*aśvaṃ na tvā vāravantam*).

"Like a horse with a tail"—the tail serves to ward off gadflies; "gadfly" (*daṃśa*) is derived from the root *daṃś* (to bite). "Like a terrifying beast, roaming, dwelling in the mountains"—like a terrifying beast, he roams and dwells in the mountains. "Beast" (*mṛga*) is derived from the root *mṛj* (to move); "terrifying" (*bhīma*) means that people are afraid of him. *Bhīṣma* is also derived from this same root. "Roaming" (*kucara*) refers to one who performs despicable actions. Alternatively, if it is a designation for a deity, it means "where does he not roam? "Dwelling in the mountains" (*giriṣṭhā*) means staying on a mountain; "mountain" (*giri*) is a peak.

It is "samudgīrṇaḥ" (vomited forth). A mountain (*parvata*) possesses joints (*parvan*). Furthermore, *parva* is derived from the root *pṛṇāti* (to fill) or *prīṇāti* (to please); it refers to the joint of a half-month (*ardhamāsa-parva*), because the gods please [the sacrificer] therein. The rest follows that same pattern due to the commonality of their joints. It resides in the clouds; for the cloud (*megha*) is also a mountain (*giri*) for this very reason. Those names which belong to the deities who are primarily praised are called "daivata" (pertaining to the deities). We shall explain those later on. Here, however, are the *naighaṇṭuka* (lexical) and *naigama* (etymological) words. 1.20.

The traditional recitation (samāmnāya) therein consists of four categories; other than these are the particles (nipātas), such as *vāyuḥ*, *vā tvā*, *na nūnam*, *nūnam*, *sā ta ṛcā*, *antvo akṣaṇvantaḥ*, *niṣṭvaktrāsaḥ*, and *havirbhiḥ*. Furthermore, there are those that are meaningful, such as *yaḥ*, *yatho hi nu*, *athāpīdam*, *sthāṇur ayam*, *uta tvaḥ paśyan*, and *uta tvaḥ sakhye*—these constitute twenty.
Thus ends the first chapter in the first six-chapter section of the *Nirukta*.
Now begins the second chapter.

Now, as for etymological derivation (*nirvacana*): those words in which accent and grammatical formation are capable [of yielding meaning] and are endowed with a localized modification, one should derive them accordingly.

Now, when the meaning is not directly connected [to the etymological derivation] or when the modification is not comprehensive, one should examine it through some commonality of function. Even when no such commonality exists, one should provide an etymological explanation based on a commonality of phonemes or letters; one must never fail to provide an explanation. One should not pay heed to the grammatical refinement alone, for linguistic functions are subject to various scopes. One should adjust the case endings according to the actual sense.

In the case of *pratta* and *avatta*, only the initial portion of the verbal root remains. Furthermore, there is the elision of the initial [augment] in place of the cessation of the root *as*: as in *staḥ* and *santi*. Moreover, there is the elision of the final [element]: as in *gatvā* and *gatam*.
Furthermore, there is the elision of the penultimate vowel: as in *jagmatuḥ* and *jagmuḥ*.

Furthermore, there is modification by means of an affix (*upadhāvikāra*), as in *rājā* and *daṇḍī*. Moreover, there is the elision of a phoneme (*varṇalopa*), as in *tattvā yāmi*. Furthermore, there is the elision of two phonemes, as in *tṛcaḥ*. Moreover, there is a transposition of the initial [phoneme], as in *jyotiḥ*, *ghanaḥ*, *binduḥ*, and *vāṭyaḥ*. Furthermore, there is a transposition of both the initial and final [phonemes], as in *stokāḥ*, *rajjuḥ*, *sikatāḥ*, and *tarkuḥ*. Moreover, there is the displacement of the final [phoneme].

*oghaḥ*, *meghaḥ*, *nādhaḥ*, *gādhaḥ*, *vadhūḥ*, and *madhu*. Furthermore, there is the addition of a phoneme (*varṇopajana*): *āsthat*, *dvāraḥ*, and *bharūja*. Now, when a verbal root (*dhātu*) has a semivowel (*antasthā*) immediately following a vowel, they designate that as the locus of roots with two constituent elements (*dviprakṛti*). In that case, if one [form] is established while another is not applicable, one should desire to explain it by means of the other. Even therein, some have few derivations. For example: *ūtiḥ*, *mṛduḥ*, *pṛthuḥ*, *pṛṣataḥ*, and *kuṇāru*.

Moreover, there are Vedic derivatives spoken from common (bhāṣika) verbal roots, such as *damūnāḥ* and *kṣetrasādhāḥ*. Furthermore, there are common words spoken from Vedic derivatives, such as *uṣṇam* and *ghṛtam*. Moreover, in some cases the original forms (*prakṛti*) themselves are spoken, while in others the modified forms (*vikṛti*) are spoken.

The root *śavati* means "to go" and is used only among the Kambojas; the Kambojas are so called because they eat wool (*kaṃbala*) or because they eat what is desirable (*kamanīya*). Wool is indeed desirable. Among the Āryas, however, they speak of its derivative form, *śava*. The root *dāti* is used in the sense of "cutting" among those in the East, while *dātra* is used in the North. In this manner, one should explain single words. Now, regarding Taddhita derivatives and compounds—whether consisting of two members or more—one should explain them by dividing them into successive parts, from the first to the last. For example: "A man who is liable to a fine" (*daṇḍyaḥ puruṣaḥ*) means "one who deserves a fine" (*daṇḍamarhati*).

Or, it is called *daṇḍa* because one is equipped with it (*saṃpadyate*). The word *daṇḍa* is derived from the root *dā*, in the sense of holding or supporting; people say, "Akrūra gives a jewel. According to Aupamanyava, it is from the root *dam*, meaning to restrain. In the sense of reproach, it refers to one who drags a staff; it is the girth-rope of a horse. It serves the side (*kakṣa*). *Kakṣa* is derived from the root *gāh*, meaning to plunge into. The suffix *ksa* is a name-forming element. Or, it is from the root *khyā*, where the reduplication is meaningless; the question being, "What is proclaimed (*khyāna*) in this? Or, it is from the root *kaṣ*. Because of that similarity, it is called the "side" (*kakṣa*) of a human being.

Because of the commonality of their arm-pits, [the term] *rājapuruṣaḥ* (king’s man) refers to a man who belongs to the king. *Rājā* is derived from the root *rāj* (to shine). *Puruṣaḥ* is one who devours (*ṣāt*) in the city (*puri*), or one who lies (*śayaḥ*) in the city; or it is derived from the root *pṛ* (to fill), for he fills the interior, with reference to the inner person (*antarapuruṣa*).
"Than whom there is nothing further, than whom there is nothing else, than whom there is none smaller and none greater."

"Like a tree, he stands firm, alone, in heaven; by that Puruṣa all this is filled. Thus also there is a Vedic verse. *Viśvakadrākarṣaḥ*. The root *vi-cakra* is said to mean "to go" (*śvagati*). *Drāti* is a term of reproach regarding motion. *Kadrāti* is a reproach regarding the act of going. In *cakadrāti kadrāti*, the repetition is meaningless for the existing form. That which possesses this [quality] is *viśvakadraḥ*.

"Of auspicious complexion and form. His form is as if of auspicious complexion; it becomes auspicious and desirable. *Varṇa* is derived from the root *vṛṇoti* (to choose); *rūpa* is derived from the root *rocate* (to shine). Thus one should explain [words] through secondary derivatives (*taddhita*) and compounds (*samāsa*), but not by means of single words. One should not explain them to one who is unacquainted with grammar, nor to one who has not approached [the teacher], nor to one who does not know "this" (the Self). For there is always envy toward the knowledge of one who does not understand. However, one should explain them to one who has approached [the teacher], or to one who is capable of understanding, or to one who is intelligent, or to one who is ascetic. "Knowledge indeed came to a Brahmin and said: 'Guard me; I am your treasure.'"
Do not speak this powerful [teaching] to one who is censorious, dishonest, or uncontrolled; may I thereby become possessed of such power.

He who fills one's ears with that which is not false, bringing about freedom from suffering and bestowing immortality—him one should regard as both father and mother; one should never do him harm, nor speak ill of him.
Those Brahmins who, having been taught by their teacher, do not honor him in word, thought, or deed—
just as they are not worthy of being fed by the teacher, so too that sacred learning does not nourish them.
O Brahmin, teach this to one whom you know to be pure, vigilant, intelligent, and endowed with celibacy;
to one who would not deceive you nor speak ill of you—to such a guardian of the treasure, O Brahmin, you should speak it.
Thus [it is called] "the treasure" (nidhi) and "the storehouse" (śevadhi).
Now, therefore, we shall set them forth in their proper order.

*Gauḥ* is a name for the earth, because she has gone far away (*dūraṃ gatā*), and because beings go (*gacchanti*) upon her. Or rather, *go* is a formative suffix (*vokaḥ*) used for naming. Furthermore, it is also a name for cattle for this very reason. Moreover, there are Vedic citations (*nigamāḥ*) regarding her that treat her as a whole through a secondary derivative (*tāddhita*): "Mix the intoxicating drink with cows."

Thus regarding *payas* (milk). *Matsara* is Soma; it is derived from the root *mad*, meaning "to satisfy. *Matsara* is a name for greed; by means of it, wealth becomes fully acquired (*abhimatta*). *Payas* is derived either from the root *pā* ("to drink") or *pyā* ("to swell"). *Kṣīra* is derived from the root *kṣar* ("to flow"). *Ghasera* is a formative suffix used to create names, as in the word *uśīra*.

Regarding the phrase "milking the stalk, they sit upon the cow," this refers to the skin of the pressing-vessel. A *aṃśu* (stalk) is eight finger-breadths in measure; or rather, it is called *aṃśu* because it provides well-being (*śam*) to the eater (*ana*).
It is derived from the root *car* (to move), or it is called "elevated" (*uccṛta*).
Moreover, it consists of skin (*carman*) and phlegm (*śleṣman*).
"Thou art bound with cow-hides; display thy vigor!"
Thus, in the praise of the chariot; and furthermore: "Sinew and phlegm, bound together with cow-hides, fly forth when discharged.
Thus, in the praise of the arrow.
Furthermore, "gaur" is mentioned. If it is "gavyā," it is a secondary derivative (*taddhita*); if not, then [it is used as] "gavyā gamayati iṣūn.
[The verse continues: "O tree, let the cow move through the tree; then the bird [will go] toward the men-eaters who have arrived."

In every tree, in every bow. Or, it stands having encompassed the earth (*kṣām*); *kṣā* is from the root *kṣi*, meaning "to dwell. The cow (*gauḥ*) bellowed (*mīmayat*), for it makes sound; *mīmayati* is a verb whose action is making sound. Thence the birds fly forth to devour men. *Viri* is a name for a bird, from the root *vī*, meaning "to go. Furthermore, the word *iṣu* (arrow) here also comes from this same root. The Sun (*āditya*) is also called *go*. And there, in that rough cow...

"It possesses mountains and is radiant," says Aupamanyava. Moreover, one of its rays shines toward the moon; therefore, this should be regarded as such. Its radiance comes from the sun. "Suṣumṇa, the ray of the sun, the moon, the Gandharva"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (nigama). That [moon] is also called *go* (the cow).
Regarding this, it is said: "They perceived the *go* here."
Thus it is said. We shall explain this further below. All rays are called *gāvaḥ* (cows).
"We desire to go to those abodes of yours where the many-horned, tireless cows are;
there indeed shines down that highest step of the wide-striding Bull in great abundance."

We desire to go to those abodes of yours where there are cows with many horns—*bhūri* being a name for "much," so called because it prevails; *śṛṅga* is derived from the root *śri* (to resort to), or *śṛ* (to crush), or *śam* (to be peaceful), or "risen for protection," or "emerged from the head. *Ayāsaḥ* means "unwearied" or "moving. There, the supreme station of Viṣṇu, whose stride is vast (*urugāyasya*), shines forth abundantly as the most excellent. *Pāda* is that which is stepped upon; it is called *pada* because it is the place of its placement.
He who made this does not know it; he who saw it is far removed from it.
Enveloped within his mother’s womb, he who possesses abundant offspring has entered into destruction.

"He who has many offspring falls into distress"—so say the Parivrājakas. "It is the act of raining"—so say the etymologists (*nairuktāḥ*). Regarding the words "he who made him" (*ya īṃ cakāra*), the roots *kṛ* (to make) and *kṛ* (to scatter) are ambiguous in their application to the act of raining. "The middle one does not know him"—the middle one is he who saw him established in the sun. "He is in the womb of his mother"—the mother is the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*); for in it all beings are produced. The womb is the intermediate region; it is a great limb. It is enveloped by the wind. This other [physical] womb is derived from this very same [principle]; it is completely enclosed. He who has many offspring falls upon the earth through the act of raining.

Śākapūṇi resolved, "I shall know all the deities. To him, a deity of both genders appeared. He did not recognize her. He asked her, "May I know you? She directed this Ṛc to him: "This is my deity"— "This one snorts, by whom the cow is covered; she bellows a lowing sound, resting upon the cleft.
By her thoughts she has indeed humbled the mortal; becoming lightning, she has stripped away her covering. (RV 1.164.42)

This is that which makes sound, by which the cow has been set in motion and bellows; she utters the "māyu" sound, or rather, she bellows toward the sun. This is the voice of the intermediate region (mādhyamikā), resting upon the thundering cloud. By means of her mental powers—that is, her ritual acts—she humbles the mortal. Becoming lightning, she rends asunder the covering (vavri). "Vavri" is a name for form; it is so called because it covers. Having concealed the earth with rain, she takes it back again.

The next fifteen [names] are those of gold (*hiraṇya*). Why "gold"? Because it is carried away (*hriyate*) when being stretched out; or because it is carried from person to person; or because it is a source of delight (*hitaramaṇa*); or it may derive from the root *haryati*, meaning the act of desiring. The next sixteen [names] are those of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Why "intermediate space"? Because it is situated between (*antara*) and pervades (*kṣānta*); or because "these two are within it" (*antareme*); or because it does not perish within bodies (*śarīreṣu antarakṣaya*).

In this context, the word *samudra* is associated with the earthly ocean (*pārthiva-samudra*). Why is it called *samudra*? Because from it the waters flow forth (*sam-ud-dravanti*); because the waters flow toward it (*sam-abhi-dravanti*); because beings rejoice within it (*sam-modante*); because it consists of water (*sam-udaka*); or because it moistens thoroughly (*sam-unatti*). This is the analysis of its parts.

Regarding this, they relate an ancient history: Devāpi Ārṣṭiṣeṇa and Śantanu, both descendants of Kuru, were brothers. That Śantanu, being the younger, was consecrated [as king]. Devāpi, however, devoted himself to asceticism. Then, for twelve years, the god did not send rain upon the kingdom of Śantanu. The brahmins said to him, "An unrighteous act has been committed by you; you have bypassed your elder brother and been consecrated. Therefore, the god does not rain for you."

That Śantanu sought to instruct Devāpi in the kingship. Devāpi said to him, "I shall be your domestic priest, and I shall perform the sacrifices for you. This hymn of his is intended for one who desires rain. Regarding this, there is this verse (RV 8.92.1):
"Arṣṭiṣeṇa, the seer Devāpi, having sat down to the office of the Hotṛ and being cognizant of the gods' favor, released from the upper ocean the celestial waters, the rains, toward the lower ocean."

Ārṣṭiṣeṇa is the son of Ṛṣṭiṣeṇa, or rather, the son of Iṣitasena. *Senā* means "possessing a lord" (*seśvarā*), or it has the same meaning as *samānagati*. A *putra* protects (*trāyate*) in many ways (*puru*); or [it is so called] from the act of depositing (*niparaṇa*); or because he protects one from the *punnaraka* (the hell of repeated death). The seer (*ṛṣi*) sat down for the office of the *hotṛ*. He is a seer because of his vision; according to Aupamanyava, it is because he saw the *stomas*.

"That which the self-existent Brahman sent down to these [sages] as they were performing penance—that is the *ṛṣitva* (seership) of the ṛṣis," so it is known. Devāpi, through his attainment of the gods, through praise, and through giving, being wise and conscious, [attained] the auspicious mind of the gods. He [went] from the northern [ocean] to the lower ocean. "Northern" means more elevated; "lower" means below. By saying "it does not flow downwards," upward motion is prohibited. The following verse is for further explanation: "When Devāpi, the domestic priest (*purohita*) for Śantanu, was chosen for the office of *hotṛ*, he shone forth with compassion."
Bestowing it, Bṛhaspati granted this speech to him, which is heard by the gods and wins the rain.

"Śaṃtanu"—either meaning "may he extend peace," or "may there be peace for him through his body. As the *purohita*, they place him in front. Chosen for the office of the *hotṛ* priest, he meditated with compassion.

"God-hearing": the gods hear him as one who prays for rain. "Rarāṇaḥ": the gift has been bestowed. Bṛhaspati was the *brahmán* priest; he bestowed speech upon him. "Bṛhat" has already been explained. 12.

The six subsequent [names] are common to both the Sky (*div*) and the Sun (*āditya*). However, those which belong primarily to him we shall explain below. Why "Āditya"? Because he takes up (*ādatte*) essences; because he takes up the luster of lights; or because he is blazing with luster (*ādīpto bhāsā*); or because he is the son of Aditi. Yet, this [name] has little usage; it receives its own hymn only in the *ārcābhyāmnāya*: "Sūrya, the son of Aditi."

"The son of Aditi. In this same way, there are praises of other deities as well that refer to them as being of the nature of Ādityas; for example, those of Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Dakṣa, Bhaga, and Aṃśa. Furthermore, there are praises of Mitra and Varuṇa together: "O Ādityas, lords of the gift" (meaning lords of giving). Moreover, there is praise of Mitra alone:
"May that mortal, O Mitra, be foremost who exerts himself for you with his vow, O Āditya."
Thus there is also a Vedic verse:
"Now, O Āditya Varuṇa, we [abide] in your vow.
"Vow" (*vrata*) is a name for action; it is so called because it restrains (*vārayati*) one from activity.

This other vow also derives its name from this very fact that it "chooses" (vṛṇoti) the existent; thus food is also called a *vrata*, because it covers (āvṛṇoti) the body. The sun is *Svar*. He is one who moves well (*su-araṇaḥ*), one who impels well (*su-īraṇaḥ*). He is well-moved toward the essences (*rasān*); he is well-moved toward the light of the luminaries; or rather, he is well-moved toward radiance (*bhās*). By this, the sky (*dyauḥ*) is explained. The sun is *Pṛśni*. According to the etymologists (*nairuktāḥ*), he is so called because he has "eaten" (*prāśnute*) his color. He is touched by the essences; he is the toucher of the light of the luminaries; or rather, he is touched by radiance. Now, as for the sky: it is touched by the luminaries and by those who perform meritorious deeds.

The *nāka* is the Āditya; he is the leader, the guide of lights. And then there is *dyauḥ*. *Ka* is a name for happiness (*sukha*). That which is prohibited would be prohibited [here]. For there is nothing that is not *nāka* for one who has gone to that world, nor is there anything that is not happiness for one who has gone to that world; for only those who perform meritorious deeds go there. The *go* is the Āditya; he causes the juices (*rasas*) to move; he moves in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). And then there is *dyauḥ*, because she has gone far away from the earth, and because the lights move within her.

The sun becomes *viṣṭabh* (the pervader), having entered the essences, having entered the luster of the lights, or as it is said, "having entered the luster. Now, the sky (*dyauḥ*): it is entered by the lights and by those who perform meritorious deeds.

The sun becomes *nabhas* (the leader), the leader of the lusters, the guide of the lights; or rather, it may be *bhana*, the opposite [of *na-bhā*], meaning "it does not fail to shine" (*na na bhāti*). By this, the sky is explained. 14.

The next fifteen [sections] are names of rays (*raśmi*). A ray is so called because of its restraining (*yamanāt*) [power]. Of these, the first five are common to the rays of a horse. The next eight are names of the directions (*diś*). Why "direction" (*diś*)? From the root *diś*, meaning "to point out. Or else, from "to sit down" (*āsadanāt*), or from "to reach" (*abhyaśanāt*). In that context, the term *kāṣṭhā* applies even to many beings; the directions are the *kāṣṭhās*.

Having traversed, they stand still. The quarters (kāṣṭhā) become the intermediate directions; having traversed one another, they stand still. The sun also is called a quarter; having traversed, it stands still. The fire at the end of the world (ājyanta) also is called a quarter; having traversed, it stands still. The waters also are called quarters; having traversed, they stand still—thus [it refers] to stationary things.
Within these quarters that do not stand still and have no fixed dwelling, the body is deposited.

"The waters flow through the secret place of Vṛtra; he whose enemy was Indra lay long in darkness. The cloud is the body placed in the midst of the non-stationary, non-abiding, fixed expanses (kāṣṭhā). "Body" (*śarīram*) is derived from the root *śṛ* ("to crush") or from *śam* ("to pacify"). "The waters flow through the secret place of Vṛtra" means they know it thoroughly. "Long" (*dīrgham*) is from the root *drāgh* ("to stretch"). "Darkness" (*tamaḥ*) is from the root *tan* ("to extend"). "He lay" (*āśayat*) is from the root *śī* ("to lie down"). "Whose enemy was Indra" (*indraśatruḥ*): Indra is his pacifier or his destroyer; therefore, he is "Indra-Enemy."

Who, then, is Vṛtra? The etymologists say he is the cloud; the historians say he is the Asura, the son of Tvaṣṭṛ. From the action of mixing water and light, the act of raining is produced. In that regard, descriptions of battle occur by way of metaphor. Indeed, both the Vedic mantras and the Brāhmaṇa discourses speak of him as a serpent. Because of the swelling of his body, he blocked the channels [of the waters]. When he was slain, the waters flowed forth. Regarding this, there is a Ṛgvedic verse:
"The waters stood obstructed, having the Dāsa as their lord and the serpent as their guardian, like the cows held captive by the Paṇi."
The opening of the waters that was covered, he threw it open after slaying Vṛtra.

*Dasapatnīḥ* means having the *dāsa* as their lord; *dāsa* is derived from the root *das*, for he destroys (upadāsayati) actions. *Ahigopā atiṣṭhan* means they stood protected by the serpent (*ahi*); *ahi* is so called because it moves (*eti*) through the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

This other [word] *ahi* is derived from this very same root, with the prefix elided: it means "he strikes" (*āhanti*). The waters were obstructed by him, as cows are by a *paṇi*. A *paṇi* is a merchant; he is so called because of bargaining (*paṇana*). A merchant displays his wares (*paṇya*) for sale. When the opening of the waters was covered, that opening is called *bhara*; it comes from the root *bharati* (to support). He slew Vṛtra; he closed it off. *Vṛtra* is derived from the root *vṛṇoti* (to cover), or from *vartati* (to turn), or from *vardhati* (to grow).

"That which he covered (avṛṇot) is the Vṛtra-nature of Vṛtra," so it is known. "That which he rolled forward (avartata) is the Vṛtra-nature of Vṛtra," so it is known. "That which he grew (avardhata) is the Vṛtra-nature of Vṛtra," so it is known. 17

The next twenty-three [names] are those of Night (*rātri*). Why "Night"? Because she causes the night-wandering beings to take great delight; she causes others to cease and makes them steady. Or it may be from the root *rā*, meaning "to give," for dewdrops are given forth (*pradīyante*) upon her. The next sixteen [names] are those of Dawn (*uṣas*). Why "Dawn"? Because she shines (*ucchatīti*) truly. She is the latter part of the night. Regarding her, there is this verse (RV 7.79.2): "This most excellent light among lights has come; the bright, far-reaching signal has been born.
As the mother yields to the impulse of Savitṛ, even so has Night yielded her womb to Dawn."

This most excellent light among lights has arrived; it has been born as a wondrous beacon, most wise and most pervasive. Just as Night yielded her place for the procreation of Savitṛ, even so Night has yielded her womb, her station, to the Dawn. The womb of the woman is joined with her; the embryo is within her. Regarding this, there is another verse:
Radiant with her radiant calf, the bright one has come; the black one has departed from her dwellings.
Of common kinship, immortal, following one after the other, the two heavens move along, changing their colors.

*Ruśadvatsā sūryavatsā*: *ruśat* is a name for color; it comes from the root *ruc*, meaning "to shine. He calls the sun her calf because of their association, or because [the sun] carries away her essence (*rasa*). *Ruśatī* means "shining white"; *śvetyā* comes from the root *śvit*, "to become white. "The dark one has entered her dwellings": the night is dark-colored; *kṛṣṇa* comes from the root *kṛṣ*, meaning a low or inferior color. Now he praises these two: "of common kinship" means having a common bond; "immortal" means having the nature of not dying; "following one another" means with reference to each other.

The two move across the sky; they themselves are the two heavens (*dyāvau*), because of their shining (*dyotanāt*). Or rather, it may be that "the two move" means "they move by means of her. Not failing (*amināne*), they act within one another.

The following twelve words are names of the day (*ahan*). Why "day" (*ahaḥ*)? Because actions are brought forward (*upāharanti*) in it. This is its irregular form (*nipātaḥ*) occurring in the verse addressed to Vaiśvānara (RV 7.99.1): "The black day and the white day revolve through the spaces with their manifestations."
Being born as Vaiśvānara, Agni has outshone the darkness, just as a king surpasses his enemies.

The day is black and the night is white; the day is bright and the night is dark. These two dust-clouds revolve through activities that are to be known and those that are to be realized, like the fire Vaiśvānara when he is born, like the rising sun, the king of all lights, or like Agni who has struck down the darkness with his light.

The next thirty [sections] are names of clouds. Why "megha" (cloud)? Because it "moists" (*mehati*) while existing. It shares its names with mountains, namely *upara* and *upala*. A cloud is *upara* or *upala*; in it the clouds cease (*uparamante*), or rather, the waters have ceased there. Regarding them, this verse occurs: "The first ones stood at the measuring of the gods; their fierce ones went forth from the cutting-tool. Three heat the earth, two carry the moisture (*purīṣa*) as the rain-cloud. 21. *devānāṃ māne prathamā atiṣṭhankṛntatrādeṣāmuprā udāyan | trayaḥ tapanti pṛthivīmanūpā dvā bṛbūkaṃ vahataḥ purīṣam* ||
