The first [group] stood at the creation of the gods; they were the middle classes of deities. "First" (*prathama*) is a name for the principal; he becomes preeminent. The intermediate space is a "cutting" (*kṛntatra*); it is the "cleaving" (*vikartana*) of the clouds. Through the cleaving of the clouds, water is produced. Three heat the earth: Parjanya, Vāyu, and Āditya. They ripen the plants with cold, heat, and rain. They are called *anūpāḥ* because they "sow after" (*anu-vapanti*) the worlds according to their respective functions. This other [terrestrial] *anūpa* (marshland) comes from this very same root.

It was moistened by water; or rather, it might be "anv-ā-bhita" (enveloped from behind), as in the case of "prāk" (eastward). For that, there would be "anūpa" (moisture-rich land), as in the case of "prācīnam" (eastern). Two carry the *bṛbūka* (flood/water): Vāyu and Āditya, [carrying] the water. *Bṛbūka* is a name for water, derived from the root *bravīti*, meaning "to sound," or from *bhraṃśati*, "to fall. *Purīṣa* is from the root *pṛṇāti* (to fill) or *pūrayati* (to fill). 22.

The next fifty-seven [sections] concern Speech (*vāc*). Why "Speech"? From the root *vac* (to speak). Regarding that, there are Vedic citations (*nigama*) for the word *sarasvatī* that treat it both as a river and as a deity. Of these, we shall explain later those that treat it as a deity; here, however, it is treated as a river: "She, like one who digs up lotus-stalks, has shattered the ridges of the mountains with her surging powers and her mighty waves.
For the sake of protection, let us invoke Sarasvatī—the slayer of the Pārāvatas—with well-fashioned hymns and meditations. (RV 6.61.2)

This [river] is with its *śuṣma*s—*śuṣma* being a name for strength; it is so called because it dries up (*śoṣayati*) that which exists. *Bisa* comes from the root *bis*, meaning "to split," or from the sense of "growing. A *sānu* is something elevated; or rather, it is "raised up" (*samunnunna*). With its great waves. *Pārāvataghnī* means "slaying those on the far shore"; *pāra* is "the further side" and *avāra* is "the near side. May we worship Sarasvatī, the river, with well-performed rites and beautiful hymns for the sake of protection. There are one hundred and one subsequent words for water. Why is it called *udaka*? Because it moistens (*unatti*).

The following thirty-seven [names] are those of rivers. Why "rivers" (*nadyaḥ*)? Because they flow (*nadanti*); they possess sound. Their usage in the *Naighaṇṭuka* is frequent; it is, as it were, a marvel due to their preeminence.

Regarding this, they relate an ancient history (*itihāsa*). The seer Viśvāmitra was the domestic priest (*purohita*) of Sudās, the son of Pijavana. Viśvāmitra means "friend of all"; he is one with whom everything is well-integrated. Sudās means "one who gives auspiciously. Paijavana is the son of Pijavana; furthermore, Pijavana is so called because his speed (*java*) is to be envied, or because his movement is unimpeded. Taking his wealth, he came to the confluence of the Vipāś and Śutudrī rivers. The others followed him. That Viśvāmitra praised the rivers, saying, "Become fordable! (*gādhā bhavata*).
There is also the dual number; there is also the plural number. Of these, we shall explain that which follows the dual later on. Now, as for this plural number:
"Delight yourselves in my pleasant speech, O you who follow the *ṛta*, for a moment with your movements!
With a lofty hymn, seeking help, the son of Kuśika has called out toward the river."

Cease from my speech, which is worthy of Soma and brings about the attainment of Soma. *Ṛtāvarīḥ* means "possessing *ṛta*. *Ṛta* is a name for water; it is so called because it flows toward (*prati-ṛta*). *Muhūrta* refers to moments, whether by movements or by descents. A *muhūrta* is a momentary season (*muhuḥ-ṛtu*). *Ṛtu* comes from the root *ṛ*, meaning "to go. Time is like a momentary flash (*muhur-mūhla*). It is also [called] *abhīkṣṇa*. *Abhīkṣṇa* becomes *abhikṣaṇa*. *Kṣaṇa* comes from the root *kṣaṇoti*; time is that which wears away (*prakṣṇutaḥ*). *Kāla* comes from the root *kālayati*, meaning "to go."

I call upon the Sindhu with a lofty, great hymn of inspiration—by the impulse of the mind, by praise, and by wisdom—for the sake of winning [the prize]. The son of Kuśika: King Kuśika was so named from the root *kruś*, meaning "to cry out," or perhaps from *kraṃś*, meaning "to make manifest"; or it may mean "one who skillfully proclaims wealth. The rivers replied:
"Indra, whose arm wields the thunderbolt, dug us out; he struck down Vṛtra, the confining barrier of the rivers.
The god Savitṛ, the fair-handed, led us forth; at his impulsion, we, the wide ones, flow on."

Indra, whose arm wields the thunderbolt, has rescued us. *Radati* is a verb meaning "to dig. He struck down Vṛtra, the dam of the rivers—this has already been explained. The god Savitṛ led [us] forth; he is "supāṇi," one with beautiful hands. *Pāṇi* [is derived] from the root *paṇāyati*, which means "to honor. Having taken hold of their hands, they honor the gods. "In his impulsion, we go upon the wide expanses. *Urvī* is from the root *ūrṇoti* (to cover); Aurṇavābha says it is from the root *vṛṇoti* (to choose). Having rejected [the narrow path], they finally heard [the call].
"O singer (*kāra*), may we hear your words, you who have come from afar with wagon and chariot."
She bows down to him like a swelling woman, like a maiden for her suitor; she belongs eternally to you.

We have heard your words, O maker; come from afar with your wagon and your chariot. We bend down to you as a nursing woman bends toward her son, or as a maiden embraces a man—*ninamā* means "we bend down. The next twenty-six verses contain names of horses. Of these, the last eight are in the plural. Why is he called *aśva*? Because he traverses (*aśnute*) the path, or because he is a great eater (*mahāśana*).
In that context, *dadhikrā* means either "he who moves while bestowing" (*dadhat krāmati*) or "he who cries out while bestowing" (*dadhat krandati*).

Or [it is so called] because it assumes a form (*ākāra*). Its *nigamas* (scriptural citations) are like those of the horse and like those of the deity. Of these, those that are like the deity we shall explain later; now, as for those like the horse:
"Or this vigorous steed, though bound by the neck, at the girth, and in the mouth, speeds toward the whip.
Dadhikrā, having strengthened his resolve, springs along the curves of the paths. (RV 4.40.2)

Moreover, that vigorous steed, full of trembling, swiftly traverses the path along its course. It is bound by the neck; "neck" (*grīvā*) is derived from *girasati* ("to swallow"), or from *gṛṇāti* ("to praise"), or from *gṛhṇāti* ("to seize"). Furthermore, the phrase "in the armpit" (*kakṣe āsani*) has been explained. *Kratum* refers to *Dadhikrāḥ*—either his action or his wisdom. *Anusaṃtavītvat*: this is a Vedic usage (*nigama*) with the original root form of *tanoti* ("to extend"). *Pathām aṅkāṃsi* means the crooked places of the paths. "Path" (*panthāḥ*) is derived from *patati* ("to fly"), or from *padyate* ("to go"), or from *panthati* ("to traverse"). *Aṅkaḥ* is derived from *añcati* ("to bend").

"Āpanīphaṇat" is derived from the root *phaṇ* in the *carkarīta* (intensive) formation. They say there are ten subsequent [meanings] for the sake of understanding their association. The eleven following verbal roots have "to blaze" (*jvalati*) as their action; there are exactly that many subsequent names for "blazing. 28. Names, names. 28.

Now follows the Nirvacana-mogha; the knowledge of the King indeed [is this]. Hereafter we shall enumerate [the hymns]: "On every tree" (vṛkṣavṛkṣe), "as many as there are dwellings" (tāvāṃ vāstūni), "he who made them" (ya īṃ cakāra), "this one bleats" (ayaṃ sa śiṅkte), "names of gold" (hiraṇyanāmāni), "Ārṣṭiṣeṇa," "when Devāpi" (yaddevāpiḥ), "common [verses]" (sādhāraṇāni), "Svar, Āditya," "names of rays" (raśmināmāni), "of those standing still" (atiṣṭhantīnām), "Dāsapatnī," "names of nights" (rātrināmāni), "this best" (idaṃ śreṣṭham), "the white calf" (ruśadvatsā), "and the black" (ahaśca kṛṣṇam), "in the dwelling of the gods" (devānāṃ māne), "names of speech" (vāṅnāmāni), "with vigor, rejoice" (iyaṃ śuṣmebhi ramadhvam), "may Indra for me" (ma indro asmān), "of Kārūtas" (āte kārāvutasya), "possessing strength" (vājī)—[these] twenty-eight.

Thus ends the second chapter in the first six books of the *Nirukta*. Now begins the third chapter. Hereafter follow twenty-six names of action (*karman*). Why "action" (*karman*)? Because it is performed (*kriyate*) while existing. Hereafter follow fifteen names of offspring (*apatya*). Why "offspring" (*apatya*)? Because it falls away from [the parent] (*apatatam*), or because one does not fall by means of it. It is just as [the term] "progeny" (*prajā*) is used for the offspring of a progenitor. We shall cite examples from the *Ṛgveda* regarding this meaning. 1.
For the wealth of one who is free from strife is indeed a source of security; may we be masters of eternal riches.
O Agni, there is no offspring of another for one who is heedless; do not lead us astray from the path.

For one must avoid, not approach, the wealth of a stranger (*araṇa*). A stranger is one who is unrelated. "Wealth" (*rekṇas*) is a name for riches; it is left behind when one departs. May we be masters of eternal wealth, as if of ancestral property. O Agni, there is no offspring remaining from one born of another. "Offspring" (*śeṣa*) is a name for progeny; it is that which remains when one departs. That belongs to one who is mindless or negligent. [The prayer continues: "Do not lead us astray from our path. The following verse serves to provide a further explanation: "For one should not seize the wealth of a stranger, even if he is very kind; for a son born of another womb is to be considered [as such] in one's mind."
Then indeed he returns again to his own dwelling; may the new prize-winning steed come toward us with longing.

Indeed, he should not be taken [as his own], even though he is harmless and most pleasant; nor should a half-brother be considered by the mind as "this is my son. Then he returns again to that very home from which he came; "home" (*okaḥ*) is said to be the name for a dwelling place. "May the vigorous one, the impeller, come to us, overcoming our rivals—he who is newly born is indeed the son. Now, those who favor the daughter's inheritance cite this verse, while some say it is the son's inheritance:
"The wise bearer, instructing, honoring the ordinance of Truth, [knows] the lineage of the daughter's granddaughter."
Where the father, bestowing the marriage-portion upon his daughter, hastened with a willing mind.

The bearer (the father) instructs his daughter regarding her state of being a mother through the act of procreation. "Daughter" (*duhitā*) means one who is placed far away (*dūre hitā*), or from the root *duh* (to milk). She has approached the grandson; that is, the son of the daughter (*dauhitra*) is the son of the son (*pautra*). This is known by the wise man of the sacrifice of procreation, or rather, of semen. [He knows this] of him who is produced from limb after limb, born from the heart, and firmly established in the mother. Honoring the ordinance, he recognizes that sons born of union are heirs without distinction.
This very point is expressed in two verses of the Ṛgveda: "From limb after limb you are produced; you are born from the heart."
"You are indeed the self named 'son'; live for a hundred autumns. Thus [it is said].
According to dharma, the inheritance of sons occurs without distinction;
so Manu Svāyambhuva declared regarding the creation of pairs at the beginning.
"Some say there are no daughters; therefore, the male is the heir and the female is not an heir—so it is known.
Therefore, they cast out a daughter when she is born, but not a son."
And thus:

"The giving, selling, and abandonment of women exist, but not those of men. Some say, "They also exist for men," because of the example seen in the case of Śunaḥśepa. Another [view] is that it refers to the statement concerning a woman without brothers: "Those sisters who go there, all dressed in red garments..."
Like sisters who have no brothers, they stand with their paths destroyed.

"Like a brotherless maiden, they stand for the sake of the ancestral rite and the offering of funeral cakes, their paths blocked. Thus is the figurative explanation of the "brotherless one" (abhrātṛkā). The following verse provides a further etymological interpretation: Like a brotherless woman, she comes toward us; like one ascending the funeral mound to win riches;
like a longing wife well-attired for her husband; Dawn, like a laughing woman, bares her bosom.

Like a woman without a brother, she approaches her father’s [ancestors] face-to-face for the sake of the act of procreation and the offering of funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*), but not her husband. Like a courtesan from the Deccan who climbs onto a pit to obtain wealth, so does she climb onto the *sabhā-sthāṇu* (the pillar of the assembly hall). It is derived from the root *gṛ* (to swallow/to take). He is one whose promise is true. Thereupon, a woman who is childless or husbandless climbs upon it. There they strike her with a die (*akṣa*). She obtains the inheritance. The word *garta* also refers to the collection of the cremation ground; it is derived from the root *gur* (to swallow/to take). He becomes one who has swallowed [his enemies]. *Śmaśāna* means "lying in the *śman*"; *śman* is the body.

*Śarīram* is derived from the root *śṛ* (to crush) or from *śam* (to pacify). *Śmaśru* is hair; it rests upon the face (*śman*). It is derived from the root *lū* (to cut) or from *lī* (to dissolve). One should not expose the lower part [of the sacrificial post]; for if one were to expose the lower part, the sacrificer would stand in a pit and be liable to die prematurely.
Thus there is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*).

The chariot (*ratha*) is also called a *gartá*. [It is derived] from the root *gṛ*, meaning "to praise"; it is the most highly praised vehicle. There is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) which says: "O Varuṇa and Mitra, ascend the *gartá*."

"Like a wife desiring her husband, well-adorned at the proper seasons, Dawn, like a smiling woman, reveals her forms as she displays her teeth. There are four similes here. "One should not marry a girl who has no brother, for her offspring belongs to him"—this is the explicit prohibition against marrying a girl without a brother. And there is the father's status as a son: "When the father effects the emission of seed in his unmarried daughter, he unites himself with her through mental union."
Now they cite this prohibition against the inheritance of a sister: "Some say the eldest [son] belongs to the appointed daughter (*putrikā*).
"He has not left his own inheritance for his sister; he made her a womb, a treasure-store for the winner.
When the mothers have generated the bearer, one shall be the performer of good deeds, while the other shall be the one who suffers."

Not to a *jāmi*, that is, a sister; for others produce offspring upon her as a *jāmi*. Or it may derive from the root *jam*, meaning "to go," for she is one who is prone to depart [from the family]. To them, the son born of oneself gives the inheritance (*riktha*); he has bestowed it. And he made her the vessel for depositing the embryo. Of the giver, the one who took her hand—when the mothers gave birth to the son as the bearer (*vahni*) and the woman as the non-bearer (*avahni*). One becomes the progenitor of the lineage, the male heir; the other, having been diminished, is given away to another as a *jāmi*.
The next twenty-five [constellations] are those named after humans.

Why "men" (*manuṣyāḥ*)? Because they sew together their actions after having reflected; they were created by one who reflects. The root *manasyati* refers to the state of being possessed of mind (*manasvin*). [They are] the offspring of Manu, or [descended] from Manu. Regarding this, there are Vedic citations (*nigama*) for the term *pañcajanāḥ* (the five peoples):
"May I today think the first thought of speech, by which we gods may overcome the Asuras.
O eaters of strength, worthy of sacrifice, you five peoples, enjoy my oblation! (RV 10.53.4)

"May I now consider that which is beyond speech, by which we gods may overcome the Asuras. The Asuras are so called because they have been cast away (*as-tāḥ*) from their positions, or rather, from their places (*sthānebhyaḥ*). Alternatively, *asu* is a name for breath; it resides within the body, and they possess it (*tena tadvantaḥ*). He created the gods from *su* (well-being); that is the "god-nature" (*suratva*) of the gods. He created the Asuras from *asu*; that is the "Asura-nature" (*asuratva*) of the Asuras. Thus it is known.

"Eaters of strength (*ūrj*), and worthy of sacrifice; eaters of food (*anna*) and worthy of sacrifice. *Ūrj* is a name for food, because it gives strength (*ūrjayati*). Or [it means] "well-cooked" and "well-cut. "O five peoples (*pañcajana*), enjoy my oblation!"—some say these are the Gandharvas, the Pitṛs, the Devas, the Asuras, and the Rakṣases. Aupamanyava says they are the four castes with the Niṣāda as the fifth. Why "Niṣāda"? Because he is one who sits down (*niṣadana*). The etymologists (*nairukta*) say: "In him evil is seated (*niṣaṇṇa*). "With the five-peopled clan (*viś*)" means with the clan belonging to the five peoples (*pañcajanīna*). "Five" is a distinct number.

It is common to females, males, and neuters. The following twelve are names of the arms. Why "bāhu"? Because one performs actions by means of them (*prabādhate*). The following twenty-two are names of the fingers. Why "aṅguli"? Because they go forward (*agragāminyaḥ*), or because they glide forward (*agragālinyaḥ*), or because they act at the front (*agrakāriṇyaḥ*), or because they move forward (*agrasāriṇyaḥ*), or because they mark (*aṅkanāḥ*), or because they bend (*añcanāḥ*), or perhaps simply because of their being anointed (*abhyañjanāt*). Of these, there is this verse: 8.
Sing praise to those who have ten guardians, ten girths, ten yokes, and ten harnesses;
to those with ten reins, who are ageless, and who carry ten loads as ten yoked steeds.

The *avanayaḥ* are the fingers; they advance (*avanti*) the actions. The *kakṣyāḥ* reveal the actions. The *yoktrāṇi* are explained as "bindings" (*yojanāni*). The *abhīśavaḥ* are those by which actions are directed toward (*abhyaśnuvate*). *Daśadhuraḥ* means "ten yokes" for those that carry while being harnessed. *Dhūr* comes from the root *dhurv*, meaning "to injure. This other [meaning of] *dhūr* also arises from this same root. It strikes down the carrying [burden]. Or it comes from the root *dhṛ*, "to support.
The eighteen subsequent verbal roots have the sense of "shining" (*kānti*).

The next twenty-eight [words] are names for food (*anna*). Why "food"? Because it is eaten by beings; or because it comes from the root *ad* (to eat). The ten subsequent verbal roots have the sense of eating. The next twenty-eight are names for strength (*bala*). Why "strength"? Because it bears a burden; from the root *bhṛ* (to bear). The next twenty-eight are names for wealth (*dhana*). Why "wealth"? Because it satisfies one who exists. The next nine are names for a cow (*go*).
The ten subsequent verbal roots have the sense of becoming angry.
There are eleven subsequent names for "anger.
There are one hundred and twenty-two subsequent elements (*dhātu*) whose function is motion.

There are twenty-six subsequent names for "quickly. Why "quickly"? Because the dragging away is abbreviated. There are eleven subsequent names for "near. Why "near"? Because it has been brought close. There are forty-six subsequent names for "battle" (*saṃgrāma*). Why "battle"? Because of coming together, or because of making an agreement, or because two villages have come together.
Regarding that, there are indeed these explanatory verses (*nigama*) for the word *khala*:
"I alone overcome this one; I alone overcome two. What can even three do?
Like a threshing-floor, I strike down the many. Why do the enemy, who are not Indra, revile me? I alone overcome this one; I am the one who overcomes.

I overcome my rivals. Why do two do this to me? Three! One is the number; two is the swifter number; three is the most transcendent number; four is the most moving number. Eight [comes] from the root *aś* (to pervade). Nine (*nava*) means "not desirable" (*na vananīya*), or "not reached" (*na āpta*). Ten (*daśa*) means "stretched out" (*dasta*), or "having seen the goal" (*dṛṣṭārtha*). Twenty (*viṃśati*) is two tens. A hundred (*śata*) is ten tens. A thousand (*sahasra*) is a thousandfold. Myriad (*ayuta*), million (*prayuta*), and ten million (*niyuta*) are each a tenfold repetition of the preceding.

*Arbuda* becomes *megha* (cloud). *Araṇa* means water; that [cloud] gives it. Or, it is called *ambuda* because it shines while possessing water (*ambumat*), or because it comes into being while possessing water. Just as it becomes great and vast when raining, so too is it called *arbuda*. "Upon the threshing floor (*khale*) I strike down many enemies (*parṣan*). As on a threshing floor, I strike down many enemies. *Khala* is a name for battle. It is derived either from the root *khal* (to crush) or *skhal* (to stumble). This other [worldly] threshing floor is also derived from this same root, for it is crowded together.

"Why do my enemies, who are not Indra, revile me? For they do not know Indra; for I am indeed Indra, while the others are non-Indras. Or [it means]: "The other ones are non-Indras. The next ten verbal roots have the sense of pervading (*vyāpti*). Among them, there are two names: *ākṣāṇaḥ* (the one who reaches) and *āśnuvānaḥ* (the one who attains); *āpānaḥ* (the one who obtains) and *āpnuvānaḥ* (the one who acquires). The next thirty-three verbal roots have the sense of killing (*vadhakarma*). Among them, the word *viyātaḥ* means "he causes to stretch out" (*viyātayati*), or "he stretches out" (*viyātayati*). "O Ākhaṇḍala, you are invoked!"
He is broken; he is shattered into pieces.
According to the rule *talid antike vadhau*, the object is compounded with the sense of proximity or destruction. From the root *tālayati* (to strike), [it means] "being present.
O Lord of Prayer (*brahmaṇaspati*), may we, through you, increase well and bestow desirable wealth upon men.
Those enemies of ours who are far away, and those who lie close at hand—crush them all, so that they have no wealth.

O Brahmaṇaspati, through you, our excellent nourisher, may we obtain from men those desirable riches—both those which are far away, like lightning (*talita*), and those which are near; whether they be enemies characterized by non-giving, or those whose intellect is set on non-giving. Crush them, the ones who possess no wealth (*anapnasaḥ*). *Apnas* is a name for form (*rūpa*); it is so called because one attains (*āpnoti*) it. Śākapūṇi says that *talit* becomes *vidyut* (lightning), for it causes one to tremble (*avalālayati*) and is seen even from afar. However, this might also be intended as a name for "nearness": "Even though far, you shine forth as if close at hand";
meaning, although you are far, you appear as if you were near.

The next eighteen [names] are names of Vajra. Why "Vajra"? Because he avoids (*varjayati*) what is existent (*sataḥ*). In that regard, the word *kutsa* comes from the root *kṛt* (to cut). Kutsa is a seer (*ṛṣi*); according to Aupamanyava, he is the maker of hymns (*stoma*). Furthermore, his function is indeed that of a slayer, as in: "Indra, the friend of that [Kutsa], slew Śuṣṇa.
The four subsequent verbal roots pertain to the functions of sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).
The next four [hymns] contain the names of Īśvara. In this regard, *it* (in) means "by means of sovereignty" (*aiśvaryeṇa*), or "by which sovereignty has been won" (*sanitam anena aiśvaryam*).
"Where the fair-winged ones, toward the portion of immortality, uninterruptedly sing toward the assemblies;
there the Lord, the guardian of the entire world, the wise one, has entered into me, the simple. (RV 10.121.1)

Wherein the *suparṇas*—the well-flying rays of the sun—[guard] the portion of immortality, that is, of water; they, being unblinking, either sing toward it through their knowledge, or they move toward it. Āditya is the lord, the protector of all beings. "May he, the wise one, enter me here as a child"—*dhīraḥ* means possessed of wisdom; *pākaḥ* means one who is to be matured; [thus] Āditya is one whose wisdom is fully ripened.

Such is the description of the Upaniṣad. This concludes the section concerning the deities (*adhidaivata*). Now, that which concerns the self (*adhyātma*): Wherein the well-flying senses—[which are] a portion of immortality and of knowledge—unwinking, either "sing toward" (*abhisvaranti*) by means of perception, or "move toward" (*abhiprayanti*). The Lord (*īśvara*) is the protector of all the senses, the Self (*ātman*). "May that wise one enter here into my ripeness" (*pāka*); "wise" (*dhīra*) means possessed of intelligence (*dhīmān*). "Ripeness" (*pāka*) is that which is to be matured; [thus] the Self is one whose wisdom is fully matured. Thus he declares the course of the Self. 12

The following twelve are names for "much" (*bahu*). Why "much"? Because it prevails over what exists. The following eleven are names for "short" (*hrasva*). "Short" (*hrasva*) is from the root *hras* (to diminish). The following twenty-five are names for "great" (*mahat*). Why "great"? Śākapūṇi says: because by its measure it leaves others behind; or, because it is worthy of being magnified (*maṃhanīya*). The words *bahu*, *vavakṣitha*, and *vivakṣase* are derived either from the root *vac* (to speak) or *vah* (to carry), with reduplication. The following twenty-two are names for "house" (*gṛha*). Why "house"? Because they receive (*gṛhṇanti*) the virtuous. The following ten roots denote the acts of service.

The next twenty terms are names for happiness (*sukha*). Why is it called "happiness"? Because it is well-satisfied (*suhita*) with respect to the voids (*kha*). Furthermore, the word *kha* is derived from the root *khan*. The next sixteen terms are names for form (*rūpa*). Form is derived from the root *ruc*. The next ten terms are names for that which is praiseworthy.
The next eleven terms are names for wisdom (*prajñā*).

The subsequent six [sections] concern names that are true (*satyanāman*). Why "true" (*satya*)? Because it extends (*tāyate*) toward the good (*satsu*), or because it originates from what is real (*sat*). The eight subsequent words are verbal roots whose action is "to see," beginning with *aya* and so forth; these names are unmixed.
There are ninety-nine words for the enumeration of all words.
Now, therefore, follow the similes.
Gārgya says that what is "that-not-that" (atattat) is "resembling that" (tatsadṛśa).
This is their function:
they compare a lesser or less renowned thing with a greater or more renowned thing by means of a quality;
or even, conversely, a greater thing with a lesser one. 13.
Like two thieves who have abandoned their bodies, seeking the forest, they are bound with ten cords.

"Body-protectors" (*tanūtyak*) means those who have abandoned their bodies. "Forest-goers" (*vanargū*) means those who go to the forest. He compares the two arms to thieves, for they are the churners of fire. According to the etymologists (*nairuktāḥ*), a "thief" (*taskaraḥ*) is so called because he performs that which is evil; or it may derive from the root *tan* (to stretch), meaning one whose actions are continuous, or whose actions pertain to day and night. They were bound with ten cords; that is, they were bound. In this context, the quality intended is strength. "Where indeed at night, where by day, O Aśvins? Where do you approach? Where have you dwelt?
Who has brought you to your dwelling-place, as a widow brings her brother-in-law, or as a young woman brings her husband? (Ṛgveda 1.34.7)

"Who are you two at night? Where are you by day? Where do you go? Where do you dwell? Who is it for you on the bed, like a widow for her brother-in-law? Why "brother-in-law" (*devara*)? He is called the second husband (*dvitīyo varaḥ*). A "widow" (*vidhavā*) is so called because she is one whose husband (*dhava*) has departed (*vidhātṛkā*), or from *vidhavana* (shaking), or from *vidhāvana* (running away)—so says Carmaśiras. Alternatively, *dhava* is a name for a man; she is a widow due to separation from him. *Devara* is derived from the root *div* (to play/shine). *Marya* means a human being, subject to the law of death (*maraṇadharmā*). *Yoṣā* comes from the root *yu* (to join).
He establishes himself in his dwelling place. Now, the particles have already been explained above. "Yathā" (as) is a comparison of action: as the wind, as the forest, as the ocean trembles.
Shining like fires.
The self perishes from consumption, like one who has seized a living being.

Or from "attaining" (āpti); or from "reaching" (āpti). Or rather, he may be like one who has reached [his goal]. As long as he has become all-pervasive. "Those whose chests are adorned with gold, brilliant like fire"—those who are brilliant like fire, whose chests are adorned with gold.
One should fear even four [dice] while they are being thrown, until they have been laid down.
One should not long for what is ill-spoken.

"O wise ones, hold him fast. Just as one would fear a gambler, so indeed should one fear ill-spoken words; one should never long for ill-spoken words. The prefix *ā* has already been explained above. Furthermore, it is seen in the sense of comparison, as in "the lover [attains] fortune" (*jāra ā bhagam*), meaning "like a lover, [he attains] fortune.
Here, the Sun is called the "lover" (*jāra*), the one who causes the night to age away; he is likewise the [lover] of the lights. To this effect there is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*).

"May the lover of our mother-in-law hear us"—thus he addresses the Dawn as his sister, either because of their constant association or because she carries away the essence (of things). Or rather, it may be intended that this refers to a human lover; in that case, the word *strībhaga* would apply [to the Dawn], derived from the root *bhaj*.
"The ram" (*meṣa*) is a comparison with a living being.
"Having become a ram, he advances.
*Meṣaḥ* is derived from the root *miṣati*; likewise, *paśuḥ* is derived from the root *paśyati*. "Agni" is a comparison based on form.
He is golden-hued, golden-eyed, the Son of the Waters;
indeed, he is golden-colored. His form is like that of one who is golden-colored—so it is said.
"Taṃ pratnathā pūrvathā viśvathemathā" means "as of old, as formerly, as universally, as now.

"Pratna iva, pūrva iva, viśva iva, ima iva" [is explained as follows]: "This one is more recent than that one; that one is more ancient than this one. "Amuthā" means "as that one"; this has been explained. "Vat" is a completed comparison, as in "like Brāhmaṇas, like Vṛṣalas. A Vṛṣala is one who has the character (*śīla*) of a bull (*vṛṣan*), or rather, one whose character is not that of a bull. 16
O Jātavedas, like Priyamedha, Atri, and Virūpa,
and like Aṅgiras, you whose vows are great, hear the invocation of Praskaṇva.

Priyamedha: his wisdom (*medhā*) is dear. Just as it was for these seers (*ṛṣi*), so hear the invocation of Praskaṇva. Praskaṇva is the son of Kaṇva; he originates from Kaṇva. As for "the tip": Bhr̥gu came into being in the flame; Bhr̥gu [is so called] because he was being broiled (*bhṛjyamāna*) in the body. Aṅgiras [was born] in the embers; embers are so called because they mark (*aṅkana*). Regarding this very point, they said, "Let him go to the third [state]," and thus he became Atri—not three (*na trayaḥ*). Vaikhānasa [is so called] from digging (*vikhanana*); Bhāradvāja from supporting (*bharaṇa*). Virūpa means having various forms (*nānārūpa*). Mahivrata means one of great vows (*mahāvrata*). 17.

Now, they call those [names] where the comparison is elided "Arthopamānas" (comparisons by meaning). "Lion" or "tiger" is used in a sense of praise; "dog" or "crow" is used in a sense of censure. "Crow" (*kāka*) is an imitation of its sound; this is common among birds. Aupamanyava says that there is no imitation of sound [in these cases]. A crow is so called because it is to be driven away (*apakālayitavya*). A partridge (*tittiri*) is so called because of its crossing (*taraṇa*), or perhaps because it is speckled like a sesame seed (*tila*). A *kapiñjala* is so called because it is worn out (*jīrṇa*) like a monkey (*kapi*), or because it moves (*javate*) like a monkey, or because it is slightly reddish-brown (*piṅgala*).

Or, it is called *piñjara* because it fans out (*piñjayati*) a desirable sound. A dog is *śvā* or *śuyāyī*; this is from the root *śū*, which denotes the act of moving, or from *śvas*. A lion is *siṃha* because of its power to endure (*sahanāt*), or it may be from the root *hiṃs*, in its reversed form, or from the root *han* preceded by the prefix *sam*. Or, it is called *siṃha* because it kills after having gathered together (*saṃhāya*). A tiger is *vyāghra* because it kills by opening wide (*vyāghrāṇāt*), or because it kills after having gaped (*vyādāya*).
The subsequent forty-four verbal roots denote the act of praising (*arcati*).

The next twenty-four [names] are those of the wise. Why "medhāvī" (wise)? Because he possesses *medhā* (wisdom). *Medhā* is placed in the mind (*mati*). The next thirteen are names of the praisers (*stotṛ*). A praiser (*stotṛ*) is so called because of praising (*stavana*). The next fifteen are names of sacrifice (*yajña*). Why "yajña"? The etymologists say it is because the act of sacrificing (*yajati*) is well-known. Or, it is because one becomes a petitioner (*yācña*). Or, it is because one becomes possessed of *yajus* verses. According to Aupamanyava, it is because he has many black antelope skins (*kṛṣṇājina*). Or, it is because the *yajus* verses lead him. The next eight are names of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Why "ṛtvik"? Because he is a mover (*īraṇaḥ*).

"Ṛg becomes *yaṣṭṛ*," says Śākapūṇi; or rather, "he becomes a performer of seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtuyājī*). The seventeen subsequent verbal roots have the sense of begging; the ten subsequent verbal roots have the sense of giving.
The four subsequent elements [of the suffix] are for the purpose of expressing the act of requesting (*adhyeṣaṇā*).
"He sleeps" (*svapiti*) and "he lies down" (*sasti*)—these two express the act of sleeping.

The fourteen subsequent items are names for a well (*kūpa*). Why "well"? Because drinking (*pāna*) occurs there, or because it comes from the root *kup*. The fourteen subsequent items are names for a thief (*stena*). Why "thief"?
"The etymologists [say] that it is called *saṃstyāna* because evil is condensed (*saṃstyāna*) within it.
The next six [words] have names that are determined or hidden.

The next five are names for "far" (*dūra*). Why "far"? Because it is "run away from" (*druta*) or "difficult to reach" (*duraya*). The next six are names for "ancient" (*purāṇa*). Why "ancient"? Because it was "new" (*nava*) in the past. The next six are names for "new. Why "new"? Because it has been "brought forth" (*ānīta*). 19.

The subsequent names are in pairs, twenty-six in total. "In *prapitve* [and] *abhīke*" refers to that which is near; *prapitve* means when [the time] has arrived, and *abhīke* means in close proximity. "Come quickly to us in *āpitve*, in *prapitve*;
even in *abhīke*, you are the creator of wide space."

There are also two Vedic citations: "dabhram" and "arbhakam" are words for the small. "Dabhram" is derived from the root *dabh* (to deceive or harm); it is very easily deceived. "Arbhakam" means that which has been diminished. [The mantras are: "Come close to me, do not touch me; do not think my things are small.
"Homage to the great ones, homage to the small ones."
Thus there are also two Vedic citations:
regarding the word *tiraḥ* as it occurs [in the text], it means "crossed over" (*tirastīrṇa*); regarding the word *sataḥ*, it means "spread out" (*saṃsṛta*).
"O invincible ones, come around with your wide-reaching course even across the desert."
Like a vessel, he goes about shattering the Rākṣasas.

There are also two Vedic citations: "tvo nema" refers to a half; "tvaḥ" means fallen away; "nemaḥ" means removed. "Ardham" [is derived] from the root *hṛ* (to carry) in its reverse sense, or it may be from *dhṛ* (to hold); it means that which has been set aside. Or it may be from *ṛdh* (to prosper); it is the most prosperous division. "One praises one, another reviles.
"Half are the gods, half are the asuras."
There are also two explanatory passages (*nigama*) regarding this:

"The *ṛkṣas* by means of the *stṛs*" refers to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). [The word] *nakṣatra* is derived from the root *nakṣ*, meaning "to move. And there is a Brāhmaṇa passage stating, "These are not *kṣatras* (protectors/rulers). They appear as if raised up (*udīrṇa*), like *ṛkṣas*; they appear as if strewn, like *stṛs*.
"These bears that are placed on high,
looking at heaven as it were with their stars"— there are also two such Vedic citations.

"By the ants, the *upajihvikā*"—this refers to the *sīmikā* (ants). They are called *vamrī* because of their vomiting (*vamanāt*). They are called *sīmikā* because of their creeping (*syamanāt*). They are called *upajihvikā* because they are to be smelled closely (*upajighryaḥ*). Regarding this, there are two Vedic citations (*nigama*): "The *upajihvikā* eats the son given by the ants, who do not give; when the ant creeps over him. Thus [the words] occur in the sacred texts.

*Ūrdara* and *kṛdara* are terms for a granary. *Ūrdara* is that which is opened wide (*uddīrṇa*); or rather, it is "opened wide" (*dīrṇa*) for the sake of nourishment (*ūrj*). Regarding this, there is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*): "Do not fill that *ūrdara* with barley. This means he fills it, as it were, with barley like an *ūrdara*. *Kṛdara* is that which has its opening made (*kṛtadara*).
"Kindled, he anoints the churner of prayers"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (Nigama).
*Rambha* and *pināka* are names for a staff (*daṇḍa*). They "take hold of" (*prārabhante*) it as *rambha*.
"Like an old man [clinging] to a staff, we have clung to you"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (*nigama*). "We take hold of you, as the aged [take hold of] a staff.
With this [staff], he crushes the *pināka* (the bow).
"Clad in a hide, with the Pināka bow in hand, and with his bow drawn"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (*nigama*).

*Menā* and *gnā* are [terms] for women. Women [are so called] from the root *styai*, which has the sense of the action of modesty (*apatrapaṇa*). They are *menāḥ* because they honor (*mānayanti*) them; they are *gnāḥ* because they go (*gacchanti*) toward them.
"Even these [beings] you brought forth from their birth;
the Gnas cut you out, the Apas stretched you out"— these two are also Vedic citations.
"Śepo vaitasaḥ" refers to the male organ. Śepaḥ is derived from the root *śap*, meaning "to touch.
Vaitasaḥ means "it extends for a span (*vitastam*). [As it is said: "In whom we, desiring, shall insert the phallus."
"Three times a day you have struck me with a reed"—
these two Vedic citations also exist.
This refers to the instruction regarding the *ayaina* sacrifice.
"May we worship you, O Agni, with this fuel"—thus for a woman.
"With this [oblation] I approach your Agni"—thus for a neuter.
"With this husband, unite your body."
Thus for a male.
"May he attend," "may he attend upon"—this is for one who serves. "May he who is swift attend us; may he who is swift serve us."
Be mindful of us for our well-being; attend to us for our well-being.
"Svasti" is a name for non-destruction. The root *as* is highly honored; thus, "su-asti" means "well-being.
The roots *bhyas* and *rej* signify fear and trembling, respectively.
"From whose fury the two worlds trembled, O Agni, and the earth shakes before his sacrificial rites"—
these are also two Vedic citations (nigamas).
The following twenty-four verses are names of Heaven and Earth.
Regarding these two, there is this [verse]: "Which of these two is the earlier, which the later? When they were born, O sages, who indeed knows?"
He sustains the universe by his own self; when the two days revolve like two wheels, they bear their name.

Which of these two is the former, and which is the latter? How were they born? Who among the poets truly knows them? They both sustain everything by themselves; whatever is their work, they both revolve. The two days—day and night—are like two wheels joined together. Thus he proclaims the greatness of Heaven and Earth. 22.

The names of actions are to be gathered; for the instructing bearer of the oblation is not to be seized, like a sister for her brother. Today, those names of men are for the ten lords of the earth; through you, we [attain] this, where the fair-winged ones [soar]. The many names are like those who abandon their bodies; wherever they are, like the Priyamedhas, they honor the fourfold [sacrifice]. Now, with ellipses of comparison, he worships them in pairs: "Which is the first?"—twenty-two [verses].
Thus ends the third chapter in the first six books of the Nirukta.
Now begins the fourth chapter.

It has been stated that there are multiple words with a single meaning; now we shall enumerate those single words with multiple meanings, as well as Vedic citations (*nigama*) whose grammatical refinements (*saṃskāra*) are not understood. These are called the *Aikapadika* (Single-Word Section).
As for "jahā," it means "having struck. 4.1 Who indeed, O mortal, being unprovoked, has spoken thus to a friend: "Who among us seeks to harm?"

*Maryā* is a name for humans; or it may be a designation for a boundary (*maryādā*). A boundary is the demarcation between those within the boundary and those outside. *Methati* is a verb whose function is to revile. "Who indeed has ever struck one who is sinless? "Who flees out of fear of us? "A snare becomes a trap. That which is laid down is a *nidhā*. A *pāśyā* is a collection of snares (*pāśa*). A *pāśa* comes from the root *pāśayati* (to bind). [From] "unbinding" [comes] *vipāśanāt*.
"The birds with beautiful wings, the Priyamedha seers, approached Indra while imploring him. (Ṛgveda 10.108.2)
Drive away the darkness, fill our eyes with light, and release us like those bound in a prison.

The word *vayaḥ* is a plural form of *vi*. The well-flying rays of the sun approached Indra, making a request: "Uncover the eye that has been cast down. The word *cakṣus* is derived either from the root *khyāti* (to perceive) or from *caṣṭe* (to see). [Fill it]—that is, make full, or give. Release us who are bound as if by snares—from the sides, from the hips, and from the head.

The *pārśva* (side) is a limb consisting of ribs (*parśu*). *Parśu* comes from the root *spr̥ś* (to touch); it is that which touches the region of the back. *Pṛṣṭha* (back) comes from the root *spr̥ś*; it is touched by the limbs. *Aṅga* (limb) comes from *aṅganā* (moving) or from *añcana* (bending). *Śroṇi* (hip/loins) comes from the root *śroṇati*, a verb denoting the act of moving; as one walks, the hip seems to move. *Doḥ* (arm) becomes *śitāma*. *Doḥ* comes from the root *dravati* (to run). Regarding *yoni*, Śākapūṇi says it becomes *śitāma*. It is *viṣita* (stretched out). Taiṭīki says *yakr̥t* (liver) becomes *śyāma*. *Śyāma* comes from the root *śyāyate* (to become dark).

Regarding the liver (*yakṛt*): Gālava says it is so called because it is "cut" (*kṛtyate*) in some way or another. As for *śitimāṃsa* (the dark-fleshed) and *medas* (fat): *śiti* comes from the root *śyai* (to congeal). *Māṃsa* is either from *māna* (measuring) or *mānasa* (belonging to the mind), or because the mind (*manas*) settles within it. *Medas* comes from the root *med* (to be fat).
"O Indra, whatever wonderful wealth there is of yours to bestow, O wielder of the stone, O possessor of riches, bring that to us with both hands. (RV 8.21.14)

"O Indra, whatever wealth there is that is worthy of admiration and worthy of honor—whether it be that which exists here for me or that which does not—" these are the three middle feet [of the verse]. "That must be given by you to us. "O wielder of the stone (adrivan). It is called *adri* because one crushes (*ādṛṇāti*) with it; or rather, it may be from the root *atti*, as it is known: "They eat the Soma (*somādaḥ*).
"Rādhaḥ" is a name for wealth, for they prosper (*rādhnuvanti*) by means of it. Therefore, you who possess both kinds of wealth, bring that to us with both hands. Both hands are closed together.

*Damūnā* means either "one who has a taming mind," or "one whose mind is inclined toward giving," or "one whose mind is subdued. Alternatively, *dama* is a name for the house; he may be one whose mind is fixed upon that. *Manas* comes from the root *man* (to think). "Welcome as the domestic friend, the guest in the home, come to this our sacrifice, O wise one!
Having struck down all assailants, O Agni, bring hither the possessions of those who act like enemies. (RV 1.1.5)

The ribs pain me on all sides like rival wives; the middle parts bite me like rats gnawing at unspun threads. Or rather, it may be a designation of one’s own limbs: they bite the *śiśnas*. My desires, O Śatakratu, torment me. O Dyāvāpṛthivī, you two know of this, my praiser, O Lord of a Hundred Powers! The ribs—meaning the ribs of the well—pain me on all sides like rival wives. Like rats, they gnaw at the unspun threads. Or it may be a designation of one’s own limbs: "they bite the *śiśnas*. My middle parts—meaning my desires—torment me. "O Śatakratu, [know] my praiser. "O Heaven and Earth, you two know of this for me."

This hymn appeared to Trita when he was cast down into a well. Therein it consists of a mixture of *brahman*, historical narratives (*itihāsa*), *ṛc* verses, and songs (*gāthā*). Trita was one who had crossed over most widely through his wisdom. Or rather, it may be intended as a mere enumeration of names: Ekata, Dvita, and Trita—thus there were three.
"May we partake of your pressed juice with an eager mind, like ancestral wealth.
O King Soma, prolong our lifespans, as the sun lengthens the days. (RV 8.48.3)

Whether by means of *īṣaṇa*, *vaiṣaṇa*, or *vārṣaṇa*, may we partake with our minds of this pressed [Soma], as if of ancestral wealth. And do thou, O King Soma, increase our lifespans, as the sun increases the days, the days that are *vesarāṇi*—meaning either "dwelling-places," "expellings," or "goings. [The forms] *kuratana*, *kartana*, *hantana*, and *yātana* are meaningless insertions (*upajana*). *Jaṭhara* means the belly; it is that in which what has been eaten (*jagdha*) is held or deposited.
"O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts, a bull for the battle, drink the Soma according to thy wont for exhilaration. (RV 3.47.1)
Pour the wave of honeyed juice into your own belly; you have been the king of the pressed juices from of old.

O Indra, accompanied by the Maruts and possessing those powers, you are the bull, the showerer of waters. Drink the Soma for the sake of the delightful battle; drink according to your wonted food, for exhilaration and for victory. Pour the wave of honey into your own belly—“honey” refers to Soma by way of metaphor, as it causes intoxication; this other [common] honey is derived from the same root. You are the king even over the Soma-pressings of former days. 4.8 *Titau* is a filter; it is so called because it is stretched (*tata*) or because it is new (*tnava*), or because it is pressed down to the size of a sesame seed (*tila*). 4.9
Where the wise have fashioned speech with their mind, purifying it like groats through a sieve—there friends recognize their friendships; auspicious is the mark placed upon their speech.

"Like winnowing grain with a fan, they purify it. *Saktu* comes from the root *sac*; it is difficult to winnow. Or it may come from the root *kas* in its reverse form; it becomes scattered. "Where the wise have drawn forth speech with their mind, [that is] wisdom (*prajñāna*). The wise are those possessed of wisdom, possessed of meditation (*dhyāna*). There, as friends, they recognize their friendships. "Auspicious is their mark placed upon their speech. *Bhadra* has been explained by means of *bhaga*. It is that which is to be enjoyed and that which is to be approached by living beings.

Or [the word *lakṣmī*] may mean "she who delights beings. Or it is like a vessel (*bhājana*). It may come from *lakṣ*, meaning "attainment" (*lābha*), or from *lakṣaṇa*, "marking," or from *lāñchana*, "branding. Or it may derive from the root *laṣ*, in the sense of "desiring to obtain" (*prepsā-karman*); or from *lag*, in the sense of "embracing" (*āśleṣa-karman*); or from *lajj*, in the sense of "lack of praise" (*aślāghā-karman*). We shall explain the word *śipre* later on. That is the divinity of the Sun, that is his majesty: in the midst of his work, he has gathered together what was spread out.
When he has unyoked his bay steeds from the sixth [station], then Night spreads her garment over all.

That is the divinity of the Sun, that is his greatness, that while deeds are being performed, he who is spread out is withdrawn in the midst of them. When he has yoked the carriers—the rays of the Sun—or, as it were, the bay horses—then Night spreads her garment for everyone; she, the dawn, withdraws the day from all. Or perhaps it may be used in a comparative sense: "as Night spreads her garment. Even so there is a Vedic verse: "She weaves it out again, spreading it together; she has gathered it from every side. (RV 4.11)
For you shall be seen united with Indra, who is fearless; both of you are joyful and equal in splendor.

For you are seen by Indra as he comes together with his fearless host—you two are exhilarated and intoxicating; or perhaps it may be "with that exhilarating one. This has been explained by the phrase "of equal splendor" (4.12).
"With their limbs at the ends, slender in the middle, well-formed, divine coursers."

Like swans, they strive in rows when the horses have reached the divine course. Their ends are smooth, their ends are stirred, or their ends are broad; their middles are compact, or their middles are joined together, or their middles are heads. Moreover, the sun is the head, because it lies over all beings and stands in their midst. This other [physical] head also comes from that very same source; the senses are supported upon it. They are "conquerors" (*saṃśūraṇāsaḥ*); *śūra* is derived from the root *śavati*, meaning "to go."

Divine, born of heaven; swift, they are the extenders. Like swans, they strive in rows. "Swans" (haṃsāḥ) [is derived] from the root *han*, for they traverse the path; "row" (śreṇiḥ) [is derived] from the root *śri*, for they become closely joined together. When they have impelled, when they have reached—the divine course, the birth, the race—[so do] the horses.
There is a praise of the horse as being of the nature of Āditya: "The horse was fashioned from Āditya.
There is also this Vedic verse (nigama): "The Vasus fashioned the horse from the Sun.
4.13 "When you, longing for the woods, went to your mothers, the waters."
O Agni, that return of yours is not to be forgotten, since you, though far away, have become present here.

Whether he is being measured, being honored, or desiring; [he approaches] the forests. When you went to your mothers, the waters, becoming tranquil, that turning back of yours, O Agni, is not forgotten—since you, though far away, become present here as soon as you are born.
They lead him away like a beast, thinking him to be Lodha.

They lead away the greedy seer, regarding him as a sacrificial animal—him who is sharp and possesses the brilliance of fire, whose radiance is purifying; or rather, one who lies along [the path], or one who consumes.
Like two pupils in an unblemished, new, small wooden bowl.
The two tawny ones shine in their journeys.

"Kanīnake" means "two girls. A girl (*kanyā*) is so called because she is desirable (*kamanīyā*). Or perhaps it comes from the root *kan*, meaning "to shine," as in the thought, "Where is she to be led? These are designations for the two bases [of the eyes]. Śākapūṇi says they are locative singular forms. They refer to two wooden blocks (*dārupādvaḥ*) that have lost their original form. "Dāru" comes from the root *dṛ* (to split) or from *drū* (to run); hence it is also called *dru*. "Nave" means newly born; "arbhake" means small or undeveloped. Just as those two shine upon their respective bases, so do the two brown ones (*babhrū*) shine during the journeys. This is a praise of the two brown horses.
"This he gave to me, and this he gave to me"—thus the seer spoke after reflecting.
"Suvāstu upon the ford. Suvāstu is a river; *tugva* means a ford, for they cross over it quickly.
The Maruts bend down for us again; the Maruts bend down for us again. We shall explain the word *nasanta* later on.
O Indra, with those exhilarating drinks of yours that are impetuous and far-reaching, urge Indra to grant us wealth.
With those exhilarations of yours that are striking and deceptive, urge Indra on to bestow wealth.
The breast of the pure one has been seen; like Nodhas, she has revealed her dear secrets.
Having settled at the place of eating, awakening us, she has come again as the most constant among the long-lived ones.

The *śundhyu* was displayed. The *śundhyu* is the sun, because of its purifying (*śodhana*) nature. Its breast is the sky (*adhyūḍham*), for this other breast [of the dawn] is likewise supported upon it. A bird is also called *śundhyu*, precisely because of its purifying nature; it moves in the water. The waters also are called *śundhyu*, precisely because of their purifying nature. Nodhas is the name of a seer (*ṛṣi*); he bestows newness (*navanam dadhāti*). Just as he makes his desires manifest through praise, so does Uṣas make her forms manifest. She is *admásat*; *adma* is food, or she is "one who sits at the food" (*admásadinī*), or "one who wins food" (*adyasāninī*).
Awakening those who sleep, she has come again as the most constant of those who return repeatedly; she has come again as the most eternal of those who return repeatedly.
They are armed with axes and are impetuous—whether called *īṣiṇaḥ*, or *vaiṣiṇaḥ*, or *ārṣiṇaḥ*. "Vāśī" is a name for speech; they are true because they speak (*vāśyate*).

"Recite, O Adhvaryu! Respond to me! Let us both prepare an acceptable offering for Indra. They consider this to be a praise directed toward the pressing-stones (*abhiṣavaṇa*) and their proclamation; however, it is specifically praised as being addressed to Indra. We shall explain the word *paritakmyā* later. (4.16) *Suvite*: well-gone, well-traversed, or well-faring; or else, "in offspring. "Place me in the *suvita*," so also occurs in a Vedic citation (*nigama*).
*dayati* has many meanings:
"May we be compassionate toward [others] with our new [wealth]"—thus it has the sense of compassion (*dayā*).
"He alone who bestows wealth"—thus it has the sense of giving (*dāna*) or distribution (*vibhāga*).
"The terrible one with evil courses consumes the forests"—this refers to the act of burning. "Evil-coursing" means difficult to restrain.
"The possessor of wealth, destroying the enemies"—this refers to the act of harming.
These Soma drops have been pressed; O Aśvins, you who travel at dawn, drink them together in harmony!
For I have awakened you both for protection and for praise, as the bird, crying out in the darkness, rouses me.
Regarding the word *dayamāna*: *nū cid* is a particle used for both the old and the new forms; it is also [used] with *ca*. [Examples include: *adyā cin nū cit tad apo nadīnām*.
The same is the work of the rivers, both now and of old;
the abode of riches, both now and of old—the abode of riches, both now and of old. "Riches" (rayi) is a name for wealth.
May we know this of you, the boundless one, for the granting of that gift which is the act of bestowing.

May we know that gift of yours which is unfailing (*akūpāra*). The Āditya is also called *akūpāra*; he is *akūpāra* because his further shore (*pāra*) is distant. The ocean is also called *akūpāra*; it is *akūpāra* because its further shore is great. A tortoise is also called *akūpāra*; *akūpāra* means "it does not reach a well" (*kūpa*); a tortoise protects the marsh (*kaccha*), or it protects by means of the marsh, or it drinks by means of the marsh. *Kaccha* is *khaccha*, meaning "clear" (*khacchada*). This other [word for] a river-marsch (*nadī-kaccha*) is derived from this very same root.

Kam is water; by it [the world] is covered. *Śiśīte śṛṅge rakṣase vinikṣe*: he sharpens his two horns for the purpose of piercing the demon. *Rakṣaḥ* means that which is to be protected from; or, it pierces in secret (*rahasi kṣaṇoti*); or, it perishes at night (*rātrau nakṣate*).
Agni is swift with his swift horses.

"May they be well-born with those who are well-born," or "may they be of good offspring with those of good offspring"; "may they, being easy of access, spread out at this sacrifice," meaning "having a good way of proceeding. 4.18
May the gods always be present for our prosperity, our protectors day after day,
never failing, never negligent. May the gods always be there for our growth, our protectors, day by day, never failing, never heedless.
The seer Cyavana is one who causes the hymns to move;
there are also Vedic citations (nigamas) concerning him that call him "Cyavāna":
"O you two, you fashioned Cyavana, who was like an old chariot, into a youth again for the sake of movement."

"You two fashioned Cyavana—the ancient, the one from of old—like a chariot, making him young again for the sake of movement. The root *yu* means "to join" (*prayauti*); the root *takṣ* has the sense of "to do" (*karoti*). *Rajas* comes from the root *rañj*. Light is called *rajas*; water is called *rajas*; the worlds are called *rajāṃsi*; blood and the two eyes are called *rajasī*. There is also a Vedic verse (nigama) that says: "The brilliant, thundering [clouds] move through the various *rajāṃsi*. *Hara* comes from the root *hṛ*. Light is called *hara*; water is called *hara*; the worlds are called *harāṃsi*; blood and the two eyes are called *harasī*.
"O Agni, with your heat, burn; crush [the enemy]!"—thus also there is a Vedic verse.
"They have offered, discerning"; "they have offered, becoming conscious.
The root *vi-ant* has many meanings.
"Entering with reverence the station of the god"—this refers to the action of seeing.

"O hero, enjoy the sacrificial cake"—this refers to the action of eating. "Enjoy and drink of the milk of the cow; eat and drink of the milk of the cow. *Usriyā* is a name for a cow. Her enjoyments flow forth (*usrāvin*); and [the word] *usra* [is also used].
O Indra, with hymns at the pressing of the juice, those seeking wealth and providing good guidance have celebrated you, having prepared the offering with milk.
They have offered praise while fashioning [the soma] with the rays of light.

Pour forth the golden-hued [soma] into the lap of the wooden vessel; fashion it with stone-made axes. Pour forth the golden-hued one into the lap of the wooden vessel—that is, into that which is made of wood. Soma is golden-hued (*hari*); this other [meaning of *hari*] also derives from this very root. Fashion it with stone-made axes—or rather, with axes made of stone; or perhaps with words (*vāgbhiḥ*).
May he be bold against the man who is treacherous; may those who worship the phallus not attain our truth.

May he prevail over the man who is treacherous, the malicious one; may those who worship the phallus, lacking self-restraint, not reach us. He pierces the phallus; may they not attain our truth—our truth being either reality or sacrifice.
Indeed, those later ages shall surely come when kinsmen shall commit acts unbecoming to kin.
Place your arm around another man as a bull; O fortunate one, seek someone other than me as your husband.

Those future ages will come when sisters shall perform the acts of non-sisters; "sister" (*jāmi*) is a name for redundancy, or for the offspring of a fool, or for the birth of one of the same lineage. "Lay your arm around the bull; seek another husband, O fortunate one, me!"—this has been explained.
Heaven is my father, my progenitor; there is my navel. This great earth is my kin, my mother.
Between the two upturned bowls (the heaven and earth) is the womb; therein the father deposited the embryo of his daughter.

Heaven is my father—my protector, or rather, my guardian and progenitor. Here, this great earth is my mother, my kinsman (*bandhu*). She is called *bandhu* because she binds (*bandhana*) [us to her]; she is called *nābhi* because she connects (*sannahana*). From the *nābhi* (the navel), embryos are joined and born; so they say. For this very reason, they call one's own people "those who share the same navel" (*sanābhayaḥ*) and "those who share the same bond" (*sabandhavaḥ*). A kinsman (*jñāti*) is so called because of their mutual recognition (*saṃjñāna*). Within the two upturned vessels is the womb.

"Ut-tāna" means stretched out; or rather, one who is stretched upwards. Therein, the father—Parjanya—places the embryo within the daughter—the earth. "Śaṃyu" means possessing happiness. Thus, "bestow upon us well-being and freedom from harm. "Rapas" and "ripra" are both names for evil. [It means] the allaying of diseases and the warding off of fears. Furthermore, Śaṃyu is said to be the son of Bṛhaspati. Therefore:
"We choose that path of Śaṃyu, the way for the sacrifice, the way for the performance of the sacrifice."
Thus also there is a Vedic verse: "The going is for the sacrifice, the going is for the lord of the sacrifice.
(4.21) Aditi, the undecaying mother of the gods; (4.22) Aditi is heaven, Aditi is the mid-air, Aditi is the mother, she is the father, she is the son.
The All-Gods are Aditi, the five peoples are Aditi; Aditi is what has been born, and Aditi is what is yet to be born.
Thus he describes the manifestation (*vibhūti*) of Aditi; or, "these [worlds] belong to Aditi. Regarding *yameḥ* [in *yamerire*], the Bhṛgus have recited it.
And indeed, as they pursue him like a thief who has stripped away a garment, the people cry out after him in battles;
he, though appearing lowly and exhausted like a falcon, hastens toward fame and toward the herd of cattle.

"Is he not like a *vastramathin*, a 'clothes-stealer'—*vastra* being derived from the root *vas* (to wear)—a thief (*tāyu*), according to the etymologists, so called because evil is gathered (*saṃstyāna*) within him? Or it may be from the root *tan* (to stretch). The people lament for him in battles; *bhara* is a name for battle, derived either from the root *bhr* (to carry) or *hṛ* (to seize). He is 'going low,' moving downward;
he is 'collected low,' while he is 'collected high. Like a hawk that has swooped down."

The hawk goes toward that which is worthy of praise, and toward glory accompanied by cattle—a herd, namely glory accompanied by cattle; both praise and the herd, or wealth and the herd. "Herd" (*yūtha*) comes from the root *yu* ("to join"); it is that which is joined together. The pious man, kindling him, praises him with a well-disposed mind;
he sings. "Mandī" [is derived] from the root *mand*, meaning "to praise.
"Sing forth a word full of nourishment for the gladdened one; sing forth a word full of nourishment for the gladdened one."
"Gau" has thus been explained (4.24). Here he says: "The name of Tvaṣṭṛ, which is hidden even from thought, is here indeed in the dwelling of the moon."

In this regard, the rays of the sun considered the name of the cow (*go*) to be their own: *apīcyam*, meaning diminished (*apacitam*), gone away (*apagatam*), covered over (*apihitam*), or hidden (*antarhitam*) there in the abode of the moon.
The word *gātu* has been explained. There is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) which says: "May they create a path (*gātum*) for the people at dawn."
*Daṃsayaḥ* means deeds; they cause these to be seen.
"The *daṃsayaḥ* for Kutsa and for Manu" — such also is a Vedic verse (*nigama*).
"He has grown strong; no affliction reaches him."

He praised him; distress does not reach him. *Aṃhati*, *aṃhaḥ*, and *āṃhuḥ* are derived from the root *han* (to strike). They are formed with the prefix *ni* elided and the suffix *upa* changed. From the opposite [of non-distress]. "O Bṛhaspati, you strike down the one who hates" (*piyāru*). "O Bṛhaspati, you drive away the one who reviles the gods" (*devapīyu*). *Pīyati* is a verb meaning "to injure. He separates heaven and earth. From the act of separating (*viyavana*).
"Separated from the common [state], at a distance and an end.

"Common" (*samāna*) means merely equal (*sammāna*). "Mātrā" is derived from "measure" (*māna*). "Distance" (*dūra*) has already been explained. "End" (*anta*) is that which is extended (*atata*). "Ṛdhak" is a term used to express separation. Furthermore, it is also seen in the sense of "to prosper" (*ṛdhnoti*): "You have prospered separately; you have sacrificed separately."

"Thou hast prospered; thou hast prospered," and "thou hast performed the sacrifice. In the case of *asyāḥ* and *asya*, when used as a first mention (*prathamādeśa*), the accent is udātta; in the case of a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*), it is anudātta. The udātta is for a more intense meaning, while the anudātta is for a lesser meaning. "O thou who art rich in goats, come hither for our gain, being ungrudging, O giver of wealth!

O thou who art rich in goats, [come] for those seeking glory! Be present for this our gain, being ungrudging—that is, not angry—being a giver. 'Giver' (*rarivān*) is the reduplicated form of 'giving' (*rāti*). By 'rich in goats,' he refers to Pūṣan. 'Rich in goats' means having goats as his people (*ajā ajanāḥ*)."
Now follows the unaccented portion: "May he who is her husband live a long life for a hundred autumns;
may he who is her husband live a long life for a hundred autumns. The herbs become ripe in autumn, or rather, the waters have ripened.
The word "asya" (of him) is explained by the word "asyāḥ" (of her). 4.25:
Of this lovely, gray-haired Hotṛ-priest, there is a middle brother who is voracious;
his third brother has ghee upon his back. Here I beheld the Lord of the People, who has seven sons.

Of this lovely one, worthy of being sought after; of the gray-haired one, the protector; of the Hotṛ, the one to be invoked—his middle brother is Aśana. [He is called] *bhrātṛ* from the root *bhṛ*, meaning "to carry"; he carries his portion, or rather, he is to be supported. The third brother is Ghṛtapṛṣṭha, who is this Agni here. There I beheld the protector or guardian of all, the Lord of the People (*viśpati*), the one with seven sons—that is, the one whose seventh son is the serpent—or else, "seven" is a number of those who have crept forth.
They say there are seven rays of the sun. 4.26
Seven yoke the chariot that has a single wheel; a single horse, bearing seven names, draws it.
The wheel has three naves, is ageless, and is manly; upon it all these worlds stand.

Seven harness the chariot that has one wheel and moves alone. The word *cakra* comes from the root *cak* (to shine), or from *car* (to move), or from *kram* (to stride). A single horse draws it; he who has seven names is the Āditya. Seven rays direct juices toward him, or seven ṛṣis praise him—so it is said. This other [word] *saptanāman* likewise comes from this same [root], from *abhisannāma* (directing together). The latter half-verse has the year as its primary subject: "The wheel has three naves. The year consists of three seasons: summer, the rainy season, and winter.

The *saṃvatsara* (year) is so called because living beings dwell together (*saṃvasante*) in it. *Grīṣma* (summer) is so called because the vital juices (*rasāḥ*) are swallowed up (*grasyante*) in it. *Varṣā* (the rainy season) is so called because Parjanya rains upon them. *Hemanta* (winter) is so called because it possesses frost (*himavān*). Furthermore, *hima* (frost) is derived either from the root *han* (to strike) or from the root *hi* (to impel). *Ajaram* means that which has the nature of being ageless. *Anarvam* means unopposed or unrivalled by anything else. In that [year], all these beings come together and rest; he praises that year with its various measures. "In the five-spoked wheel as it revolves"—this refers to the five seasons.
"There are five seasons of the year," so says the Brāhmaṇa. By combining the winter and the cool season, they say there are six seasons established.
Thus by way of the six seasons; the spokes are fixed in the hub according to the seasons. Furthermore, "six" is from the root *sah* (to endure).
"The twelve-spoked wheel does not decay"—there is one wheel with twelve felloes.
Thus regarding the months. "The months [are so called] because of measuring. The rim is firmly fixed; upon it thirty spokes are set together, and sixty unswerving linchpins.
Indeed, there are three hundred and sixty days and nights in a year;
such is the Brāhmaṇa in brief.
Seven hundred and twenty remained.
Indeed, seven hundred and twenty are the days and nights of the year; thus says the Brāhmaṇa in its various divisions. 4.27

"Of one purpose are these birds of fair wings; since Indra is pleased, he is the master of the house. They have heated me with fervor, O Marut-possessor; they cling to me like parched grain in a sieve. With Indra, the winds are united, striving for the body; like two pupils, they are seen near at hand. May we find the gods in prosperity! Aditi is my heaven, Aditi is the earth; may she protect us from this lovely one. Seven harness the seven-and-twenty.
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the first hexad of the *Nirukta*. Now begins the fifth chapter.
He found the giver at the crossing of the rivers; he found the giver, the cloud that has been well-bathed.
The most effective hymn among invocations is the messenger calling you two heroes;

the hymn, the best carrier of invocations, is the messenger calling the two heroes. Heroes—men—dance in their deeds. "Messenger" is derived from *javati* (to hasten), or *dravati* (to run), or *vārayati* (to ward off).

"You are the messenger of the gods among mortals"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (*nigama*). "Bellowing" (*vāvaśānaḥ*) is derived either from the root *vaṣṭi* or from *vāśyati*. "Bellowing toward the seven ruddy sisters"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse.
"Worthy of choice" (*vāryam*) is from the root *vṛṇoti*. And also "most excellent" (*varatamam*). "That worthy-of-choice we choose, the most excellent protector"—[so it is said].
We choose that desirable thing; the most excellent thing to be protected. You are the protectors—or [the phrase may mean] "for you.
*Andhas* is a name for food; it is that which is to be meditated upon.
"With the vessels, pour out the exhilarating food (*andhas*)."

"Let them pour intoxicating liquor here into the *amatra*. *Amatra* means a vessel; they rejoice in it together (*amā*). Furthermore, it is unconstructed (*anirmita*). It is called a *pātra* because of drinking. Darkness (*tamas*) is also called *andha*. In it there is neither meditation nor vision; they speak of it as "blind darkness" (*andhatamas*). This other [meaning of] *andha* also derives from this very same root.
There is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*): "Let the one with eyes see, for the blind does not perceive. (5.1)
"Unceasing, with many streams, full of water"—or "not clinging," or "not casting away. [The two] have many streams and possess water.
The root *vanuṣyati* has the sense of "killing. It remains an ununderstood formation (*anavagata-saṃskāra*).
"May we overcome those who attack us. Thus also occurs a Vedic verse (*nigama*).

"He who attacks the one whose sacrifice is long-extended—may we conquer that evil-minded one in battles. He who seeks to strike down the one whose sacrifice is long-protracted—may we conquer him in battles. "Evil-minded" (*dūḍhya*) means one of wicked intellect, one of sinful intellect. "Sinful" (*pāpa*) refers to one who drinks what should not be drunk; or, "sinning," he falls downward; or it may be derived from the root *pāpaty*. The verb *taruṣyati* has the same meaning: "With Indra as our ally, may we overcome Vṛtra."
Thus there is also a Vedic citation: "Mandana is from the root *bhand*, meaning 'to praise.
'The much-beloved sage Bhandanādhāman praises'—thus there is also a Vedic citation.
And: 'He, through his praising, raises up [the cows] rich in offspring.'"

"Go quickly by another way, O burner! Go swiftly by another way, O burner!"—by speaking thus as if addressing someone with "burner," it becomes an improper speech; therefore, he should be called *āhana*. The seer is a river (*nada*); [the word comes] from the root *nad*, meaning "to praise.
"The desire of the obstructing river has come upon me."
"Desire has come upon me, who am crying out and being obstructed; upon me, whose procreative power is blocked, a celibate student. Thus they report the lamentation of the seer’s daughter (5.2).
"Soma has flowed, for whom neither heaven and earth, nor the desert, nor the mid-air, nor the mountains could contain him.
Some say [the word] is derived from the root *aś* (to reach).
"In the marshy land, the owner of cattle dwells with his cattle; Soma flows for those who have milked.
"The hyena devours the lion as he comes toward it.

Regarding the word *kṣiyati*, some say the former [example] is a citation of usage (*nigama*) for the sense of "dwelling" (*kṣi*), while the latter is a citation of usage for the sense of "flowing" (*kṣar*). "When the owner of cattle dwells in the marshy land with his cattle, then Soma flows for those who have milked," so it is said. Śākapūṇi, however, maintains that all citations of usage for *kṣiyati* refer to the sense of "dwelling."

*Śvātram* is a name for "quickly. It means "it extends swiftly. That which is winged, that which is swift, that which is stationary, and that which is moving—whatever is quick, Agni Jātavedas has made it so. *Ūtiḥ* means protection from distress.
"Come to us like a chariot for our aid"—thus there is also a Vedic verse (nigama).
We shall explain the word *hāsamāne* later on.
"The ant (*vamraka*) crept up to Indra with its feet."
Or by drinks, or by spies—
he found him, the pure one, like ripe grain.
This is the dream-like, intermediate light, whose appearance is transient.
He perceived that very [reality] as blazing intensely;
and Śambhu is existence in two ways, both through his own power (svadhā) and through his inherent nature.
Existence is twofold, in the middle station and in the highest station; Śambhu is the source of bliss.
They seek him like a herd seeks a deer;
the *praiṣas* (calls) are like hunters seeking a deer. 5.3 The cloud becomes a boar; it is the food of the boar.
"You have eaten the best food," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"He pierced the boar through the rock," such also is a Vedic verse (nigama).

This other [meaning of] *varāha* is derived from this very same [root]. "It digs up roots"—either meaning "it digs up the best root" or "it digs up large roots. "O Indra, the boar who steals [the grain]," such also is a Vedic verse.
The Aṅgirasas are also called boars;
[it says] "Brahmaṇaspati with the bulls, the boars.
Furthermore, these middle groups of gods are also called boars.

Beholding the golden-wheeled boars with tusks as they run about, the days become *svasarāṇi*; or rather, they are themselves *sārīṇi*. The Sun (*svar*) is he who causes these to move (*sārayati*). "Like the rays of light, the *svasarāṇi*," so also there is a Vedic verse (*nigama*).
The singers of the Gāyatrī hymns sing to you; those who recite the Ṛks praise you with Ṛks.
O Śatakratu, the Brahmans have raised you up as one would a sacrificial post.

The singers of the *gāyatrī* chant to you; the reciters of the *ṛk* praise your *ṛk*. O Lord of a hundred powers (*śatakratu*), the priests have raised you up like a pole. A pole (*vaṃśa*) is so called because it lies in the forest (*vanaśaya*), or perhaps because it is heard from the forest (*vananāt*).
The felly (*pavī*) is the rim of a chariot wheel, for it purifies (*vipunāti*) the earth. And with the felly of the chariots, they split the mountain by their might.

"The Maruts struck him with their razor-edged thunderbolts. There are also two such Vedic citations (*nigama*). "Vakṣas" has been explained. "Dhanvan" is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); from it the waters flow forth.
"It shines across the bow," so also says a Vedic verse (*nigama*).
"Sinam" means food; it binds all beings.
"With which you bring sustenance for your friends," so also says a Vedic verse.
By this, "itthāmuthā" is explained.
"Sacā" means "together with. "Vasubhiḥ sacā bhuvā" means "being together with the Vasus," that is, being together with the Vasus.

The particle *cit* is unaccented (*anudātta*); it has already been explained above. However, here it occurs as accented (*udātta*) when it is a name for cattle: *cid asi manāsi*, "Thou art conscious, thou art mindful"; or, "enjoyments are known through thee. Or [it means] "thou perceivest. The prefix *ā*—the vowel *ā*—has already been explained above. Furthermore, it is seen in the sense of "above" (*adhi*): *abhra ām̐ apaḥ*, "the waters are upon the cloud," meaning "the waters are over the cloud. *Dyumna* is from the root *dyut* (to shine). It means either glory or food.
Bestow upon us splendor and treasure; bestow upon us both splendor and treasure.
5.5 *Pavitra* is derived from the root *pū* (to purify). A mantra is called *pavitra*;
for there is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) which says: "By means of which *pavitra*, the gods always purify themselves."
The rays are called the purifier; there is also a Vedic verse (nigama) that says: "Purified by the hands, pressed by men with stones. Water is also called the purifier.
Having a hundred purifiers, rejoicing with their own call, possessing abundant waters—Agni is called the purifier;
Vāyu is called the purifier; Soma is called the purifier; Sūrya is called the purifier; Indra is called the purifier. May Agni, the purifier, purify me; may Vāyu, Soma, Sūrya, and Indra [purify me].
"May the purifiers purify thee. Thus also there is a Vedic verse (nigama).
Like the shelter of a great hunter's arrow.
I, having given much, invoke you alone. *Ari* means enemy (*amitra*), from the root *ṛcchati*.

*Īśvara* also [derives] from this very same [root]. Having observed that oblations intended for other deities are offered into Agni, one might say this: "In the shelter of the great *todas*, as if in the shelter of the great *tudasya*. *Svañcaḥ* means he who moves beautifully.
"Pouring oblations, he whose back is glistening with clarified butter, moving with ease"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (*nigama*).

"Śipiviṣṭa" and "Viṣṇu" are two names of Viṣṇu. According to Aupamanyava, the former has a deprecatory sense. "O Viṣṇu, what was there to be concealed from you, that you declared, 'I am Śipiviṣṭa'? (RV 7.99.6).
Do not conceal this form from us, that you appeared in another guise during the encounter.

"O Viṣṇu, what is this that is unknown to you? It is something not to be made known, since you say, 'I am shrouded like a phallus,' while failing to grasp the reins.
