Or perhaps it is only praise that is intended: O Viṣṇu, what is this that is well-known to you? It is something to be made known, namely when you say, 'I am Śipiviṣṭa,' having grasped the reins."

"Śipayaḥ" here refers to the rays; he becomes possessed by them. "Mā varpo asmad apa gūha etat"—*varpas* is a name for form (*rūpa*), so called because it covers (*vṛṇoti*). When you appear in another form in battle, in the conflict, with your rays withdrawn. The following verse is for a more extensive explanation:
**5.8** O Śipiviṣṭa, today I proclaim your noble name, I who know the sacred ordinances (*vayunāni*).
I sing of you, the powerful one, who surpasses those lacking power, dwelling in the far distance of this world-space.

Therefore, O Śipiviṣṭa, I, being noble, praise that name of yours today; for I am noble, the lord of hymns, and you are noble—or rather, "you are noble. I praise you, the powerful one, who are beyond the reach of the powerless. "Tavasa" is a name for the Great One. He is praised as being beyond this world, in the distance, in the transcendent realm. "Āghṛṇi" means one whose wrath has come forth;

"ā ghṛṇe saṃ saṃcāvahai" means "O you of wrathful aspect, let us two come together in harmony"; "āgatahṛṇe saṃsevāvahai" means "O you whose wrath has arrived, let us two serve together. "Pṛthujrayas" means one of wide-reaching speed.

With his wide-reaching course, he has shortened the life of the Dasyu; he has caused the life of the Dasyu to perish. (5.9) The men, with their prayers and the movement of their hands, have generated from the two fire-sticks the praiseworthy Agni—the far-seeing, the lord of the house, the active one.

The fingers are the rays; they are placed in the ritual acts. These two [the fire-drills] are turned toward the fire, or rather, it is born from their friction. By the movement of the hands, by the motion of the hands, they have generated the praiseworthy one, visible from afar, the lord of the house, the mindful one. With a single stroke, Indra drank at once thirty lakes of Soma, out of his desire for it.

He drank with a single draught; "sākam" means together. Indra [drank] of the soma's *kāṇukā*. This means either "the desirable ones," or "the traversed ones," or "the prepared ones"; or it means "Indra is the desirer of the soma. Or it means "a blow to the joints" (*kaṇeghāta*); that is, struck in the joints, or struck by desire (*kānti*).

Regarding this, the ritualists declare: "In the midday pressing, there are thirty *uktha*-vessels dedicated to a single deity; they drink from these at this time by means of a single setting down (*pratidhāna*). These are here called "lakes" (*sarāṃsi*). "There are thirty days and nights of the waning half-month, and thirty of the waxing half-month," say the etymologists (*nairuktāḥ*). Thus, those rays which are the waters belonging to the moon that are about to come, they drink them during the waning half-month. To this effect there is also a scriptural verse (*nigama*): "The imperishable ones drink [the waters] whose abode is imperishable."
They cause that [Soma] to swell during the *pūrvapakṣa* (the waxing fortnight). Nevertheless, there is a scriptural citation (*nigama*) stating: "Just as the gods cause Aṃśu to swell.

The mantra is addressed to the *adhvaryu*, because the subject matter concerns the cow. Alternatively, it may be intended as a command, because it possesses the form of an imperative: "O *adhvaryu*, perform the service; perform it well; perform it, O *adhvaryu*! Furthermore, Agni is also called *adhvaryu*.
For you, O Adhrigu, O powerful one—[the term] *adhrigú* refers to one whose movement is unrestrained;
Indra also is called *adhrigu*. There is also a Vedic citation (nigama) which says: "O Adhrigus, [bring] the oblation for Indra."
Praise, hymn, and proclamation! Through this praise we are accompanied by Indra;
through this hymn we are accompanied by Indra.
5.11 Āpāntamanyu, Tṛpala-prabharmā, Dhuni, Śimīvan, Śaru, and Ṛjīṣin.
Soma has encompassed all forests from that [place]; no counter-measures have deceived Indra within his reach.

One whose anger is cast down; one who strikes sharply; one who strikes swiftly; one who strikes with a broad stroke; whether Soma or Indra; *dhuni* is from the root *dhū* (to shake); *śimi* is a name for action, derived either from *śam* (to pacify), or from *śak* (to be able). *Ṛjīṣī* refers to Soma: that which remains over when the Soma is being purified is the *ṛjīṣa*; it is what has been left behind. Because of that, Soma is *ṛjīṣī*. Furthermore, there is a Vedic passage concerning Indra: "The wielder of the *ṛjīṣa*, the wielder of the thunderbolt. And:
"That is his portion of the two bay horses, the parched grains (*dhānāḥ*). The *dhānāḥ* are those placed in a frying pan, or they are those placed in a vessel.

"May your two bay horses eat the parched grains; may they smell the *ṛjīṣa*. Thus there is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*). By means of the prefix *ā*, accompanied by repetition, he takes the suffix *upadhā*. The root *babhasti* has the meaning "to eat. Soma [consumes] all forests and trees. No counter-measures (*pratimānāni*) can overcome Indra from this side. Those by which they attempt to measure him do not overcome him; failing to reach him from this side, they perish. Some say that Indra is the primary subject here. Others say it is a description of the ritual action of Soma according to the *Nighaṇṭu*. Yet others say both are primary subjects. [The word *śmaśā*] is derived either from *śu* (quickly) and *aśnute* (he pervades), or from *śmā* and *aśnute*.
"ava śmaśā rudhadvāḥ" (RV 10.95.14), "avārudhat śmaśā vāra" (RV 10.95.15).

Urvaśī is an Apsaras. She extends over the wide [spaces] (urvabhyaḥ aśnute); she extends from her thighs (ūrubhyām aśnute). Or, her desire (vaśaḥ) is vast (uruḥ). An Apsaras is one who moves about (apsāriṇī). Alternatively, *apsa* is a name for form (*rūpa*); it comes from the root *apsāti*. It is that which is desirable to see; it is worthy of being beheld, or rather, worthy of being pervaded. Śākapūṇi says it is so called because it is clearly visible.
"Yadapsaḥ"—this refers to that which is not to be consumed.

"Apso nāma"—this refers to the pervasive [element]. That becomes possessed of form; or rather, "it was taken by her," or "it was given to her. Upon seeing her, the seed of Mitra and Varuṇa spilled. This ṛc is addressed to that [event]. 5.13
And you, O Vasiṣṭha, are the son of Mitra and Varuṇa, born from the mind of Urvaśī, O Brahman;
all the gods received you as a fallen drop by means of divine prayer within the lotus-leaf.

You also, O Vasiṣṭha, are the son of Mitrāvaruṇa; you were born from the mind of Urvaśī, O Brahman. The fallen drop [was recovered] by divine prayer (*brahman*). That drop was gathered together; it becomes fit for consumption. All the gods supported you upon the *puṣkara*. The *puṣkara* is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); it nourishes all beings. Water is the *puṣkara*; it is that which brings honor, that which is to be honored. This other [well-known] *puṣkara* (lotus) is also derived from this very same root. It is *puṣkara* or *vapuṣkara*. A flower (*puṣpa*) is from the root *puṣp* (to blossom).
*Vayuna* is from the root *vi* (to discern); it means either radiance or wisdom. 5.14

He, spreading out the darkness that was without discernment, made it possessed of discernment by means of the sun. He spread out that darkness which is non-cognition; he made it possessed of cognition by means of the sun.
Vājapastyam: having the dwelling place of strength.
"May we know him whose abode is strength"—thus there is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*).
In *vājagandhya*, the word *gadhya* is the final member of the compound. "May we attain him who possesses the fragrance of strength"—thus there is also a Vedic verse.

The word *gadhya* is derived from the root *grah* (to seize). There is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) which says: "Desiring to win the prize like a straight-running horse that seizes its prey. In this context, the root *gadhyati* has the sense of the act of mixing.
"Clung to, closely clung to"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (*nigama*). "Kaurayāṇa means one whose vehicle is made. "Pākasthāman is Kaurayāṇa"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse.
"Taurayāṇa means one whose vehicle is swift. "As such a Taurayāṇa, O Indra, come to the sacrifice with the Maruts as your friends, in harmony with them."
Thus there is also a Vedic verse (nigama):
"The shameless one, whose vehicle is shamelessness;
act with haste, O shameless one! Thus there is also a Vedic verse.
"Harayāṇaḥ" means "carrying away.
"Rajataṃ harayāṇe" (silver in the carrying-away)—thus also there is a Vedic verse (*nigama*).
"He who is invoked at every rite, steadfast, has accepted the hymns of praise."
*vrandī* is derived from the root *vrad*, meaning "to soften.

(5.15) When you, roaring, strike down the woods upon the head of the wind, even that of Śuṣṇa the subduer; when you strike down upon the head of the wind, the sound-maker, even that of Śuṣṇa the Āditya, the dryer; or when you are repeatedly roaring at the woods; or [it means] "by means of slaughter."

"He has become stiffened and paralyzed"—thus also occurs a Vedic passage (nigama). Both the roots *vīlayati* and *vrīlayati* have the sense of causing rigidity; they are employed together with the preceding [root].
"Niṣṣapī" means one who desires women; that is, one from whom the *sapa-* [impulse] has departed.
*Sapas* is derived from the root *sap*, which means "to touch.
"O Maghavan, do not abandon us like one who is negligent (*niṣṣapī*). Just as such a person destroys wealth, do not you likewise abandon us.

"Tūrṇāśa" means water; it quickly reaches [the earth]. "Like the *tūrṇāśa* from the mountain," thus there is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*). "Kṣumpa" is the mushroom; that which is shaken (*kṣubhyate*). 5.16
When will he trample with his foot the man who offers no gifts, like a mushroom?
When indeed will Indra listen to our songs?

When will he kick the mortal who does not worship him, as one kicks a clump of grass with his foot? When, indeed, will Indra listen to our songs? "Aṅga" is a word for "quickly"; it becomes "aṅkita" (marked) when it is bent down.
*Nicumpuṇaḥ* refers to Soma; *nicāntapṛṇaḥ* means "he satisfies by drinking. 5.17: These pressed juices, accompanied by their wives, go forth eagerly for the feast.
The gliding one, the stirrer of the waters.
These pressed juices, accompanied by their wives, the waters, go seeking [the gods] and desiring to drink.
The *nicumpuṇa* goes;

the ocean also is called *nicumpuṇa*, for it is filled by flowing down (*ni-cum-*) into it. The *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is also called *nicumpuṇa*, because they murmur softly (*nīcaiḥ kvaṇanti*) in it, or because they place [the offerings] low (*nīcaiḥ dadhati*).
"O *avabhṛtha*, O *nicumpuṇa*!"—thus there is also a Vedic citation (*nigama*).
[The words] *nicumpuṇa* and *nicuṅkuṇa* [are used]. *Padi* means "one who goes," as in that which moves (*yat padyate*). 5.18
To him Indra grants excellent cows, fine gold, and many horses—
great wealth for him who, O early-rising one, releases you as you come with riches, like a bird caught in a snare.

He becomes well-provided with cattle, well-endowed with gold, and possessed of good horses; and Indra bestows great vigor upon him who offers food to you as you arrive, O guest coming at dawn. As a boy releases his foot from a snare, so he releases himself from the snare, from the bond, from the fetter, and from the tether. *Pādu* comes from the root *pad* (to go). He makes the light manifest and hides the chaff; thus his foot is not released from its covering.

The sun reveals its light; it hides the *busa*. *Busa* is a name for water. It is derived from the root *brū*, meaning "to sound," or from *bhraṃś*, "to fall. When it rains, it causes the water to fall [from the sky], and it takes that back up again with its rays (5.19).

The moon is called *vṛka* ("wolf"). This is because its light is spread out (*vivṛta-jyotiṣka*), or because its light is transformed (*vikṛta-jyotiṣka*), or because its light strides forth (*vikrānta-jyotiṣka*) (5.20):
"The ruddy wolf, who makes the months, indeed saw him as he went along the path. (RV 1.116.17)
Having perceived it, she rises up like a carpenter fashioning a back-rib; O Heaven and Earth, witness this wealth of mine.

Aruṇa is the one who shines forth. The Moon becomes the maker of months and the maker of half-months. The Wolf (Vṛka) beheld the host of stars as they moved along their paths; having observed them, he overtakes them, for by whichever [path] the Moon is about to be yoked, [he follows it]. Like one suffering from back pain while carving [wood], [the Moon says]: "O Heaven and Earth, know this of me. The Sun also is called Vṛka, because he encompasses (vṛṅkte).
The quail invoked you, O Aśvins, when you released her from the mouth of the wolf.
Uṣas, seized by the Āditya, called upon the Aśvins; the Aśvins liberated her—such is the narrative. The dog is also called "wolf" (vṛka) because of its tearing (vikartana).
"Even the wolf, the restrainer, the churner of the breast"—that is, the churner of the sheep's breast.
The ram (*uraṇa*) is so called because it possesses wool (*ūrṇā*). The word *ūrṇā* is derived from the root *vṛ* (to choose) or from *ūṛṇoti* (to cover).
Furthermore, the female wolf (*vṛkī*) is also called *vṛkī*.
[As in the verse: "His father made Ṛjrāśva blind, who had given a hundred rams to the she-wolf."
Thus also there is a Vedic citation:

*joṣavākam* is a name whose specific meaning is unknown; it is something that should be approved. 5.21 "O Indra and Agni, those who praise you while the [Soma] juices are pressed, you who increase the cosmic order (*ṛta*)..."
O gods, you do not consume even the speech of one who speaks with a heart full of devotion.

O Indra and Agni, you eat the portion of him who praises you when the *soma* juices have been pressed; but as for this man who speaks words of approval (*joṣavākam*) while muttering prayers (*vijañjapaḥ*), you do not eat the portion of that godless man whose offerings are rejected. *Kṛttiḥ* is from the root *kṛt* (to cut); it means either glory or food. "O Indra, may your great skin be our protection."

"O Indra, your protection is very great, like a skin in the atmosphere. This other [word] *kṛtti* is derived from this same root; it means "made of thread" (*sūtramayī*). Or, it is used in the sense of a comparison. "There he whose garment is a skin, who holds the Pināka bow in his hand, whose bow is unstrung;
wearing a skin, come hither, bearing the Pināka—thus there is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*)."
Let not the distress of any malicious hater strike us down,
as a wave strikes a ship.

May not the distress of the evil-minded, the wicked-minded, or the hatred of anyone from all sides strike us down, as a wave strikes a ship. The word *ūrmi* is derived from the root *ūrṇoti*. The word *nauḥ* (ship) is that which is to be propelled forward; or it is derived from the root *namati*. How then could it be a noun with an unaccented base? Yet its declensional forms are observed [in the Veda]: "And so, O Vasu, sharpen us together in this."
Thus in the locative case; *śiśīti* has the sense of "giving.
"Protect us from every malicious person" (*uruṣyā ṇo aghāyataḥ samasmāt*)—thus in the ablative case; *uruṣyati* is intransitive. Furthermore, it also occurs in the nominative plural.
He who is not to be harmed, who is equal in his own dwelling— 5.23—
the lover of the waters fills [them] with oblation, he who is a fulfiller, O heroes; he is the father of the cloud, the one who observes all people.

He is the one who causes the oblation to digest through the waters. *Piparti* and *papuriḥ* are either derivations from the root *pṛṇāti* (to satisfy) or from *prīṇāti* (to please). He is the father because he protects the performed ritual act;
he is Āditya. *Śamba* is a name for the thunderbolt (*vajra*), derived either from the root *śam* (to pacify) or from *śāt* (to cut down).
"O you who are fierce, with that *śamba* which is much-invoked"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (*nigama*).
"The *kepayas* are those who are base (*kapūya*). Regarding "base": it refers to a contemptible action; it is something difficult to purify. 5.24
Separately, for the most part, they performed their first invocations of the gods, seeking glorious deeds that are difficult to surpass.
Those who were unable to board the sacrificial ship settled down in the marshy ground like birds.

They went apart. They spread out separately. The first invocations of the gods—those who called upon the gods, who performed deeds worthy of renown, achievements difficult for others to emulate—they were those who were able to board the sacrificial ship.

But those who were unable to board the sacrificial ship, they settled down right there; they settled down right here; they settled down in debt, or rather, in this very world. *Īrma* is a name for the arm; it becomes more extended.
All these pressings you have made swift for yourself, O Son of Strength, those which you have taken up for yourselves.

You quickly take up all these positions, O Son of Power, those which you assume for yourselves: the shoulder-guard, the protection against distress, the bow, or the armor. Armor is that which is fastened; it is that which is well-fitted; or rather, it is that which is fitted to the body. "Satisfy the horses; win what is beneficial; make the chariot one that brings well-being."
As he descended into the boat-like Drona, the wheel of his chariot sank and its axle broke while he was pouring out water for the kings.

"Refresh the horses; conquer with full vigor! May victory be beneficial for you! Make the chariot a vehicle of well-being. The *droṇa* is made of wood (*druma*). It is called *āhāva* because of its calling out (*āhvāna*). It is called *āvaha* because of its bringing forth (*āvahana*). Because it is dug out (*avata*) and has been excavated, it becomes great.

"An iron wheel, a stone wheel, or a whetstone wheel," so it is said. "The quiver of the shoulder. May your shoulder-protectors be like a quiver; a *kośa* (quiver) is derived from the root *kuṣ*, for it is scraped away (*vikuṣita*). This other [word] *kośa* (treasury) has the same origin: it becomes great when accumulated and merely heaped up. "Pour out for the protection of men"—that is, for the protection of the leaders. He compares the battle to the work of digging a well.

They call the palate *kākuda*. The tongue is *kokuvā*; it is placed within this [palate]. Or, *jihvā* is *kokuvā* because, while cooing (*kokūyamānā*), it utters the phonemes. Or it may be derived from the root *kukūyati*, which denotes the act of making sound. *Jihvā* is *johuvā*. The palate (*tālu*) is from the root *tṛ*; it is the most crossed-over (*tīrṇatama*) part of the body. Or it may be from the root *lat*, used in reverse; as in *tala*. *Latā* would be the non-reversed form.
"O Varuṇa, you are a good god, whose seven rivers flow along the palate like a hollow tube. (RV 8.69.12)
"You are a good god, a giver of auspicious gifts; O God, you upon whose palate the seven rivers flow like breath, as if into a hollow tube. Thus there is a Vedic verse.

You are Sudeva, the auspicious god; or you are Kamanīyadeva, O Varuṇa. You, whose seven rivers—*sindhu* being so called from flowing (*sravaṇāt*)—whose seven streams there are, flow along your palate (*kākud*). *Sūrmi* means an auspicious wave; it is like a hollow stream. Regarding *vīriṭa*, Taiṭiki says that the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*) is so called because it weaves (*vayati*) what is before and stretches out (*irate*) what is after; for "wings" (*vayāṃsi*) or "lights" (*bhāṃsi*) move within it. They cite this very verse in this regard. There is also a traditional interpretation (*nigama*). 5.27
The sacrificial grass, easy to tread upon, has been spread out for them; like two lords of the people, they hasten to the assembly.
At the first invocation of the dawns, Vāyu with his team and Pūṣan come for our well-being, O wide-hipped Dawn.
The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) of these [gods] is easy of access; they go forth toward it. "E-yāte" means the two protectors or guardians of all.

*Bīriṭam* is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). It is either a multitude of fears or of lights. Or perhaps it may be used in a comparative sense: "like two kings who are lords of all. In the *bīriṭa*, that is, in the assembly of men, at the first invocation during the departure of the night. And Vāyu, accompanied by his team (*niyutvān*), and Pūṣan, for the sake of well-being. "Ni-yutvān" means he whose horses are *niyuts*.
They are called *niyuts* either because of their restraint (*niyamana*) or because of their harnessing (*niyojana*). Śākapūṇi says: "Toward the one who has reached [the goal]."
*Parīm* has been explained [in the previous section]. *Enām* is explained by this [particle] *enām*, *asyāḥ*, and *asya*.
*Sṛṇiḥ* is a goad (*aṅkuśa*), because of its causing [the animal] to run (*saraṇāt*). *Aṅkuśaḥ* is derived from the root *añc* (to bend); or it is so called because it is bent (*ākucitaḥ*).
"May the enemy come closer to the cooked [food]. Thus there is also a Vedic verse (nigama).
"May he come from the very closest; may the cooked medicine come. "May it come"—so [it is said]. 5.28.

Sasni, Aścantī, and the boar sing of thee; they praise thee as the purifier many times. What is thine? What is offered to thee? O Agni, O hero! One protects while another is wrathful. Urvaśī is an *apsaras*; thou art he. When indeed shall the mortal be with his wife? The wolf is well-disposed; the moon is ruddy. May he [be] for me. O Indra and Agni! Do not [let him be] the lover of our entire oblation. Separately they went forth; may the benevolent one satisfy the horses. He has turned away. Twenty-eight.
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the first six books of the Nirukta.
Now the sixth chapter:
O Agni, you are born from the days, you are born from the kindling-sticks, you are born from the stone;
you are born from the woods, you are born from the plants, O Lord of men, you are born pure.

"O Agni, you [are so] by days and by nights. You are *āśuśukṣaṇi*. Both *āśu* and *śu* are names for "swift" (*kṣipra*). *Kṣaṇi* is the latter [member of the compound], derived from the root *kṣaṇoti*. Alternatively, [the name means] "one who quickly (*āśu*) consumes (*kṣaṇoti*) with heat (*śucā*)," or "one who bestows (*sanoti*). *Śuk* is from the root *śuc*. Or, the nominative case is used in the sense of the ablative; for such is the connection in the sentence: the prefix *ā* is first, and the following part is that which intends to be expressed—namely, "desiring to cause to shine quickly" (*āśu-śocayiṣuḥ*). *Śuci* is from the root *śuc*, a verb meaning "to blaze. This other [word] *śuci* (pure) comes from this very same root. The etymologists say: "The evil has been poured out (*niḥṣikta*) from him."
O Indra, may you bring us across all regions; for the *āśās* (regions) become so because of reaching (*āsadanāt*).

The *diśas* (quarters) become so because of pervading (*abhy-aśanāt*). The *upadiśas* (intermediate quarters) become so because of being near (*upa-āsanāt*). A *kāśis* is a fist (*muṣṭi*), because of manifesting (*prakāśanāt*), or because of closing (*mocanāt*), or because of seizing (*moṣaṇāt*), or because of bewildering (*mohanāt*). O Indra, when you, O Bounteous One, grasp these two boundless worlds, that is your *kāśis*.
O Indra, you who are without enemies, you have shattered the enclosure of the cow, fearing no blow from the foe;
you have made the paths easy for the cows to pass, as they low toward the one invoked by many, opening the way for their release.

Alātṛṇa means "one who is sufficient to crush. Alātardana means "one who is sufficient to destroy. Megha is derived from *miha* (to sprinkle). Vala is derived from *vṛṇoti* (he covers). Vraja is derived from *vrajati* (he moves); it refers to the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). Of this cow—the speech of the intermediate region—he cried out (*vyāra*) out of fear before being slain. He made the paths easy to traverse for the release of the cows; he made the paths well-traveled for the driving forth of the cattle. The voices (*vāṇīḥ*) blew toward the one invoked by many; or "waters" (*āpaḥ*) because of their flowing, or "speeches" (*vācaḥ*) because of their speaking. Water is called *bahubhir-āhūtam* (invoked by many). *Dhamati* is a verb meaning "to go. "Uproot the demon, O Indra, root and all; cut him down, and crush his fresh middle part!"
How long have you made the *sallūka* plant your missile, O Brahman, for the sake of burning the enemy?

"Uproot the Rakṣas, O Indra, together with its root"—the "root" (mūla) is so called because of its being loosened (mocana), or because of its being stolen away (moṣaṇa), or because of its being deluded (mohana). "Cut through the middle; crush the tip. The "tip" (agra) is that which has come to the front. From how far a distance? It is "salalūka," meaning thoroughly agitated or greedy; the etymologists say it means "evil-doing" (pāpaka). Or it may be "sararuka," derived from the root *sṛ* (to move) in the reduplicated form. "Tapuṣi" is from the root *tap* (to heat). "Hetis" is from the root *han* (to strike). "That very one, thus fashioned, lying down"—his "milk" (payas) is "sukha" (pleasant); his milk is pleasant. "Visruhas" are the waters; they are so called because of their flowing forth (*visravaṇa*).
"Like a bird, the seven shoots have grown forth. Thus there is also a Vedic verse (nigama).
"Vīrudhas" are plants (oṣadhayaḥ), because they grow forth (virohaṇāt). "The vīrudhas that carry one across [to safety]"—thus there is also a Vedic verse.

*Nakṣaddābham*: "attacking the unassailable," or "he overcomes by means of reaching. There is also a Vedic verse: *nakṣāhaṃ tatuṃ parvateṣṭhām*. *Askṛdhoyuḥ*: "one whose life is not cut short"; *kṛdh* is a name for something short; it means "cut off."
"He who is unassailable, the ancient one, the possessor of all. Thus there is also a Vedic verse (nigama):
"The supporters, the destroyers of enemies, the bringers of wealth—those supporters have placed Pūṣan upon the chariot; they bear the god to bestow glory."
"May they bring Pūṣan on the chariot; they are the looseners and the takers away. [They bring] the glory of the people, the glory born of birth.
Bṛbaduktha is one of great hymns (mahaduktha). 'A hymn (uktha) is to be recited for him'—or rather, he is Bṛbaduktha himself. 'We invoke Bṛhaduktha'—thus also there is a Vedic verse (nigama)."
Soma is *ṛdūdara* (soft-bellied). [He is] soft-bellied; or rather, [the term refers to] those who are soft-bellied.
There is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) that says: "May he be united with his soft-bellied friend.
We shall explain the term *ṛdūpe* further below.
"Pulūkāmaḥ" means "one who has many desires. For there is also a Vedic verse (nigama) that says: "The mortal man indeed has many desires. "Asinvatī" means "not devouring."
"Consuming, she devours much," so there is also a Vedic verse (nigama).
"The *kapana*s are *kapana*s; they are worms," so there is also a Vedic verse: "O wise ones, shake the tree like *kapana*s. *Bhāṛjīka* means one whose light is well-established.
"The one whose banner is smoke, blazing with kindled fuel"—thus there is also a Vedic verse (nigama).
"The rivers break asunder"; they break the banks.
"Crushed together, Indra’s enemy was ground to pieces"—thus there is also a Vedic verse.

*Jūrṇi* is derived from *jūrvati* (to consume), or from *dravati* (to run), or from *dūnāti* (to burn). There is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) that says: "The swift *jūrṇi* shall carry [the oblation]. And:
"May the bird go around you both with a glowing mind."
"He has pervaded the heat; food has come for the forest. 6.4 Upalaprakṣiṇī: she scatters [food] upon the millstones, or she is one who throws [food] onto the millstones.
Indra asked the sages: "In a time of famine, by what means do you live? One among them replied:
A cart, a female cannibal, cattle, a net, a chariot, a forest,
the ocean, a mountain, and a king— these are the nine means of subsistence during a famine.
Thus she is explained by the words themselves:
"I am indeed a singer, a physician, a protector of the house;
seeking various riches, we have stood waiting like cows for the herd—O Indu, flow around for Indra."

"I am a doer; I am the maker of hymns; therefore, I am a physician. "Therefore" (*tataḥ*) is a name for lineage, or [it refers to] the father or the son. "The one who grinds stones" (*upalaprakṣiṇī*) is the one who prepares groats (*saktukārikā*). "Nanā" is derived from the root *nam* (to bow); she is either the mother or the daughter. "Those of various minds" (*nānādhiyaḥ*) are those of various activities. "Seeking wealth" (*vasūyavaḥ*) means desiring riches. "We have followed after [the world] like cattle" (*anvāsthitāḥ smo gāva iva lokam*). "O Indu, flow around for Indra"—this is a prayer. Sitting, he cuts the upright [hair] upon the lap (*upasi*). "In the lap" (*upasthe*). He becomes a merchant who knows the parts (*prakalavid*). He knows both the parts (*kalāḥ*) and the sub-parts (*prakalāḥ*).

"O you who have evil friends, O you who are skilled in reproach!"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (nigama). "The one who performs excessive sacrifice. He sacrifices excessively. "Pūṣan attends upon the one who performs excessive sacrifice"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse. 6.5

"You behold, O Lord; for you behold both kinds of wealth, O King"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (*nigama*). "Of the great dwelling, of the dweller"—"O Aśvins, [bestow it] upon Kaṇva"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse.
6.6 "Our kinship is with you"—the meaning is "we.
"Come to us, O Nāsatyas, with delight"—the meaning is "toward us."
"O Bull, with our equal manly powers—
meaning, with us— grant us [wealth], O Maghavan, O consumer of the soma-residue— meaning, for us.
May he drive the hatred far away from us— even from afar— meaning, from us."
"Like the thigh (ūrva), our desire has spread wide"—meaning, "among us.
"O Vasus, bestow treasures upon us"—meaning, "upon ourselves.

*Pāthaḥ* is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). It is explained by the word *pathā*. There is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) which says: "Like a falcon flying, he follows the *pāthaḥ*. Water is also called *pāthaḥ*, because of the act of drinking (*pāna*).
"He beholds the course of these rivers"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (nigama).
Food also is called *pātha*, because it is indeed a drink (*pāna*). "O wise one, bring [the oblation] to the path of the gods"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse.
"In the impulse, in the instigation; in the impulse of the god Savitṛ"—thus also there is a Vedic verse. "Saprathas" means wide on all sides.
"O Agni, you are far-extending"—thus there is also a Vedic verse (nigama). "The assemblies, the acts of knowing"—thus there is also a Vedic verse: "Impelling the assemblies.
6.7 "Like those who come for the sun, may all partake of Indra's portion."
O you who are born and being born with vigor, we look toward the riches as if toward our allotted portion.

They, having taken their stand together, wait upon the Sun; or rather, it may be for the sake of comparison: "they wait upon Indra as if upon the Sun. Desiring to share all of Indra’s riches—riches which he distributes among those already born and those yet to be born—we meditate upon that portion [of his]. With *ojas*, with strength. *Ojas* is derived either from the root *ujj*, "to exert," or from *ubj*, "to press down," or from *ā-śri*, "to resort to," or from *ā-śrap*, "to cook. Now, this other *āśis* (blessing) is derived from the root *ā-śās*, "to hope for. There is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) stating: "The cows [provide] the *āśir* (milk-mixture) for Indra. And also: "May that true blessing of mine be among the gods."
When you, O mortal, having attained your enjoyment, did swallow and awaken the plants; when you, O mortal, having reached your enjoyment, did swallow the plants as the greatest devourer—
*jigartiḥ* means either one whose action is swallowing, or one whose action is praising, or one whose action is seizing.
"O Wise One, we are not deluded; O Agni, you alone truly know your greatness. We are deluded; you are undeluded. We do not know your greatness, O Agni, but you know it.
'Exerting himself, praising'—there is also a Vedic verse [to this effect]: 'He who, exerting himself with sacrifices, offers worship to you two.'"
The god is grace directed toward the gods;
the god is grace manifested toward the gods. It is derived from the root *kṛp* ("to be gracious") or from the root *kalp* ("to be fit").

6.8 For I have heard that you two are more generous givers than a brother-in-law or even than a husband's brother. Therefore, O Indra and Agni, as the Soma flows forth, I generate a new hymn of praise for you both.

For I have heard that you two are most liberal givers, even more so than a son-in-law (*vijāmātṛ*). [The term] *asusamāpta* refers to a son-in-law; the people of the South (*Dākṣiṇātyas*) constantly call a purchased husband a *vijāmātṛ*. By *asusamāpta*, a bridegroom (*vara*) who is not yet fully established is intended. *Jāmātṛ*: *jā* means offspring; its producer is the son-in-law. Or rather, it may be from a brother-in-law (*syāla*). Also, "even from a brother-in-law. The Naidānas say a brother-in-law is so called because he is close through marriage. Or, "he scatters parched grains (*lāja*)," thus he is a *syāla*. *Lāja* comes from the root *lāj* (to parch). *Sya* is a winnowing basket (*śūrpa*), from the root *syai* (to pour out). A winnowing basket is for winnowing food. Or it comes from the root *śṛ* (to destroy).
Now, through the offering of Soma, O Indra and Agni, I generate for you two a new, ever-fresher hymn.
We shall explain the verse beginning with "omāsaḥ" later on.
(RV 1.9) "O Brahmaṇaspati, make the Soma-presser resound."
[He who is] Kakṣīvat, the son of Uśij.

O Brahmaṇaspati, make me, the presser of Soma juices, resplendent, even as Kakṣīvat was—Kakṣīvat being one who possesses a girth-band (kakṣyā), and Auśija being the son of Uśij; Uśij [is so called] from the root *uś*, meaning "to desire" or "to shine. Or perhaps it is intended here that he was simply a man with a girth-band (*manuṣyakakṣa*). O Brahmaṇaspati, make me, the presser of Soma juices, resplendent.
O Indra and Soma, burn up the one who speaks evil against us, like a vessel of hot food placed upon the fire.
Bestow hatred upon the hater of prayer, the flesh-eater, the one of terrible aspect, the Kimīdin, so that he may never prosper.

O Indra and Soma, [protect] the praiser of the sinner; *agha* is from the root *han* (to strike), with its prefix shortened, as in "he strikes. *Tapuḥ* is from the root *tap* (to heat). *Caru* is a mound of earth; it comes from the root *car* (to move).

From this [word] waters flow forth. "To the hater of Brahman, to the eater of raw flesh (kravyād), to the one of terrible report. Regarding "raw flesh" (*kravya*), the etymologists say it is produced from what is cut apart (*vikṛtta*). "Bestow hatred," meaning "without lack" (*anavāyam*) and "without deficiency" (*anavayavam*), so that others may not separate [us]. Or, "those who are without hatred. "To the *kimīdin*": he moves about asking, "What now? or "What is this? What is this? He moves about as a slanderer (*piśuna*); a slanderer is so called from the root *piṃśati* ("to tear apart"), for he tears apart [the truth]. "Make your strength wide-spreading like a net; go like a king with his elephant-herd."
Rushing along your swift course, you are the archer; pierce the demons with your most scorching shafts.

Display your power—*pājaḥ* from *pā* (to protect)—like a wide net; *prasitiḥ* from *pra-si* (to extend), or it means a thread, or a net. Go forth like a king, accompanied by his ministers, or by his attendants, or by his own forces, with a host that brings nourishment (*irābhṛt*), free from fear, or with elephants. Pursuing them with a swift net—*tṛṣvī* is a name for the swift, derived either from *tṛ* (to cross) or *tvar* (to hasten)—you are the dark one (*asitā*). Pierce the demons with your most scorching weapons—*tapiṣṭhaiḥ* meaning most heated, or most satisfying, or most crushing.
Whatever disease (*amīvā*) of evil name has entered your embryo or lies within your womb...

The [verse regarding] *amīvā* is explained by this [same analysis]. A *durṇāman* is one with an evil name; a *krimi* (worm) is one that fattens upon raw flesh (*kravya*). It may derive from the root *kram*, in the sense of the action of moving, or from *kram*, in the sense of "stepping over. As it is said: "Stepping over all misfortunes," meaning stepping over all movements toward miserable states of existence. *Apvā* is so called because when one is pierced by it, one is driven away (*apavīyate*). It is either a disease or fear. Regarding this, there is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*): "O *apvā*, go away! *Amati* is the absence of *mati*; *mati* is that which consists of the self (*ātman*).
Regarding this, there is also a Vedic verse: "He whose *mati* shines upward in his own domain."
*Śruṣṭi* is a name for "quickly. *Āśu-aṣṭi* [is another]. O Agni, you who desire the sacrifice, worship them—the Bhaga, the Nāsatyas, and Purandhi—with quick obedience.

O Agni, at this sacrifice (*adhvara*), worship those who desire [the offering]—Bhaga with swift obedience, and the two Nāsatyas, the Aśvins. Regarding the term *nāsatyau*: Aurṇavābha says they are simply "the two truthful ones" (*satyau*); Āgrāyaṇa says they are "the two leaders of truth" (*satyasya praṇetārau*); or rather, they were born from the nose (*nāsikā*). *Puraṃdhiḥ* means "possessing much wisdom. Who is *puraṃdhiḥ*? One view is that Bhaga is mentioned first, and this is a subsequent reference (*anvādeśa*) to him; another view is that it is Indra, for he is the most active in deeds and the greatest shatterer of fortresses (*purām*). Yet another view is that it is Varuṇa.

He praises that [light] with wisdom: "Behold now this most wondrous power of the sage," so says a Vedic verse (*nigama*). *Ruśat* is a name for color; it comes from the root *ruc*, meaning "to shine. "The radiant power of the kindled one has been seen," so says a Vedic verse.

"O gods, destroyers of enemies, you have kinship with us; you have affinity with us. "You have kinship" means, O gods, you possess the state of being born from the same source as those who destroy the harmful. "You have affinity": *āpya* comes from the root *āp* (to reach). "The bounteous giver, the giver of auspicious gifts"—"May Tvaṣṭṛ, the bounteous giver, bestow riches upon us," so says a Vedic verse.
"Suvidatra" means one who possesses auspicious knowledge. There is also a Vedic verse (nigama) that says: "O Agni, come hither with those who possess auspicious knowledge.
"Ānuṣak" is a term for succession. It means "connected in sequence. There is also a Vedic verse that says: "They spread the sacrificial grass in succession."
"Turvaṇi is the swift winner. "He, Turvaṇi, is great in manly power, O dustless one"—thus there is also a Vedic verse (nigama).
"The god is the lover of songs (girvaṇas). "They win him over with songs. "A lofty [hymn] is pleasing to the lover of songs"—thus there is also a Vedic verse. 6.14

Seated upon the unmanifested and the manifested dust, those who fashioned these beings—unimpelled by breath, yet impelled by breath, impelled by the wind—those intermediate hosts of gods, satisfying the earth with their essence, create living beings. They performed sacrifice; this is the response to what was previously stated.
"O Indra, that spear of yours is well-anointed," or "it is smeared," or "it is anointed. Just as it was established, so did he find it through his creative vision.
In whatever manner he was established, he found it through his insight; like a father, the Dawn has been made to grow old through sacrifices.
Like the Dawn, the protector has been born through sacrifices.
They have come toward you, well-pleased; all the strengths have become foremost.

They set forth, taking pleasure [in the journey], and all became [united]. Or rather, it means "by going at the head" (*agragamanena*), or "by leading the way" (*agragaraṇena*), or "those who speak first" (*agravādinaḥ*). Alternatively, one may take the prefix *agra-* as being without specific meaning.
"Eat indeed, O Indra; these oblations have been set forth. Accept them with favor, both the cooked food and the Soma."
"O Indra, accept with favor these oblations that have been set forth; *cana* is a name for food. The root *pacati* has become a noun [meaning 'cooked' or 'matured'].
Regarding this, there is also a Vedic verse (nigama): 'They both took hold of him from the fatness by means of the cooked offering.'"

Or rather, there may be a dual number for both the fat and the animal; it would be a dual form expressing the essence (*sāttvam*). For where the meaning of the singular is well-established, that [dual] occurs, as in:
"O Agni, the two sacrificial cakes are being cooked. Likewise, "the *śurudhas* are the waters" means they restrain (*saṃrundhanti*) suffering (*śucam*).

"For the powers of *ṛta* are many," so indeed there is a Vedic verse (*nigama*). "Aminas" means one who is immeasurable in extent, or one who is unassailable; "aminaḥ sahobhiḥ" (unassailable by his powers), so too there is a Vedic verse.

The waters become *jajjhatīḥ*, making a sound; "the Maruts are like those that *jajjhati*," so there is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*). *Apratiṣkutaḥ* means "unopposed" or "unrebutted," or alternatively, "unstumbling."

"Unopposed for us"—thus also occurs a Vedic citation (*nigama*). *Śāśadānaḥ* means "repeatedly striking down" or "being repeatedly struck down. "Repeatedly striking down his own thought"—thus also occurs a Vedic citation.
(6.16) *Sṛpraḥ* is from the root *sṛp* ("to glide"). This other word *sṛpra* is derived from that very same root; it means either clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) or oil (*tailam*).
"Sṛprakarasnā mūtaye"—there is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) thus.
*Karasnau* refers to the two arms; they are the two who immerse themselves in ritual actions (*karman*).
By this, *suśipra* is also explained.
There is also a Vedic verse (nigama): "O fair-jawed one, in the battle for cattle!

Here, *śipre* refers to the jaws or the nostrils. *Hanu* is derived from the root *han*; *nāsikā* is derived from the root *nas*. There is also another Vedic verse: "Open your jaws; release the two streams!"
*Dhenā* is derived from *dhā*, "to bestow.
*Raṃsu* is from *ram*, "to delight. Regarding this, there is also a Vedic verse (nigama): "He is perceived by his wondrous, delightful radiance."

"Dvibarhā" means one who is preeminent in two places: in the middle station and in the highest station. Furthermore, there is a Vedic verse (nigama) which says, "And he is doubly great, undiminished by his powers. "Akra" is from the root *kram*, meaning "to step upon" or "to ascend."
"A bull bearing [the prize] in the assembly of the great ones"—such is also a Vedic verse (nigama).
"Choosing" means making wide room. "Thou goest as a messenger from of old, choosing"—such is also a Vedic verse. Waters are called *stiya* because of their flowing (*styāyanāt*).
"The bull of the rivers, the steer of the standing waters"—thus there is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*).
"Stipāḥ" means the protector of the standing waters; or, he protects those who have approached him.
"May you be our protector of the standing waters and also our protector of our bodies"—thus there is also a Vedic verse.

*Jabāru* means "moving swiftly," "aging," or "heating. *Jabāru* is that which has been placed upon the front (*agra*). There is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) to this effect. *Jarūtham* and *garūtham* are derived from the root *gṛ* (to praise).
"Slay Jarūtha; bestow abundance for the sake of wealth"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (*nigama*).
*Kuliśa* is a name for the thunderbolt (*vajra*); it is that which shatters the bank. "Like shoulders severed by a thunderbolt, the serpent lies pressed close against the earth."

The trunk of a tree is firmly fixed; this other [trunk] is likewise from that very same source. It is fixed upon the body. A serpent lies coiled, embracing the earth. *Tuja* is derived from the root *tuñj*, meaning "to give.
6.17 At every gift, at every bestowal, those hymns of Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, which are superior—no one finds his perfect praise.

With every gift, with every superior hymn of praise for Indra, the wielder of the thunderbolt, I find no end to this eulogy—[a hymn] of crushing power, of overwhelming force. "The Asura of great renown was made by crushing power"—thus also occurs a Vedic citation (Nigama). 6.18

Whoever presses Soma for him—be it from the distilling vat or from the udder—that man indeed becomes radiant. The powerful Maghavan drives away his sin and his misfortune; he who is bright of body and wise in speech.

*Ghraṃsa* is a name for the day; in it, the juices (*rasas*) are swallowed. The cow’s udder (*ūdhas*) becomes more uplifted; or rather, it is "bound up" (*uponnaddham*). Because of the commonality of providing moisture (*sneha*), the night also is called the udder. He who presses the *soma* for him either by day or by night becomes radiant during the day. *Apohati* means he strikes away, *śakra*, the one who desires to stretch out—that is, the one devoid of the continuity of dharma, the one who fancies himself adorned but is no sacrificer. *Tanūśubhram* means the one who beautifies the body. *Maghavā* is he who possesses wealth. *Kavāsakhaḥ* is he whose companions (*sakhas*) are contemptible (*kupūyas*).
Indra pierced the strongholds of Ilībiśa;
Indra shattered Śuṣṇa, the horned one, who lay within the cave.
To him, the lord, the possessor of manifold power, bring forth the thunderbolt with haste against Vṛtra.
He does not break through the mountain ridges, desiring to cross the waters so that he may flow over the floods.

"Strike him! Swiftly, with haste! The Lord [Indra] against Vṛtra with the thunderbolt. Or: "Of how much measure? Of what extent? Or: "Of advancing measure. "Break the joints of the cloud as if of a cow. "Desiring to release the floods for the flowing of the waters. *Bhṛmi* is from the root *bhram* (to wander). "Thou art *bhṛmi*, the maker of seers among mortals"—thus there is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*). *Viṣpita* means "attained" or "reached. "May he carry us across this attained [distress]"—thus there is also a Vedic verse. 6.20
May Tvaṣṭṛ, who is well-disposed toward us, release that wonderful, most desirable, and manifold [gift] for our nourishment and wealth from his own self, like a navel-center.

"May he, swift, great, and well-prepared, by himself, may Tvaṣṭṛ release [the wealth] for the nourishment of riches"—thus [he is] *asmayu*, desiring us. *Rāspinaḥ* means "one who speaks" (*rāspī*), from either the root *rap* or *ras*.
There is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) regarding *rāspinasyāyoḥ*.
The root *ṛñjati* has the sense of adorning or preparing.
"Come to us with straight power at the dawning of strengths"—thus there is also a Vedic verse (nigama).
"Straight" is also an epithet for him. "May Varuṇa lead us with straight guidance"—thus there is also a Vedic verse.
"O you whose wealth is ready, O you whose wealth is attained!
O Indra, address the two bay steeds whose wealth is ready!"—thus also there is a Vedic verse (Nigama).
"Further our sacrifice with the worship of the gods; further our prayer for the winning of riches."
Open up your udders for the union with the Cosmic Order; O Waters, be gracious and responsive to us.
Send forth our sacrifice for the worship of the gods; send forth the sacred prayer (*brahman*) for the winning of wealth.

For the application of *ṛta*, for the application of the sacrifice—or rather, for the sacrificial cart. The cart is called *śakaṭa* because it is covered with dung (*śakṛt*), or because it moves slowly (*śanakaiḥ-takati*), or because it makes a sound as it moves (*śabdena-takati*). O Waters, be pleasant and ready to listen for us! O Waters, be pleasant for us! Indra, bestowing much that is desirable—Indra, giving much that is worthy of being won—Indra, the king of both worlds while they increase, bestows his gifts upon the people and upon men.

He casts away those who do not press the soma while they are prospering; he bestows [the soma] upon those who do press it. He is the king of both, of that which is celestial and of that which is terrestrial. "Coṣkūyamāṇaḥ"—this is the reduplication (*carkarīta-vṛtta*) of the root *coṣkūyati*;
the meaning is "excellent" (*sumat*) by itself. "The well-disposed one has approached with a prayer for wisdom;
may it come to me of its own accord—that mind of mine which has been meditated upon through sacrifice. This is the mantra from the Aśvamedha.
In the *diviṣṭis*, that is, in the pursuits for heaven;
[there was] abundant wealth consisting of a hundred horses from Kuruṅga in the *diviṣṭis*.
"Abundant" (*sthūra*): it becomes great merely by being approached. "Minute" (*aṇu*) follows "larger" (*sthavīyas*). The prefix has its name elided, as in the word *saṃprati*.

Kuruṅga was a king. Or [the name] Kuru is derived from *kuru-gamana* (going to the Kurus) or *kula-gamana* (going to the family). *Kuru* comes from the root *kṛt* (to cut); it also has the meaning "cruel. *Kula* comes from the root *kuṣ* (to tear); it means "that which is torn apart. *Dūta* has already been explained. The root *jinva* signifies the act of pleasing.
"The rains quicken the earth; the fires quicken the sky"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (nigama).

"He is a great vessel, measureless, or indeed immeasurable. "The great vessel, overflowing in the struggle"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse. "The wielder of the thunderbolt is praised as equal to the Ṛc. He is praised as equal by means of the Ṛc, O wielder of the thunderbolt.
"Anarśarāti" means a gift that is not base or foul; "aślīla" means evil or wicked, and "aśrimat" means uneven. "Praise Anarśarāti, the giver of wealth"—thus also occurs in the *Nigama*.
"Anarvā" means one who is unopposed by another. "Exalt with new hymns Bṛhaspati, the unopposed bull, whose tongue is sweet."

Unrivaled and unopposed by another; the bull; with a pleasant tongue—that is, a tongue that gladdens, or perhaps a tongue that delights; Bṛhaspati—magnify him with new hymns (*arkas*), that is, with praiseworthy songs of praise (*stomas*). "Asāmi" means not deficient; it is derived from the root *syati*. "O you of good gifts, you bear strength that is never deficient."

O you who bestow auspicious gifts, maintain your strength until it is fully completed. Let me not provoke you, like a restless wild beast at the soma-pressings, with my constant prayer for the flowing soma; for who would not entreat one who is all-powerful?

I have never been angry with you because of the pressing of Soma, always entreating you with song, with chanting, and with praise—as one might [entreat] a wild beast. I was not angry during the libations, thinking, "Who would not entreat the Lord? *Galda* refers to the vessels (the veins); the pressing is placed within them. "May the drops enter you; may they enter the *galda*, the vessels. These two words take different case endings; the meaning here is "into the vessels for the purpose of pressing" (6.24).
"We do not consider ourselves evil, nor powerless, nor dejected;

we do not consider ourselves evil, nor poor, nor lacking in brilliance," so said the seer. "We possess within us holy living (*brahmacarya*), study, austerity, and the act of giving. Bakura is Bhāskara (the Sun); he is terrifying, or he runs while shining.
O Aśvins, you who are wonder-workers (*dasra*), you plow barley with the wolf and milk nourishment for mankind.
With the Bakura weapon, you blew away the Dasyu; you created vast light for the Ārya.
"Sowing barley as if with a wolf," O Aśvins. The wolf is so called because of its tearing; the plow (*lāṅgala*) is so called from the root *lag* (to cling).

Or it is like a tail (*lāṅgūla*); the tail (*lāgūla*) is from the root *lag*. Or from *laṅg*; or from *laṃb* (to hang down). "Milking food for man, beautiful to behold, crushing the Dasyu with a bright flame, or with water. The noble one (*arya*) is the son of a lord. The Bekanāṭas are indeed usurers; or those who deal in double [interest]; or those who give double; or those who desire double.
Indra [overcomes] all the Bekanāṭas, and by his power he overcomes the Paṇis.

Indra is he who [overcomes] all the Bekanāṭas—the "day-seers," that is, those who see the sun, or those who think, "We see these days, but not the future ones. He overcomes them through his action, as well as the Paṇis, the merchants. 6.26
O Ādityas, protect us with life before we are struck down;
for how indeed are you hearers of our invocation?

"May he run toward us while we are still alive, before our slaughter! Where indeed are you, O ye who hear our call?"—this is what they declare as the seer's vision regarding fish that have fallen into a net. The fish move about in the water; or rather, they become intoxicated with one another for the sake of devouring each other. A *jāla* (net) is that which moves in the water (*jala-cara*), or that which is born in the water (*jala-bhava*), or that which lies in the water (*jala-śaya*).
*Aṃhuraḥ* means "one who possesses distress" (*aṃhas-vān*); *aṃhūraṇa* is also a term used for him.
"Making wide space from narrowness"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (*nigama*).
"The seers fashioned seven boundaries; even one who goes beyond only one of them becomes possessed of sin.

The seers established seven boundaries. Even by transgressing just one of them, one becomes sinful. [These are: theft, violating the teacher's bed, killing a Brahmin, killing an embryo, drinking liquor, repeatedly performing evil deeds, and making a false claim regarding a grave offense.
*Bata* is an indeclinable particle [used] in the senses of distress and compassion (6.27). "Alas, alas! You are such a man, O Yama; we have found neither your mind nor your heart.
Surely another woman will embrace you, as a girth-band encircles a yoked horse, or as a creeper clings to a tree."

"Alas, you have become one who has passed beyond strength! Alas, O Yama, you are weak! I do not recognize either your mind or your heart. Surely another shall embrace you, as a creeper (*libujā*) embraces a tree, or as a girth-belt (*kakṣyā*) embraces a yoked horse. *Libujā* is a climbing plant (*vratati*); it is so called because "it clings" (*līyate*) while dividing [the tree], and because it is a choice (*vrata*) among creepers, and because of its spreading (*tanana*). "Vātāpya" means water; for the wind (*vāta*) causes this to swell (*āpyāyayati*).
There is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) which says: "Purifying himself, he reaches the all-shining vātāpya."

"In the forest, Vāyu was not placed; he delighted in the forest. [The word] *vāyo* is the son of *vī*. Or rather, it means "observing" (*cāyan*) or "desiring" (*kāmayamāna*). Śākalya has composed [the text] with both *veti* and *ya iti*. However, had it been so, the verb would have been accented on the first syllable (*udātta*). Furthermore, the meaning would remain incomplete. [The form] *ratharyati* is established as one who desires to obtain that; or it means "he desires a chariot."
"This god speeds along in his chariot"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (Nigama).
"Make our nourishment swell like a cow that does not stray;
[make it] one that does not stray."
"Ādhava" is derived from "ādhavana" (shaking/stirring).
There is also a Vedic verse (nigama) which says: "The means for the thoughts and the sustainer of the sages.
"Anavabrava" means one whose speech is never cast down or disparaged.
"Like Indra, the maker of victory, he is unassailable"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (Nigama).
"O one-eyed, misshapen, and deformed Arayi, go to the mountain, O ever-seeking one! With the powers of Śirimbiṭha, we drive you away with them."

Regarding *adāyin*, *kāṇa*, and *vikaṭa*: Aupamanyava says that *kāṇa* means "one whose vision has failed. Alternatively, it may derive from the root *kan* in the sense of the action of becoming minute (*aṇubhāva*). Or it may derive from the root *kaṇ*, which is stated to mean the becoming minute of sound; as in the expression "it resounds faintly" (*anukaṇati*). Because of the minuteness of its measure, it is *kaṇa*; because of the minuteness of its vision, it is *kāṇa*. Aupamanyava says that *vikaṭa* means "one whose gait has failed. Or it may derive from the root *kuṭ* in the sense of being distorted; he becomes distorted (*vikuṭita*). [As in the command: "Go to the mountain! [And] "O you who always produce sound after [the wind]!"

"By the beings of Śirimbiṭha. Śirimbiṭha is a cloud; it is shattered (*śīryate*) in the *biṭha*. *Biṭha* is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*); *biṭha* is explained by *bīriṭa*. It would mean "by its beings," that is, by the waters. Having sacrificed with them, we drive away [misfortune]. Or alternatively, Śirimbiṭha was Bhāradvāja, afflicted by *kālakarṇī* (the ill-omened ear). He caused misfortune (*alakṣmī*) to perish. It would mean "by his beings," that is, by his ritual acts. Having sacrificed with them, we drive away [misfortune]; the root *cātayati* means "to destroy. Parāśara was born from the aged Vasiṣṭha who had been cast away (*parāśīrṇa*).
"Parāśara, Śatayātu, and Vasiṣṭha"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (nigama).
Indra also is called Parāśara; "Indra became the Parāśara of the Yātus"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse. "Parāśara" means one who utterly destroys (parā-śātayitā) the Yātus.

*Krivirdatī* means "one with jagged teeth. There is also a Vedic verse: "Where your lightning bolt, *krivirdatī*, strikes. *Karūlatī* means "one with cut teeth. Or rather, having seen some god with cut teeth, one might have spoken thus. (6.30)
O Āduri, may the divine Aryaman grant you what is most desirable, again and again.
May Pūṣan grant us what is desirable; may Bhaga grant us what is desirable; may the god Karūlatī grant us what is desirable.

The left side is desirable (*vananīya*). *Āduri* means from *ādaraṇa* (reverence). Regarding that, who is *karūlatī*? One view is that *bhaga* is its subsequent designation; another is that it is *pūṣan*. He is toothless. "Pūṣan is toothless"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"O Indra, [subdue] the tribes that speak harshly.
O Indra, make us humans—those whose minds are toward giving—gentle in speech.
"This cruel man regards me as if I were without a protector;
this fool, wishing to shatter me, regards me as if I were weak.

Here, "desiring this" (*idam-yu*) means desiring this object. Furthermore, it is also used in the sense of the object itself, as in "Indra is a seeker of wealth" (*vasu-yu*), where the meaning is "possessing wealth."
"Indra is the seeker of horses, the seeker of cattle, the seeker of chariots, the seeker of wealth"—thus also occurs a *nigama*.

"What do your cows among the Kīkaṭas do? They do not yield the milk-mixture (*āśira*), nor do they heat the *gharma* vessel. Bring to us the wealth of Pramaganda; O Maghavan, make Naicāśākha subject to us."

"What do your cows do among the Kīkaṭas?"—the country called Kīkaṭa is an abode of non-Aryans. What have the Kīkaṭas done? It means "what by their actions," or it expresses a desire for something. They do not even milk [their cows] with curds; they do not heat the *gharma* vessel in the sacrificial hall. "Bring to us the wealth of Pramaganda. A *maganda* is a usurer; one who gives thinking, "He will come back to me again" is a *māṅgada*. His offspring is a *pramaganda*: one born into a family of extreme usurers.

Or [the word *prārdaka* refers to] one who is a *pramada*, desiring that "this world alone exists, not the other"; or it is a *paṇḍaka*. A *paṇḍaka* is a *paṇḍaga*; or a *prārdaka* because he crushes (*prārdati*) the testicles. He causes the two testicles (*āṇḍau*) to feel shame (*vrīḍayati*), as they are like two *āṇis* (axle-pins). That [place] is the *naicāśākha*; *nīcāśākha* means having low branches (*nīcaiḥ śākhaḥ*). Branches (*śākhāḥ*) come from the root *śak* (to be able). An *āṇi* comes from *araṇ* (to move). [The mantra says: "O Maghavan, subject us to that. The root *radh* signifies coming under control.

*Bunda* is an arrow; or it is a piercer (*bhinda*); or it is a giver of fear (*bhayada*); or it is so called because it flies while shining (*bhāsamānaḥ*). "Powerful is your well-made, pleasant bow; excellent is the golden arrow. (6.32)
Both your arms are worthy of battle, well-fashioned, and though they are of soft form, they are increasers of softness.

Your bow is well-crafted, pleasant, and very easy to handle, whether it be of great reach, wide range, or immense scope. Your arrow-head is made of gold. Both your arms are beautiful and fit for battle. They are of soft form, yet they strike with piercing force; they strike with speed, strike with sound, strike from afar, or strike upon the vital organs. They pierce with a crushing blow, or they pierce with speed (or strike with sound, or strike from afar).
He pierced [the enemy] from the mountains and brought away the cooked rice.
Indra [struck] the most self-surrendering Bunda.

He pierced [the clouds] from the mountains and held the cooked rice; [he held] the cloud that bestows water. Indra [held] the *bunda* most well-strung. *Vṛnda* is explained by *bunda*. And *vṛndāraka* [is derived from it]. 6.34 This one who is the Hotṛ—what indeed is he? To whom does Yama belong? Whatever the gods agree upon, that they carry out.
Day by day he is born, month by month; thus, O gods, you have established him as the bearer of oblations.

This one who is the Hotṛ, the agent, carries forth some food for Yama—that which the gods partake of. Day by day he is born; month by month; or half-month by half-month. Then the gods established him as the bearer of oblations. *Ulba* is from the root *ūrṇoti* (to cover) or from *vṛṇoti* (to choose). "That *ulba* was great; that was firm," so there is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*).
*Ṛbīsam* means "devoid of luster," "stripped of luster," "hidden from luster," or "gone from luster.
"With snow you two warded off the burning fire; you bestowed upon him nourishing strength."
O Aśvins, you raised up Atri, who had been cast into the cauldron, together with all his followers, in safety.

With the water of the snowfall at the end of summer, you two warded off the scorching heat of the fire. And for this Agni, you bestowed nourishing strength. That fire which was within the *ṛbīsa* (the earth's womb), within the plants and trees, and within the waters—that you two brought forth, with all its hosts and all its names. "Host" (*gaṇa*) is so called because of numbering (*gaṇanāt*), and also because of quality (*guṇa*). When the plants rise up after rain and living beings [awaken] upon the earth, that is the form of the Aśvins; with that he praises them, he praises them. 6.36

O Agni, you who are the devourer, root out the *ajāsaḥ* and the *upalaprakṣiṇī*. O Karūru, we are here for you; I have heard them as if they were seeking refuge. O Indra, [drink] the Soma, the resonant one; O Indras, make the Somas [ready]. Perform your heroic deeds at the sacrifice; there is help for us. Proclaim it in the unformed [space]; let it be spread at every stroke. He who is for us—for him alone is that. Urge on our fourth [portion]; do not [hold back] this praise. Let not the wicked ones seize you like barley with a wolf. Bless us, O cow! O stingy one, O one-eyed one, [give] wealth after wealth. What is yours? To the one of many clans, he has cast it away. This one who is the Hotṛ [has done so] with frost to the fire. Thirty-six.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the first six books of the *Nirukta*; thus the section on individual words (*naigama-kāṇḍa*) and the first half are completed;
now the second six books (*uttara-ṣaṭka*) begins.

Now begins the seventh chapter. Om! Now, therefore, concerning the deities (*daivata*). Those names which belong to the deities who are praised for their preeminence are called "the section on deities" (*daivata*).
This is the investigation of the deities.
Whatever desire a seer has, and whichever deity he intends to seek lordship over when he offers praise, that mantra becomes dedicated to that deity.
These ṛcs are of three kinds:
those composed in the third person (parokṣakṛtāḥ), those composed in the second person (pratyakṣakṛtāḥ), and those concerning the self (ādhyātmikyaḥ).
In that regard, those [mantras] composed in the absence [of the deity] are joined with all case-endings of nouns; and [they contain] the third person forms of the verb:
"Indra rules over heaven, Indra rules over earth;
to Indra alone the singers sing loudly."
These Tr̥tsus, serving zealously under Indra—
sing a Sāman for Indra!
Without Indra, no domain whatsoever flows pure.
"I shall now proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra;
in Indra, desires have been directed. Thus [it is said].
Now follow the forms made in the direct [address] through the use of the second person and by this pronoun "thou" (*tvam*).
"O Indra, [bestow] from thy power...
"O Indra, strike down our enemies.
Thus it is; moreover, the singers are addressed directly, while those worthy of praise are addressed indirectly.
"By no means praise anything else! O Kaṇvas, sing forth! Come hither, O Kuśikas, and take heed! Thus [he said].
Now follow the internal applications for the Supreme Person, by means of this pronoun "I" (*aham*). For example: "Indra Vaikuṇṭha," the *Labasūkta*, and the *Vāgāmbhṛṇīya*. 7.2

The majority of mantras are those addressed to deities who are beyond perception (*parokṣa*) and those addressed to deities who are perceptible (*pratyakṣa*); those concerning the inner self (*ādhyātmika*) are few.
Furthermore, they often consist of praise alone rather than a formal benediction (*āśīrvāda*), as in this hymn: "I shall proclaim the heroic deeds of Indra. Thus it is in this very *sūkta*.
Moreover, there are indeed benedictions, not praises, such as:

"May I be well-eyed with my two eyes; may I be radiant of countenance; may I be well-hearing with my two ears. This [type of formula] is abundant among the Adhvaryu priests and in sacrificial mantras.
Furthermore, there are also oaths and curses.
"May I die this very day if I am a sorcerer;
may he then be separated from his ten terrible sons.
Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, there is the desire to express a certain state of being.
There was neither death nor immortality at that time;
there was only darkness hidden by darkness.
Furthermore, there was a sign of lamentation arising from some state of being.
"May Sudeva fly away today, never to return; I do not know whether I am ignorant or whether I possess knowledge.
Thus [he speaks], and furthermore, there are both censures and praises.
"He who eats alone becomes solely a vessel for sin;
this house of the eater is like a lotus pond.
Thus, in the Akṣasūkta, there is both a censure of gambling and a praise of agriculture.
Thus, through various high and low intentions, the visionary insights of the seers (*ṛṣi*) arise.
7.3 Now, regarding those mantras whose deities have not been specifically prescribed, there is an investigation into their deities:
whatever deity belongs to that sacrifice or that constituent part of the sacrifice, they have that as their deity.
Now, as for those other than the sacrifice:
the ritualists call them *prājāpatya*,
while the etymologists call them *nārāśaṃsa*.
Or rather, that [deity] might be Kāmadevatā,
or perhaps Prāyodevatā; for there is a common practice in the world [to designate deities] as "having the gods as deity," "having guests as deity," or "having the ancestors as deity."
"A mantra has a deity as its object of sacrifice.

For even those who are not deities are praised as if they were deities, such as the things beginning with horses and ending with plants. Furthermore, there are eight pairs [of deities]. One should not think that these are merely adventitious attributes of the deities; for this is directly perceived. Due to the great majesty (*māhābhāgya*) of the deity, a single self is praised in many ways. Other deities become the various limbs of that one self. Moreover, it is said that the seers praise [the deities] through the various natures of living beings, and because of the universal nature of their essence.
They arise from one another; they have one another as their material cause;
they are born of karma;
they are born of the self.

The self alone becomes their chariot; the self is the horse; the self is the weapon; the self is the arrows; the self is everything for the god. 7.4 Regarding this, the etymologists (nairuktāḥ) say there are only three deities:
Agni, whose station is the earth; Vāyu or Indra, whose station is the intermediate space; and Sūrya, whose station is the sky.
Due to their great majesty, each one of them has many names; or rather, because of the diversity of their functions,
just as there are the titles Hotṛ, Adhvaryu, Brahman, and Udgātṛ even for a single person.

Or rather, they should be distinct; for there are separate praises and separate designations. As for the argument that "because of the separateness of the ritual acts," even many [priests] may perform the acts by dividing them.
In this regard, the unity of configuration and the unity of enjoyment are to be disregarded.

For example, there is unity of place, as in "humans, animals, and gods on earth," and unity of enjoyment is also observed. For instance, the earth has enjoyment through rain, and through wind and the sun; and fire has enjoyment through the rest of the world.
In this regard, it is like a kingdom of men (7.5).
Now follows the consideration of the forms of the deities:
one view is that they are anthropomorphic.
Praises are offered by those possessing volition;
likewise are the designations.
Moreover, they are praised by means of the constituent parts (aṅga) that pertain to the human form.
Lofty are your arms, O Indra, you who are steadfast,
when you grasp the *kāśī* [spear], O Maghavan;
and also by means of substances associated with manly exploits.
Come, O Indra, with your two bay horses;
your wife is auspicious and your home is a source of delight.
Moreover, [you are honored] by deeds that manifest your manly prowess.
"O Lord of the Path, drink of what has been set forth;
O you whose ears hear, listen to our call. (7.6) "They should be non-human," is another [view].

Rather, that which is seen in human form is as follows: fire, wind, the sun, the earth, and the moon. As for the statement that praises are "as if endowed with consciousness," even insentient things are praised in this way, such as those beginning with the axle and ending with the plants.
Furthermore, regarding the statement that they are praised by means of limbs having human form, this also applies to insentient objects:
"They neigh toward [the sacrifice] with their green horses."
Thus ends the praise of the pressing-stones (*grāvastuti*).
As for that which concerns the substances associated with the *puruṣavidhi* rites, that too is of the same nature.
"He has yoked the easy-moving chariot drawn by the horses of the Sindhu."
Thus ends the praise of the river.
As for that which was said regarding "rites performed according to human form," that too is exactly like this:
"Even before the Hotṛ priest, they attained the right to eat the sacrificial oblation."
Thus [it is] the Grāvastut [priest] alone. Or rather, they may be of both kinds.

Or rather, while being of the nature of persons, these may have ritual action as their essence, just as the sacrifice is the essence of the sacrificer. And this is the established rule for narrative accounts. 7.7
It has been stated previously that there are only three deities. We shall now explain their association with their respective portions (*bhakti*).
Now, these [verses] belong to the portions of Agni.

This world, the morning pressing, spring, the *gāyatrī* metre, the *trivṛt* hymn-form, and the *rathaṃtara* chant; and those groups of deities enumerated in the first position; and the females, namely Agnāyī and Pṛthivī—this is its [the Fire’s] domain. Now, its function: the carrying of oblations and the summoning of the deities.
And whatever pertains to the range of vision is indeed the work of fire. Now, its associated deities are Indra, Soma, Varuṇa, Parjanya, and the Seasons.
And the oblation dedicated to Agni and Viṣṇu.

However, no hymn of praise consisting of ten verses is found among the *Ṛgveda* collections; nevertheless, there is an oblation for Agni and Pūṣan, though it is not a hymn of praise. In this regard, they cite this verse as an example of a distributed praise (7.8).
May Pūṣan, the wise guardian of the world whose cattle are never lost, drive you forth from here.
May he entrust you to these ancestors and to Agni, who is well-disposed toward the gods.

"May Pūṣan cause you to move from here—he who is wise, whose cattle are never lost, the guardian of the world. For this Āditya is indeed the protector (*gopāyitā*) of all beings. "He shall entrust you to these Fathers"—this third quarter-verse is subject to doubt. One view is that it is a reference (*anvādeśa*) to him [Pūṣan] from the preceding [quarter]. Another view is that it is a mention (*prakīrtana*) of him [Agni] from the subsequent [quarter]: "Agni for the gods who are well-disposed; wealth is *suvidatra*. It is derived from the root *vid* with one prefix, or it may be from the root *dā* with two prefixes. 7.9
Now, these belong to Indra:

the intermediate world, the midday pressing, the summer season, the triṣṭubh metre, the fifteenfold stoma, the bṛhat sāman, and those groups of gods who are enumerated as belonging to the middle station.
And as for the women;

furthermore, his bestowing of the essence of action was the slaying of Vṛtra, and whatever feat of strength there was, that too was indeed the work of Indra. Now, his associated deities are as follows.
Agni, Soma, Varuṇa, Pūṣan, Bṛhaspati, Brahmaṇaspati, Parvata, Kutsa, Viṣṇu,
and Vāyu; furthermore, Mitra is praised together with Varuṇa, Soma with Pūṣan and Rudra, and Pūṣan with Agni (or Vāyu, according to a variant reading).
And by means of the wind, Parjanya [is sustained]. 7.10. Now these are the divisions of Āditya:

yonder world is the third pressing; the rainy season is the *jagatī* meter, the seventeenfold hymn-form (*saptadaśastoma*), and the *vairūpa* chant; and those hosts of gods who are enumerated in the highest station.
And as for women;
furthermore, its function is the taking up of sap by means of rays and the holding of that sap—whatever is thus conveyed is indeed the work of the Sun.
This is the praise [of the Sun] in conjunction with the Moon, the Wind, and the Year.
Within these very arrangements of stations (*sthānavyūha*), one should determine the remaining distribution (*bhakti*) according to the season, the metre, the *stoma*, and the *pṛṣṭha* chant.
"Autumn, the *anuṣṭubh* metre, the twenty-one-fold *stoma*, and the *vairāja* sāman" are those whose abode is the earth.
"Winter, the *paṅkti* metre, the twenty-seven-fold *stoma*, and the *śākvara* sāman" are those whose abode is the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*).

"Śiśira, aticchandas, the thirty-threefold stoma, and the raivata sāman"—these are the divisions of the day. 7.11. Mantras are so called because of their power to reflect; the meters (*chandas*) because they cover; and the *stoma* because of its power to praise.
The *yajus* is derived from the root *yaj* (to sacrifice);
the *sāman* is measured by the *ṛc*,
or else it is derived from the root *as* (to throw).
"The *ṛc* is equal to thought," say the Naidānas.
The *gāyatrī* is so called from the root *gā*, meaning "to praise";
or it is "threefold in its movement," or the reverse. And the Brāhmaṇa says: "It sprang forth from the mouth of the one who was singing."

The *uṣṇih* is so called because it has been bathed (*utsnātā*). Or it may derive from the root *snih*, meaning "to love" or "to shine," as in "she who possesses a turban" (*uṣṇīṣiṇī*), which is a metaphorical expression; for *uṣṇīṣa* comes from the root *snā*. The *kakubh* is so called because it is "exalted" (*kakubhinī*). *Kakup* and *kubja* both derive from the root *kuj* ("to croak") or from the root *ubj* ("to bend"). The *anuṣṭubh* is so called because of its "repeated chanting" (*anuṣṭobhana*). For the *Brāhmaṇa* states: "It repeatedly chants after the three-footed *gāyatrī* with a fourth foot. The *bṛhatī* is so called because of its "expansion" (*paribarhaṇa*). The *paṅkti* has five feet. The *triṣṭubh* "chants" (*stobhati*) with its final foot.
But what is *tritā*? It is the most crossed-over (*tīrṇatama*) among the meters; it is the threefold (*trivṛt*) thunderbolt. It "stobhas" (resounds) for that [thunderbolt];
because it stobbed thrice, that is the *triṣṭubh*-ness of the *triṣṭubh*. Thus it is known.
7.12 The *jagatī* is the most gone-to (*gatatama*) among the meters, or it is the gait of water-dwellers.
"He created it while melting," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
She is *Virāj* because of her shining forth (*virājanāt*), or because of her ruling (*virādhanāt*), or because of her bestowing abundantly (*viprāpaṇāt*).
Through shining forth she has complete syllables; through ruling she has deficient syllables; through bestowing abundantly she has redundant syllables.
The "ant-middled" (*pipīlikamadhyā*) is an illustrative example. The word *pipīlikā* [is derived] from the root *pela*, meaning "to move.

Thus have these deities been enumerated; they are for the most part recipients of hymns (*sūkta*), recipients of oblations (*havis*), and recipients of verses (*ṛc*). Some, however, are recipients of particles (*nipāta*).
Then, having joined them with their respective designations, he impels the oblation:

"For Indra, the slayer of Vṛtra; for Indra, the overcomer of Vṛtra; for Indra, the deliverer from distress. Some authorities recite these as well, but they are more numerous according to the traditional recension.
As for that which constitutes a distinct cognition, it is recited as a praise of the principal [deity].
Alternatively, the seer praises the deities through their ritual functions, such as "Vṛtrahā" (Slayer of Vṛtra) and "Purandara" (Destroyer of Forts).
Some indeed recite these as well; however, because they are more numerous than the [principal] recitation, they serve merely as phonetic supplements (*vyañjana*) to that designation.
Just as one says: "Give rice to the hungry Brahmin; [give] ointment to the one who has bathed; [give] water to the thirsty. 7.13 Now, therefore, we shall set forth the sequence:
Fire has the earth as its locus; we shall explain that first.
Why "agni"? He is a leader (*agraṇī*). He is led to the forefront in sacrifices.
Or, he leads (*nayati*) his own body (*aṅga*) while bowing down. "He is not wettable" (*aknopana*), says Sthaulāṣṭhīvi;

he does not cause to moisten, he does not cause to become oily. Śākapūṇi says he is born from three verbal roots: from *ita*, from *akta* (anointed) or *dagdha* (burnt), and from *nīta* (led). He takes the letter *a* from the root *eti* (to go), the letter *g* from either *añjati* (to anoint) or *dahati* (to burn), with *nī* following. Of him, this verse occurs: 7.14.
I praise Agni, the domestic priest, the divine minister of the sacrifice,
the invoker, the bestower of most abundant treasures.
