"I praise Agni; I entreat Agni. *Īli* is a word for the act of entreating, or for the act of honoring. "Purohita" has been explained, as has "sacrifice" (*yajña*). [He is called] "God" (*deva*) because of giving, or because of kindling, or because of shining; or because he dwells in heaven (*dyu*). That which is a god is a deity. "Hotṛ" means one who offers oblations; Aurṇavābha says it is from the root *hu* (to sacrifice), thus "Hotṛ. "Most bestowing of jewels" means the most excellent giver of delightful riches. Regarding him, there is this other verse:
"Agni is to be praised by the ancient seers and by the modern ones as well; may he bring the gods here. (7.15)
"Agni, who was to be praised by the ancient seers and is to be honored by us who are newer—may he bring the gods here.
One should not think, "This alone is Agni"; for these two other lights are also called Agnis. Therefore, from among them, the middle one [is intended]:
"May they advance toward Agni like women at a gathering, beautiful and smiling."
The streams of clarified butter reach the fuel; enjoying them, Jātavedas takes delight in them.

Bowing down like women toward a gathering—*samana* being so called either from *sam-anana* (coming together), or from *sam-mānana* (honoring)—the beautiful ones, smiling, [approach] Agni; this is a simile. The streams of clarified butter, the streams of water, reach the fuel-sticks (*samidhaḥ*). The root *nas* means either "to reach" or "to bend. Being pleased by them, Jātavedas desires them; *haryati* is a verb meaning "to desire to obtain," as in the expression "he moves about desiring."

"A wave rich in sweetness has arisen from the ocean"—thus they consider this to refer to Āditya; for the Brāhmaṇa says, "For he rises from the waters of the ocean. Furthermore, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "Agni is all the deities. The following verse serves to provide a further etymological explanation:
"They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni; and he is the divine, fair-winged Garutman."
The wise speak of the one Reality in many ways; they call it Agni, Yama, and Mātariśvan.

The wise speak of this very great Self as Agni in many ways—as Indra, Mitra, Varuṇa, Agni, and the celestial Garuḍa. "Celestial" (divya) means born in heaven; "Garuḍa" means one who goes in a flock, or one whose self is heavy, or the Great Self. He who partakes of the hymn and for whom the oblation is prepared—he is indeed this Agni. These two subsequent lights partake of this very name as a mere designation. 7.18

Why is he called Jātavedas? Because he knows (*veda*) what has been born (*jātāni*); or because beings know him; or because he is found (*vidyate*) at every birth; or because his wealth (*vitto*) is born; or because his riches (*dhana*) are born; or because his knowledge (*vidyā*) is born, or his wisdom (*prajñāna*) is born.

"Since, once born, he found the cattle," that is why Jātavedas is called Jātavedas—so says the Brāhmaṇa. And: "Therefore, during all the seasons, the cattle creep toward Agni. Regarding him, there is this verse (RV 1.99.1): "Let us press the Soma for Jātavedas; may he burn away the wealth (*vedas*) of him who acts with hostility."
May he, Agni, carry us across all difficulties, as one crosses a river with a boat, beyond all misfortunes.

"Jātavedase"—this refers to the *jātavedasyā* [verse]. Likewise, "to Jātavedas we press the Soma for worship. For the sake of impulsion—that is, for the pressing—the immortal King Soma is [offered] for the purpose of sacrifice; thus we say. "He burns up"—he certainly burns, he reduces to ashes. The meaning is that Soma bestows [the goal]. "May He carry us across all difficulties"—that is, across all impassable places. Just as one crosses a river with a boat, so He carries us across the river, the river that is difficult due to its waters, possessing great banks.
"Over misfortunes, Agni"—he carries us across misfortunes. Of him, there is this other verse (inserted):
"Now indeed, urge on Jātavedas, the vigorous steed, so that he may sit upon this our sacrificial grass."

"Drive away Jātavedas who has attained [his goal] through his deeds. Or rather, it may be used in a comparative sense: "Like a horse, [drive away] Jātavedas," as in "May he sit upon this our sacrificial grass (barhis).
Thus, this very single *jātavedas*-verse in the *gāyatrī* meter is found among the *daśatayīs*.
Whatever is addressed to Agni may be employed in the place of the *jātavedas* verses.
He should not think, "This alone is Agni. For these two other lights are also called Jātavedas. Of these, the middle one is [the fire] from which [the others proceed].
"They hasten toward him like maidens to a gathering"—this has been explained previously.
Now, this is the sun.

"Behold that Jātavedas... We shall explain this later. That Agni who partakes of the hymn and for whom the oblation is set aside—he alone is Jātavedas. These two subsequent lights also partake of this very name as a designation. Why "Vaiśvānara"? Because he leads all men; or, all men lead him. Or rather, he may be Viśvānara himself. All beings are turned toward him; thus he is Vaiśvānara. Regarding him, there is this verse: 7.21. "Behold that Jātavedas... We shall explain this later. "Behold that Jātavedas... We shall explain this later. That Agni who partakes of the hymn and for whom the oblation is
May we abide in the good-will of Vaiśvānara; for he is the king, the glory of all beings.
Born from here, he beholds this entire universe; Vaiśvānara strives in harmony with the Sun.

Born from this [earth], he beholds all this; Vaiśvānara unites with the sun. May we abide in the auspicious thought of that Vaiśvānara who is the king of all beings and the one to be sought for refuge. Now, who is Vaiśvānara? The teachers say it is the intermediate [fire] (the lightning), for they praise him by means of his act of raining:
"Let me now proclaim the greatness of the bull, whom the Pūrus attend as the slayer of Vṛtra.
Agni Vaiśvānara, having struck down the Dasyu, shook the quarters and shattered Śambara. (RV 3.18.4)

I shall explain that greatness and majesty of the Bull, the showerer of waters, whom the Pūrus—men who are to be fulfilled—attend upon and serve, desiring rain, for he is the slayer of Vṛtra, the destroyer of the clouds. *Dasyu* comes from the root *das*, in the sense of "to destroy"; the juices perish within him, or he destroys the ritual acts. Agni Vaiśvānara, striking him down, shook off the waters and split the firmament; he struck down Śambara, the cloud. Thus say the ancient ritualists: "That is the Sun."

The ascent of these worlds is traditionally taught as the ascent of the *savana*s (pressings). Following that ascent, a descent is intended to be performed. To imitate that process, the Hotṛ priest begins the *agnimāruta* śastra with the Vaiśvānara hymn. He should also pay attention to the *stotriya* verse, for it belongs to Agni. From there, he proceeds to the deities of the middle station: Rudra and the Maruts.
Then, having reached Agni, who is situated here in this world, he recites the *stotriya* right here.

Furthermore, there is a cake on twelve potsherds for Vaiśvānara; for his ritual action is twelvefold. Moreover, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "Yonder sun is indeed Agni Vaiśvānara. Furthermore, there is a *nivit* verse dedicated to Sūrya-Vaiśvānara: "He who shines upon the sky and upon the earth."
For he indeed illuminates heaven and earth;
moreover, there is a hymn belonging to the Chandomas dedicated to Sūrya-Vaiśvānara:
"He shone with his back toward heaven."
For it is said: "He, being praised in heaven, has shone forth.
Furthermore, there is a hymn beginning with *haviṣpāntīyam*, dedicated to Sūrya and Vaiśvānara;
Śākapūṇi maintains that this very Agni is Vaiśvānara. Moreover, these two [deities] mentioned subsequently are Viśva and Nara.

The luminous one is Vaiśvānara, who is born from those two. But how is he born from these two? When the lightning strikes a shelter, as long as it has not yet been taken up, it remains characterized by the intermediate state, with water as its fuel and the body as its extinguisher. At the very moment it is being taken up, it becomes one whose extinguisher is water and whose radiance is the body.

Now, from the sun: when the sun has first turned toward the north, having wiped clean a bronze vessel or a gem, he holds it at the focal point where dry cow-dung does not touch it; there it blazes up. This very fire is thus produced. Moreover, it is said: "Vaiśvānara strives with the sun. Yet, the self does not strive with itself; one thing is made to strive by another. From here he places this [fire], and from there the rays of that [sun] appear. Seeing the meeting of their two splendors—the rays from there and the flames from here—one would speak thus.

Now, as for those final hymns—whether they belong to Bhaga, Savitṛ, Sūrya, Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, or the Viśvedevas—in them there would have been references to Vaiśvānara; and one would have praised him through the act of Āditya, saying, "He rises," "He sets," or "He moves across. For it is indeed in the hymns addressed to Agni that there are references to Vaiśvānara; and one praises him through the act of Agni, saying, "Thou carriest," "Thou cookest," or "Thou burnest."
As for the statement that "he praises him by means of the act of rain," this is also appropriate here:
"This same water rises up and flows down through the days;
Parjanya quickens the earth, and the fires quicken the sky."
Thus it is explained by the words themselves (nigadavyākhyātā). 7.23:
The well-winged bay horses, clothed in the waters, fly up to heaven as their path;
they have returned from the seat of Ṛta, and since then the earth is moistened with clarified butter.

The night is the dark downward path of the sun; the *harayaḥ* are the golden-winged carriers, the rays of the sun. When they turn back from there toward this side, together with their place—the water—from the sun, then the earth is moistened by *ghṛta*, that is, by water. *Ghṛta* is a name for water, derived from the root *ghṛ*, meaning "to sprinkle. Furthermore, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage [to this effect].

"Agni indeed impels the rain from here; having become the sky, he rains while covering the dwellings; the Maruts lead forth the released rain. When indeed that sun revolves around Agni with his rays, then it rains. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "the descent is intended after the ascent," this occurs because of the scriptural injunction.
Moreover, regarding the statement "there is a cake for Vaiśvānara on twelve potsherds," there is no fixed rule as to how many potsherds there shall be.
For there is indeed a cake on one potsherd for Sūrya and one on five potsherds for Vaiśvānara.
As for the Brāhmaṇa passage that occurs [regarding this], Brāhmaṇas are indeed full of various figurative expressions: "Vaiśvānara is the earth; Vaiśvānara is the year; Vaiśvānara is the Brāhmaṇa.
And as for the statement that the *nivit* formula belongs to both Sūrya and Vaiśvānara, it belongs to him who shines upon the human clans (*viś*); for he indeed shines upon the human clans.

As for this statement that "the *sūkta* used in the *Chandomas* is dedicated to Sūrya-Vaiśvānara," it belongs to this very [deity]. "Offered by the Jamadagnis"—the Jamadagnis are either those whose fires have been well-kindled (*prajamita*), or those whose fires are blazing (*prajvalita*). By them, he is offered. (As for this statement that "the *sūkta* used in the *Chandomas* is dedicated to Sūrya-Vaiśvānara," it belongs to this very [deity]: "Offered by the Yamadagnis"—the Yamadagnis are either those whose fires have been well-restrained (*prayamita*), or those whose fires are blazing. By them, he is offered. [This is a variant reading.]*)
As for the statement that this hymn, *Haviṣpāntīya*, is dedicated to Sūrya-Vaiśvānara, it belongs to this very [deity]:

"The oblation-drinker, ageless, finding the light, touching the sky, offered as a welcome gift in Agni—for the bearing of that world and for its upholding, the gods have spread themselves out according to their own inherent power. (RV 10.88.1)

The oblation is the water that is ageless, known by the sun, touching the heavens, offered into the fire, and well-pleasing. For its supporting, its nourishing, and its sustaining—for all these activities—the gods spread out this Agni with food. And so it is also said:
"In the lap of the waters, the mighty ones seized him; the subjects stood near the king who is worthy of praise."
Mātariśvan brought Agni Vaiśvānara as a messenger from afar, from Vivasvat.

In the lap of the waters, in the great expanse of the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), the great ones sat; indeed, the divine hosts of the middle region took hold of him. They waited upon him like subjects waiting upon a king. He is worthy of praise, or rather, he possesses hymns of praise; he is worthy of adoration, or rather, he is worthy of worship. Today, the messenger of the gods brought him from Vivasvat, the Āditya. Vivasvat is "the radiant one," meaning either the one who has impelled [him] or the one from whom he has departed. Or else, it refers to Mātariśvan as the bringer of this Agni Vaiśvānara. Mātariśvan is the wind.
He breathes in the mother, the intermediate space; or rather, "the mother neighs. Then he praises him with these two [verses] in all his stations, beginning from the feet:
"The head of the earth becomes Agni by night; from him the sun is born rising in the morning.
But this is the creative power (*māyā*) of the worshipful ones, that he moves swiftly through the waters, knowing [his way]."

The *mūrdhan* (head) is that in which the formed (*mūrta*) is placed. He who is the head of all beings becomes the fire at night; from him the sun is born in the morning as he rises—it is he indeed. But they consider this to be the wisdom of the gods worthy of sacrifice, those who accomplish the sacrifice. Since he performs his work within the waters, knowing them, he moves swiftly through all stations. Of this, the following verse serves for further explanation: "By means of praise (*stoma*), the gods generated Agni in heaven with their powers, filling both worlds."
They made him threefold for existence; he ripens the plants of every form.

For with praise (*stoma*), the gods generated Agni in heaven by means of their powers and ritual acts to fill heaven and earth; they made him threefold for the sake of becoming threefold—on earth, in the intermediate space, and in heaven—so says Śākapūṇi.

"That which is his third [part] in heaven, that is this Āditya," so says the Brāhmaṇa. Having thus made it into Agni, he praises it; then he praises it by making it into Āditya with this [verse]. 7.28
When the gods worthy of the sweet sacrifice [beheld] Sūrya, the son of Aditi, in heaven;
when the two moving ones became a pair, then all the worlds beheld them from the beginning.

When all the gods worthy of sacrifice placed him, Sūrya, the son of Aditi, in heaven; when the two moving pairs appeared, always traveling together—Uṣas and Āditya. Why "mithunau" (a pair)? The root *mi* has the meaning of "to lean upon" (*śrayati*). The suffix *thu* is a name-forming suffix, or rather, it is the letter *tha*. Or [it is] the root *nī* followed by the suffix *van*. They lean upon one another and lead each other. Or they desire (*vanutaḥ*) one another. The human pair also originates from this very same [root]: they rub against (*methantau*) one another and desire one another. Then, having made him into fire by means of this [verse], he praises him: 7.29.

Where the lower and the higher speak, which of us two, the leaders of the sacrifice, knows? Only those friends have succeeded in reaching the common feast; they have attained the sacrifice—who will declare this?

Where the two divine Hotṛ-priests dispute—"This Agni here and that one in the middle, which of us two knows more in the sacrifice?"—they are unable [to decide]. That is the *sahamadanam* (the place of joint exhilaration), for those officiating priests of common renown who share in the sacrifice [think], "Who among us will speak this out?
The following verse is for the further explanation of that:
"As much as the face of the Dawn, O Mātariśvan, when the fair-winged one settles upon her. (RV 10.189.2)
Just then, a Brahmin, approaching the sacrifice and sitting down below the Hotṛ, bestows [the sacrificial gift].
As much as the dawn becomes visible, or rather, as much as it is seen.

There is an application of a simile in its present sense, as in "place it here as it were. [The words] *suparṇyaḥ* mean "those of good flight. "These nights dwell in Mātariśvan, who is of the color of light; he places them down for so long while approaching the sacrifice, as a Brāhmaṇa Hotṛ sits down lower than this Agni, the Hotṛ. But the *hotṛjapa* (the muttering of the Hotṛ) belongs to Agni Vaiśvānara. "O God Savitṛ, they choose you, Agni, for the office of Hotṛ, together with your father Vaiśvānara. By this, he speaks of this very Agni as Savitṛ.

The progenitor of all, whether he be the middle or the highest father—whoever partakes of the hymn and for whom the oblation is set forth, he indeed is this Agni Vaiśvānara. These two latter lights partake of this very name as a designation; they partake, they partake. 7.31

Now, therefore, follows the section on the deities (*daivata*). Indra is the deity of heaven; these are the deities whose actions are performed out of sight. Now, regarding the consideration of their forms: it has been stated that there are only three deities who are not anthropomorphic (*apurushavidha*). Pūṣan is among them. Now follow these divisions belonging to Indra, and then these divisions belonging to Āditya. Because of the act of thinking (*manana*), they are called *mantra*s. Because they have gone to the world (*jagatī*), they are the *gatatama*. Now, therefore, we shall enumerate them in order: "I praise Agni" (*agnim īḷe*); Agni with the ancients; they flow toward Indra; Mitra; Jātavedas. Why? Because he is truly born (*pra-nūnam vai jāta*). Jātavedas; Vaiśvānara. Why? Because of Vaiśvānara's preeminence (*pra-nū*).
The greatness, the black path, the drinker of oblations in the lap of the waters—the head of the world when it is reached by praise, where these two speak as much as is measured by thirty-one.
Thus ends the first chapter in the sixth book [of the Uttarāṣaṭka]. Thus ends the seventh chapter in the Nirukta. Now begins the eighth chapter.

Why "draviṇodas"? Wealth is called *draviṇa*. Because people run toward it (*abhidravanti*), or because strength is *draviṇa*, since by means of it they run forward; its giver is *draviṇodas*. Regarding him, there is this verse (8.1): [Verse follows]
The givers of wealth, with pressing-stones in hand at the sacrifice,
honor the god at the rites who bestows riches.

"You are the giver of wealth (*draviṇodā*). [The word] *draviṇasaḥ* means either "those who possess wealth," or "those who seek wealth," or "those who desire wealth. Or [it may mean] "may he drink from that wealth. They honor the god at the sacrifices; they beg, they praise, they magnify, or they worship him. Who, then, is the giver of wealth? "Indra," says Krauṣṭuki; for he is the greatest giver of strength and riches, and all his actions consist of the exercise of power.
"He was born from *ojas*, and I consider him such," so he says; and furthermore, he speaks of Agni as the *draviṇodas*. Yet this [Agni] is born from that [other]:
"He who generated the fire between the two stones"—thus also there is a *nigama* (Vedic citation).
Moreover, in the Ṛtuyāja offerings, there are references to the Draviṇodas; for them, however, the cup is designated as the "Indra-drink.
Furthermore, he praises him with the term "Soma-drinker," and he also says:
"May the Draviṇodas drink from the cup of the Draviṇodas."

"This Agni alone is Draviṇodās," says Śākapūṇi; for it is only in the hymns addressed to Agni that there occur references to the Draviṇodās. There is also a Vedic citation (nigama) stating: "The gods maintained Agni as the bestower of wealth (draviṇodās).
As for the statement that he is the greatest giver of strength and wealth, sovereignty is found among all the deities.

As for the statement, "I consider him born of vigor," this fire also is born when being churned by vigor—that is, by strength. Therefore, he calls him "the son of strength, the offspring of strength, the child of strength. And as for the statement, "Agni Draviṇodas," here the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are called Draviṇodas; they are the givers of the oblation (*havis*), and they produce him.
"He is the son of the seers, the sovereign ruler"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (Nigama).

As for the statement that "the drinking by Indra" belongs to them again as their vessel, that is merely a figurative designation (bhakti), just as all Soma vessels are called "Vāyavya. Furthermore, the claim that he praises him by means of the drinking of Soma is also applicable in this case.
"Drink the Soma, rejoicing, with your throngs of attendants"—thus also occurs a Vedic verse (*nigama*).
As for this [phrase], "May Draviṇodas drink, O Draviṇodasa," that belongs to this very [deity].
"O Lord of the Forest (*vanaspate*), let those carriers by whom you go be exhilarated; do not cause harm, but settle yourself."
O bold one, drawing near and exerting yourself, drink the Soma from the Neṣṭṛ’s cup with the seasonal rites, O giver of wealth!

Now, therefore, the *āprīs* (propitiatory verses). Why are they called *āprīs*? From the root *āp* ("to reach") or from *prī* ("to please"). "He propitiates with the *āprīs*"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. Of these, the fuel (*idhma*) comes first. It is called *idhma* because it kindles (*samindhana*). Regarding this, there is this verse: "Kindled today in the house of man, O Jātavedas, as a god you sacrifice to the gods.
Bring them hither, O you of Mitra-like luster, you who are observant; you are the messenger, the seer, the wise one. (RV 3.27.1)
"Kindled today in the house of every man, O Jātavedas, you, a god, sacrifice to the gods.

And bring them hither, O you who are great as Mitra! You are the wise messenger, the seer, the one possessed of keen insight and expanded consciousness. Regarding the word *yajñedhma*, Kāṭhaka says it means "the fuel of the sacrifice," while Śākapūṇi says it means "Agni."

"Tanūnapāt [is] the clarified butter," says Kāṭhaka; "Napāt" is the name of the offspring immediately following [the body]. It is most clearly defined. Here, the "body" (*tanū*) is said to be the cow. In her, enjoyments are spread out (*tatā*); from her, milk is produced; from the milk, clarified butter is produced. "Agni," says Śākapūṇi. Here, the "bodies" (*tanvaḥ*) are said to be the waters. They are spread out in the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*). From them, plants and trees are produced; from the plants and trees, this [Agni] is produced. Regarding him, there is this verse (RV 10.70.2):
"O Tanūnapāt, with sweetness, season and prepare the paths by which they go, O fair-tongued one!"
Gratifying my prayers with your wisdom and our sacrifice, perform our ritual among the gods.
We shall praise with sacrifices the greatness of these worshipful ones, who are praised by men—the gods who are wise, pure, and sustainers of prayer, who relish both kinds of oblations.

We praise with sacrifices the greatness of these worshipful ones who are praised by men—those who perform good deeds, who are pure, and who maintain the sacred thought (*dhī*). May the gods make both kinds of oblations palatable: the *soma* and the others; or, as it is said, the *tantra* (fixed) and the *āvāpika* (inserted) rites. *Iḷe* is derived from the root *iḍ*, meaning "to praise," or from *indh*, "to kindle. Regarding this, there is this verse:
"Being invoked, worthy of praise, and venerable, come, O Agni, in harmony with the Vasus!
You are the great Hotṛ-priest of the gods; as such, being impelled, sacrifice for us as the most skilled sacrificer. (RV 8.7)

He is to be summoned, praised, and saluted: "Come hither, O Agni, together with the Vasus, in harmony; you are the great Hotṛ-priest of the gods. *Yahva* is a name for the great one; he is both "gone" (*yāta*) and "summoned" (*hūta*). Being impelled (*iṣita*), he sacrifices for these [gods] as the most excellent sacrificer (*yajīyān*). *Iṣita* means either "impelled" or "commanded," or "entreated. *Yajīyān* means "more excellent at sacrificing. *Barhis* is so called because of its spreading out. Regarding this, there is this verse (RV 10.70.4): "The sacred grass (*barhis*) is strewn eastward according to the direction of the earth; it is spread out at the beginning of the days for her dwelling. It extends further and wider, a pleasant seat for the gods and for Aditi."

"The sacrificial grass (barhis) is strewn eastward according to the direction of the earth, for her clothing, at the beginning of the days, in the forenoon. It is spread out—that is, more widely scattered, or more extensively extended. "Varīyaḥ" means more excellent, or more spacious. It is "syona" for the gods and for Aditi. "Syona" is a name for comfort; it is derived from the root *sī* (to lie down). They rest upon it, or rather, it is that which is to be resorted to. Or, [the word] "dvāraḥ" (doors) is derived from *ju* (to hasten), or *dru* (to run), or *vṛ* (to ward off). Regarding these, there is this verse (RV 8.9).
Let the spacious doors open wide, like women adorning themselves for their husbands; O divine, lofty, all-impelling doors, be easy of access for the gods.

"May they, possessing ornaments, extend themselves in width like wives to their husbands; the thighs, shining beautifully in the act of sexual union—the thighs being the most excellent limb. The divine doors—lofty, great, all-encompassing, for everything comes through them at the sacrifice. ‘The doors of the house,’ says Kāṭhaka; ‘Agni,’ says Śākapūṇi. Dawn and Night—Dawn and Night. Dawn has been explained. ‘Night’ is a name for the night; she anoints all beings with dew. Or rather, ‘Naktā’ means she whose color is unmanifest. Of these two, there is this verse (8.10):"
May the two worshipful ones, Dawn and Night, pressing on together, sit down in their proper place;
the two celestial maidens, lofty and richly adorned, assuming a splendor of radiant hues.

"Whether it means 'causing them to tremble,' or 'causing them to sleep well,' or 'may they sit down,' or 'may they settle down'—the two divine women who have approached the sacrificial ground; the two vast and great ones; the two well-adorned with beautiful ornaments; bestowing upon [Agni] a splendor whose form is bright—the word *śukra* comes from the root *śuc*, meaning 'to blaze'; *peśas* is a name for form, derived from the root *piṃś*, as it becomes 'well-fashioned' (*vipiśita*)—the two divine Hotṛs, the two divine Hotṛ-priests: this Agni here and that one there in the intermediate space. Of these two, this is the verse. (8.11)
The two divine Hotṛ-priests, the first, eloquent ones, being mindful, shall sacrifice for Manu’s rite;
they, the poets, impel [the gods] at the assemblies, pointing toward the east the light by their direction.
The two divine Hotṛ-priests, the first ones of beautiful speech, fashioning the sacrifice for the worship of man;

impelling [the sacrificers] at the rites, the two performers who point out that the sacrifice is to be offered in the eastern direction. Three goddesses—three divine females. Of them, this is the verse (RV 10.70.8):
"May Bhāratī come quickly to our sacrifice, and Ilā, making it manifest here like a human; may the three goddesses, Sarasvatī and the others, sit upon this pleasant, soft seat outside."

May Bhāratī come quickly to our sacrifice; Bhārata is Āditya, and his light is *bhās*. And may Ilā, perceiving here like a human being—these three goddesses, Sarasvatī and [Bhāratī], who perform good deeds—sit upon this pleasant sacrificial grass (*barhis*).

Regarding Tvaṣṭṛ, the etymologists say he is so called because "he swiftly pervades" (*tūrṇam aśnute*); or it may be from the root *tviṣ*, which means "to shine," or from the root *tvakṣ*, which means "to fashion. Of him, there is this verse:
"He who fashioned these two, Heaven and Earth, the parents, and all beings with their forms. (RV 10.70.4)
O Hotṛ, being impelled today, you who are more skilled in sacrifice, worship here as a wise one the god Tvaṣṭṛ.

Him who created these two, Heaven and Earth, the progenitors, and all beings with their forms—worship that god Tvaṣṭṛ here today, O wise one, as the most skilled sacrificer, impelled by the Hotṛ. They say that Tvaṣṭṛ is the intermediate one; he is recorded in the middle station. Śākapūṇi says he is Agni. Of him there is this other verse: "The lovely, desirable one grows within them; upright in the lap of those that lie horizontal, he increases, self-glorious."
Both wives of Tvaṣṭṛ were afraid of him as he was being born; turning toward him, they both find pleasure in the lion.

Until the end of his life, he prospers beautifully among these [women]. "Beautiful" (*cāru*) is derived from the root *car* (to move). "Crookedly" (*jihmam*) is from the root *hī* (to go). "Upright" (*ūrdhvam*) means raised upward. "Self-glorious" (*svayaśāḥ*) means having glory inherent in himself. "In the lap" (*upasthe*) means in the place of rest. Both [Heaven and Earth] were afraid of Tvaṣṭṛ as he was being born. "Facing him, they take pleasure in the lion"—or rather, it refers to Heaven and Earth; or to Day and Night; or to the two kindling-sticks (*araṇī*). "Facing him, they attend upon the lion," that is, the conqueror. 8.15 The *vanaspati* has been explained. This is its verse: 8.16
Release [the victim] by yourself, making it ready for its time; let the gods partake of the oblations according to the seasons.
Let Vanaspati, the divine Agni the immolator, sweeten the offering with honey and ghee.

"May he release himself by means of himself, anointing the food of the gods at every appointed time, the oblations at each proper season. May these three—the Lord of the Forest, the Sacrificer, and the divine Agni—make the offering palatable with honey and with ghee.
"What is this 'Lord of the Forest'? asks Kāṭhaka. "The sacrificial post," says Kāṭhaka. "Agni," says Śākapūṇi. Regarding him, there is this other verse:
"They anoint you, O Lord of the Forest, at the sacrifice, those seeking the gods, with divine honey."
Whatever wealth you have standing above, bestow that here; or whatever is in the dwelling-place within the lap of this mother.

"O Lord of the Forest, desiring the gods, they anoint you at the sacrifice with divine honey and with ghee. When you stand upright, you will bestow riches upon us. Or, as for your dwelling place made within the lap of this mother—Śākapūṇi says it is Agni. Regarding this, there is another verse: 8.18.
O Vanaspati with golden leaves, you carry the oblations to the gods; from of old your purpose has been directed toward them.
Moving clockwise, having fastened the sacrificial cord, you bear [the offerings] along the straightest paths of Truth.

O Vanaspati, golden-leaved one, whose leaves are the *ṛta*, carry the oblations to the gods—or perhaps "golden-leaved" may be used here in the sense of "comparable to gold," meaning "having leaves of golden color. From of old has been your purpose; that is your ancient purpose which we declare to you: "Carry [the offerings] along the straightest paths of the sacrifice—by the most level, or by the most radiant, or by the most glowing ones. Regarding this, there is another verse: "O Vanaspati, having bound it with the most refined cord, you who know the sacred ordinances (*vayunāni*), carry the offerings to the gods, O seeker of honor; and proclaim the giver among the immortals."

O Lord of the Forest, having bound [the victim] with a most beautiful cord, you who know the ways, who understand the insights, bring the gods to the sacrifice and carry the offerings of the donor. And announce the donor among the immortal gods. Regarding the *svāhā*-utterances:
"Svāhā" means "He has spoken this," or "The good voice has spoken," or "He has spoken what is his own," or "He offers the oblation well-sacrificed. Of these, there is this verse:
"As soon as he was born, Agni measured out the sacrifice; he became the leader of the gods. (RV 10.52.3)
May the gods eat the oblation consecrated with Svāhā in the speech of this Hotṛ, according to the direction of Ṛta.

"Being born at once, he fashioned the sacrifice; Agni became the leader of the gods. At the direction of this Hotṛ, in the speech of the Ṛta, let the gods eat the oblation consecrated with Svāhā in his mouth"—thus they sacrifice.
Thus have these Āprī deities been enumerated.
Now, what are the deities of the *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s? Some say they belong to Agni (8.21).

O gods, grant me the fore-sacrifices and the after-sacrifices in their entirety, a portion of the oblation rich in vigor; grant me the fatness of the waters and the essence of the plants, and may there be long life for me from Agni.
May the fore-offerings and the after-offerings be yours alone; may the portions of the oblation be full of vigor.
O Agni, let this entire sacrifice be yours; may the four quarters bow down before you.

"The *prayāja*s belong to Agni, and the *anuyāja*s belong to Agni"—so says the Brāhmaṇa. "The meters are the deities," so says another [Brāhmaṇa]. "The *prayāja*s are indeed the meters, and the *anuyāja*s are the meters"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"The seasons are the deities," so says another [Brāhmaṇa].
"The seasonal sacrifices (*prayāja*) are indeed the seasons, and the subsequent sacrifices (*anuyāja*) are the seasons," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"The deities of the animal sacrifice" is another [view]. "The *prayāja*s are indeed cattle, and the *anuyāja*s are cattle," so says the Brāhmaṇa.
"The deities of the vital breaths" is yet another [view].

"The *prayāja*s are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*); the *anuyāja*s are indeed the vital breaths," so says the Brāhmaṇa. "The deities are the self (*ātman*)," so says another [Brāhmaṇa]. "The *prayāja*s are indeed the self; the *anuyāja*s are indeed the self," so says the Brāhmaṇa.

The established rule, however, is that they belong to Agni; the others are merely [metaphorical] applications. But for what purpose is this stated? "One should meditate in the mind upon whichever deity the oblation has been taken for when about to utter the *vaṣaṭ*," so it is known from scripture.

These are the eleven *aprī*-hymns. Among them, those of Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Vadhryaśva, and Gṛtsamada contain the *nārāśaṃsa* verses. Those of Medhātithi and Dīrghatamas contain both [the *tanūnapāt* and the *nārāśaṃsa*]. The others contain the *tanūnapāt* verses. 8.22

*Draviṇodāḥ*: Why "draviṇodāḥ"? Because he bestows wealth (*draviṇasaḥ*) and he is the one who increases it. Now follow the *Āprī* verses: "Enkindled today," "Tanūnapāt," "Narāśaṃsa," "Being invoked," "The forward-pointing sacrificial grass," "The wide-extending ones," "The swelling ones," "The two divine Hotṛ-priests for our sacrifice," "These two who enter [the altar]," "The Lord of the Forest," "They release [the victim] for you, O Lord of the Forest," "Having bound [it] with a cord," "Just born," "My fore-offerings"—twenty-two in total.
Thus ends the second chapter in the Uttarashatka;
thus the eighth chapter of the Nirukta is completed.
Now begins the ninth chapter.

Now we shall enumerate in order those beings that have the earth as their abode and receive praise. Of these, the horse comes first. The horse has already been explained. Regarding it, there is this verse: "The horse, the drawer of the chariot, brings ease; he neighs toward the attendants.
The penis desires the two hairy testicles, like a frog in the water. Flow, O Indu, for Indra. (9.1)

The horse is a carrier; it is a comfortable carrier, a carrier of the chariot. "Sukham" (comfort) is a name for what is auspicious (*kalyāṇa*). It becomes auspicious, meritorious, and well-being. Or, it is that by which one goes to well-being. Or, it is a gladdener, a protector, or a guardian. It reaches the remainder; it wards off water. "Mā naḥ" has been explained. Regarding this, there is this verse: 9.2 May Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Āyu, Indra, Ṛbhukṣan, and the Maruts not overlook us.
We shall proclaim in the assembly the heroic deeds of the steed, born of the gods, the swift courser.

Or rather: we shall proclaim at the sacrifice and in the assembly the heroic deeds of the steed, the swift courser, who was born for the gods as he speeds along. May you, Mitra, Varuṇa, Aryaman, Āyu, Vāyu, Indra—the one of wide dwelling—and the Maruts, the king of the Ṛbhus, not overlook us. *Śakuni* means "he is able to lift himself up," or "he is able to cry out," or "he is able to fly. Or it means "may he be a bringer of peace from every side. Or it is derived from the root *śak* (to be able). Regarding him, there is this verse:
"Chanting loudly, proclaiming his own birth, he sends forth his voice like a rower propelling a boat."
And may you be a source of good fortune in our omens; may no universal misfortune overcome you.
Speak auspiciously from the right; speak auspiciously from the left;
speak auspiciously to us from the front; speak auspiciously from behind, O Kapiñjala!
Thus it is explained by its very utterance (*nigada*).

Gṛtsamada is one who is "skilled" (*gṛtsamadanah*). *Gṛtsa* is a name for the wise; it is derived from the root *gṛ*, meaning "to praise. Maṇḍūkas are so called because they "dive" (*majjanāt*). Or they are derived from *mad*, meaning "to rejoice," or from *mand*, meaning "to be satisfied. According to the grammarians, they are derived from *maṇḍayati*. Alternatively, their dwelling place (*oka*) is "essence" (*maṇḍa*). *Maṇḍa* is derived from *mad* or *mud*. Of them, this [verse] occurs: 9.5.
Having lain dormant for a year, these Brahmins who observe their vows,
the frogs, have uttered their voices, which are quickened by Parjanya.

Having lain for a year, the Brāhmaṇas, observing their vows and remaining silent, spoke. Or rather, it may be used in a figurative sense: "like Brāhmaṇas who observe their vows. The frogs uttered speech that was pleasing to Parjanya.
Vasiṣṭha, desiring rain, praised Parjanya; the frogs rejoiced in him. Seeing them rejoicing, he praised them further. This verse concerning them occurs [at 9.6]:
"Speak forth, O female frog! Do not speak too loudly, O Tāduri!"

"Leap in the middle of the heart, grasping with four feet"—this [verse] is explained by its very recitation (*nigada*). Alternatively, "dice" (*akṣāḥ*) are so called because they reach (*aśnuvate*) these things, or because they reach out toward these things. Regarding them, there is this verse (9.7):
"The dangling ones from the high [tree] exhilarate me, born in the windy place, rolling about on the gambling board."
Like the draught of Soma from Mount Mujavant, may the wakeful Vibhīdaka fruit bring me refreshment.

The quivering fruits of the great *vibhītaka* tree intoxicate me. They are born in the wind, they are driven by the wind. Existing in a salt-flat (*iriṇa*), for a salt-flat is "without grass" (*nirṛṇa*); it comes from the root *ṛṇāti*. It is "without a shore" (*apārṇa*); or rather, it is because the plants have departed from it. Its consumption is like that of the *maujavata* soma; the *maujavata* is born on Mount *Mūjavat*. Mount *Mūjavat* is "possessing *muñja* grass. The *muñja* grass is so called because it is released from the reed (*iṣīkā*). The word *iṣīkā* comes from the root *iṣ*, meaning "to go. This other [kind of] reed comes from the same root. The *vibhītaka* is so called from "breaking apart" (*vibhedana*).

*Jāgṛviḥ* means "the wakeful one" because of his vigilance. He has revealed [this] to me. He praises them with the first verse; he censures them with the subsequent verses. They declare this to be the *ārṣa* (the seer’s own composition) of the seer Akṣaparidyūna.
Let these speak forth, let us speak forth; utter the word to the speaking pressing-stones!
When you, O swift stones, mountains, and possessors of Soma, together bring forth the sound and the roar for Indra.
Let these speak; let us speak. Speak the word to the pressing-stones as they speak.
O stones (*adrayaḥ*), mountains that are not to be split (*adaraṇīyāḥ*), you who are swift and quick-acting, [speak] together with the Soma.
*Śloka* is from the root *śru* (to hear); *ghoṣa* is from the root *ghuṣ* (to sound). Or: "O you possessors of Soma, stand here!"
Or [it is called] "in the houses of the Soma-drinker.
That mantra by which men are praised is the *nārāśaṃsa*; of it there is this [verse]: 9.9.
With my inspired thought, I offer forth abundant hymns of praise for Bhāvya, who dwells by the river and who,
the unconquered king seeking glory, measured out a thousand libations for me.

"Amandān"—not dull, not foolish, or not small. A child (*bāla*) must be supported by one who possesses strength (*balavat*). Or [it means] "ambā" (mother) is sufficient for him; or "ambā" (strength) is his; or *bala* (strength) is separated by a negation. "I offer with *manīṣā*"—by the impulse of the mind, by praise, or by wisdom. Of King Bhāvayavya, who dwells beyond the Sindhu river, who fashioned for me a thousand sacrificial gifts (*savān*), the unconquered king—meaning "one who has not been overcome" or "one who does not hasten"—desiring praise. 9.10
O Lord of the Forest, may you be firm of limb; as our friend, be our furtherer and a provider of heroic sons.
You are bound with cow-hide; be steadfast. May your rider conquer all that is to be won.

"O Lord of the Forest, be firm of limb! Be our friend, a furtherer, a hero of goodly heroes, a possessor of auspicious heroes. You are bound with cow-hides; be strong—meaning, take firm stand! May your rider conquer all that is to be conquered! "Dundubhi" is an imitation of sound, or it may mean "the tree has burst. It may also derive from the root *dundubhyati*, which denotes the action of making sound. Regarding this, there is this verse (RV 10.147.1): "Make the earth and the sky resound! Let the world scattered in many places take heed of you."
O Drum, in harmony with Indra and the gods, drive the enemies far, even to the furthest distance.

Make the earth and the sky resound! Let them perceive your roar in many ways—whatever is established, whether stationary or moving. O drum, in harmony with Indra and with the gods, drive the enemies far, even further away. The quiver is the repository of arrows; concerning it, this [verse] occurs: 9.13.
The father of many, the son of many, the quiver makes a whizzing sound as it moves forward into the fray;
bound upon the back and set in motion, it conquers all encounters and all hostile armies.

"Father of many, he whose son is many"—this refers to the arrows. "He seems to smile as he is being uncovered. This is either an imitation of sound, or [it comes] from the root *sañc* (to join), or from *kṛ* with the prefix *sam* (to scatter). It has been explained that "bound upon the back, he conquers when impelled. *Hastaghna* means "that which is struck in the hand. Regarding this, there is the following verse: 9.14.
Like a serpent with its coils, it encircles the arm, warding off the strike of the bowstring;
the hand-guard, knowing all secret ways, as a man, shall protect the man from every side.
Like a serpent with its coils, it encircles the arm, protecting it from being struck by the bowstring.
The hand-guard (hastaghna), knowing all forms of wisdom, becomes a man of great mind; or rather, it is so called from the root *puṃsati* (to protect).
The reins have been explained. Regarding them, this verse occurs: "Standing in the chariot, the skilled charioteer guides the horses forward wherever he desires.
Marvel at the greatness of the reins; the traces hold back the mind from behind."

Standing on the chariot, the skillful driver, the auspicious charioteer, guides the horses forward wherever he desires. I honor the greatness of the reins; the horses follow behind, guided by the reins which are attached to the mind.
The word *dhanus* is derived from the root *dhanv*, which means "to go" or "to kill"; arrows fly forth from it. Of this [word], there is this verse (RV 6.75.3):
"With the bow may we win cattle, with the bow the prize of battle; with the bow may we conquer fierce contending hosts.
The bow turns back the enemy's advance; with the bow may we conquer all the quarters."
Thus, it is explained by its very utterance (*nigadavyākhyātā*). *Samadaḥ* means "possessing intoxication" (*samadaḥ*) from the root *mad*, or "great joy" (*sammadaḥ*) from the root *mad*.
*Jyā* is derived either from *ji* ("to conquer") or *jināti* ("to overcome"). Or [it is so called] because "she sends forth arrows. Regarding this, there is this verse:
"As if about to speak, she goes near the ear, embracing her dear friend. (RV 10.71.4)
Like a woman, she twangs upon the stretched bow; this bowstring carries us across in the assembly.
As if about to speak, she approaches; embracing her friend, the arrow, as it were, she goes toward Karna.

Like a woman, she whistles—that is, she makes a sound. She is stretched upon the bow, the bowstring, crossing over in the assembly, that is, in battle. The word *iṣu* comes from the root *iṣ*, meaning "to go," or from the root meaning "to kill. Regarding this [arrow], there is this verse (RV 10.18): "She clothes herself in beautiful feathers; the deer is her tooth; bound with cow-hides, she flies forth when discharged."
Where men run together and apart, there may the archers grant us protection.

"Clad in the fair-winged [eagle]," he says, referring to the arrows. Its shaft is made of *mṛga* wood; or rather, it is so called from the root *mṛg* (to seek). "Furnished with cow-hair, she flies forth when discharged"—this has been explained. "Where men rush together and flee apart, there may our arrows grant us protection, a refuge in battles.

They call the horse-whip *kaśā*. The whip makes fear manifest to the horse; or perhaps from the root *kṛṣ* (to draw), because of its slenderness. Furthermore, speech makes meanings manifest. [The word] *khaśayā*.
Or it is from the root *kruś* (to cry out). This [verse] belongs to the horse-whip:
"They strike upon their backs; they beat upon their haunches. O horse-whip, you who are wise, urge on the horses for those who desire them."

They strike their shoulders, their thighs, and their running limbs; "thigh" (*sakthi*) is derived from the root *sac* (to cling), for the body clings to it. And they strike their hips; "hip" (*jaghana*) is derived from the root *jaṅghan* (to strike). O wise one, of keen intellect, urge on the horses in the encounters, in the rushings, in the battles.
Or [it refers to] the mortar, the wide-maker; or the upward-opening one; or the strength-maker.
"Make wide space for me," he said; that became the *ulūkhala*.
"This *ulūkhala* is indeed 'the maker of wide space' (*urukara*)," they say cryptically (*parokṣeṇa*). Thus says the Brāhmaṇa.
Of this [verse], there is this [sacred text]: 9.20.
For even though you, O mortar, are joined in every single house,
here speak most brilliantly, like the drum of the conquerors.
Thus it is explained by its very utterance (nigada).

9.21 Or, he is a *vṛṣabha* because he showers forth offspring; or, he overflows with semen. He is a *vṛṣabha* because his activity is that of raining, due to his showering [of seed]. Of him, there is this verse: 9.22
Bellowing and bellowing loudly as they approached, they urged on the bull in the midst of the contest;
with him, Mudgala won a well-nourished prize of a hundred thousand cattle in the struggle.

"It approached, crying out"—this has been explained. "He made the bull urinate in the midst," meaning either "conquering" or "driving away. By that [act], he won the well-nourished king. The root *bhṛ* (in *bharvati*) signifies the act of eating. Indeed, Mudgala won a thousand well-nourished cows in the contest (*pradhana*). *Pradhana* is a name for battle; it is so called because wealth is scattered (*prakīrṇa*) therein.

The *drughaṇa* is a mallet made of wood. Regarding this, they relate an ancient legend: the seer Mudgala Bhārmyaśva, having yoked both a bull and a wooden mallet, engaged in battle and won the prize. A verse concerning this occurs [in the Ṛgveda]:
"Behold this yoke-fellow of the bull, the wooden mallet lying in the midst of the race-course—by means of which Mudgala won a hundred thousand cattle in the contests for booty. (9.23)

Behold this mace, the companion of the bull, lying in the midst of the race-course—the one by which Mudgala won a hundred thousand cattle in the *pṛtanājyas*. *Pṛtanājya* is a name for battle; it is so called either from the word *pṛtanā* (army/battle), or from the act of conquering (*jaya*).

Mudgala is "possessing beans" (*mudga-vān*), or "swallowing beans" (*mudga-gila*). Or, he is so called because he swallows intoxication (*mada*); thus he is *madaṅgila*. Or, he is *mudaṅgila*, [meaning] one who swallows joy (*muda*). Bhārmyāśva is the son of Bhṛmyaśva.

Bhṛmyaśva is so called because his horses are "nourishing" (*bhṛmi*) or because he supports (*bharana*) the horses. *Pituḥ* is a name for food; it is derived from the root *pā* (to drink), or *pā* (to drink), or *pyā* (to swell). Regarding him, there is this verse: 9.24.
Now I shall praise the drinker, the possessor of great laws and power,
by whose might Trita shattered Vṛtra limb from limb.

I praise that father, the sustainer of great strength— *taviṣī* being a name for strength, derived either from the root *tavati* meaning "to increase" or from the root *tan* meaning "to extend"— he by whose might and power Trita,
Indra existing in three places (*tristhāna*), shattered Vṛtra, who was jointless (*viparvan*).
The rivers have been explained. Of them, this [verse] occurs:

"O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudrī, Paruṣṇī—accept this hymn of praise from me! O Marudvṛdhā, together with the Asiknī, listen; and with the Vitastā and Suṣomā, hear [this] at the Ārjīkīya"—such is the collective meaning. Now, the etymological explanation of each word: Gaṅgā, from "going" (gam). Yamunā, because she goes forth quickly (prayuvatī), or because she goes apart (praviyutaṃ). Sarasvatī: *sara* is a name for water; it comes from the root *sṛ* (to flow); she possesses that. Śutudrī, from "flowing swiftly" (*śudrāviṇī*), or "flowing rapidly" (*kṣipradrāviṇī*), or because she flows as if pierced by speed (*āśu tunnaiva*).
They call her Irāvatī; she possesses joints and flows in a winding course.
Asiknī means blackish-white; "white" (sita) is a name for color, and its negation is "blackish" (asita). Marudvṛdhā refers to all rivers, for the Maruts cause them to swell.

The Vitastā, the Vidagdhā, the Vivṛddhā, and the Mahākūlā—they call her Ārjīkīyā, or Vipāṭ. She either originates from the Ṛjīka mountain, or she flows straight (ṛjugāminī). She is called Vipāṭ because of "tearing apart" (vipāṭana), or because of "untying" (vipāśana), or because of "delivering" (viprāpaṇa). When Vasiṣṭha was about to die, his bonds were unloosed (vyapāśyanta) upon her; therefore she is called Vipāṭ. Formerly she was Uruñjirā, the Suṣomā, and the Sindhu. Because other rivers flow toward her, she is the Sindhu. She is *sindhu* because of "flowing" (syandana). Water is *āpaḥ* from the root *āp* ("to reach"). Regarding them, there is this verse (RV 10.75.5): 9.26.1–3 The Sindhu is the best of rivers, the most glorious, the most powerful, and the most famous. She has surpassed all the flowing streams with her greatness. O Sindhu, you have surpassed all the flowing streams with your greatness. O Sindhu, you have surpassed all the flowing streams with your greatness. 9.26.4 The Sindhu has surpassed the Sarasvatī, the Śutudrī, the Vitastā, the Ārjīkīyā, and the Marudvṛdhā. The Sindhu has surpassed the Tr̥ṣṭāmā, the Susartu, the Rathaspūtī, and the Sarayu. 9.26.5 The Sindhu has surpassed the Gomatī, the Kubhā, the Krumu, the Mehatnu, and the R̥jīkā. The Sindhu has surpassed the Anitabhā, the Sr̥tvatī, the Svāśasā, and the Pr̥thuśravas. 9.26.6 The Sindhu has surpassed the Ārjīkīyā, the Tr̥ṣṭāmā, the Susartu, and the Rathaspūtī. The Sindhu has surpassed the Sarayu, the Śutudrī, the Vitastā, and the Ārjīkīyā. 9.26.7 The Sindhu has surpassed the Gomatī, the Kubhā, the Krumu, the Mehatnu, and the R̥jīkā. The Sindhu has surpassed the Anitabhā, the Sr̥tvatī, the Svāśasā, and the Pr̥thuśravas. 9.26.8 The Sindhu has surpassed the Ārjīkīyā, the Tr̥ṣṭāmā, the Susartu, and the Rathaspūtī. The Sindhu has surpassed the Sarayu, the Śutudrī, the Vitastā, and the Ārjīkīyā. 9.26.9 The Sindhu has surpassed the Gomatī, the Kubhā, the Krumu, the Mehatnu, and the R̥jīkā. The Sindhu has surpassed the Anitabhā, the Sr̥tvatī, the Svāśasā, and the Pr̥thuśravas. 9.26.10 The Sindhu has surpassed the Ārjīkīyā, the Tr̥ṣṭāmā, the Susartu, and the Rathaspūtī. The Sindhu has surpassed the Sarayu, the Śutudrī, the Vitastā, and the Ārjīkīyā. 9.26.11 The Sindhu has surpassed the Gomatī, the Kubhā, the Krumu, the Mehatnu, and the R̥jīkā. The Sindhu has surpassed the Anitabhā, the Sr̥tvatī, the Svāśasā, and the Pr̥thuśravas. 9.26.12 The Sindhu has surpassed the Ārjīkīyā, the Tr̥ṣṭāmā, the Susartu, and the Rathaspūtī. The Sindhu has surpassed the Sarayu, the Śutudrī, the Vitastā, and the Ārjīkīyā. 9.26.13 The Sindhu has surpassed the Gomatī, the Kubhā, the Krumu, the Mehatnu, and the R̥jīkā. The Sindhu has surpassed the Anitabhā, the Sr̥tvatī, the Svāśasā, and the Pr̥thuśravas. 9.26.14 The Sindhu has surpassed the Ārjīkīyā, the Tr̥ṣṭāmā, the Susartu, and the Rathaspūtī. The Sindhu has surpassed the Sarayu, the Śutudrī, the Vitastā, and the Ārjīkīyā. 9.26.15 The Sindhu has surpassed the Gomatī, the Kubhā, the Krumu, the Mehatnu, and the R̥jīkā. The Sindhu has surpassed the Anitabhā, the Sr̥tvatī, the Svāśasā, and the Pr̥thuśravas. 9.26.16 The Sindhu has surpassed the Ārjīkīyā, the Tr̥ṣṭāmā, the Susartu, and the Rathaspūtī. The Sindhu has surpassed the Sarayu, the Śutudrī, the Vitastā, and the Ārjīkīyā. 9.26.17 The Sindhu has surpassed the Gomatī, the Kubhā, the Krumu, the Mehatnu, and the R̥jīkā. The Sindhu has surpassed the Anitabhā, the Sr̥tvatī, the Svāśasā, and the Pr̥thuśravas. 9.26.18 The Sindhu has surpassed the Ārjīkīyā, the Tr̥ṣṭāmā, the Susartu, and the Rathaspūtī. The Sindhu has surpassed the Sarayu, the Śutudrī, the Vitastā, and the Ārjīkīyā. 9.26.19 The Sindhu has surpassed the Gomatī, the Kubhā, the Krumu, the Mehatnu, and the R̥jīkā. The Sindhu has surpassed the Anitabhā, the Sr̥tvatī, the Svāśasā, and the Pr̥thuśravas. 9.26.20 The Sindhu has surpassed the Ārjīkīyā, the Tr̥ṣṭāmā, the Susartu, and the Rathaspūtī. The Sindhu has surpassed the Sarayu, the Śutudrī, the Vitastā, and the Ārjīkīyā. 9.26.21 The Sindhu has surpassed the Gomatī, the Kubhā, the Krumu, the Mehatnu, and the R̥jīkā. The Sindhu has surpassed the Anitabhā, the Sr̥tvatī, the Svāśasā, and the Pr̥thuśravas. 9.26.22 The Sindhu has surpassed the Ārjīkīyā, the Tr̥ṣṭāmā, the Susartu, and the Rathaspūtī. The Sindhu has surpassed the Sarayu, the Śutudrī, the Vitastā, and the Ārjīkīyā. 9.26.23 The Sindhu has surpassed the Gomatī, the Kubhā, the Krumu, the Mehatnu, and the R̥jīkā. The Sindhu has surpassed the Anitabhā, the Sr̥tvatī, the Svāśasā, and the Pr̥thuśravas. 9.26.24 The Sindhu has surpassed the Ārjīkīyā, the Tr̥ṣṭāmā, the Susartu, and the Rathaspūtī. The Sindhu has surpassed the Sarayu, the Śutudrī, the Vitastā,
O Waters, you are indeed sources of bliss;
grant us strength for great joy and for the sake of vision.
"Ye are waters, sources of happiness; grant us food for our great delight and for a beautiful vision.

Regarding the plants (*oṣadhayaḥ*): they are so called because "they cause to heal" (*oṣadhyanti*), or "they burn away as they suck" (*oṣanty enā dhayanti*), or "they suck away the disease" (*doṣaṃ dhayanti*). Of them, this verse occurs:
"The plants that were born first, three ages before the gods... (RV 10.97.1)
I know indeed the hundred and seven abodes of the tawny ones.

The plants that were born first, three ages before the gods—I consider those to be the brown ones, meaning those of brown color, or perhaps those that carry away or support. They have one hundred and seven abodes. There are three kinds of abodes: places, names, and births; it is these births that are intended here. Or, since there are seven hundred vital points (*marman*) in a person, they place [the plants] within them. Night has been explained; this is its verse (RV 10.127). 9.28.28.1–3 yā óṣadhīḥ pūrvā jātā devebhyas triyugám purā | mánai nu tá babhrūṇām áham śatám dhāmāni saptá ca || śatám dhāmāni saptá ca | trīṇi bhavanti | sthānāni | nāmāni | janmānīti | janmāny atrābhipretāni | saptaśatám puruṣásya marmaṇām téṣv enā dadhatīti vā | rātrír vyākhyātā | tasyā eṣā bhavati || 9.28.28.4 śatám vo amba dhāmāni sahasram uta vo ruhaḥ | adhā śatakratvo yūyám imám me agadaṃ kṛta || śatám vo amba dhāmāni sahasram uta vo ruhaḥ | adhā śatakratvo yūyám imám me agadaṃ kṛta || 9.28.28.5 óṣadhīḥ prati modadhvam púṣpavatīḥ prasūvarīḥ | aśvā iva sajitvarīr vīrudhaḥ pārayiṣṇvaḥ || óṣadhīḥ prati modadhvam púṣpavatīḥ prasūvarīḥ | aśvā iva sajitvarīr vīrudhaḥ pārayiṣṇvaḥ || 9.28.28.6 púṣpavatīḥ prasūvarīr máhyaṃ O Night, you have reached the earthly realm through the abodes of your father;
vast one, you spread across the seats of heaven, and the brilliant darkness rolls forward.

O Night, you have filled the earthly realm; with your stations, you pervade the abodes of the mid-region and of heaven. Great and vast, you spread yourself out; the brilliant darkness rolls around. Araṇyānī is the mistress of the forest. "The forest is shoreless," it is said; or rather, she is one who finds no delight in the village, having departed from it. Of her, this verse occurs: "Araṇyānī, O Araṇyānī! You who seem to vanish away."
Why do you not ask the way to the village? Is it that fear does not find you? 3.

He addresses her as "Araṇyānī": "O Araṇyānī, you who vanish away like forests toward the distant regions, why do you not ask for the way to the village? Does fear not seize you? The particle *iva* is used here in the sense of "as it were" or "almost. *Śraddhā* (faith) arises from the act of believing. Regarding this, there is this verse:
"By faith the fire is kindled; by faith the oblation is offered.
We proclaim faith upon the head of Bhaga with our speech. (9.30)

Through faith the fire is properly kindled; through faith the oblation is properly offered. We proclaim faith at the head—the principal limb—of Bhaga, the lord of fortune, by means of this speech. Pṛthivī has been explained. Regarding her, there is this verse (9.31): "O Earth, be pleasant, thornless, and a place of rest."
Grant us that protection which is far-extending.

"Be pleasant to us, O Earth; be thornless and a place of rest. A "thorn" (*ṛkṣara*) is so called from the root *ṛcch* ("to go"). It may also be derived from *kaṇṭap*, or from *kṛnt* ("to cut"), or from *kaṇṭ* as a verb meaning "to move," for it is most prominent. Grant us protection; let them grant us refuge, broad on all sides.
*Apvā* has been explained; here is a verse concerning her (RV 10.97.14):
"O *Apvā*, bewildering the minds of these men, seize their limbs and depart!"
Advance against them; burn them with sorrows in their hearts; let the enemies be possessed by blinding darkness.
Bewildering the minds and understandings of these [enemies], seize their limbs, O Apvā;
go forth! Advance! Burn their hearts with sorrows! Let the enemies be enveloped in blinding darkness.
Agnāyī is the wife of Agni; this is her [hymn]. 9.33
Here I invoke Indrāṇī for well-being, Varuṇānī for prosperity,
and Agnāyī for the drinking of Soma.

Thus it is explained by its very utterance (nigada). 9.34 Now, therefore, follow the eight pairs: the mortar and pestle. The mortar has been explained; the pestle is that which moves repeatedly (*muhuḥ saraḥ*). Regarding these two, there is this verse:
9.35 "The two most effective sacrificers, the best at winning booty—these two indeed are held aloft."
Like two tawny steeds devouring the darkness.
The two *āyava* are those most worthy of sharing in the foods; for they are carried aloft like two bay horses (*harī*) while consuming the offerings.
The two *havirdhāna*s are the repositories of the oblations. Regarding them, there is this verse (9.36):
"May the gods worthy of sacrifice sit upon your lap, O guileless ones."
Come here today for the drinking of the Soma.
"May you two sit upon the lap, the place of rest—O you who are not to be harmed, O gods worthy of sacrifice, fulfillers of the sacrifice, come here today for the drinking of Soma.
Heaven and Earth have been explained. Of these two, there is this verse (RV 1.22.13):
"May Heaven and Earth today make this our [offering] successful, reaching to the sky..."
May they present the sacrifice to the gods.
May Heaven and Earth today present this our means of accomplishment, this heaven-touching sacrifice, among the gods.
The Vipāś and Śutudrī have been explained. Of these two, there is this [verse]:
"From the lap of the mountains, longing, like two mares let loose, vying with each other... (RV 3.33.1).
Like two bright mother cows licking their calves, the Vipāś and Śutudrī hasten with their waters.

From the vicinity, from the proximity of the mountains. Desiring, longing. Or like two horses unyoked; or "fallen apart" (*viṣaṇṇe*); or "laughing together. *Hāsati* means "in rivalry" or "rejoicing. Like two beautiful cows, the two mothers, licking each other, the Vipāś and Śutudrī flow swiftly with their waters. Or "the two bow-ends" (*ārtnī*, *artanyau*); or "the two forest-dwellers" (*araṇyau*); or "the two non-harming ones" (*ariṣaṇyau*). Regarding these two, there is this [verse]: 9.39.
Moving together like a woman to her husband, may they bear [the arrow] in their lap like a mother her son;
acting in concert, may these two bow-ends, quivering together, pierce the enemies and strike down the foes.

Acting together like two women of one mind, may they bear [us] in their lap as a mother bears her son. Being in harmony, may they drive away our enemies; these two, acting in concert, strike down our foes. Śuna and Sīra: Śuna is Vāyu, for he moves swiftly through the atmosphere; Sīra is Āditya, because of his movement. Regarding them, there is this verse: "O Śuna and Sīra, enjoy this speech; the milk which you created in heaven."
Sprinkle this [earth] with water.
Thus, this [verse] is explained by its very recitation (*nigada*).
"The two divine ones who take pleasure" (*devī joṣṭrī*) refers to the two goddesses who cause delight; or it refers to Heaven and Earth;
or it refers to Day and Night; or, according to Kāṭhaka, it refers to the grain and the year. This is the formal injunction (*saṃpreṣa*) regarding them. 9.41

The two divine ladies, the lovers, the bestowers of wealth, of whom one drives away hostilities and the other brings desirable riches to the sacrificer—may they both partake of the offering at the winning of wealth; sacrifice!

The two goddesses are the *joṣṭrī* (the two who enjoy). They are the two goddesses who cause enjoyment. They are the two possessors of wealth (*vasudhānī*). Of these two, one drives away and carries off the two-fold hostilities, while the other brings to the sacrificer desirable riches, for the winning of wealth and for the bestowing of wealth. Let them partake, drink, or desire [the offering]. "Sacrifice! is the call to action (*saṃpraiṣaḥ*).

The two goddesses are the *ūrjāhutī* (the two offerings of strength). They are the two goddesses who bring strength. Or they are Heaven and Earth; or they are Day and Night, according to Kāṭhaka. Or, as Kāṭhaka says, they are the Crop and the Year. For these two, this is the call to action. 9.42

The two goddesses, Ūrjā and Āhutī—one shall bring us food and vigor, the other the shared meal and the drinking together; may we, sharing with the new, be mindful of the old, and with the old, of the new. May those two, Ūrjā and Āhutī, bestowing vigor, grant us that vigor; may they partake of the gift of wealth for the sake of obtaining wealth. Sacrifice!

The two goddesses are Ūrjāhutī (the two offerings of strength). Of the two goddesses, they are Ūrjāhvānyau (the two who invoke strength). One brings food and sap; the other brings eating together and drinking together. May we, through the new [grain], be mindful of the old; through the old, the new. To that strength, O Ūrjāhutī, you two, bestowing strength, have bestowed it—for the winning of wealth and for the granting of wealth. Let them partake, let them drink, or let them desire. "Sacrifice! is the call; "Sacrifice! is the call. 9.43

Now, those which the horse shall carry—may Mitra, neighing loudly, speak auspiciously for us; speak forth throughout the year! Let the trembling ones not approach me; let them speak of intoxicating things through their connection with the sacrifice. O Lord of the Forest, make them hiss like a serpent with its coils; standing upon the chariot, as if about to drive the cows across the desert, he has clothed himself in the fair-winged one. They strike him down, for even when you, the bull, have roared downward, this is that food; now come to me. Those herbs which are most helpful, the nights, the forest regions, and Agni with faith.

"May their mind here be pleasant, O Indrāṇī"—then follow eight *ājyā* verses: "O Heaven and Earth for us," "Forward toward the mountains," "They come hither," "O Śuna and Sīra," "The two goddesses who delight," "The goddesses, the two offerings of strength"—[these] thirty-four [verses]. (Total: forty-three.)
Thus ends the third chapter in the Uttarashatka;
thus ends the ninth chapter in the Nirukta.
Now begins the tenth chapter.
Now, therefore, the deities of the middle station.

Of these, Vāyu is the first to arrive. [The word] *vāyuḥ* is from the root *vā*; or it may be from *veti*, a verb meaning "to go. According to Sthaulāṣṭhīvi, it is from the root *eti*. The letter *v* is meaningless. Regarding him, there is this verse: "O Vāyu, come hither! These Soma juices, well-prepared, are here. (RV 7.92.1)
Protect them; hear our invocation.
"O Vāyu, come! These Soma juices are beautiful and well-prepared;
Speeding with might toward the powerful Indra, the chariot-horses on well-wheeled wheels have rushed toward glory;
they hasten straightway, for the immortality of Vāyu shall never fail.

Having rushed forward toward Indra as he was exerting his strength, the chariot-steeds—the draft-horses that carry the chariot—should, moving straight on, convey food to him for the yoking of the chariot with its beautiful wheels: both new and old. *Śrava* is a name for food; it is so called because it is heard (*śrūyate*). And there is this portion of Vāyu so that it may not fail him. Some say it has Indra as its primary deity, while others say it is a description of Vāyu’s action according to the *Nighaṇṭu*. Yet another view holds it has both as its primary deities. *Varuṇa* is so called because he covers (*vṛṇoti*). Regarding him, there is this verse (10.3).
Varuṇa has released the cloud, pouring down its waters; he has spread it across the two worlds and the mid-air.
With that, the King of the entire universe moistens the earth, as rain does for the barley.

Varuṇa has his gate turned downward; he [controls] the *kabandha*, the cloud. *Kavana* means water; it is held (*dhīyate*) therein. Water also is called *kabandha*. The root *bandh* is used in the sense of non-restraint; and the cloud is unrestrained. He pours forth [rain], [encompassing] heaven, earth, and the intermediate space by his greatness. As the king of the entire world, he moistens the earth with rain as if sowing barley. Of him, there is this other verse:
"Let us truly praise him with a song, and with the hymns of the fathers... (RV 10.4)"
He who, through the praises of Nābhāka, dwells at the source of the rivers as their middle brother among the seven sisters—he, the unassailable one, is equal to himself in his own abode.

I praise him with a harmonious song, with a chant, with hymns of praise, and with the meditative chants (*stoma*) of the ancestors, and with the eulogies of Nābhāka. Nābhāka was a seer (*ṛṣi*). At the rising of these flowing waters, he spoke to this seven-sistered one with words, identifying her as "the middle one. Now, it is said: "May all others perish!"—may all others not exist, those who hate us, the evil-minded, the wicked-minded, those of sinful intent.

Rudra is so called because he cries out (*rauti*) from existence; or because he runs about while crying repeatedly (*rorūyamāṇaḥ*); or from the root *rud*, "to cause to weep. "Because he cried (*arodat*), that is the Rudra-nature of Rudra," so says the *Kāṭhaka*. "Because he wept (*arodīt*), that is the Rudra-nature of Rudra," so says the *Hāridravika*. Regarding him, there is this verse (RV 7.46.1):
"Bring these songs for Rudra, who has a firm bow, swift arrows, a divine nature, and self-sustaining power;
for the invincible, the conqueror, the wise ordainer, whose weapons are sharp—may he hear us!"

To this Rudra—of the firm bow, of the swift arrows, the god who possesses food, the invincible one whom others cannot overcome, the conqueror, the ordainer, the wielder of sharp weapons—to him bring these songs; may he hear us. *Tigma* comes from the root *tij*, meaning "to sharpen," referring to the act of exertion; *āyudha* comes from *ā-yudh*, meaning "to fight. Regarding this, there is another verse:
That bolt of yours which, discharged from heaven, moves across the earth—may it spare us.
O you whose breath is sweet, may your thousand medicines protect us; do not harm our children or our descendants.

That missile of yours which has been launched from heaven, from the sky—that missile, whether derived from the root *dyut* (to shine) or *didyut* (to flash)—moves upon the earth. *Kṣmā* means the earth; it moves upon that, or it moves by means of her, or it moves making the earth tremble. May she spare us. O you whose word is true, there are a thousand healing remedies for you. Do not harm us, nor our sons, nor our grandsons. *Toka* comes from the root *tud* (to push); *tanaya* comes from the root *tan* (to stretch). Agni is also called Rudra. Regarding him, this verse occurs:
"O Jarābodha, perceive that; provide it for every people worthy of sacrifice."
A beautiful hymn for Rudra.

*Jarā* is praise; it is derived from the root *jar*, meaning "to praise. Understand that [praise]; or, by means of it, [be] an awakener. Perform that; do that for the sacrifice of every human being—a beautiful hymn (*stoma*) for Rudra. Indra either splits (*dṛṇāti*) nourishment (*irā*), or he gives nourishment, or he bestows nourishment, or he distributes nourishment, or he sustains nourishment. Or he rushes toward Indra, or he delights in Indra, or he kindles all beings.

"Because he kindled him with the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), that is the 'Indra-nature' (*indratva*) of Indra"—thus it is known. "It is the Āgrayaṇa because of this making" (from the root *kṛ*); "it is the Aupamanyava because of this seeing" (from the root *dṛś*). [The name] is derived from the root *ind*, which signifies the act of exercising sovereignty; or one who is "indant," a shatterer of enemies, or a driver away [of them], and one who causes the sacrificers to take heed.
Regarding him, there is this verse (RV 8.6.19): "You shattered [the mountain], you opened up the channels; you set free the obstructed floods.
O Indra, when you split the great mountain asunder, you let loose the streams and struck down the Dānava."

He released the spring; or because of its flowing out, or because of its being cast up, or because of its streaming forth, or from the root *un* (to moisten). He opened his channels. You released the water-filled oceans—these collections in the midst [of the sky]—which were being obstructed. The root *ramṇāti* has the sense of restraining, or it has the sense of releasing. O Indra, when you opened the great mountain—the cloud—you released its streams; you struck it down, which has the sense of giving. Regarding this, there is another verse:
"He who, as soon as born, was the first wise god, who by his power encompassed the gods."
He at whose might the two worlds trembled from his manly strength—he, O people, is Indra.

"He who, as soon as he was born, the first wise god, by his will and his action, overcame, encompassed, protected, or transcended the gods—he before whose power even heaven and earth trembled through the greatness of his manly strength—He, O people, is Indra.
This is the joy of a seer who has perceived the truth, joined with a narrative.

*Parjanya* is from the root *tṛp* (to satisfy), with the initial and final syllables transposed; he is the one who satisfies the people (*janya*), or the supreme conqueror, or the supreme progenitor, or the one who procures the essences. Regarding him, there is this verse: 10.10.
He strikes down the trees and he slays the demons; the entire world trembles before his great weapon.
Even the innocent man flees from the one of virile power when Parjanya, thundering, smites the evildoers.

He strikes down the trees; he strikes down the *rakṣases*. All beings are afraid of him because of his great slaughter, for his slaughter is indeed great. Even one who is innocent flees in fear when Parjanya, possessing the power of rain, strikes the evildoers, the doers of evil, while thundering. Bṛhaspati is the protector (*pātā*) or the guardian (*pālayitā*) of the great. Regarding him, there is this verse: 10.11 He beheld the honey fastened within, like a fish dwelling in shallow water.
Bṛhaspati, having split it open with a loud cry, brought it forth as one draws a cup from a tree.

He beheld honey enveloped by a cloud that possessed food, like a wretched fish dwelling in the water. He drew it forth from the tree as if it were a *camasa* cup. Why "cup" (*camasa*)? Because they sip (*camanti*) from it. Bṛhaspati, with a loud sound, having split it open—Brahmaṇaspati being either the protector (*pātā*) or the guardian (*pālayitā*) of sacred knowledge (*brahman*). Regarding him, there is this verse:
10.12 Brahmaṇaspati split apart the stone-mouthed, watery vessel that poured forth honey, by his might.

All those who behold the light have drunk from that very [fountain]; together they have poured out the oceanic spring. It is full of food, it flows with moisture; it is unassailable, the honey-streaming [fountain] of Brahmaṇaspati. Yama has pierced it through with vigor and strength; all the rays, beholding the sun, drink from that very [fountain]. Together they pour out much for him—the oceanic spring, full of water.

The Lord of the Field (*kṣetrasya patiḥ*). "Field" (*kṣetra*) is derived from the root *kṣi*, meaning "to dwell. He is its protector or guardian. Regarding him, this verse occurs: Through the Lord of the Field, our well-wisher, may we conquer.
May he, who nourishes the village horse, be gracious to us in such a state.
"May we conquer through the Lord of the Field as if with a well-nourished [ally].

Bring us cattle and horses, nourished and providing nourishment! May he be gracious to us in such a state, whether by strength or by wealth. The root *mṛl* has the sense of giving. Of this [deity], there is another verse:
"O Lord of the Field, milk for us a honeyed wave, as a cow yields her milk! (10.15)
"May the lords of truth (ṛta) show us mercy—[the Soma] dripping with honey, well-purified like clarified butter.

O Lord of the Field, milk for us a wave rich in sweetness, as a cow milks her milk. [The phrase] "dripping with honey, well-purified like clarified butter" refers to the water. "May the protectors or guardians of our truth show us mercy"—the root *mṛ* (in *mṛlayantu*) signifies the act of showing compassion, or perhaps the act of honoring. Now, it is one thing that when there is a common expression within the same verse, it becomes a tautology (*jāmi*).

"Just as [in the mantra] *madhumantaṃ madhuścutam*"; furthermore, that which occurs within the same foot with identical verbal expression becomes *jāmi*. "Just as [in the mantra] *hiraṇyarūpaḥ sa hiraṇyasaṃdṛk*";
furthermore, whatever distinction exists constitutes non-*jāmi*.
Like a frog from the water, like a frog from the water—so it is said.

Regarding Vāstoṣpati: *vāstu* is derived from the root *vas*, meaning "to dwell"; he is either the protector (*pātā*) or the guardian (*pālayitā*) of that dwelling. Of him, there is this verse (10.16): "O Vāstoṣpati, driving away disease, entering all forms..."
Be a most gracious friend to us.

O Vāstoṣpati, entering all forms with a mind free from malice, be our friend and one who is very gracious. *Śeva* is a name for happiness; it is derived from the root *śiṣ*. The letter *v* is a name-formative (*nāmakaraṇa*), an internal substitute for the final consonant, and its vowel quality is optionally modified. *Śiva* is also a form of this word. Whatever form he desires, that very form the deity becomes.
There is also a Vedic verse (nigama) which says: "The Bountiful One assumes every form.
*Vācaspati* is the protector or guardian of speech. Regarding him, there is this [verse]: 10.17.
Come again, O Lord of Speech, together with the divine mind;
O Lord of Abode, cause my very body to rest within me alone.
Thus she [the goddess] has been explained by her very name.
Apāṃ Napāt (the Son of Waters) has been explained by [the section on] Tanūnapāt. This is his [hymn]:
"He who shines without fuel within the waters, whom the sages invoke at the sacrifices. (RV 2.35.4)
O Son of the Waters, grant us the honey-sweet waters, by which Indra was strengthened for heroic valor.

He who shines within without fuel, whom the wise praise at the sacrifices—he is Apāṃnapāt. Grant us waters rich in sweetness for the pressing, by which Indra increases for heroic power and for deeds of valor. Yama restrains the living; of him this verse occurs: "Pay honor with an oblation to Yama, the king, the son of Vivasvat, the assembler of people, who has departed along the great slopes, having spied out the path for many."
"Having gone forth," meaning one who has returned from the journey. Regarding the words "downward slopes, upward slopes, and downward hollows":
the root *ava* signifies the act of going. [He is the one] who has reached out his hand along the path for many.
"Vaivasvata" means the assembler of people. "Yama the King, honor him with an oblation"—the root *duvasyati* signifies the act of attaining.
Agni is also called Yama; these *ṛc*-verses proclaim him:
"Like an army let loose, he bestows fear; like an archer’s missile, he is terrible in appearance. (10.20)
"Yama indeed was born; Yama is the progeny of birth. He is the lover of maidens and the husband of wives.

To him, O people, let us go for our dwelling, as cows reach their home when the fire is kindled. Thus are the two-footed verses. Like an army let loose, he bestows either fear or strength. Like the bolt of an archer, he has a terrifying aspect—either a terrifying aspect, a powerful aspect, an aspect of glory, a great aspect, or a radiant aspect. "Yama indeed was born, united with Indra. Here and there are the two mothers, the Yamas. Such also is a Vedic citation (*nigama*). He is like one born as Yama; Yama is he who is yet to be born.

The lover of maidens; the one who causes the girls to grow old; the husband of women; the protector of wives—for they become preeminent through their connection with sacrifice.
