Regarding this, there is also a Vedic verse (nigama): "The third [fire] is your husband. [We offer] to you that which moves, moving along; with the oblation of cattle; and with the dwelling, that which dwells; with the oblation of plants. May we reach home, just as cows reach their stall, [reaching] what is kindled and enriched with enjoyments.

Mitra [is so called] because he protects from death; or because, gathering together, he moves; or from the root *med* (to gladden). Regarding him, there is this verse: "Mitra, speaking, impels men; Mitra has supported both the earth and the sky.
Mitra gazes upon the people with unblinking eyes; unto Mitra offer the oblation accompanied by clarified butter."

Mitra leads forth the people, proclaiming and making a sound. Mitra alone upholds both the earth and the sky. "Mitra gazes intently upon the *kṛṣṭīs* (peoples) with unblinking eyes"—*kṛṣṭīs* is a name for human beings; they are so called because they perform actions (*karman*) or because their bodies are fashioned (*vikṛṣṭa*). "Offer an oblation rich in ghee to Mitra"—this has been explained. The root *hu* denotes the act of giving. He is either one who desires (*kāmana*), or one who strides (*kramaṇa*), or one who is blissful (*sukha*). Regarding him, there is this verse: "In the beginning, the Golden Embryo (*Hiraṇyagarbha*) came into being. Once born, he was the sole Lord of all that exists. (10.22)
He has supported this earth and this heaven; to what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?

Hiraṇyagarbha is a golden embryo; or, he whose embryo is made of gold. The word *garbha* comes from the root *gṛbh* (to seize), in the sense of "praising" (*gṛṇāti*), or "swallowing up" (*girati*) misfortunes. For when a woman seizes qualities (*guṇa*) and her qualities are seized [by him], then she becomes pregnant (*garbha*). "In the beginning he came into being; once born, he became the sole lord of all that exists. He supports both the earth and the sky. To what god shall we offer worship with our oblation?"—this has been explained. The root *vidh* signifies the act of giving. *Sarasvant* has been explained. This is his verse: 10.23.
O Sarasvatī, those waves of yours which are honeyed and dripping with clarity— with those, be our protector.
Thus she is explained by her very utterance (10.24).
Viśvakarman is the maker of all; of him this [verse] occurs (10.25):
"Viśvakarman, the wise, the far-reaching, the ordainer, the disposer, and the supreme seer."
Their desired offerings rejoice together with the sacrificial food where they say there is one beyond the seven seers.

Viśvakarman, whose mind is manifold, is the pervader, the supporter, and the ordainer; he is the supreme beholder of beings. Whatever is desired, beloved, traversed, gone, thought, or bowed to among them, all rejoice together with the waters where these lights of the seven seers are. Beyond them is the Āditya; they become one in him—thus with respect to the deities.

Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*). Viśvakarman is the one whose mind is manifested, the pervasive one, the Ordainer (*dhātṛ*), and the Disposer (*vidhātṛ*). He is the supreme revealer of the senses. Whatever among these is desired, or beloved, or traversed, or gone, or thought, or bowed to—these rejoice together with food where these seven groups of the seers' senses are. Beyond these is the Self (*ātman*); [the text] declares the course of the Self, that "they all become one in this."
Regarding this, they relate an ancient legend: Viśvakarman Bhauvana offered all beings as a sacrifice in the Sarvamedha; at the very end, he even offered himself.
Concerning this, there is this Ṛgvedic verse:
"He who offered all these worlds... and so forth.
For a more extensive explanation of this, here is the following verse (10.26):
"O Viśvakarman, increasing through the oblation, sacrifice yourself to both the earth and the sky!
Let other people around us be confounded; here, let the bountiful Maghavan be our patron."
O Viśvakarman, growing strong by means of the oblation, sacrifice yourself to both the earth and the sky.
Let other people around us, our rivals, be confounded. May Maghavan be our patron here, the one who knows all.
Tārkṣya has been explained by Tvaṣṭṛ. He dwells in the traversed mid-air; he swiftly protects his purpose, or [the name] comes from the root *aś* (to reach). Of him, this is the verse: 10.27.
We invoke here for our well-being that swift Tārkṣya, the prize-winner impelled by the gods, the victorious overcomer of chariots, whose rim is unharmed, who conquers in battle, and who is fleet.
"Abundantly provided with food; *jūti* means movement or delight; *devajūtam* means moved by the gods, gone to the gods, or beloved by the gods;

powerful, a deliverer of chariots, with uninjured fellies, the winner of battles—the swift Tārkṣya we invoke here for our well-being. Whom else but the god of the middle region could he have thus addressed?
Of him there is this other verse:

He who by his might has at once overspread the five peoples, as the sun with its light overspreads the waters— he whose strength wins thousands and hundreds, no one can restrain his impetus, any more than one can hold back a young arrow.

He who, even instantly, spreads forth the waters with his vital power and strength, like the sun with its light over the five tribes of men—his course wins a thousandfold, it wins a hundredfold. They do not hold him back, for he is like an arrow made of reeds that shoots forth. *Manyu* is from the root *man*, meaning "to shine" or "to be angry. From it the arrows take their name, for they are impelled by him. Regarding him, this verse occurs:

"O Manyu, borne on the same chariot with you, may the Maruts—who are unassailable, rejoicing, and armed with sharp-pointed shafts—advance against us, these heroes who have the form of fire, whetting their weapons in their exultation. (RV 10.83.6)
O Manyu, having mounted the same chariot with you, may the men—breaking things asunder, exulting, unassailable, accompanied by the Maruts, possessing sharp arrows, and whetting their weapons—advance.
They have the appearance of fire and perform the deeds of fire; or rather, they are "armed" and "clad in armor. Dadhikrā has been explained. This is his [verse]:
Dadhikrā has overspread the five peoples with his might, as the sun has spread the waters with his light.
May the swift steed, winning thousands and hundreds, fill these words with sweetness.

Dadhikrā spreads the waters with his might and strength, as the sun [spreads] the light over the five races of men. He is the winner of thousands, the winner of hundreds; he is the prize-winner (*vājī*), the one who stirs, the steed (*arvan*) that rushes forward. "May he endow these our words with honeyed water," [he says]. *Madhu* is from the root *dhamati* in its reverse form. Savitṛ is the impeller of all; of him this [verse] occurs:
Savitṛ has propped up the earth with supports; Savitṛ has made the sky firm where there is no pillar.
Savitṛ has milked the ocean, the roaring expanse of the atmosphere, which was bound fast in the trackless realm, as one might milk a horse.

Savitṛ caused the earth to rest with his supports in the supportless atmosphere; Savitṛ made the sky firm. He milked the moving cloud in the atmosphere like a horse, [the cloud] bound in the unmeasured—meaning either "bound in the swift" or "not hurrying," or "not moving quickly. [The name] Savitṛ means "one who has risen together. Who else other than the Midmost (the Sun) would he have thus described? The Āditya is also called Savitṛ; and so he is praised in the Hiraṇyastūpa hymn. The seer Hiraṇyastūpa, while praising, uttered this hymn. This verse occurs as a salutation to that [deity]: 10.32.
As Hiraṇyastūpa, the Aṅgiras, invoked thee, O Savitṛ, for this prize of booty, so do I,
praising and adoring thee for protection, remain ever watchful for thee, like one who partakes of the Soma-stalk.

*Hiraṇyastūpaḥ*: a stūpa made of gold; or, he whose stūpa is made of gold. A *stūpa* is so called from the root *styā*, meaning a mass or heap. "As the Aṅgirasas offered thee oblations, O Savitṛ, for this food (*vāja*), so do I worship thee. Praising thee for protection, I have awakened to thee as one awakens to the stalk of Soma. *Tvaṣṭṛ* has already been explained. This is his [hymn]: 10.33.
Tvaṣṭṛ, the divine Savitṛ of all forms, has nourished all creatures and brought them forth in many ways; he is the creator of all these worlds. Great is the singular divine sovereignty of the gods.

Tvaṣṭṛ is a god, the impeller (*savitṛ*) who possesses all forms; he nourishes creatures by bestowing vital fluids and generates these [beings] in many ways. Furthermore, all these beings and the waters belong to him. Among the gods, he alone possesses the quality of being an *asura*—that is, either the state of possessing wisdom (*prajñāvat*), or the state of being unassailable (*anava*), or alternatively, "asura" is a name for wisdom itself. He casts away (*asyati*) misfortunes, and misfortunes are cast away from him. His quality of being an *asura* has its initial syllable elided [in the compound].
Vāta is so called because he blows (*vāti*) what exists. Regarding him, there is this verse (10.34):
"O Wind, let that which is healing blow upon us—what is auspicious and brings delight to our heart."
May he prolong our lives.
May the Wind blow toward us with medicines—both auspicious and delightful for our heart—and may he increase our lifespan. Agni has already been explained; here is his [hymn]:
"Thou art summoned hither to this beautiful sacrifice for the protection of the draught."
O Agni, come with the Maruts.

And for him you are summoned to this beautiful sacrifice for the drinking of Soma; "O Agni, come together with the Maruts"—whom else but the Middle One (Indra) would he have thus addressed? Of him there is this other verse:
"I pour out for thee the Soma-mead for the first draught."
O Agni, come with the Maruts.
"I send you forth for the first drinking, for the first draught—the Soma-like honey, that which consists of Soma. O Agni, may he come together with the Maruts.
(10.37) *Vena* is derived from the root *ven*, meaning "to desire. Regarding this, there is this verse:
(10.38) "This *Vena* impels those born of the speckled [cloud], whose womb is light, in the measurement of the mid-air."
At this confluence of the waters, the wise lick him with their hymns, as if he were the child of the Sun.
This Vena impels those whose womb is the speckled one—that is, whose womb is of variegated color—or rather, the waters.

He has light as his amnion; light serves as his amnion. It is called *jarāyu* because it decays (*jarayā*) the embryo, or because it is worn away by decay. At the meeting-place of the waters and the sun, the inspired ones lick him with their hymns—as they would a child. They lick, praise, magnify, or honor him. A child is worthy of being praised (*śaṃsaniya*). Or perhaps the word comes from *śiśīti*, a verb meaning "to give. The embryo is one that is obtained after a long time.
Asunīti. She leads away the breaths. Her verse is this (10.39): "O Asunīti, maintain the mind within us; extend our life-span well for the sake of living.
Grant us delight in the sight of the sun; do thou increase our body with clarified butter."
O Asunīti, maintain the mind within us for long life; increase our lifespan and bring us under control so that we may behold the sun.
The root *radh* is also seen in the sense of coming under one’s power;
thus there is also a Vedic verse: "O King Soma, may we not come under the power of the enemy."
"Strengthen yourself and your body with clarified butter.
*Ṛta* has been explained. Regarding it, there is this verse (10.40):
"For the gifts of *ṛta* are many; the thought of *ṛta* destroys wickedness."
The song of Truth has pierced the ears of the deaf, awakening and shining forth for the living man.

For the powers of *ṛta* are many; its wisdom destroys things that are to be avoided. The resonance of *ṛta* pierces the ears even of the deaf—the deaf one being one whose hearing is bound—awakening his ears and shining forth for the *āyu*, the human being who moves, as a light or as water.
*Indu* [comes] from the root *indh* (to kindle) or from *und* (to moisten). Regarding this, there is this verse:
"May I proclaim this to the future *indu*, he who, like a victim to be offered, stirs the prayer with his impetuousness; the demon-slayer stirs the prayer."
May he himself, through our curses, strike down the evil-minded one with his weapons;
may the reviler flow away downward, and flow away like a trivial thing.

I declare this to the fortunate Indu, who is worthy of invocation—whether he be possessed of arrows, possessed of food, or possessed of desire—who stirs our thoughts, who is the slayer of demons, and who stirs [all] by his might. May he himself strike down with weapons the evil-minded one who reviles us; may the speaker of evil flow away, and from that, may he flow away like a trivial thing. People consider a meaning more significant when it occurs in proximity, as for example: "Oh, how beautiful! Oh, how beautiful!"
That is the characteristic of Parucchepa. Parucchepa is a seer (*ṛṣi*). He is so called because his heels (*śepas*) are jointed (*paru*), or because his heels are on every joint (*paruṣi-paruṣi*).

Thus, these twenty-seven names of deities have been enumerated; they partake of the hymns (*sūkta*) and partake of the oblations (*havis*). Among them, these do not partake of the oblations: Vena, Asunīti, Ṛta, Indu, and Prajāpati—either the protector (*pātā*) or the guardian (*pālayitā*) of creatures. Regarding him, there is this verse (10.42).
O Prajāpati, none other than you has encompassed all these created beings.
Whatever desire we have as we offer this oblation to you, may that be ours; may we be masters of riches.
"O Prajāpati, for no one other than you has encompassed all these created beings. Whatever desire we offer to you with this oblation, may that be ours; may we be masters of riches.
This is the prayer of benediction.
The serpent has been explained. This is his [verse]:
"With hymns I praise Ahi, the son of the waters, as he sits at the base of the rivers in the mid-air regions."
With hymns (*ukthaiḥ*), I praise Ahi, who is born of the waters, dwelling in the depths of the rivers, in the mists, and in the waters.

"The depth" (*budhnam*) refers to the intermediate space (*antarikṣam*). Or rather: "In this [depth] the waters are bound and held. This other [term] *budhna* is derived from the same root: "In this [body] the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are bound and held. That which is Ahi is *Budhnya*. The intermediate space is the "depth," because he dwells therein. Of him, there is this verse: 10.44.
May Ahibudhnya not deliver us to harm; may the sacrifice of this upholder of truth not fail.
May Ahibudhnya not deliver us to injury, nor may the sacrificial fire-pan of this seeker of sacrifice fail. Suparṇa has been explained. Of him, there is this verse:
"The single-winged bird entered the ocean; he gazes upon this entire world."
I beheld him from nearby with a longing mind; the mother licked him, and he licked the mother.

"The single eagle enters the ocean; he gazes upon all these beings. I beheld him from nearby with a simple mind"—thus there arises joy for the seer who has perceived the reality. This is connected with a narrative. "The mother licks him; this is the speech of the intermediate realm. He, in turn, licks his mother. Purūravas roars in many ways. Regarding him, there is this [verse]: 10.46.
While he was being born, the Gnas sat beside him, and they, self-praised, strengthened him;
for you, O Purūravas, the gods strengthened you for great battle and for the slaying of the Dasyus.

When he was being born, they were gathered together. The *ap* (waters) are so called because of their movement, or perhaps because they are the wives of the gods. And they strengthened him—the rivers that flow by their own impulse, moving of their own accord. And for the sake of great battle, O Purūravas, for a delightful conflict, and for the slaying of the Dasyus, the gods strengthened you.

Now, therefore, come hither, O Vāyu, who dwells in the intermediate space; you who have not been let loose, whose waters flow downward. To this high place, O Rudra, [bring] that missile of yours. From the one awakened by age, [he] shattered the trees. As soon as he was born, he ate the bound [trees]. The stone-faced [missile], the Avata, and the Lord of the Field—[worship] the Lord of the Field with the Lord of the Field.

O Lord of the Field, O dispeller of disease, come back again; he who has gone away without fuel—like an army let loose, like Mitra toward the people—Hiraṇyagarbha; those who are yours, O Sarasvatī; Viśvakarman, the maker of all;
the wise one, O Viśvakarman, with the oblation; that very one, even instantly; he whom you, Manyu, [have favored], Dadhikrā.
Savitṛ with his restraints; the golden-tufted god Tvaṣṭṛ; may Vāta blow hither; toward that one; for you, O lover, the lover yearns;

this lover has been led forth by the breath of life; for this is the Truth; may I proclaim that for you; O Prajāpati; with hymns of praise; let not the serpent alone [be our foe]; the fair-winged one; in this [collection], forty-seven [verses].
Thus ends the fourth chapter in the Uttaraṣaṭka;
thus the tenth chapter of the Nirukta is completed.
Now begins the eleventh chapter.
The Śyena has been explained. This is his [hymn]:
"Having seized him, the Śyena brought the Soma—ten thousand and ten thousand libations together.
Thereupon Purandhi abandoned her enemies; in the intoxication of Soma, the wise one [left behind] the foolish. (RV 4.26.7)

Taking [the Soma], Śyena carried it away—the thousand *sava*s and ten thousand together, intending the "thousandfold thousand-offering" (*sahasrasāvyam*). In that context, there are ten thousand partakers of the Soma;

or, by association with that, there are ten thousand sacrificial gifts (*dakṣiṇā*). In that regard, [it is said]: "Puraṃdhi abandoned the non-givers, the enemies," and "In the exhilaration of Soma, the wise one [is] among the foolish. And in the hymn dedicated to Indra, he is praised for the drinking of Soma; therefore, they consider him to be Indra.

*Soma* is an *oṣadhi* (plant/herb) derived from the root *su* (to press), because they press it out. Its usage in the *naighaṇṭuka* (lexicographical) sense is frequent, occurring almost as if it were a marvel due to its preeminence.
We shall cite examples from among its *pāvamānī* verses for illustration:
"Flow on, O Soma, with your most sweet and most intoxicating stream. (RV 9.1.1)
Pressed for Indra to drink.
Thus this [verse] has been explained by its very recitation.
Now there is this other [verse]: "Or rather, he thinks of the moon as having drunk the *soma* when they are grinding the plant. (11.3)
That Soma which the Brahmins know, no one at all eats of it.

"He thinks he has drunk Soma when they crush the plant"—this refers to the Soma that is pressed without ritual efficacy. "Soma, whom the Brahmins know"—this refers to the sacrifice. "No one eats of it who is not a sacrificer. Now, with respect to the deities: "He thinks he has drunk Soma when they crush the plant"—this refers to the Soma pressed by the *Yajus* formulas. "Soma, whom the Brahmins know as the Moon"—"no one eats of it who is not a god. Now there is this other verse concerning that very Moon: "O God, when they drink from you, you swell up again."
Vāyu is the protector of Soma; the month is the form of the Samans.
"When they drink you, O god, from that you swell again"—this refers to the *nārāśaṃsa* cups, or else to the bright and dark fortnights. Vāyu is the protector of Soma;

he calls Vāyu his protector because of their association, or because of [Vāyu's] carrying away the essence. Soma is the form of the months among the years. He is an herb by virtue of its specific forms, or else he is the Moon.

And this moon is called *candramas*. It is either because the mother is *candra* (the moon), or because its measure is lunar (*cāndra*). *Candra* comes from the root *cand*, which means "to shine. From this [root] also comes the word *candana*. It moves beautifully (*cāru dramati*), or it moves for a long time (*ciraṃ dramati*). Or it is derived from *cam* with the prefix *pra*. *Cāru* is from the root *ruc* with a reversed meaning.
Regarding this, there is this verse: "Being born again and again, he becomes ever new; as the banner of the days, he goes to the forefront of the dawns. (RV 7.89.5)
Bestowing a portion upon the gods as he approaches, the moon extends a long life.

"He becomes ever new as he is born"—this refers to the beginning of the bright fortnight (pūrvapakṣa). "The banner of days, the leader of the dawns, goes at their head"—this refers to the end of the dark fortnight (aparapakṣa). Some say that the second quarter [of the verse] has Āditya as its deity. "He ordains the portion for the gods as he comes"—this refers to the sacrifice performed during the half-months. "The moon increases long life; death causes one to die"—so says Sata. Or, "he causes the dead to fall away," so says Śatabalākṣa Maudgalya. Of him, this [verse] occurs: 11.6.
Go away, O Death, along your own path, which is distinct from the path of the gods;
I speak to you who have eyes and hear: do not harm our progeny, nor our heroic sons.

O Death, go away! O Death, go away for certain! O Death, go away for certain! This has been told by him, O Death: "He causes the dead to fall away, O Death. Whether from *mader* or *muder*, for them this [verse] occurs:
11.7 This is indeed the brilliant encounter of the two impetuous ones; O Indra and Viṣṇu, the drinker of the pressed juice protects you both.
You protect the mortal against that which is aimed at him, as you protect the swift bolt of the archer Kṛśānu.
Thus, she is explained by her very name.
Viśvānara has been explained. Of him, this [verse] occurs:
"Sing forth for the great one, who rejoices in the soma-juice—for Viśvānara, the all-encompassing—[for him] who exists in all."
Of that Indra, whose victorious power is great, and whose fame and manly valor the two worlds revere.

"Pray you all to the hymn of praise for the great one, the giver of food (andhas), who is exhilarated, who rejoices, who is being praised, or who is making sound; for Viśvānara, who has pervaded all things, for Indra, in whose pleasure there is very great strength, and great fame worthy of hearing, and manly power that bends men down. 'May Heaven and Earth serve you!'—who else but the Middle One (Indra) would he have thus addressed?
Of him, there is this other verse:
'Upward Savitṛ, the god Viśvānara, has extended his immortal light, common to all people.'"
He has caused to rise the light, the immortal, common to all people—the god Savitṛ, the friend of all men. Dhātṛ is the ordainer of all; regarding him, this verse occurs:
May Dhātṛ grant to the donor long-lasting life that extends forward.
May we obtain the favor of the god whose laws are true.
May Dhātṛ grant to the giver an increased and inexhaustible livelihood. May we meditate upon the auspicious benevolence and the wise mind of the god whose nature is truth.
Vidhātṛ has been explained by [the analysis of] Dhātṛ; this is his occurrence in a verse addressed to many deities (11.11).

"Under the law of King Varuṇa, under the protection of Bṛhaspati and Anumati, today, O Maghavan, under your praise, O Dhātṛ and Vidhātṛ, I have partaken of the Soma-jars. Thus, impelled by these deities, I have partaken of the Soma-jars. Why "kalaśa"? Because measures (kalā) rest within it; both *kali* and *kalā* derive from the root *kṛ* (to scatter). Its measures are scattered. 11.12.

Now, therefore, follow the hosts of gods who dwell in the middle station. Of these, the Maruts are the first to arrive. They are called Maruts because they are measured in their speech (*mita-rāviṇaḥ*), or because they shine with measured light (*mita-rociṇaḥ*), or because they run greatly (*mahad dravanti*). Regarding them, there is this verse:
"O Maruts, come hither on your lightning-bright, well-sounding chariots, armed with spears and winged with horses.
Fly toward us like birds with our most abundant food-offering, O you of wondrous power."

O Maruts, come with your lightning-laden chariots—chariots that are well-praised, or that move beautifully, or that shine beautifully, or that possess brilliant splendor. Come with your spears, with those winged by horses—that is, those that fly like horses—and with most excellent food, swooping down upon us like birds. They are possessed of good *māyā*, or they are performers of auspicious deeds, or they are of auspicious wisdom. The Rudras have been explained; this is their verse: "O Rudras, accompanied by Indra, being of one accord, come on your golden chariots for our welfare!
This prayer of ours is offered toward you, like a spring from heaven to one who thirsts for water."

Come, O Rudras, in harmony with Indra, for the sake of our well-being and for the performance of the rite. This prayer of ours seeks you even more; it is like springs of water from heaven for one parched with thirst. *Tṛṣṇaj* comes from *tṛṣ*, "to thirst"; *udanyu* comes from *udanyati*, "to desire water. As for the *Ṛbhus*: they are so called because they shine widely (*uru bhānti*), or because they shine by means of the cosmic order (*ṛta*), or because they come into being through the cosmic order.
Regarding them, there is this verse: "Having performed their work with skill and swiftness, the mortals, as priests, attained immortality.
The *Ṛbhus*, sons of Sudhanvan, with the eye of the sun, were united with their sacred thoughts within the year. (RV 1.110.4)

Having performed their deeds with swiftness, the *volhāraḥ*—the wise ones, being mortals, attained immortality. The *Ṛbhus*, sons of Sudhanvan, renowned as heroes or possessing heroic wisdom, were united in the year through their inspired thoughts and ritual acts.

*Ṛbhu*, *Vibhvan*, and *Vāja* were the three sons of Sudhanvan Āṅgirasa. Of these, there are Vedic citations (*nigama*) in the plural form for the first and the last, but not for the middle one. Thus, due to the plural usage of *Ṛbhu* and the praise of the *camasa* (the cup), there are many hymns in the *Daśatayīs* [the ten maṇḍalas].
The rays of the Sun are also called *Ṛbhus*. "O *Ṛbhus*, since you were in the house of Agohya, you do not follow after this [world] today."
"Agohya" means the Āditya who is not to be hidden. "In his house there is no sleeping"—meaning, as long as you are there, so long are you not here.
The Aṅgirases have been explained; of them, this verse occurs:
"The Ṛṣis are indeed multiformed, they whose inspiration is profound."
They are the sons of Aṅgiras; they were born from Agni.

The Ṛṣis are multiform; they are either those of profound deeds or those of profound wisdom. They are the sons of Aṅgiras; they were born from Agni—thus [is described] the birth from Agni. The Pitṛs have been explained. Of them, this verse occurs: 11.17.

May the fathers who are below, those who are above, and those who are in the middle rise up—those Soma-loving ancestors who have gone to the life-breath, who are harmless and knowers of Truth; may they protect us in our invocations.

May the lower ancestors rise up; may the higher ones rise up; may the middle ancestors rise up—those who are worthy of Soma, who have attained the essence of Soma, and who follow after the vital breath (*asu*) and the life-force (*prāṇa*). Free from cruelty, free from enmity, whether they are knowers of truth or knowers of sacrifice, may those ancestors come to us at our invocations.
They say that Yama is the middle one; therefore, they consider the middle ancestors to be his.

The Aṅgirases have been explained. The Pitṛs (Fathers) have been explained. The Bhṛgus have been explained. The Atharvans possess *atharvan* [as their characteristic]. The root *tharv* has the sense of "moving about. Its negation [forms *atharvan*]. This verse is common to them:

11.18 The Aṅgirases, the Pitṛs, the Navagvas, the Atharvans, and the Bhṛgus who are worthy of Soma—may we abide in the benevolent thought of those worthy of sacrifice, and also in their auspicious goodwill.

The Aṅgirases are our fathers; they are those who have attained the new [knowledge], or those who have attained the fresh butter (*navanīta*). The Atharvans and the Bhṛgus are the Somyas, those who prepare the *soma*. May we abide in their auspicious thought—their benevolent intention—and in the auspicious, praiseworthy, or worthy vessel-like mind of these ones who are worthy of sacrifice. The etymologists say that they are the middle group of gods; "fathers" is merely a designation. Furthermore, the seers (*ṛṣis*) are also praised:
"Their growth is like that of the sun, their light is such; their greatness is as profound as the ocean. (RV 10.62.2)
Like the swift rush of the wind, your hymn of praise, O Vasiṣṭhas, cannot be followed by another.
Thus, for example:

*āptyā* from the root *āp*. This is their irregular form (*nipāta*) occurring in a verse addressed to Indra: "I would praise the one of many forms, the skillful, the most bountiful, the *āptya* among the *āptyas*. (RV 1.111.20)
He displays his power with his might against the seven Dānus; he overcomes many counter-measures.

He is to be praised; he is multiform; he has become vast; he is the most sovereign lord. He is to be attained; among those things to be attained, he attains them. He who, by his might and strength—whether it be the seven givers or the seven Dānavas—overcomes many counter-measures. *Sākṣati* is a verb meaning "to attain. Now, therefore, follow the deities of the middle region, the females. Of these, Aditi is the first to come. Aditi has already been explained. Her verse is as follows:
"O Aditi, at the birth of Dakṣa, or in his sacred law (*vrata*), you seek to win over the two kings, Mitra and Varuṇa."
Aryaman, whose path is unassailable, who possesses many chariots, and who is the priest of the sevenfold sacrifice among beings of diverse forms.

At the birth of Dakṣa, in the vow, in the ritual act—O two kings, Mitra and Varuṇa, you attend upon [him]. *Vivāsati* means "to serve" (*paricaryāyām*). "The possessor of oblations desires to win over" (*haviṣmān āvivāsati*)—this is either from the sense of "to hope for" (*āśāsteḥ*). "He whose path is unassailable" (*atūrtapanthā*) means one whose path is not hurried (*atvaramāṇapanthāḥ*). "Possessing many chariots" (*bahurathaḥ*). Aryaman is Āditya; he restrains the enemies (*arīn niyacchati*). "The seven-priest" (*saptahotā*): either seven rays cause the essences to flow toward him, or seven seers praise him. In births of diverse forms, in actions, and in consummations.
"It is said that Dakṣa is Āditya; he is praised among the Ādityas. And [it is said]: 'Aditi is the daughter of Dakṣa (Dākṣāyaṇī);
from Aditi was Dakṣa born, and from Dakṣa, Aditi.
How is this possible? They would have to be of the same birth. Or rather, by the nature of the gods, they may be born from one another and be each other's source."
Agni is also called Aditi. Of him, this [verse] occurs:
"To whomsoever you, O possessor of excellent wealth, grant sinlessness, O Aditi, in your fullness;
whomsoever you impel with auspicious power, may we be those who possess your wealth accompanied by progeny."

"To whomsoever you, O possessor of excellent wealth (*sudraviṇas*), grant freedom from sin (*anāgastvam*)—that is, freedom from transgression (*anaparādhatvam*)—O Aditi, in all series of ritual acts; [the word] *āgas* is derived from the root *gam* with the prefix *ā*; *enas* from the root *i*; *kilbiṣam* from *kilbhid*, meaning fear for one who performs good deeds, or that which shatters his fame—whom you impel with auspicious power (*śavas*), with strength (*balena*), and with wealth (*rādhas*) consisting of progeny, may we be those very ones here.

*Saramā* is so called because of her constant movement (*saraṇāt*). Regarding her, there is this verse (RV 10.108.1): "What did she desire when Saramā came hither? For the path is far, wearisome, and leads away to distant lands?"
What was our distress? What was the surrounding darkness? How did you cross the waters of the Rasā?

"Desiring what did she run this way? For the road was far. Jaguri comes from the root *gam* (to go). She was pursued by those turning away. What purpose for gain did you have toward us? What was the protection? *Paritakmyā* means night; *takman* surrounds her. *Takman* is a name for heat, derived from the root *tak* (to burn). How did you cross the waters of the *rasā*? *Rasā* is a river, from the root *ras* (meaning 'to sound'). Or rather, how did you [cross] those liquid waters?"—thus is the narrative concerning the divine bitch sent by Indra, who mated with the Paṇis, the Asuras.
Sarasvatī has been explained. Of her, this [verse] occurs:
"May the purifying Sarasvatī, rich in prizes through her prizes, who possesses wealth through her wisdom, desire our sacrifice."
May Sarasvatī, our purifier, rich in food with her foods, desire our sacrifice—she who is wealthy in wisdom, wealthy in ritual action. Of her, there is this other verse:
Sarasvatī, a great flood, makes herself known by her signal; she rules over all inspired thoughts.

The great flood, Sarasvatī, makes known and brings to consciousness by her signal—by her action or by her wisdom—and she shines forth over all these forms of knowledge. Speech is established among the objects of meaning; therefore, they consider her to be the speech of the middle region. Speech has been explained. Of her, this [verse] occurs: "What the voice speaks, though it be unconscious things—the delightful queen of the gods has sat down.
She has milked out fourfold vigor and milks; where indeed has her highest part gone? (RV 8.100.11)

That which they speak with their voice—unconscious and unknowing—the Queen of the Gods has sat down, exhilarated. She has milked strength and milks into the four quarters. "Where indeed has her highest part gone?"—some say it goes to the earth; others say it is carried away by the rays of the sun. Of this, there is another verse: "The gods generated divine speech; animals of every form speak it. (RV 10.71.1)
May that cow, Speech, yielding for us pleasant refreshment and vigor, come to us with fair praise.

The gods generated divine speech; animals of every form speak it—both those with distinct voices and those with indistinct voices. May that cow, Speech, come to us, yielding for our delight both food and flavor, well-milked.

Regarding Anumati and Rākā, the etymologists say they are the two wives of the gods; the ritualists say they are the two full moons. It is known thus: "That which is the earlier full moon is Anumati; that which is the later is Rākā.
Anumati is so called because of her being approved (*anumananāt*). Of her, this [verse] occurs: 11.29.
O Anumati, do thou approve;
grant us well-being and further our power and skill; prolong our lives.

Grant your approval, O Anumati; bring us happiness. Bestow food upon our offspring and increase our lifespan. *Rākā* is so called from the root *rā*, meaning the act of giving. Regarding her, there is this verse (11.30): "I invoke Rākā, who is easily summoned, with a beautiful hymn of praise. May the fortunate one hear us and take notice of us by herself."
May she sew the waters with an unbroken needle; may she grant a heroic son, a giver of hundreds, worthy of praise.

I invoke Rākā, who is well-invoked, with a beautiful hymn. May she, the fortunate one, hear us; may she perceive us by herself. May she sew together the work of procreation with a needle that does not break.
The word *sūcī* (needle) is derived from the root *sīv* (to sew). May she grant a hero, a giver of a hundred, worthy of praise (*ukthya*), whose virtues are to be proclaimed.
"Sinīvālī and Kuhū are the two wives of the gods," say the etymologists (nairuktāḥ). "They are the two new-moon nights (amāvāsye)," say the ritualists (yājñikāḥ).

It is known thus: "The earlier new moon is Sinīvālī; the later one is Kuhū. *Sinīvālī*: *sina* is food (*anna*); she nourishes (*sināti*) living beings. *Vāla* is a joint (*parva*), derived from the root *vṛ* (to choose/cover). She is "possessing food" (*annavatī*) in that [joint], or she is "possessing hair" (*vālinī*).

Or rather, because of its smallness, the moon is to be served by it as if by Vālī. Regarding this, there is a verse (RV 2.32.6): "O Sinīvālī, broad-hipped one, you who are the sister of the gods—enjoy the offered oblation; O goddess, grant us progeny."

Sinīvālī! O broad-hipped one! *Stuka* comes from the root *styai*, meaning a mass; thus, "one with a mass of broad hair," or "one with broad praise. You who are the sister of the gods—*svasā* means "she who is well-seated" (*su-asā*), or "she who sits among her own people" (*sveṣu sīdati*). Accept the oblation and the food; O Goddess, bestow progeny upon us.
*Kuhū* comes from the root *guh*, or it means "where has she been?"; or "being where, is she invoked?"; or "where does she offer the offered oblation? Regarding her, this verse occurs: 11.32.
I repeatedly invoke Kuhu, the well-performing one, who is skilled in action and easy to call upon at this sacrifice.
May she grant us the renown of our ancestors; O Goddess, let us worship you with this oblation.

I invoke at this sacrifice Kuhū, the well-performed one whose deeds are known among those who are to be invoked. May she grant us the renown of the ancestors—or, as it were, ancestral wealth; or, as it were, ancestral glory. "To thee, O Goddess, we shall pay worship with an oblation"—this has been explained.
Yamī has been explained. This is her [hymn]:
"O Yamī, may another indeed embrace you, and may you embrace another, as a creeper embraces a tree."
Either you must desire his mind, or he yours; establish a most auspicious bond of mutual understanding.

"For you are one, and another shall embrace you, as a creeper embraces a tree. Desire his mind, or let his be yours; then make an agreement with him—[with] Subhadrā, the auspicious and blessed one. Thus [it is told that] Yamī desired Yama, but he rejected her. This is the narrative (11.34). Urvaśī has been explained; this verse belongs to her (11.35).
Like lightning falling, she flashed forth, bringing to me my heart’s desires;
the hero born of the waters was well-born; may Urvaśī prolong his long life.

She who flashes like lightning, falling and illuminating, carrying away my heart’s desires—the waters of the atmospheric realm—when indeed this hero, beneficial to men, was born from the waters as water itself; or rather, he is the offspring of heroes (*narāpatya*). Well-born, most excellently born, Urvaśī now increases her long life.
*Pṛthivī* (the Earth) has already been explained; regarding her, there is this verse: 11.36.
O Pṛthivī, you bear the weight of the mountains as their support; O mighty one, you who possess flowing slopes, you quicken the earth with your greatness.
Truly, O Earth, you possess there the power to weary and shatter the mountains and the clouds.
You who enliven the ground, O you who are full of slopes, great by your magnitude—or "great" because you are possessed of water—you are Indrāṇī, the wife of Indra. This is her [hymn]. 11.37
Among these women, I have heard that Indrāṇī is most fortunate;
for her husband shall never die of old age, nor even later. Indra is superior to all.

Among these women, I have heard that Indrāṇī is most fortunate; for even in another age, her husband does not die of old age. We speak thus of him who is superior to all, including Indra. Of her, there is this other verse:
11.38 O Indrāṇī, I have no pleasure except in the friendship of Vṛṣākapi, whose dear oblation here goes among the gods.
Indra is superior to all.

"O Indrāṇī, I do not take pleasure [in anyone] except for my friend Vṛṣākapi, whose *apyam* oblation—cooked in the waters or perhaps prepared with water—reaches the gods as something dear. We speak thus of him who is Indra, superior to all. *Gaurī* means 'she shines,' from the root meaning 'to blaze. This other *gaura*, 'the fair-colored one,' comes from the same root; he is one who is praiseworthy. Regarding her, there is this verse (10.75.5):
The Gaurī has lowed, fashioning the waters; she is one-footed, two-footed, and four-footed."
She who has become eight-footed, nine-footed, and thousand-syllabled in the highest heaven.

She fashioned the white waters, hewing them out, making them. She is one-footed by means of the middle [region]; two-footed by means of the middle and the sun; four-footed by means of the quarters; eight-footed by means of the quarters and the intermediate directions; nine-footed by means of the quarters, the intermediate directions, and the sun. She has a thousand syllables and much water in the highest firmament. Regarding her, there is this other verse:
From her the oceans flow forth; thereby the four quarters of space live. Thence flows the imperishable [syllable], and by it all this universe lives.
From her the oceans flow forth; the clouds rain down; by that the beings who dwell in the quarters of space live. From that flows the imperishable water; upon that all beings depend for life.
The Cow has been explained. Of her this [verse] occurs:
The Cow lowed after her blinking calf; she made the "hiṅ" sound at its head, as if to measure it.
Muttering toward the heat within her cheeks, she utters a low moan and flows with milk.

The white cow lowed toward her calf—the blinking one, or the unblinking one, namely the Sun. He uttered the *hiṅ* sound over its head for the sake of reflection; *sṛkvāṇam* means "the flowing," and *gharmaḥ* means "the carrying. Lowing toward it, she utters her cry; she swells with milk. Or, as some say, she utters her cry toward the Sun. This is the voice of the intermediate region (*mādhyamikā*). The ritualists call her "the milker of the *gharma*";

she is a "cow" (*dhenu*) either from the root *dhayati* ("to suck") or from the root *dhinoti* ("to satisfy"). Regarding her, this verse occurs: "I invoke this well-milking cow; may the skillful milker of cows milk her."* *Ṛgveda 10.133.7*
May Savitṛ impel for us the most excellent impulse; the Gharma has been heated—this indeed I shall proclaim.

"I invoke this well-milking cow; may the milker with skillful hands milk her. May Savitṛ press for us the most excellent pressing. For water, or milk accompanied by the *yajus*-formula, is indeed the best of all pressings. "The *gharma* is kindled; I proclaim it well. This is the voice of the intermediate region (*mādhyamikā*). The ritualists call it "the milker of the *gharma*. She is called *aghnyā*, meaning "not to be killed," or perhaps "the slayer of evil" (*aghaghnī*). Regarding her, there is this verse: 11.43.
May you indeed be blessed with good pasture; may we also be blessed. Eat grass, O inviolable one, at all times, and drink pure water as you wander.
May you indeed be blessed, eating on well-tilled pasture; and may we now likewise be blessed. Eat the grass, O unslayable one! And always drink pure water as you move about.
Of her, there is this other verse:
Uttering the sound *hiṅ*, the mistress of treasures has come near, desiring her calf with her mind.
May this cow yield milk for the Aśvins; may she increase for our great good fortune.
Thus, she is explained by her very name.
*Pathyā* means well-being. *Pathin* means the intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), because she dwells therein. Of her, this [verse] occurs: 11.45.

May Svasti, the most excellent prosperity on the distant path, who possesses wealth and approaches that which is desirable, protect us at home and in the wilderness; may she, the guardian of the gods, be easy of access to us.

For well-being indeed is the best on the journey. She who approaches, rich in heritage and possessed of wealth, bringing desirable riches—may she protect us at home, may she protect us in our resting place, and may she protect us in our departure. May she be easy of access; may the goddess be our guardian, guarding the gods—or rather, may the gods guard her. Dawn has been explained; this is her [hymn]: 11.46.
The waters fled from the chariotless one, terrified of the crushing [chariot],
when the bull struck them down.

The Dawn has departed, fearing the cloud that crushes the cart. "Cart" (*anas*) comes from the root *an*, meaning "to breathe" or "to move. Alternatively, it may be used in a comparative sense: "like a cart," as *anas* means a cart. It is so called because clothing is fastened (*ānaddha*) upon it; or it may derive from the root *ani*, signifying the act of living, for people subsist upon it. The cloud is also called *anas* for this very reason, because the bull—the showerer, the intermediate deity (Indra)—has crushed it. Regarding her, there is another verse: "This is her cart, well-crushed by the Vipāś, lying [there]. (RV 10.75.6)
He has flowed across from the distant mountains.

This [food] of hers lies here well-crushed, as it were, like something else. *Vipāśī* means "one whose bonds are released. *Sasāroṣāḥ* means "those who have moved away," or "from those who have come from afar.
*Ilā* has been explained. Regarding her, this verse occurs: "May *Ilā*, the mother of the herd, or *Urvaśī*, together with the rivers, favor us. (11.48)
May Urvaśī, the one of vast heaven, being praised, come toward us as she desires the offering of the living man;
may she attend to our nourishment that provides strength.

May Ilā praise him; she who is the mother of the herd, the mother of all. May she, along with the rivers, or Urvaśī, praise him—or indeed Urvaśī herself. May she, dwelling in the vast heaven, in the great sky, being praised, covering [him] over, [praise him] for the offering that has been presented—whether it be the light of the living man’s journey, or water. May she attend to our nourishment of food.
Rodasī is the wife of Rudra; regarding her, this verse occurs:
“We now invoke the Marut’s chariot, which seeks renown.”
In whom Rodasī has taken her stand, bringing delightful gifts together with the Maruts.
We invoke the swift Marut-host, like a cloud worthy of renown, upon whom there stands together with the Maruts the two worlds, Rodasī, bearing most delightful waters. 11.50

The Śyena has been explained. [He] takes [the Soma]. With the most sweet [verse], he thinks of the Soma: "When, O God, you, ever new, [think of me]... "Beyond death, O Tveṣa... "Thus, your greatness... "Upward the light... "May Dhātṛ grant [the Soma]... Regarding the Soma, now follow the groups of gods belonging to the middle station: "With lightning-bright [horses], the Rudras, having performed their work... "The various-formed ones, for peace... "May the lower Aṅgirases raise us up... "Like the sun, I would praise [them]... Now follow the women belonging to the middle station: "Of Dakṣa, for whom you [are]... "Desiring what? "O Purifier, for us [is] the great flood..."

"Whatever speech the goddess speaks," "I have found Vāc," "Anumati, Rākā, I [have found] Sinīvālī, Kuhū; I [have found] Urvaśī," "Like lightning, she is bright," "I am Indrāṇī," "Indrāṇī," "Gaurī has lowed," "From her the oceans [flow]," "Gaurī has lowed," "Come hither," "From the well-grazed pasture," "Making the sound *hiṅ*," "Blessing indeed," "Nourishment," "This of hers," "Toward our chariot," "Now the Marut-host"—these are fifty [verses].
Thus ends the fifth chapter in the Uttarashatka;
thus the eleventh chapter of the Nirukta is completed.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Now, therefore, follow the deities residing in the sky. Of these, the Aśvins are the first to arrive.

The Aśvins are so called because they pervade (*vyaśnuvāte*) everything: one with sap, the other with light. "The Aśvins are [so called] because of their horses," says Aurnavābha. Who, then, are the Aśvins? Some say they are heaven and earth; some say they are day and night; some say they are the sun and the moon; and the historians say they are two righteous kings. Their time is after midnight, during the expansion of the light. For the middle portion, which is free from darkness, is the luminous portion, the Sun. Regarding them, there is this verse (12.1):
In the dwellings you two moved about, dark as two rams;
when indeed, O Aśvins, did you come hither to the gods?
Thus, this [verse] is explained by its very recitation.

Of those two who are simultaneous, who perform the same rite, and who have mostly completed their praise, this half-verse occurs because of their lack of formal association (*asaṃstava*). One is called Vāsātya; the other is said to be the son of Uṣas.
Regarding these two, there is this other verse:
"Born here and there, they have both lowed together with their own stainless bodies.
One is the victorious friend of the one who offers good sacrifices; the other is the fortunate son of heaven."

In this birth and that birth, they two are praised with their own names by a body unstained by evil: one is Jiṣṇu Vāmana, the impeller of a very great force; the other is the fortunate son of Heaven, Āditya, who is borne along. Of these two, there is this other verse:
"Awaken the two Aśvins, yoked at dawn; let them come here."
For the drinking of this Soma.
"Awaken the two Aśvins, the practitioners of yoga; let them come here to drink this soma.
Regarding these two, there is this other verse:
"Worship the Aśvins at dawn; urge them on. There is no [offering] in the evening that is acceptable to the gods."
Moreover, another besides us sacrifices; each preceding sacrificer has been more bountiful.

"Worship the Aśvins at dawn; send them forth, for there is no sacrifice to the gods in the evening—this is unpleasing. Even another besides us sacrifices, and he has surpassed us. Each sacrificer who comes earlier is more worthy of gain, the most excellent winner.

Their time extends until sunrise; during that interval, other deities are offered. *Uṣas* [is derived] from the root *vaṣṭi*, meaning "to desire"; the other, the intermediate one, is from the root *ucchati*. Of her, this [verse] occurs: 12.5.
O Uṣas, rich in prizes, bring that wonderful wealth to us,
by which we may support both our children and our grandchildren.
O Uṣas, bring that desirable wealth, rich in food, for us, so that we may obtain sons and grandsons. Regarding her, there is this other verse:
"Truly, these Dawns have displayed their banner; in the eastern half of the firmament, they spread their light.
Like bold warriors preparing their weapons, the ruddy cows, the mothers, come forth toward us."

These very dawns have made their banner—their sign of recognition. The plural number may be used for the sake of honoring the singular. They anoint themselves with light in the eastern half of the intermediate region (*antarikṣa*), like bold warriors preparing their weapons; here *niḥ* stands in place of *sam*. There is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) which says: "I go to their appointed place, like a woman to her lover. They move toward [the sun]; they are called "cows" (*gāvaḥ*) because of their going, "ruddy ones" (*aruṣīḥ*) because of their shining, and "mothers" (*mātaraḥ*) because they are the makers of light. Sūryā is the wife of Sūrya; she is the one most recently released [from the darkness]. Regarding her, there is this verse (12.7):
Ascend the *sukiṃśuka*, the *śalmali*, the one of universal form, golden-hued, well-rolling, and with beautiful wheels;
O Sūryā, ascend to the world of immortality, and make it pleasant for your husband to carry you away.

*Su-kaśanam*: "having beautiful branches," meaning "possessing all forms. Or, it may be used in the sense of comparison, as in "like a *śalmali* tree with beautiful *kiṃśuka* blossoms. *Kiṃśuka* is derived from the root *kraṃś*, in the sense of making manifest. The *śalmali* is "well-reed" (*su-śara*) or "possessing reeds" (*śaravat*). "Ascend to the world of immortality, O Sūryā; make the bridal procession pleasant for thy husband. Thus says the Brāhmaṇa: "Savitṛ gave Sūryā to King Soma, or to Prajāpati.
*Vṛṣākapāyī* is the wife of *Vṛṣākapi*. She is the one most recently released [from her husband]. Regarding her, there is this verse (12.8).
O Vṛṣākapi’s wife, O wealthy one, you who have good sons and a good daughter-in-law, eat the bulls, O Indra! This dear oblation, which brings about all that is desired—Indra is superior to all.

O Vṛṣākapāyī, O wealthy one, you who have good sons, O daughter-in-law with a son of middle age, with speech that is moderate—whether she is called *snuṣā* because she is a good rider (*sādhu-sādinī*), or a good winner (*sādhu-sāninī*), or because she wins (*sanoti*) her own offspring—may Indra eat these bulls for you, these gathered offerings of the midday pressing. "Bulls" (*ukṣaṇaḥ*) is from the root *ukṣ*, meaning "to grow"; or they are so called because they sprinkle (*ukṣanti*) with water. Make dear this oblation which brings an accumulation of happiness. We speak thus of him who is higher than all, Indra, the Āditya. *Saraṇyūḥ* is so called from "running" (*saraṇāt*). Regarding her, there is this verse (XII.9).

They concealed the immortal one from mortals; having made her of similar form, they gave her to Vivasvat. And she brought forth the two Aśvins when that [child] was born; Saraṇyū abandoned the two pairs of twins.

They concealed the immortal one from mortals; having made her of similar appearance (*savarṇā*), they gave her to Vivasvat. The Aśvins also brought back that which had been there. Saraṇyū abandoned two pairs: the intermediate speech and the speech of the intermediate region, according to the etymologists (*nairuktāḥ*); and Yama and Yamī, according to the historians (*aitihāsikāḥ*). Regarding this, they relate a historical narrative: Saraṇyū, the daughter of Tvaṣṭṛ, bore twin children, Yama and Yamī, to Vivasvat the Āditya. Having substituted another woman of similar appearance (*savarṇā*) and having assumed the form of a horse, she fled away.
That Vivasvat Āditya, having assumed the form of a horse, pursued her and united with her. From that, the two Aśvins were born; from Svarṇā, Manu was born. Regarding this, there is this verse:
"Tvaṣṭṛ prepared [the wedding] for his daughter to be led away; to this, the entire world assembles.
The mother of Yama, being led away, the great wife of Vivasvat, vanished. (RV 10.17.1–2)

"Tvaṣṭṛ performs the carrying away of his daughter"—thus this entire world comes together; all these beings gather here. "The mother of Yama, being carried away, the great wife of Vivasvat, vanished"—that is, the night of Āditya vanishes at the rising of the sun. Savitṛ has been explained. His time is when the sky becomes free from darkness and filled with rays. Of him, there is this verse: *Savitṛ* has been explained. His time is when the sky becomes free from darkness and filled with rays. Of him, there is this verse: 12.12
The Seer puts on all forms; he has brought forth what is auspicious for the two-footed and the four-footed.
Savitṛ, the most excellent, has looked upon the firmament; he shines following the departure of the Dawn.
The wise one releases all forms of wisdom; he becomes a seer (*kavi*) of far-reaching vision—perhaps from the root *kav* [to see]. He brings forth what is auspicious for both bipeds and quadrupeds.

Savitṛ, the one to be chosen, has caused the celestial chariot (*nāka*) to be seen; he shines after the departure of the Dawn. The sacrificial animal dedicated to Savitṛ is "dark-bellied" (*adhōrāma*). This is known in the enumeration of sacrificial animals. On account of what commonality? Because at that time, darkness is below.

This [is the case] because of this similarity: "Below Rāma, below Kṛṣṇa. Because of what similarity? "Having piled the fire-altar, one should not approach a *rāmā* (a woman). A *rāmā* is approached for pleasure (*ramaṇāya*), not for religious duty (*dharmāya*). Because of this similarity, [the animal] is of the black species (*kṛṣṇajātīya*). "The *kṛkavāku* (cock) belongs to Savitṛ. This is known in the enumeration of sacrificial animals (*paśusamāmnāya*). Because of what similarity? Because it follows the description of time. The first part of the *kṛkavāku*'s cry is an imitation of the sound of the verb *vac* (to speak). *Bhaga* has been explained; its time is prior to the rising [of the sun]. Regarding this, there is this verse: 12.13.
Let us invoke the fierce Bhaga, the conqueror of the dawn, the son of Aditi who is the sustainer;
him whom even the weak man, even the swift one, and even the king, addressing as Bhaga, says, "May I partake of his favor."
"May we invoke the fierce Bhaga, the winner in the morning, the son of Aditi, who is the sustainer of all.

Even the weak man, thinking himself wealthy, [invokes him]; even the poor man; even the swift one—*turaḥ* is a name for Yama, derived either from *tṛ* (to cross over), or from *tvar* (to hasten); Yama is swift-moving through his speed. Even the king says, 'May I partake of Bhaga. They say that Bhaga is blind;
he does not see, for he has not been let go. 'He struck out his two eyes by eating the *prāśitra*,' so says the Brāhmaṇa."
"Fortune goes to the people," so it is understood.
The sun goes to the people with its rising;
"Sūrya" is derived from the root *sṛ* ("to move"), or from *sū* ("to impel"), or from *svīr* ("to be powerful"). Of this [deity], there is this verse (RV 1.50.1): 12.14.
Those rays bear aloft that god Sūrya, the Jātavedas, so that everyone may behold him.
"The rays, the banners, carry up that Jātavedas, the Sun, for the seeing of all beings. Who else but Āditya would he have spoken of in this way? Of him there is this other verse:
"The brilliant array of the gods has risen, the eye of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni."
The Sun, the soul of all that moves and stands, has filled the heavens, the earth, and the intermediate space.

The host of the gods has risen up, worthy of being sought after—the renown of Mitra, Varuṇa, and Agni. It has filled heaven and earth and the mid-region with its greatness. Sūrya is the self of all that moves and all that is stationary. Now, insofar as he nourishes the abundance of his rays, he becomes Pūṣan.
Regarding him, there is this verse: "Thy one form is bright, thy other is worshipful; thou art like the sky, possessing two days of diverse forms."
For you protect all magical powers, O self-dependent one; O Pūṣan, may your bounty here be auspicious.

One part of you is bright; another is red; one part is worthy of sacrifice; another is fit for the ritual. You possess two days of different forms, and your action is like that of heaven. You protect all forms of wisdom. You are possessed of food. O Pūṣan, may your gift here be full of vessels. Regarding this, there is another verse:
With eloquence, I have approached the protector of every path, impelled by desire, seeking light.
May he grant us riches with golden tips; may Pūṣan bring success to every prayer.

"Path by path, the lord, by his word, made by desire; having reached the sun, or rather, having reached the sun that has come near—may he grant us wealth with desirable excellence, and may Pūṣan accomplish every work for us. Now, when one is entered (viṣita), he becomes Viṣṇu. Viṣṇu is so called from the root *viś* (to enter) or from *vyaś* (to pervade). Of him, this verse occurs: "Viṣṇu strode across this [universe]; in three places he planted his step; the whole world is gathered in his footstep's dust."
That which Viṣṇu strides forth—this is it. He places his foot in three ways for the sake of a threefold existence: on the earth, in the intermediate space, and in heaven; thus says Śākapūṇi.

Aurṇavābha [says] that [the word *viṣṇupada* refers to] Samārohaṇa, Viṣṇupada, and Gayaśiras. "His footprint is hidden in the dust; it is not seen in the swelling atmosphere. Or rather, it may be used for the sake of comparison: "His footprint is hidden as if in dust," for dust (*pām̐savaḥ*) is so called because it is produced (*sūyante*) by feet, or because those who have fallen (*pannāḥ*) lie down in it, or because they become subject to contempt (*paṃsanīyāḥ*). (12.19) *Viśvānara* has been explained. This is its occurrence in a verse addressed to Indra: (12.20) "The praise of the lord of wealth, of *Viśvānara*, the one who has attained his goal..."
And with these aids of the people, I invoke the chariots.

Of Viśvānara Āditya, the unbending, of great power and strength, with his impulses, his desires, and his ways of protection for the people of men, and with the aid of the paths of chariots—I invoke Indra at this sacrifice. Varuṇa has been explained; here is a verse concerning him:
"O Purifier, with that eye wherewith thou beholdest the active folk, O Varuṇa, thou seest [all]."

*Bhuraṇyu* is a name for "swift. *Bhuraṇyu* is the bird; it leads a vast path. It is also the bearer (*volhā*) of the heavenly world. *Bhuraṇyu* is that which reaches that [world]. With this, by means of the manifestation of the Purifier (*pāvaka*), you, O Varuṇa, behold the people who are moving swiftly (*bhuraṇyantaṃ*). "We praise that of yours"—this is the completion of the sentence.
Or rather, in the following verse (12.22):
"O Purifier, with that eye by which you [behold] the people who are moving swiftly..."
O Varuṇa, you see.
You rise up to the sky, O Sūrya, measuring out the broad space with your rays as you behold all living beings.
You traverse the sky and the broad atmosphere; you measure out the days together with the nights, O Sūrya, beholding the beings that have been born, or even those yet to come.
O Purifier, with that eye wherewith you, O Varuṇa, look upon the people as they stir about.
Facing the clans of the gods, facing men, you rise up; facing all, so that we may behold the light of heaven.
Thou risest facing this all; this light is said to face this all; thou beholdest this entire world facing it.
Or rather, O Purifier Varuṇa, with that eye wherewith thou lookest upon the active folk, [with that thou beholdest this].
Therefore, you look down upon us people.
*Keśī*: "hair" (*keśa*) means rays; he possesses these, or because of shining (*kāśana*), or because of illuminating (*prakāśana*). Of him, there is this verse (X.
98.7): "The hairy one [bears] Agni, the hairy one [bears] poison, the hairy one bears the two worlds."
The one with hair is for the vision of the sun; the one with hair is called this light.

Keśin [possesses] both fire and poison; "poison" (*viṣa*) is a name for water. It is derived from *snāti* preceded by *vi*, meaning "to purify," or from *sacati* preceded by *vi*. He sustains both heaven and earth. Keśin beholds all this. "Keśin is called this light"—by this he refers to the Sun. Furthermore, these other two lights are also called "hairy" (*keśin*): fire by its smoke, and the intermediate one (the wind) by its dust. Regarding these two, there is this verse common to them:
"Three hairy ones appear in due season; one of them shears throughout the year. (RV 1.164.44)
Alone, he beholds the universe with his powers; the flash of the One is seen, but not his form.

Three long-haired ones appear in due season; at every time they look abroad. One of them shears in the year—this is Agni who burns the earth. One looks abroad upon everything through his deeds—this is Āditya. The course of one is visible, but not the form of the middle one.
Now, when he goes along shaking [the world] with his rays, he becomes Vṛṣākapi, the Shaker of the Bull. Regarding him, there is this verse:
"Come back again, O Vṛṣākapi; let us two arrange a happy course.
You who go to sleep, you who take away [our wealth], return again by the path you came."
Indra is superior to all.

"Come again, O Vṛṣākapi! Your deeds have been well-performed; let us two perform them together. This one who, by means of sleep, causes sleep to perish—the Sun by his rising—by that same path you go back as you set. We speak thus of that Āditya who is superior to all, O Indra.
Yama has been explained. Regarding him, there is this verse (RV 10.97.16): 'In the tree with beautiful leaves where Yama drinks together with the gods...'"
Here our father, the lord of the people, looks with longing toward the ancient ones.

On which tree with beautiful leaves, or in a place that is a dwelling, or perhaps for the sake of comparison—as in "like a tree with beautiful leaves": a *vṛkṣa* is so called from being cut (*vraścana*), and *palāśa* from eating (*palāśana*). Yama meets with the gods; the Āditya [meets them] with his rays. There, may he who is the protector or guardian of us all desire the ancients. *Aja Ekapād*: the Unborn has one foot; or he protects with one foot; or he drinks with one foot; or one foot belongs to him. He does not lift up his single foot.
Thus there is also a Vedic verse (nigama). This is its occurrence as a specific term in a verse addressed to the Viśvedevas (vaiśvadevī):
“May Pāvīravī, Tanyatu, Ekapāt, Aja, the Supporter of Heaven, Sindhu, and the Waters of the ocean;
may all the gods hear my words, along with Sarasvatī, together with our prayers and Purandhī. (RV 7.35.12)

The *pavi* is the barb; it is so called because it pierces the body. Similarly, the weapon is *pavīra*; Indra, possessing that, is *pavīravān*. There is also a Vedic verse (*nigama*) which says: "The wielder of the *pavīra* has stood firm. Thus, the divine speech is *pāvīravī*, and the celestial speech is also *pāvīravī*. The thunderbolt is the striker of another voice. And Aja Ekapād, the sustainer of heaven, and Sindhu, and the waters, and those of the ocean, and all the gods, and Sarasvatī together with Purandhi—the goddess of praise—may they hear these words uttered by our prayers and joined with ritual acts.
The earth has been explained. This is its occurrence in a verse addressed to Indra and Agni (RV 7.94.7):
"O Indra and Agni, whether you two are on the highest earth, on the middle one, or on the lowest, come hither from there, O showerers of blessings; drink of this pressed soma."
Thus, this has been explained by the words themselves.
The ocean has been explained. This is its occurrence in a *pāvamānī* verse (RV 9.73.3): "Those possessing the filter sit around the speech; their ancient father protects their vow.
Varuṇa has placed the great ocean within himself; the wise have found a hold in the foundations."

The middle hosts of gods, possessing the *pavitra* (purifiers) and possessing rays, sit around the speech of the mid-region. Their ancient and primeval father, the Middle One, protects their vow and their ritual action. Varuṇa places the great ocean within, as a covering. Then the wise are able to undertake ritual actions upon the supports, the waters.
Aja Ekapād has been explained. Pṛthivī has been explained. Samudra has been explained. This is their occurrence in another verse addressed to many deities (RV 10.65.8).
May Ahi Budhnya hear us, and Aja Ekapād, the Earth, and the Ocean;
may all the gods, the increasers of Truth, being invoked, and the praised mantras recited by the sages, protect us.

Moreover, let Ahirbudhnya hear us: Aja-Ekapād, Pṛthivī, Samudra, and all the gods; those who increase truth, or those who increase sacrifice; being invoked with mantras and praised—may the mantras recited by the seers protect us, and those recited by the wise. Dadhyañc is so called because he was "turned toward" (pratyakta) meditation, or because "meditation was turned toward him. Atharvan has already been explained. Manu [is so called] from "thinking" (manana). Of these, there is this occurrence in a verse addressed to Indra (Ṛgveda 1.80.16): "In which [verse] Atharvan, the father of Manu, and Dadhyañc fashioned their inspired thought (dhī)."
In him, as of old, Indra and the seers have joined together in hymns, praising his sovereign rule.

Yama and Atharvan, and Manu the father of men, and Dadhyañc—they have extended their wisdom. In him let the sacred formulations (*brahmāṇi*), the ritual acts, and the hymns (*ukthāni*) converge, as they did with Indra of old. He who is worthy of praise, being praised, attains sovereign rule.
12.34 Now, therefore, follow the groups of gods whose abode is heaven. Of these, the Ādityas are the first to arrive. The Ādityas have been explained. This is their [verse]:
12.35 "These songs, dripping with clarity (*ghṛtasnu*), I offer with the ladle to the Ādityas, the eternal kings."
May Mitra, Aryaman, and Bhaga hear us; may Varuṇa, Dakṣa, and Aṃśa, who is born of many, listen.

"Dropping ghee, flowing with ghee; streaming with ghee, pouring forth ghee"—or rather, "flowing with ghee, gliding with ghee. For a long time I offer these oblations with the *juhū* ladle to the Ādityas—for long life, or for the sake of the kings. May Mitra, Aryaman, Bhaga, Bahujāta, Dhātṛ, Dakṣa, Varuṇa, and Aṃśa hear these songs of ours.
Aṃśa is explained by [the same etymology as] Aṃśu.
The seven seers have been explained. Of them, this [verse] occurs:
"Seven seers are stationed within the body; seven guard it with constant vigilance."

Seven waters go to the world of the sleeping man; there, two gods who do not sleep and who sit at the sacrificial session remain awake. Seven seers are stationed within the body; their rays are in the sun. Seven protect [him] ever vigilantly, remaining watchful throughout the year. Those same seven waters go to the world of the sleeping man when the sun has set. There, two gods who do not sleep and who sit at the sacrificial session—Vāyu and Āditya—remain awake. This is with respect to the deities (*adhidaivata*).

Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*). Seven seers (*ṛṣi*) are established within the body: the six sense organs, and knowledge as the seventh in the self (*ātman*). These seven always protect [the body] with vigilance; they guard the body without negligence. These very seven are the "removers" (*apanānī*); when one sleeps, they go to the world where the self has set. There, two gods who do not sleep and remain seated at the sacrifice—the wise self (*prājña-ātman*) and the radiant self (*taijasa-ātman*)—are awake. Thus he describes the movement of the self. Regarding these, there is another verse: "The ladle (*camasa*) is tilted on its side, with its base turned upward, in which glory of every form is deposited."
The seven seers who were its guardians of this great [soma] trembled together.

"The ladle with its opening turned crosswise, bound above, or perhaps awakening upward, in which glory of every form is deposited; here sit the seven seers together with the rays of the sun, who were the guardians of this Great One"—thus with reference to the deities. Now, with reference to the self: "The ladle with its opening turned crosswise, bound above, or perhaps awakening upward, in which glory of every form is deposited; here sit the seven seers together with the senses, which were the guardians of this Great One"—thus he declares the course of the self.
The gods have been explained. Of them, this [verse] occurs:
May the auspicious favor of the upright gods be ours; may the bounty of the gods turn toward us.
May we abide in the friendship of the gods; may the gods extend our span of life that we may live.

May we abide in the auspicious benevolence and wisdom of the gods—those who move straight forward, or perhaps those who move according to the seasons (ṛtu). May the gift of the gods turn toward us; may we enter into the friendship of the gods. May the gods increase our lifespan for long-lived existence.
"Viśvedevas" means all the gods. Regarding them, this verse occurs: 12.39 O protectors, sustainers of the people, you Viśvedevas, come hither!
The givers [of oblations] [drink] the pressed juice of the giver.
"Whether they are protectors or those worthy of protection, all you gods sustained by humans, come here! You have given; [give] a son to the giver!

This very same *vaiśvadeva* triplet in the *gāyatrī* meter is found in the *Daśatayīs*. Whatever [verse] has many deities is employed in the place of the *vaiśvadeva*s. Śākapūṇi says it is that which has "all" (*viśva*) as its characteristic mark. However, this definition is not exhaustive. For example, there is one [verse] concerning Babhru.

Thus, these ten verses in the *dvipadā* meter are without a specific deity (*aliṅga*). Bhūtāṃśa Kāśyapa is the single deity of the *āśina* hymn. The hymn beginning with *abhitaṣṭīyam* has a single deity. The Sādhyas are gods because of their accomplishment; this verse belongs to them:
"By means of sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; those were the first ordinances. (RV 10.90.16)
Those great ones have attained the firmament, where the ancient Sādhyas, the gods, abide.
"By means of sacrifice the gods sacrificed to the sacrifice; by means of Agni the gods sacrificed to Agni. Agni was the victim; they seized him and sacrificed with him"—so says the Brāhmaṇa.
Those were the first laws (dharmas); those great ones attained the height of heaven.

Wherein dwell the ancient Sādhyas, the gods who are achievers; the etymologists say they are the "heaven-dwelling host of gods. There is the narrative that they were the first age of the gods. Because they cause everything to shine forth (*vivasate*), they are called Vasus; this is the designation for Agni with the Vasus. Therefore, they have the earth as their station. Because Indra with the Vasus causes [all] to shine forth, he is called Vāsava; therefore, they have the intermediate space as their station. The Vasus are the rays of the sun because of their shining forth (*vivāsanāt*); therefore, they have heaven as their station. Regarding them, there is this verse (RV 7.35.14):
"O gods, we have made a good path to your dwelling, you who have come to this libation, enjoying it."
Having eaten and having drunk, O all you Vasus, bestow riches upon us.
O gods, we have prepared fair paths for your coming; you who come to these libations, having taken pleasure in them, have eaten and drunk. O Vasus, bestow all treasures upon us.
Regarding them, there is this other verse:
"Here on earth the Vasus, the gods, took delight; in the wide mid-air, the radiant ones purified themselves."
O you of wide stride, prepare the path hitherward; hear this messenger of ours who has come.

On this earth the Vasus, the gods, have taken their rest. *Jmā* is the earth; on it they dwell. In the wide intermediate space (*antarikṣa*), they purify themselves, move about, and take delight. They are radiant and shining. Make these paths easy for us, with great speed. Listen to this messenger of ours, to this Agni who has come hither.
The *vājins* (the swift ones) have been explained. Of them, this is the verse:
"May the *vājins* be auspicious to us in our invocations at the assembly of the gods—those who run measuredly, who possess beautiful songs. (RV 7.38.7)
Crushing the serpent, the wolf, and the demons, drive away all diseases far from us.

May the prize-winning steeds be auspicious to us in our invocations, at the divine gathering, and at the sacrifice—those who run measuredly, those who run well-measured; those who are good-sounding, or rather, those who move beautifully, or those who shine beautifully, or those who possess beautiful luster. May they crush the serpent, the wolf, and the demons, and may they swiftly drive away from us all diseases, O divine horses! Or [the term] *devapatnyaḥ* means the wives of the gods. Regarding them, this verse occurs: "May the longing wives of the gods protect us; may they aid us toward victory and the winning of the prize."
Those who are terrestrial and those who are in the domain of the waters—may those goddesses, who are easily invoked, grant us protection.

May the wives of the gods, longing for us, protect us; may they protect us for the procreation of offspring and for the gathering of food. Those who are terrestrial and those who are in the domain of the waters—that is, in their activity—may those goddesses, who are easily invoked, grant us shelter as a refuge.
Regarding them, there is this other verse (12.45).
And may the divine wives, the consorts of the gods, come hither—Indrāṇī, Gāyī, and Aśvinī the sovereign;
may Rodasī and Varuṇānī hear us; and may the goddesses who are the mothers of the seasons come.

Moreover, let the *gnās*, the wives of the gods, come forth: Indrāṇī, the wife of Indra; Agnāyī, the wife of Agni; Aśvinī, the wife of the Aśvins; Rāṭ, who shines; Rodasī, the wife of Rudra; and Varuṇānī, the wife of Varuṇa. Let these goddesses come forth and desire [the union] which is the proper season for wives, which is the proper season for wives. 12.46

Now, therefore, [the hymns] belonging to the day-stations among the *vasāti* verses: "O you born here, yoke at dawn, worship at dawn"; "That wonderful [light] of Uṣas"; "These dawns"; "The well-branching [tree]"; "The *vṛṣākapi* verse"; "Tvaṣṭṛ concealed [the form] from his daughter"; "Savitṛ [bestows] all forms"; "The winner of the morning"; "Upwards that [sun]"; "The wonderful, bright one"; "Of your paths, path by path"; "This [is] Viṣṇu"; "Viśvānara"; [the hymn] explained as "Viśvānara"; "Of Viśvānara"; "By which, O purifier"; this group of four; "O long-haired one, [worship] Agni"; "Three long-haired ones"; "Come back again"; "In which tree"; "The daughter of the lightning" (*pāvīravī*); "If Indra and Agni"; "Possessing the filter" (*pavitravant*).

And also: "May Ahi budhnya and Atharvan [protect us]"; then the divine hosts dwelling in heaven; these songs; the seven seers; Tiryagbila; the auspicious months of the gods; "the gods, easy of access on earth, may they be gracious to us here"; "and may the wives of the gods, Agnayi and others, enjoy [the offering]"—these constitute forty-six [verses].
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the Uttarashatka;
thus the twelfth chapter of the Nirukta is completed;
and thus the Daivata-kāṇḍa and the latter half [of the work] are finished.
Now follows the supplement;
now begins the thirteenth chapter.

Now, these are called "excessive praises" (*ati-stutayaḥ*). Or rather, there should indeed be a true understanding [of them], because of the great majesty (*māhābhāgya*) of the deity. He [the author] speaks first of Agni alone.
"O Agni, you [shine] with days; you, O Āśuśukṣaṇi," as it says in this hymn.
"For without you, neither the blinking nor the perishing [exists]," this is for Varuṇa.
Now, this is for Indra. 13.1
O Indra, even if there were a hundred heavens and a hundred earths for you,
O wielder of the thunderbolt, neither the thousand suns nor the two worlds could equal you at your birth.
"O Indra, even if there were a hundred heavens and a hundred earths as thy counterparts, O Wielder of the Thunderbolt, neither a thousand suns nor even heaven and earth together could surpass thee.
Now follows this [hymn] of Āditya:
"O Vṛṣākapi, when you and Indra went to the house of the north..."
Where is that many-slaying deer, which the daughter of Kaṇva brought forth? Indra is supreme over all.

When you went upward, O Vṛṣākapi, to the house of Indra—where was that beast so full of sin? Where was that beast who eats much? The word *mṛga* comes from the root *mārṣṭi*, meaning "to move. To what region did he go, leading his wife? We say this of Āditya, for Indra is superior to all. Now, regarding these rays of Āditya (13.3): "For they have flowed forth from the presser; they have not honored Indra as a god—at which place Vṛṣākapi is, he who is my friend among the prosperous ones. Indra is superior to all."
