For they sent forth [the seed] for procreation, yet they did not consider Indra to be a god—at that time when Vṛṣākapi became intoxicated. "The noble one" means the lord; "in prosperities" means in nourishments; "my friend" means my companion, or a friend of my heart, or "he who is a friend to me";
Like two plough-shares, you are the upholders and the destroyers; like two hunters, you are the slayers and the scatterers.
Like two water-born conquerors, you are exhilarating; as such, O two, grant me old age that is free from decay and death.

Regarding the verse *sṛṇyeva*: the *sṛṇi* (hook) is of two kinds—the supporter and the slayer. Likewise, the Aśvins are also supporters. *Jarbharī* means the two supporters; *turpharītū* means the two slayers. *Naitośeva turpharī parpharīkā*: *naitośa* is the offspring of *nitośa*. Like *naitośa*, *turpharī* refers to the two swift slayers. *Udanyajeva jemanā maderū*: *udanyajeva* means like those born from water—either in oceanic jewels or lunar ones. *Jemane* means in victory. *Jemanā maderū* [refers to the two victorious, exhilarating ones].
This is my ageless amniotic membrane, this is the ageless placenta; this body born of the womb remains undecayed through the autumns.
Now follows this [hymn] of Soma: "Crossing over, the exhilarating one flows—the stream of the pressed juice."
Crossing over, the gladdening one flows swiftly.

He who praises it overcomes all evil; being slow [in speech], he runs and goes to the upward path. This is the stream of the pressed juice—the stream of the Soma that has been poured out, purified by mantra, and praised with speech. Now, this [verse] concerning the sacrifice: Four are its horns, three are its feet, two are its heads, and seven are its hands.
Bound in three ways, the bull bellows loudly; the great god has entered into mortals.
"The four horns"—these are said to be the Vedas; "his three feet" are the three Soma-pressings;
"two heads" are the Prāyaṇīya and Udayanīya offerings; "seven hands" are the seven meters; "bound in three ways" means bound by the Mantras, Brāhmaṇas, and Kalpas; "the bull bellows."

The roaring of this [sacrifice] proceeds according to the sequence of the pressings by means of the *ṛc*s, the *yajus* formulas, and the *sāman* chants; for when they recite it with the *ṛc*s, they sacrifice with the *yajus* formulas, and they praise it with the *sāman* chants. "A great god"—for this sacrifice is indeed a great god—"has entered into mortals," for it enters into human beings for the purpose of sacrifice. The following verse is for its further explanation:
"Going to heaven, they look not back; they ascend to heaven and the two worlds, those wise ones who have extended the sacrifice which flows in every direction."

"Those who sacrifice, desiring heaven, do not see; they see only this world as having gone [to the other]. "They ascend to heaven, to the two worlds—those wise ones who have extended the sacrifice that flows everywhere, that sustains all. Now, this is like a riddle of speech: "Speech has been measured out in four quarters; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in secret, do not stir; the fourth quarter of speech, humans speak."

There are four measured steps of speech; those Brahmins who are wise know them. Three, hidden in the cave, do not reveal their meaning. "Cave" (*guhā*) is derived from the root *guh* (to hide). "The fourth" (*turīya*) is derived from the root *tvar* (to hasten). What are those four steps? According to the seers (*ārṣa*), they are the syllable *oṃ* and the great utterances (*mahāvyāhṛtis*). According to the grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), they are nouns, verbs, prefixes, and particles. According to the ritualists (*yājñika*), they are the Mantras, the Kalpas, the Brāhmaṇas, and the fourth is the common vernacular.

The etymologists say that the *ṛc*s, the *yajus* formulas, and the *sāman* chants constitute [the first three], while the fourth is the colloquial speech. Some say that the speech of serpents, of birds, of small reptiles, and the fourth, the colloquial speech, belong to these. Regarding animals, there are declarations concerning the self (*ātmapravāda*) such as: "in cattle, in lutes, in wild beasts, and in the self. Furthermore, there is a Brāhmaṇa passage: "That speech, once created, became fourfold: three parts were in these very worlds, and the fourth was in cattle. That which was on earth was in Agni and in the *Rathantara*; that which was in the intermediate space was in Vāyu and in the *Vāmadevya*."

"That [speech] which is in the sky, in the sun, in the *bṛhatī* [meter], and in the thunder—then, that speech which remained over from among the animals, they placed it in the *brāhmaṇas*. Therefore, the *brāhmaṇas* speak both kinds of speech: that of the gods and that of humans. Thus [it is said]. Now, this [verse] regarding the syllable: "In the highest heaven, upon the syllables of the *ṛc*, all the gods have taken their seat. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 1.3.9)
He who does not know that—what will he do with the Ṛg-veda? But those who know it, they sit together here.

"In the imperishable syllable of the Ṛgveda, in the highest expanse, upon which all the gods are seated—whoever does not know that, what will he do with the Ṛgveda? But those who know it, they sit together in harmony. Thus he instructs the knower. "Which is this syllable? "It is 'Om', says Śākapūṇi; for in the imperishable syllable of the Ṛgveda, in the highest expanse, [the words] are placed within mantras addressed to various deities. Indeed, this is that syllable which corresponds to the entire threefold knowledge (trayī vidyā). So says the Brāhmaṇa (13.10).

"Āditya," says Śākapūṇi’s son. This is the *ṛc*: "When they worship him with every verse (*pratyṛcaḥ*)," that is, all beings; "whatever of his is other than the mantras," that becomes the *akṣara*. Here, the rays are called the gods, those who are seated upon him—this is with reference to the deities (*adhidaivata*). Now, with reference to the self (*adhyātma*): here the body is called the *ṛc*; "when they worship him with every verse," that is, all the sense organs; "whatever of it has the nature of being indestructible," that becomes the *akṣara*. Here, the senses are called the gods, those which become one in this self—these are the declarations concerning the self (*ātmapravādāḥ*). 13.11

The *akṣara* does not perish, nor is it exhausted; it is imperishable. Or, it is called *akṣa* because it is the axle (*akṣa*) of speech. Or, the axle (*akṣa*) is so called because it is the pivot (*añjana*) of a vehicle, and the other [the syllable] is like that by virtue of its commonality of functioning as a pivot. This speculative inquiry into the meaning of the mantra has been set forth both from the perspective of revealed scripture (*śruti*) and from the perspective of reasoning (*tarka*). However, mantras should not be etymologically explained in isolation; rather, they should be explained according to their specific context (*prakaraṇa*). For there is no direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of these [mantras] for one who is not a seer (*ṛṣi*) or who lacks austerity (*tapas*).

It has been stated previously that among those who possess knowledge, he who possesses more extensive learning is indeed to be praised. When the seers were departing, men said to the gods, "Who will be our seer? To them, they gave this seer named Tarka—the one who is inferred through reflection upon the meaning of the mantras and through logical reasoning. Therefore, whatever a learned reciter (anūcāna) infers, that becomes the work of a seer.
"When the Brahmins, as friends, perform the sacrifice with their minds' impulses fashioned by the heart, then some abandon the path of knowledge here;
the knowers of the sacred word (brahmāṇaḥ) move about, ascending by various means. (RV 10.71.8)

When Brahmins, as officiating priests (ṛtvij) of equal renown, perform the sacrifice together with mental impulses fashioned by the heart, they then distinguish themselves through the various activities that are to be known through the Vedas. They are called *ūhabrahmāṇaḥ*, *ūhabrahmāṇaḥ*—meaning either those for whom the *brahman* is *ūha* (inference/interpretation), or those who possess the *brahman* as their *ūha*. This knowledge consists of sacred revelation (*śruti*), intuition (*mati*), and intellect (*buddhi*). One must seek its further limit through austerity (*tapas*). This [knowledge] must not be explained away by one desiring long life; therefore, the remaining portions among the Vedic meters (*chandas*) should be disregarded. Now, regarding tradition (*āgama*): whatever deity he names, he attains the state of being that very deity; he attains it. 13.13
The deities and the constituent parts of the sacrifice have been explained. Now, therefore, we shall explain the progression along the upward path.
The Sun is the Self; for he, having risen, is the witness of action. Regarding this, they proclaim as follows: "Now, this host of Ṛg-verses proclaims this great Self."
"They call him Indra, Mitra, Varuna, and Agni. Thus [it is said].
Then this Great Self, desiring to know the Self, spoke to himself with these two [verses]: "I am Agni, Jātavedas by birth; I am the first-born. (13.14)
I am Agni, Jātavedas by birth; ghee is my eye, and ambrosia is in my mouth. I am the threefold light, the measurer of the mid-world, the eternal heat; "oblation" is my name.
I am the first-born of Cosmic Order, the name of immortality before the gods.
Whoever gives me to him, let him speak thus: "I eat the food that eats the eater."

Having thus recognized him, he appeared. He addressed him as he approached: "Reveal to another this Self, the one born of the supreme self, who is near. "I beheld the Herdsman, never resting, moving hither and thither along his paths.
Wearing the converging and diverging rays, he revolves repeatedly within the worlds."

"He revolves within the worlds. Now, this is the Great Self, characterized by *sattva*; that is the Supreme, that is Brahman, that is Truth, that is the Water (*salila*), that is the Unmanifest, that is intangible, formless, tasteless, odorless, immortal, and pure. The elemental self (*bhūtātman*) is established in that. Some say this is the "Nature of the Elements" (*bhūtaprakṛti*). That is the Field (*kṣetra*); having reached the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) through knowledge, one becomes selfless (*nirātmaka*). Now, this Great Self becomes threefold: *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

But *sattva* remains pure in the middle; on both sides are *rajas* and *tamas*. Thus, for one who is ignorant, yet becomes purified and manifests power, [the quality of] desire, aversion, and darkness conduces to the discernment of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*). The Great Self has manifestation as its mark; knowledge has the mark of darkness; and darkness has the mark of light. Space, moreover, has certainty as its mark. (13.16)

Sound is the quality of space (*ākāśa*). From space arises wind, possessing two qualities through touch. From wind arises light, possessing three qualities through form. From light arise waters, possessing four qualities through taste. From waters arises earth, possessing five qualities through smell. From earth arise the hosts of beings, both stationary and moving. This [universe] remains awake for a thousand *yuga*s of the day; at its end, about to sleep, it withdraws its limbs. The hosts of beings enter into the earth; the earth enters the waters; the waters enter light; light enters wind; and wind enters space.

Space is the mind; the mind is knowledge; knowledge is the Great Self; the Great Self is intuition; intuition is primordial nature (*prakṛti*). That [nature] sleeps for a thousand yugas, which is its night. These two, day and night, revolve incessantly. That is time; this is what constitutes the day: those people who know that the day of Brahmā extends for a thousand yugas, and that his night likewise ends after a thousand yugas—they are the ones who truly know day and night. (13.17)

As that [body] revolves, another follows it; one is perceived as "I am the creator, the seer, the distinct, and immeasurable. Through false vision, he perceives this: from fire comes the purifier, from the great elements come the atoms, from space comes wind, from wind comes breath, from fire come the eye and the speaker, from water comes moisture, and from earth comes form. One should know there are eight qualities of the earthly body: three from the mother and three from the father. The bones, sinews, and marrow are from the father; the skin, flesh, and blood are from the mother. Food and drink make up the eighth. Thus, this person is fashioned as consisting of all things and possessing all knowledge. 13.18

Whatever he pursues, that he becomes. If he pursues *dharma*, he becomes a god; if he pursues knowledge (*jñāna*), he becomes immortal; if he pursues desire (*kāma*), he falls away and enters this womb. This is the process here: from semen (*retas*) phlegm (*śleṣman*) arises; from phlegm, chyle (*rasa*); from chyle, blood (*śoṇita*); from blood, flesh (*māṃsa*); from flesh, fat (*medas*); from fat, sinews (*snāvan*); from sinews, bones (*asthi*); from bones, marrow (*majjā*).

From the marrow comes semen. This semen, when discharged into the womb, develops into a person. With an excess of semen, one becomes male; with an excess of blood, one becomes female; with an equal amount of both, one becomes a neuter; and with a divided semen, one becomes a twin. This occurs through the union of semen and blood, and through the union of the mother and father. How then is this body fully constrained? It becomes embryonic. After staying for one night, it becomes a *kalala*; after five nights, it becomes bubbles (*budbuda*).

After seven nights, it becomes a *peśī* (a fleshy mass). After fourteen nights, it becomes an *arbuda* (a bubble-like swelling). At twenty-five nights, it becomes a firm, well-defined mass (*ghana*). After one month, it becomes solid. Within two months, the head is formed. In three months, the neck is delineated. In four months, the skin is delineated. In the fifth month, nails and hair are delineated. In the sixth month, the mouth, nose, eyes, and ears develop.
In the seventh month, it becomes capable of movement. In the eighth month, it begins to perceive and form mental determinations. In the ninth month, all its limbs become fully complete.
I have died and been born again; I have been born and died again.
Indeed, thousands of various wombs have been inhabited by me.
Various foods have been eaten, and various breasts have been drunk from;
various mothers have been seen, as well as fathers and friends.
"Head-downward and being tormented, the creature, thus endowed [with suffering], should practice Sāṃkhya and Yoga, or [meditate upon] the Puruṣa as the twenty-fifth principle.

And then, in the tenth month, it is born. Once born and touched by the wind, it does not remember birth and death. At the end, there is the fruit of its auspicious and inauspicious karma. This is the measure of the body. (13.19)

The head consists of one hundred and eight joints and eight skull-bones (*kapāla*). There are sixteen fat-pads (*vapāpalāni*), nine hundred sinews (*snāyu*), and seven hundred vital points (*marman*) in a person. There are thirty-five million hairs. The heart consists of eight skull-bones, and the tongue consists of twelve skull-bones. The two testicles consist of eight *suparṇa*-bones. Likewise, the genitals, anus, and bladder—these [organs] for urine and feces, being moistened by food and drink, produce their respective functions; why is it that they do not accumulate karma, yet each overcomes the other?

Knowledge and action, as well as prior wisdom, accompany him. Immersed in the great darkness of ignorance and overwhelmed by pairs of opposites consisting of old age, death, hunger, thirst, sorrow, anger, greed, delusion, pride, fear, envy, jealousy, malice, and exhilaration, he is liberated from this state through straightforwardness and the swiftness of his movements.

Having departed from this body composed of the great elements in a mere twinkling of an eye, it proceeds through its natural state, transforms itself into a fiery body, experiences the fruit corresponding to its karma, and upon the exhaustion of that karma, returns again to this world. 13.20

Now, those who, resorting to violence and abandoning knowledge, perform great penance or perform the rites prescribed in the Vedas for a long time, they pass into smoke; from smoke, into night; from night, into the waning half of the month; from the waning half of the month, into the southern progress of the sun; from the southern progress, into the world of the fathers; from the world of the fathers, into the moon; from the moon, into the wind; from the wind, into rain; and from rain, into plants. Having become this, upon the exhaustion of that [merit], he returns again to this very world. 13.21

Now, those who, having abandoned violence and resorted to knowledge, perform great austerity, or perform the rites prescribed by knowledge—they attain the light (*arcis*). From the light, they go to the day; from the day, to the waxing fortnight; from the waxing fortnight, to the six months of the northern course of the sun; from the northern course, to the world of the gods (*devaloka*); from the world of the gods, to the sun; from the sun, to lightning. Having become a person of mind (*mānasa-puruṣa*) from lightning, they attain the world of Brahmā. They do not return again.
Since the remaining venomous serpents do not know this, therefore this must be understood. Furthermore, it is said:
"You do not perceive him who generated these [beings]; something else has come between you.
Enveloped by mist and idle talk, the reciters of hymns wander about, seeking only their own sustenance."

The wise do not know that which those who know thus declare: "The Imperishable Lord of Brahman is one thing, and what is within you is another; there has come to be a difference between these. Enveloped by mist, by darkness, and by idle talk, the chanters of hymns, who subsist on breath and follow the path of the sun, are ignorant; they speak of the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) as if they were themselves the Knower. But indeed, when the wise ones act in accordance with the Knower of the Field, they attain vigilance together with his austerity. Then he becomes one who is to be attained.

Therefore, one should desire non-attachment; through that, one should desire friendship. For this friend is the best; he is in accord with the past, the present, and the future. Why is he called "the knower" (*jñātṛ*)? From the root *jñā* (to know). Why is he called "the friend" (*sakhā*)? From the root *sakhi* (to associate). Together with the elements and the senses, they rest. The great elements together with the senses are made to perform action by means of wisdom (*prajñā*). When his support is water, his character is tranquility, and his self is Brahman—then he becomes one who has become Brahman.
He remains as a mere witness; bondage caused by knowledge does not exist. Now, we shall enumerate in order the names of the elements of the Great Self. 13.23

The swan; heat; sacrifice; the longing one; wisdom; the worm; the earth; the pervasive; the sovereign; the source of bliss; the bestower; the performer of slaughter; Soma; that which has been; the world; that which will be; the waters; the great; the sky; glory; greatness; golden-hued; mindful; well-sounding; true; the true leader; the deep; the profound; the cave; water; food; the oblation; the dwelling; the seat; cosmic order; the womb; the womb of cosmic order.

Truth, water, oblation, wealth, existence, fullness, all, the imperishable, the sacrificial grass, by name, clarified butter; waters, the purifier, the immortal, the moon, gold, heaven, creations, Śambara, the atmosphere, the sky, the firmament, the sacrificial grass, the desert, the intermediate space, the ether, the waters, the earth, the ground, the self-born, the path, the lotus, the ocean, the sea, austerity, splendor, the river, the flood, the navel.

The udder; the tree; that; which; what; the excellent Brahman; the swan; the Self—these become [the sacrificers]; they strike out the path by means of that which carries best; and he refines the bodies, which are imperishable. Sacrifice becomes the Self because they extend it for him.
Now, these hymns and these verses proclaim this great Self:
"Soma flows clear, the progenitor of thoughts, the progenitor of heaven, the progenitor of earth."
The progenitor of Agni, the progenitor of Sūrya, the progenitor of Indra, and the progenitor of Viṣṇu.

Soma flows clear, the progenitor of hymns, the progenitor of heaven, the progenitor of earth, the progenitor of Agni, the progenitor of Sūrya, the progenitor of Indra, and the progenitor of Viṣṇu. The Brahman of the gods, the leader of the poets, the seer of the sages, the buffalo of wild beasts, the hawk of vultures, the axe of the forests— Soma flows across the filter, singing aloud.

"Brahmā of the gods": for he is indeed the Brahmā of the gods—that is, of the rays of the sun whose function is to shine. "The path-finder of the seers": for he knows the path of the seers—that is, of the rays of the sun who act as seers. "The Rishi of the sages": for he is indeed the Rishi of the sages—that is, of the rays of the sun whose function is to pervade. "The buffalo of the wild beasts": for he is indeed great among the wild beasts—that is, of the rays of the sun whose function is to seek out. "The hawk of the vultures."

The hawk is the Āditya; he is so called from the root *śyai*, meaning "to go. The vulture is the Āditya; he is so called from the root *gṛdh*, meaning "to stand," for he stands upon this [world]. "The axe of the woods"—for this Āditya himself wields his functions; "of the woods" means of the rays of the Āditya, whose function is to pervade (*vana*). "Soma, singing, passes through the filter"—for he indeed passes through the filter of the rays, being praised as he does all this imperishable [light]. This is with respect to the deities (*adhidaivata*).

Now, with reference to the self (*adhyātma*). "Brahmā of the gods" (*brahmā devānām*): he too is a *brahmā*, [the master] of the gods, that is, of the senses whose function is divine play (*devana*). "The path-finder of the seers" (*padavīḥ kavīnām*): he too knows the path (*pada*) of the seers, that is, of the senses acting as seers (*kavīyamāna*). "The seer among the sages" (*ṛṣir viprāṇām*): he too is a seer (*ṛṣi*), [the leader] of the sages, that is, of the senses whose function is pervasive penetration (*vyāpana*). "The buffalo among the wild beasts" (*mahiṣo mṛgāṇām*): he too is great (*mahat*), [the preeminent] among the wild beasts, that is, of the senses whose function is seeking (*mārgaṇa*).

"The falcon among vultures"—the Self (ātman) becomes the falcon, from the root *śyai*, meaning the act of knowing; the "vultures" are the senses, from the root *gṛdh*, meaning the act of knowing, because they abide in this [Self]. "The axe among the woods"—this one also places actions within itself; "of the woods" means of the senses, which have the nature of seeking (*vana*). "Soma, singing, passes through the filter"—this one also passes through the filter, that is, the senses;
being praised, this very one experiences all this. Thus he describes the movement of the Self. 13.26
The bearer of the oblation sends forth three voices: the thought of Truth and the inspired wisdom of the sacred word.
The cows go seeking their protector; the longing prayers go toward Soma.

The fire becomes the sun; it impels three voices: the *ṛc*s, the *yajus* formulas, and the *sāman* chants—the actions of the Sun, the Truth, and the thoughts of Brahman. This indeed is all that is imperishable. Thus with respect to the deities. Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*): the fire becomes the Self; it impels three voices: knowledge, understanding, and intellect—the actions of the Self, the Truth, and the thoughts of Brahman. This very one experiences all this. Thus he declares the course of the Self.
The cows, the milch-kine, lowing toward Soma; the sages, questioning with their insights, [seek] Soma.
The pressed Soma is purified as it is being anointed; the Soma-hymns, the *arkas*, and the *triṣṭubh* verses join together in praise.

These very rays, like lowing milch-cows, desiring and longing for Soma, go toward the Āditya. In this very way, the inspired singers, the rays, inquiring with their hymns and longing for Soma, go toward the Āditya. In this very way, the pressed Soma is purified as it is being anointed. Toward him alone do the *ṛk*-verses and the *triṣṭubh*-verses sing together. Then they become one in this Āditya. This is with reference to the deities (*adhidaivata*).

Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*). These very cows, the milch-cows—the senses—go toward the self, lowing, that is, desiring Soma. In this very same way, the inspired ones (*viprāḥ*), the senses, go toward the self, questioning with their thoughts, that is, desiring Soma. In this very same way, the pressed Soma is purified while being anointed. This very self and the seven seers (*sapta ṛṣayaḥ*) come together. They become one in this self. Thus he describes the course of the self.
The ocean has surged forth in the first ordinance, generating offspring, the king of the world.
The bull, the drop, being pressed, has increased greatly upon the sheep’s-wool filter, on its summit. Soma, the Indu, has grown strong.

"The Sun has transcended the ocean in the highest firmament, generating creatures by his act of raining, the King of the world, the King of all. The bull, upon the back of the woolly filter, the great Soma, the pressed drop, has increased. This refers to the divine realm (*adhidaivata*). Now, with respect to the self (*adhyātma*): "The Self has transcended the ocean in the highest firmament, generating creatures by the act of knowledge, the King of the world, the King of all. The bull, upon the back of the woolly filter, the great Soma, the pressed drop, has increased. Thus he declares the course of the Self. (13.29)
The great Soma, the mighty one, performed that great deed when, as the embryo of the waters, he chose the gods;
as Pavamāna, he bestowed vigor upon Indra, and as Indu, he generated light in the sun.
Great is that deed which Soma, the buffalo, performed when as the embryo of the waters he chose sovereignty over the gods.

Pavamāna bestowed vigor upon Indra; Indu Āditya generated light in the sun. Indu is the self. 13.30 The gray-haired one has swallowed the running drop, who, though young, was present at the assembly of the many.
Behold the poetic power of the god; through his greatness, he who was here yesterday has died today.

The moon is "vidhu," meaning characterized by waning; "dadrāṇa" means characterized by being subdued. The young one is the moon; the gray-haired one is the sun, who swallows it; it dies instantly. That [sun] rises during the day. Thus regarding the divine realm (*adhidaivata*). Now regarding the self (*adhyātma*): the moon is "vidhu," meaning characterized by waning; "dadrāṇa" means characterized by being subdued. The young one is the great [Self]; the gray-haired one is the Self (*ātman*), which swallows it; it dies at night. Night has arisen. Thus he describes the course of the Self.
Regarding those born together, they say the seventh was born alone; the six are called the "Ṛṣis born of the gods."
Their desired offerings, ordained for each according to its place, tremble before the Sustainer as they take on their various forms.

Of the six seers born together, the sun is the seventh. Their offerings, or desires, or strides, or movements, or thoughts, or bows, rejoice together with the waters. Beyond those lights of the seven seers is the sun; they become one in him. Thus with respect to the deities. Now with respect to the self: of the six sense organs born together, the self is the seventh.

Whatever they desire, whatever is pleasing, whatever they have overcome, whatever they have attained, whatever they have thought, or whatever they have bowed to—all these rejoice together with food. Wherein these seven seers' senses exist, beyond which is the Self—these become one in Him. Thus he declares the course of the Self. 13.32 "Women indeed they are, yet they call them men; he who has eyes sees them, but the blind does not perceive them.
Only the son who is a sage understands them; he who truly knows them shall be the father of his father."

"These women indeed are the stealers of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell; being deprived of food, he who perceives them as the male sound 'Prāṇa' does not recognize his wretched state, like a blind man. The son who is a seer knows these; he who knows these becomes the father of his father. Thus he declares the course of the Self. "The seven half-embryos, the seed of the world, stand by the command of Viṣṇu in the support of the law."

"By their insights and with their minds, those wise ones, as encompassers, encompass from all sides. This Āditya swallows these seven rays of the Āditya; the word "upward" refers to that which stands in the middle. Those things which abide in him, they turn over by means of their insights and their minds; as encompassers, they encompass all actions through the act of raining. Thus with reference to the deities. Now with reference to the self (*adhyātma*): this Self swallows these seven senses; the word "upward" refers to that which stands in the middle.

Those [senses] which abide in this [body], they turn away through their steadiness and the mind; as sovereigns, they overcome all the senses by means of knowledge and action. Thus he declares the course of the Self. "I do not discern whether I am this or not;

hidden and armored, I move with the mind. I do not discern whether I am this or not; hidden and armored, I move with the mind. For those who know do not fully declare this to the wise: 'This is the sun; this is the Self.'"
Moving away and moving toward, held by the *svadhā* offering, the immortal one is of common origin with the mortal.
These two, eternal and divergent, move apart; they perceive one another, yet they do not perceive each other.
He moves westward, he moves eastward, held by *svadhā*—the immortal Āditya together with the mortal Candramas. They both go perpetually, they go everywhere, or they go in many ways.

One sees the Āditya, not the Candramas. This is with reference to the deities (*adhidaivata*). Now, with reference to the self (*adhyātma*): He moves westward, he moves eastward, held by *svadhā*—the immortal Self (*ātman*) together with the mortal mind (*manas*). They both go perpetually, they go everywhere, or they go in many ways. One sees the Self, not the mind. Thus he declares the movement of the Self. 13.36
That indeed was the eldest among all beings, from which the fierce one, of brilliant valor, was born;
as soon as he was born, he overcomes his enemies—he in whom all the protectors rejoice.

"That which exists among beings as the eldest in the worlds, from which the fierce Āditya was born, he of brilliant strength, of radiant power—having been born, he instantly overcomes his enemies. Here, the root *riṇāti* means either "to please" or "to shine. "Him all the protectors rejoice in"—this refers to the divine realm (*adhidaivata*).

Now, with reference to the self (*adhyātma*). This occurs: "Among beings, among worlds, it is the eldest, the unmanifest, from which is born the fierce one, whose strength is splendor, whose strength is knowledge; as soon as he is born, he overcomes his enemies. The root *riṇāti* means either "to please" or "to shine. "Him all the protectors (*ūmāḥ*) rejoice in"—thus he declares the course of the self. "Who today yokes to the pole of the cosmic order (*ṛta*) the vigorous, wrathful, ill-disposed oxen? He who provides for their service—the arrows in the mouth, the heart-pleasing, the bliss-bringers—he shall live. (RV 10.102.2)
"Who yokes the oxen to the pole? The rays of the sun—active, radiant, invincible, breathing life into the breaths, sharpening the arrows, and bringing delight—that is, producing happiness.

He who knows this gathered [treasure]—how does he live? Thus with respect to the divine. Now with respect to the self: "Who yokes the oxen to the pole? The senses—active, radiant, invincible, breathing life into the breaths, sharpening the arrows, and bringing delight—that is, producing happiness. He who knows this gathered [treasure] lives long. Thus he explains the course of the self. 13.38
Who flees? Who is struck down? Who is afraid? Who perceives Indra as being present nearby?
Who will speak in favor of his children, his cattle, his wealth, or his own body, or for the sake of the people?
Who indeed goes? Who gives? Who fears? Who perceives Indra as he truly is?
Who [prays] for our offspring, for progeny, and for great, delightful, and beautiful battle?
Who praises Agni with oblation and clarified butter, who shall sacrifice with the ladle according to the fixed seasons?
To whom shall the gods bring [offerings]? Who will consider the swift oblation as one well-received by the gods? Who is the one who offers the sacrifice with a welcoming heart?

"Who fills the Āditya with oblation and with ghee, who shall sacrifice with the ladle according to the fixed seasons? "To whom do the gods bring the swift offerings? Who considers himself a 'Vītihotra'—one for whom the gods are well-disposed, one for whom the gods are auspicious? This is with reference to the deities (*adhidaivata*). Now, with reference to the self (*adhyātma*): "Who fills the Self with oblation and with ghee, who shall sacrifice with the ladle according to the fixed seasons? "To whom do the gods bring the swift offerings? Who considers himself a 'Vītihotra'—one of good wisdom, one of auspicious wisdom? Thus he declares the course of the Self. 13.40
O most powerful god, you alone, as a deity, shall praise the mortal man;
O Maghavan, there is no other comforter besides you. O Indra, I speak these words to you.

O friend, you alone, O most powerful God, should praise the mortal man; for there is no other than you, O Maghavan, who is a protector, a guardian, a victor, or one who brings happiness. O Indra, I speak these words to you, joined with praise.
Two birds, companions and friends, closely embrace the same tree.
Of these two, one eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating.

Two by two they stand established, performers of righteous deeds. They call evil and sin "the surrounding. With the words, "The two fair-winged ones, yoked together, friends," he rises toward the Self and the Supreme Self. That is born in the body as a tree; the body is the tree. He establishes the two wings upon the tree.
Having eaten one of them, while not eating the other, he attains likeness and co-residence with the other. "He who knows this shines forth, not eating"—thus he declares the course of the Self. 13.42

Come, O Indra, by the paths celebrated by us; enjoy this our sacrifice as your allotted portion. They have offered it to you as one satisfies a mother-in-law, or as a maiden offers the sacrificial fat of her father’s sister. This is your share.

The gods, including Śakra, shall come; through these three sacred fords, praised as the three Śakra-fords, may Indra enjoy this sacrifice of ours and the portions of Agni and Soma. Thus the daughter of the maternal uncle is satisfied, like a wife with her husband; those who are the deities are in their proper place, and Śakra is the witness.
O wise ones, we sages invoke the sage Agni with our songs for our protection; we mortals invoke the god for our aid.

The wise know the sage (*vipra*) for the sake of protection. "Veda" is derived from the root *vid*, meaning that which is to be known. By means of the vital air (*vāyu*), he makes the body stainless. The sage, however, filling the syllable *U* situated in the heart—which resides in the lotus and is withdrawn by the syllable *A*—causes it to go to its abode in the syllable *M*. Among the vital breaths, they call the sage the drop (*bindu*), the sprinkled, the blossomed, the fiery luster, the Lord, the gold, the immortal body within the lotuses, established in the birth of immortality, and the speaker of immortality; those with immortal mouths speak thus. We invoke Agni with our songs; one should awaken Agni.
"Agni is all the deities. The following verse serves for a further explanation of this:

The swan dwelling in the pure realm, the Vasu dwelling in the atmosphere, the Hotṛ dwelling at the altar, the guest dwelling in the house; he who dwells among men, who dwells in the best, who dwells in Truth, who dwells in the sky; born of the waters, born of the kine, born of Truth, born of the mountains—He is the Eternal Law (Ṛta).

*Haṃsa* refers to the *haṃsas*, which are the rays of the sun; the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is the supreme light. "Pervaded by the earth" means that everything is pervaded by the solar orb through the practice of the act of expansion. "He abandons" refers to the world; "he abandons" refers to the *haṃsa*; "they abandon" refers to the *haṃsas*. The Supreme Self, the Supreme Swan (*paramahaṃsa*), dwells in abundance and depth through the rays of the sun; or rather, he dwells with the three [worlds]; or he dwells as fire; or he dwells with his rays. He is Suvarṇaretas, Pūṣan, and the embryos.

"Riphati"—he roars with a crooked sound; "rephantāntarikṣaṃ caret"—he moves through the atmosphere with a roar; "caratyantarikṣam"—he moves in the atmosphere, or [moves] in heaven; "bhūmigamanam vā"—or he goes to the earth. Svarbhānu is the well-born Hotṛ. The rays of the sun become the Hotṛs. "Atithir duroṇasat"—the guest dwelling in the house. "Ravanti"—all the juices resound; or they desire to act by means of their rays, or they cause them to act. Vahni draws [them] forth.

It becomes bent; thus [we have] *aśvagojā*, *adrigojā*, *dhanagojā*, and *sarvagojātiḥ*—the word *go* becomes *bahuja* (born from many) due to its splendor (*tejas*). It becomes *nigama* and *nigamyah* for the purpose of etymological derivation (*ṛṣinirvacana*). We worship Tryambaka, the fragrant, the increaser of prosperity.
May I be liberated from death, like a cucumber from its stem, but not from immortality.

Tryambaka is Rudra. We worship that Tryambaka, who is fragrant—possessing excellent fragrance—and who increases prosperity, like one who brings about nourishment. "As a cucumber [is freed] from its stem, so release me from death"—from what? This is another [verse]: 13.45 "Let us press the Soma for Jātavedas; may he burn away the wealth of him who acts with hostility. May he carry us across all difficulties, as Agni carries us beyond misfortunes, like a boat across a river."

"Jātavedas"—all this that has been born, the moving and the unmoving, exists according to the principle of origination, maintenance, and dissolution within Jātavedas; thus, "for Jātavedas, for the sake of worship, let us press the Soma. For the sake of impulsion—that is, for the pressing—the King Soma, the immortal, burns down the hostile one who obstructs the sacrifice; he burns him down with certainty, reducing him to ashes. This is the meaning: "Soma gives. May he carry us across all difficulties, all impassable places, as if across the ocean with a boat.

Like a certain helmsman who, by means of a boat, carries one across the river—the Sindhu—which flows with great currents, is difficult to traverse due to its waters, and possesses mighty waves; he carries one across misfortunes, for "duritāt" means he delivers one from misfortunes (duritāni). Regarding him, there is this other verse:
"This [water] of yours is unequalled by other waters, whatever rivers flow into the Sindhu.
Having approached it head-first, one casts off evil, just as a snake sheds its worn-out skin. (13.46)

This [is for you], unlike those others—whatever rivers flow having made the Sindhu their lord. As a snake sheds its worn-out skin, they cast off evil. *Āpas* [is derived] from the root *āp* (to reach). Regarding them, there is this verse: "Live a hundred autumns, increasing; live a hundred winters and a hundred springs.
May Indra, Agni, Savitṛ, and Bṛhaspati, through this oblation of a hundred-fold lifespan, lead him back again."

"Live for a hundred autumns, increasing in prosperity"—thus also says a Vedic hymn (*nigama*). "A hundred" refers to a long life of a hundred years. The Maruts cause me to increase. A hundred indeed becomes a hundredfold self; a hundred becomes infinite; a hundred becomes sovereign power. "A hundred" refers to a long life of a hundred years. O Vasu, let not your riches nor your aids ever deceive us. O Manava, bestow upon us all human wealth from every side.

And let not your riches, nor any of your insights, ever fail you; bring them all together as examples. This Āditya is beneficial to humanity; this is the Self (Ātman). Now he proclaims this: now this seer proclaims him, the Great Self.
"Of Vaiśvakarman, of the gods, we indeed know [this]: then there was neither non-being nor being."

And thus: This is the inquiry into the Self; this is the inquiry into all beings. He who knows this attains equality with Brahman, similarity of form with Brahman, and residence in the same world as Brahman. Homage to Brahman! Homage to the Great Being! Homage to Yāska! O you whose mind is fixed on the pure Brahman, may I be fixed on the pure Brahman! 13.48. Thus ends the supplement.
